riscos.descricao: O esquema Multi-turn costuma não gerar código correto, atribuído a problemas de truncamento da saída do LLM.
Níveis excessivos de abstração (Plan2CoT) podem aumentar a probabilidade de erros, segundo hipótese dos autores.

Na geração direta e no Code CoT o código aborda só parte da intenção, o que frequentemente resulta em código incorreto; no exemplo da Fig. 1, o modelo copiou os casos de teste públicos fornecidos como entrada.
Os passos excessivamente detalhados do Code CoT podem ficar desatualizados após modificações do código e prejudicar a manutenibilidade.
O estudo mede o número médio de tokens de entrada e saída das variantes para relacionar desempenho e possível aumento de custo; custo quantificado em tokens (Tabela 4), não em dinheiro ou tempo.

citacoes.trecho: This paper proposes a self-planning code generation approach with large language models, which consists of two phases, namely planning phase and implementation phase.

Experimental results show that self-planning code generation achieves a relative improvement of up to 25.4% in Pass@1 compared to direct code generation, and up to 11.9% compared to Chain-of-Thought code generation.
We take advantage of the ability of LLM to perform planning through few-shot prompting.
1. The plan is organized in the form of a numbered list, where each item in the list represents a step.
Then entering the implementation phase, we append the plan to the intent and feed it to LLM.
Direct generates code using LLMs in a zero-shot setting, implying only intent and no examples are available in the prompt.
Code CoT generates a chain of thought for each question by using Code CoT prompt (described in Crafting Prompt) and then generates the corresponding code.

Ground-truth Planning is set to investigate the maximum potential of the planning approach in code generation, we directly supply the model with ground-truth plans to perform the implementation phase, skipping the planning phase.

To avoid bias caused by errors in LLMs generation and inconsistencies in style, the generated Code CoT prompts are manually reviewed and adapted to the same numbered list format as the self-planning prompts.
The examples selected from the dataset for prompting will be excluded from the evaluation.
We employ a simple method to select the questions used to construct the prompts, i.e., random sampling with fixing a seed.
Prompts for our approach and all baselines are constructed utilizing the same problems.
To mitigate this concern, we utilize the existing ground-truth code to inversely generate a plan, which we then adopt as the ground-truth plan in our experiments.

Second, we establish code-davinci-002 [5] as our base model and compare self-planning approach with Direct, Few-shot, and Code CoT to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, where the Few-shot approach uses the requirements and code pairs as prompt.

Furthermore, we apply the plan generated by code-davinci-002 during the planning phase to the implementation phase of other models, aiming to investigate the impact of planning for models with varying scales.
The Multi-turn approach involves the iterative use of solution steps of plan to generate the corresponding code snippets that eventually compose the entire code, which is introduced by CodeGen [33].
Note that the one-phase approach requires labeling both the plan and the corresponding code in the prompt, as demonstrated in ‘Instance of Self-planning Prompt (One-phase)’ in Appendix G.
Zero-shot CoT uses the instruction ’Let’s think step by step’ [23] to produce intermediate steps and code.
To eliminate the effect of the generation method, we also establish the baseline Zero-shot CoT (Two-phase) for comparison, using the two-phase generation method consistent with our approach.
The Narrative Plan is an ablation of our proposed plan, i.e., it removes the form of a numbered list and is presented as narrative text.
The Narrative Code CoT is also an ablation, which makes the Code CoT the same in form as the original CoT.
Plan2CoT means incorporate both the plan and the Code CoT during code generation, i.e., we first generate a plan and then generate a Code CoT, ultimately resulting in code.
This approach helps understand the possible performance improvement in relation to possible cost increases.
In the result of the group Schemes of Planning and Implementation, we find that the multi-turn usually fails to generate correct codes.
Relatively, excessive levels of abstraction may increase the probability of errors.
In terms of cost, self-planning has a lower token usage compared to other few-shot prompting approaches.
This is related to the fact that the benchmark HumanEval provided five public test cases as additional input, and the model copied them.
In these cases, the direct and Code CoT code generation approach only addresses a limited aspect of intent, which often results in incorrect code generation.
This can adversely affect code maintainability if the solution steps do not accurately represent the current state.

Considering the inherent sensitivity of LLMs to prompts, the primary threat comes from crafting prompts, as the example selection and plan writing in this operation can affect the degree of improvement achievable by our approach.
The second major threat to our study pertains to the generalizability of experimental results.
Additionally, we utilized the unbiased version of Pass@k [5] to diminish evaluation errors that arise from sampling.
When discussing the limitations of self-planning code generation, a major limitation may be the manual crafting of prompts.
We manually validated the generated ground-truth plans on HumanEval dataset.
This updated version includes edge test cases that enhance the soundness of code evaluation in comparison to the original benchmark.
Thereafter, we perform a full manual review of the scoring results.

Contém persona/papel e objetivo em linguagem natural («You are a powerful model specialized in refactoring Java code», definição de refatoração, «You must output a refactored version of the code») → instrucao; o código anterior à refatoração do desenvolvedor, dividido em um bloco por arquivo do commit, é fornecido como insumo → contexto. Usa o símbolo «#» como delimitador. É a condição comparadora; não há condição sem ela, por isso nao/nenhum.

tecnicas.localizador: Seção 3.4.2, p. 17; Fig. 7, p. 18; Tabela 7, p. 18; Tabela 8, p. 19
tecnicas.observacao: Herda do prompt base a instrução (persona e objetivo) e o código a refatorar. Acrescenta (i) o pedido «Explain the steps you took to refactor the code and why you selected the refactoring type/types you did» → raciocinio (o pedido de explicação não está posicionado explicitamente antes do código) e (ii) a seção «# Suggested refactoring types: {refactorings developers performed on this commit with definitions}», isto é, tipos de refatoração com definições, sem exemplos → contexto; essa seção também funciona como diretriz (instrucao, categoria já presente no prompt base). O contrafactual é o pacote completo contra o zero-shot, com o mesmo modelo e os mesmos commits; o ganho não pode ser atribuído só ao raciocínio nem só às sugestões, que não são isoladas. As sugestões derivam das refatorações que o desenvolvedor fez no mesmo commit (ver heterogeneidade). Não é pacote híbrido.

tecnicas.localizador: Seção 3.4.2, p. 17; Fig. 8, p. 18; Tabela 7, p. 18; Tabela 8, p. 19
tecnicas.observacao: Herda do prompt base a instrução (idêntica à da Fig. 2) e o código a refatorar. Acrescenta um exemplo de código antes e depois da refatoração feita pelo desenvolvedor («{code_segment_before_refactoring}» seguido de «{developer_code_after_refactoring}») → exemplos e, por ser código fornecido como demonstração, contexto (D102). Segundo o texto, o exemplo usa o mesmo tipo de refatoração do commit que o LLM vai refatorar; na Fig. 8 os marcadores do exemplo e do alvo têm o mesmo nome, e o texto não esclarece se o exemplo vem do mesmo trecho (ver heterogeneidade). O contrafactual é o pacote (zero-shot + exemplo) contra o zero-shot, com o mesmo modelo e os mesmos commits.

modelos.observacao: Único modelo avaliado. Parâmetros de decodificação (temperatura, top-p, tamanho máximo) nao_informado. Inferência em 4 GPUs Nvidia A100 de 80 GB, Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS (p. 7). O desempenho de 46,3% de pass@1 no HumanEval é citado como informação de fundo (p. 2), não é resultado executado pelo estudo.

benchmarks.nome: Conjunto próprio de commits de refatoração de projetos Java Apache (dataset 20-MAD, refatorações detectadas por RMiner a partir do dataset de estudo anterior [30])
benchmarks.quantidade: 30 projetos Java; 5.194 commits de refatoração; 39.309 arquivos (p. 2, p. 7)
benchmarks.observacao: Seleção: 765 projetos Apache do 20-MAD → 195 projetos Java após filtros (≥80% Java, ≥1.021 commits, ≥1 ano de histórico) → exclusão de 135 projetos incluídos no treinamento do StarCoder2 (texto cita «the commits of the 60 projects») → exclusão dos projetos com menos que a mediana (129) de commits de refatoração → 30 projetos (p. 4). Só commits com 100% da variação de código composta por refatorações (p. 4-5). Amostra de commits por projeto com nível de confiança de 95% e margem de erro de 5% (p. 7). Testes unitários gerados por EvoSuite; o texto fala em 39.309 testes unitários gerados, mesmo número dos arquivos (p. 7). O denominador de cada taxa (por commit, arquivo ou trecho, e se a média é entre projetos) não é ligado explicitamente ao corpus na Tabela 7; a Tabela 2 indica médias e medianas «Across the 30 Projects».

metricas.nome: Unit Test Pass Rate (Pass@1, Pass@3, Pass@5)
metricas.definicao: pass@1: uma solução por trecho, aprovada se passar nos testes unitários; pass@3/pass@5: três ou até cinco soluções, aprovado se ao menos uma passar em todos os testes (p. 8). Na Tabela 7 aparece só «Unit Test Pass Rate (%)», sem indicar o k para Chain-of-thought e One-shot.

Taxa de melhoria IR = (A_before − A_after)/A_before × 100, aplicada à contagem de code smells detectados pelo DesigniteJava 2.5.2; para o LLM, calculada só sobre código cujas refatorações passam nos testes (p. 8-10).
IR aplicado a 11 métricas do Understand (acoplamento, modularidade, coesão e complexidade ciclomática, Tabela 1).
metricas.localizador: Tabela 1, p. 6; Tabela 3, p. 11; Tabela 8, p. 19

metricas.definicao: Mann-Whitney U (p < 0,05) e Cliff's delta em RQ1-RQ3; Scott-Knott sobre as distribuições por projeto em RQ4 (rank reportado só para SRR na Tabela 7 e para cada métrica na Tabela 8).

riscos.descricao: Refatorações geradas pelo StarCoder2 podem alterar a funcionalidade do código; com o prompt zero-shot, a taxa média de aprovação nos testes é 28,4% em Pass@1 e 57,2% em Pass@5 (Tabela 2), contra 100% para os desenvolvedores.

O estudo identifica alucinação do modelo, isto é, código que parece correto mas não é lógica ou sintaticamente válido, como ameaça à validade interna, e sugere que o LLM pode alucinar em algumas gerações que tentam tratar code smells complexos.

Risco de vazamento de dados: se o LLM foi treinado no mesmo código, o desempenho pode ser inflado artificialmente; mesmo com projetos fora do conjunto de treinamento, padrões semelhantes podem estar presentes no treinamento. O controle (modelo com dados de treinamento públicos e exclusão dos projetos incluídos na The Stack v2) está em mitigacoes.
riscos.localizador: Seção 1, p. 2; Seção 2.1, p. 4; Seção 4, p. 20

riscos.descricao: Na motivação, o estudo afirma, com base em literatura citada, que código gerado por LLM pode ter projeto ruim ou introduzir dívida técnica e aumentar custos de manutenção; não é risco medido no estudo.

mitigacoes.descricao: Escolha do StarCoder2-15B-Instruct, treinado no conjunto público The Stack v2, e exclusão dos 135 projetos Java incluídos no treinamento, para evitar vazamento de dados.

Verificação da funcionalidade por testes unitários gerados com EvoSuite; validação manual de 381 testes amostrados (348, 91,3%, válidos) e filtragem de padrões de testes que falham por dependências ausentes ou asserções estritas demais.
Contra alucinação, verificação da saída por testes unitários e inspeção de código inválido; o estudo reconhece que o risco permanece.
Recomendação de testes abrangentes ao usar LLMs como o StarCoder2, para garantir a correção do código refatorado.

Regeneração de várias refatorações por entrada (Pass@5) é sugerida porque o LLM pode alucinar em algumas gerações; o estudo compara SRR de Pass@1 e Pass@5, mas não mede alucinação com e sem a regeneração.
Execução de todos os experimentos no mesmo servidor, com hardware e software idênticos.

O estudo não informa se Chain-of-thought e One-shot foram avaliados com uma ou até cinco gerações por entrada.

O «20.1% higher rate» corresponde, por cálculo próprio, a 44,36 − 24,27 = 20,09 p.p.; o mesmo valor 20,1 aparece como ganho médio de aprovação de Pass@1 para Pass@3.
O texto afirma melhora de Pass@5 (57,15%) sobre «Pass@3 (8.7%)», mas a média de Pass@3 na Tabela 2 é 48,5%; 8,7% é o ganho relatado de Pass@3 para Pass@5.

Não foi registrada em `tecnicas` porque o estudo a apresenta como métrica/critério de avaliação, não como técnica de prompting investigada, e a seleção usa o oráculo de testes.
RQ1-RQ3 comparam refatorações do LLM (zero-shot) com as dos desenvolvedores; o desenvolvedor não é condição de prompting e esses contrastes não entram em `extracoes`.

Ferramentas: RMiner (RefactoringMiner) 3.0, DesigniteJava 2.5.2, Understand, EvoSuite, Apache Maven e Mockito. Geração das refatorações em cerca de 6 dias para 5.194 commits (cerca de 1,6 minuto por commit); o estudo descreve a geração em todos os commits como computacionalmente cara e demorada, motivo da amostragem.

Número de execuções independentes por condição e sementes nao_informado; o k de Pass@k é parâmetro da métrica, não número de execuções.

citacoes.trecho: Specifically, we (1) evaluate whether the code refactored by the LLM or by developers is more effective at improving code quality, (2) understand the differences between the types of refactoring applied by the LLM and developers and compare their effectiveness, and (3) evaluate whether the quality of the refactored code generated by the LLM can be improved through one-shot prompting and chain-of-thought prompting.
You are a powerful model specialized in refactoring Java code.
The LLM is specifically prompted to refactor Java code and we break the code snippets into chunks (i.e., one chunk for each file in a commit).
Zero-shot Prompt (baseline): This prompt is the baseline used in RQ1.

Chain-of-thought: Shown in Figure 7, this prompt provides suggestions for refactorings, along with the explanation of that refactoring type, by including common refactoring patterns developers perform that the LLM does not.
Explain the steps you took to refactor the code and why you selected the refactoring type/types you did.
{refactorings developers performed on this commit with definitions}
citacoes.localizador: Fig. 7, p. 18 (linha do prompt sob «# Suggested refactoring types:»)

citacoes.trecho: We provide the LLM with an example by the developer that uses the same refactoring type on the commit the LLM will refactor.
Refactorings generated by StarCoder2 can sometimes propose changes that may affect the functionality of the code.
A potential threat to internal validity is the occurrence of model hallucination, where StarCoder2 may generate code that appears correct but is not logically or syntactically valid.
Overfitting could occur if the LLM has been trained on the same code, potentially leading to artificial inflation of its performance and resulting in over-optimistic results [5].

Although we select projects not included in the StarCoder2 training dataset, there is still a possibility that similar code patterns or practices could be present in the training set of the model, which might give the LLM an advantage.
LLMs are trained using an enormous amount of open-source code; therefore, if the training code has flaws, the generated code could suffer from poor design [52] or introduce technical debts [7].
To mitigate the risk of data leakage, we choose StarCoder2-15B-instruct [24], trained on the publicly available dataset, The Stack v2 [24].
To avoid data leakage, we filter out the 135 Java projects from our initial dataset that are included in the StarCoder2.
Of the 381 unit tests, 348 tests (91.3%) were valid and functional, meaning they executed as expected without encountering the above issues.
We account for this by verifying the output through unit test evaluations and inspecting for invalid code, but hallucinations remain an inherent risk in LLM-generated code.
Therefore, it is recommended to have comprehensive testing when utilizing LLMs like StarCoder2 to ensure the correctness and integrity of the refactored code.

This suggests that regenerating refactorings multiple times can enhance the effectiveness of code smell reduction, as the LLM may hallucinate for some refactoring generations that attempt to address complex code smells.
We use the best refactoring generation from pass@5 to answer the remaining research questions.
Our findings show that One-shot prompting improves unit test pass rate over the zero-shot prompt by 6.15% and reduces code smells at a 3.52% higher rate.

When generating five refactorings per input, StarCoder2 achieves a unit test pass rate of 28.8% higher than when generating one refactoring per input, which indicates that the combination of one-shot prompting with multiple refactoring generations per input leads to the best performance.

To assess whether the prompting techniques lead to statistically significant improvements, we perform the Scott-Knott test [11] across the three distributions: zero-shot, one-shot, and chain-of-thought.
One-shot prompting consistently yields the best performance across various metrics, including code complexity and modularity, by providing a concrete example of refactoring.

Incorporating examples (i.e., one-shot prompt) or providing more explicit instructions (i.e., chain-of-thought prompt) significantly improves both the functional correctness and overall quality of the refactorings generated by StarCoder2.
citacoes.localizador: Resumo dos resultados de RQ4, p. 19

citacoes.trecho: Our findings indicate that StarCoder2 outperforms developers in reducing implementation code smells, achieving a reduction rate of 43.36%, compared to developers’ code smell reduction rate of 24.27%.
StarCoder2 reduces the initial number of code smells from 12,213 to 6,795 showing a code smell reduction rate of 44.36% for 30 projects.
The refactored code generated by StarCoder2 achieves a 57.15% unit test pass rate at Pass@5, indicating substantial improvement over Pass@1 (28.36%) and Pass@3 (8.7%).
The LLM outperforms developers in reducing 10 of the 16 types of code smells.

Furthermore, chain-of-thought prompting increases the variety of refactoring types performed by the LLM, adding seven new refactoring types not observed with zero-shot prompting: Extract Method, Rename Method, Extract Variable, Inline Method, Add Parameter, Extract Class, and Parameterize Variable.
We randomly select 381 unit tests from 39,309 generated unit tests to assess each one to determine if it is valid and functional.
Therefore, we have 5,194 commits containing a total of 39,309 files for testing the model.
Our study is based on the latest open-source version of StarCoder2-15B-Instruct-v0.1, as of the date of our study.

Base comparável: Direct prompting, executado nas mesmas tabelas com o mesmo modelo, benchmark e métrica; o contraste é do pacote CGO (geração de objetivos + uso como contexto), sem ablação de seus ingredientes. riscos.descricao: Técnicas de raciocínio por processo podem aumentar tempo de inferência e consumo de tokens; o conteúdo intermediário aumenta a geração de tokens e o custo computacional. O estudo mede só tokens médios do conteúdo intermediário como proxy (Figura 5); custo monetário e tempo não quantificados.
Mesmo com decodificação gulosa, pequenas variações podem ocorrer por erros de precisão de ponto flutuante e ambientes de execução não determinísticos.

Técnicas de prompting podem reduzir a correção em relação ao Direct prompting: few-shot ficou abaixo do Direct prompting no HumanEval com LLaMA3-8B-Instruct, e em problemas difíceis do LiveCodeBench a maioria das linhas de base ficou abaixo do Direct prompting (GPT-3.5-Turbo).
A geração de objetivos em zero-shot pode variar em formato, detalhe ou clareza entre instâncias; a qualidade dos objetivos gerados não foi avaliada (limitação declarada).

citacoes.trecho: This paper introduces Chain of Grounded Objectives (CGO), a concise goal-oriented prompting approach that embeds functional objectives into prompts to enhance code generation.
CGO first prompts the LLM to analyze the given problem and autonomously generate a compact set of objectives outlining the functional requirements of the solution.
These objectives are then incorporated as supplemental input to guide the final code generation step.
Direct prompting: Generates code solely from the problem description.
Few-shot: Includes example problems and solutions to guide the model.
CodeCoT: Utilizes Chain of Thought (CoT) with a one-shot example to generate intermediate steps and final code in two stages [11].
Zero-shot CoT: A prompt that generates a CoT Reasoning process to solve the given problem without providing example CoT and incorporates it into code generation [17].
Self-Planning: Extracts sub-tasks from the problem and generates a plan, which guides code generation in two stages [16].
Subsequently, use the generated pseudocode to write the final code in three stage.
For the implementation of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [23, 32] and Self-Planning strategies, reasoning chains were constructed based on code examples provided in the original Self-Planning approach.
Few-shot prompting was realized by randomly selecting example problems and their corresponding solutions from the same dataset.
To evaluate whether minor wording differences could significantly influence the effectiveness of the CGO approach, we conducted an experiment.

Based on our preliminary experiments, while effective, process-oriented reasoning can introduce unnecessary complexity in straightforward tasks, potentially leading to increased inference time and token consumption.
While this additional content helps guide the code generation process, it also increases token generation, thereby raising the computational cost of using LLMs.

Although greedy sampling typically produces the same output for a given prompt, minor variations may still occur due to factors such as floating-point precision errors and non-deterministic execution environments.
To account for this, we repeated the experiment 10 times per problem.
While it showed improvements in MBPP-sanitized and MBPP+, it underperformed compared to direct prompting on the HumanEval benchmarks.
Performance degradation was more apparent in hard problems, where most baselines underperformed compared to DP.
CGO generates objectives using a zero-shot approach, which may lead to variations in format, detail, or clarity across different instances.
To increase the diversity of outputs, we generated n = 10 objective samples per problem, which were subsequently used to guide the code generation process.

tecnicas.observacao: Síntese de programa a partir da questão original ou da questão aumentada automaticamente, sem exemplos: entrada aceita sem alteração, com «write a program», com «using sympy» ou com «using simulations»; o prompt é estruturado como docstring Python entre aspas triplas (p. 3, p. 8). «Write a program» foi classificado como instrucao (mesma categoria da questão dada como instrução zero-shot no prompt base) e a especificação da biblioteca e do formato docstring como restricoes; o estudo chama a biblioteca de «context», mas não há documentação ou código fornecido, por isso não se atribuiu contexto. Para parte das questões nada é acrescentado (entrada «no change to original question»). Não é informado se as variantes de entrada foram tentadas em sequência para a mesma questão (nao_informado). O único contraste executado é com GPT-3 text-davinci-002 zero-shot respondendo em texto: pacote híbrido, pois a condição difere também no modelo (Codex code-davinci-002, componente fora do escopo: selecao_modelo) e na modalidade da saída (programa executado contra resposta em texto); o ganho não é atribuível ao prompting nem a um ingrediente isolado. Os efeitos das variantes de contextualização («Best results are obtained when...») não são quantificados.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 2 (terceiro método proposto), p. 3 (Fig. 2; Automatic Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Learning), p. 4 (continuação), p. 5 (Fig. 3, painel 18.02), p. 8 (formato do prompt few-shot)
tecnicas.observacao: Aplicada somente às questões não resolvidas por zero-shot: as questões são incorporadas com text-similarity-babbage-001, e a questão mais semelhante já resolvida por zero-shot no mesmo curso, com seu código, é inserida como exemplo; se o código gerado não produz a resposta correta, acrescenta-se o par seguinte, até cinco exemplos (p. 3–4). Herda o prefixo automático («write a program using SymPy», Fig. 3, p. 5) e o formato docstring (instrucao, restricoes). Recuperação de exemplos resolvidos → contexto e exemplos; tentativas sucessivas com parada quando a saída coincide com a resposta correta → amostragem com seleção por oráculo (a resposta de referência). O 81% relatado é cumulativo (sucessos zero-shot mais sucessos few-shot nas falhas); não há condição em que few-shot seja aplicado a todas as questões, por isso a contribuição é por fase e não é isolada.

Etapa final do pipeline aplicada a 19% das questões de cursos e 18,9% das questões MATH (legenda da Fig. 2); não há condição comparável sem ela nem medida própria de efeito.

riscos.descricao: O estudo considera a possibilidade de os resultados refletirem sobreajuste aos dados de treinamento e, como controle, resolve questões de um curso (COMS3251) descrito como indisponível online e não visto pelo Codex no treinamento. O estudo não descreve verificação dessa ausência nem analisa a presença das questões do MIT ou do MATH no pré-treinamento.

Limitação de aplicabilidade: o modelo não resolve questões apresentadas como imagem ou outra modalidade não textual, questões cuja solução exige prova e problemas computacionalmente intratáveis; essas questões foram excluídas da amostra.

riscos.descricao: O estudo trata a aleatoriedade da amostragem como fator a controlar e fixa os hiperparâmetros para obter resultados determinísticos e reprodutíveis; não mede variação entre execuções.

mitigacoes.descricao: Uso de um curso descrito como não disponível online (COMS3251) para verificar que os resultados não são apenas sobreajuste; não há comparação de desempenho com e sem esse controle que meça o efeito da contaminação.
Hiperparâmetros fixos (top P = 0, temperatura = 0, penalidades = 0) em todos os experimentos de solução e explicação.

heterogeneidade.descricao: O resultado few-shot é condicional e cumulativo: few-shot só é aplicado às questões que falharam em zero-shot, e exemplos são acrescentados um a um enquanto o código não produz a resposta correta, isto é, a parada usa a resposta de referência. A taxa «automática» resulta, assim, de várias tentativas com verificação contra o gabarito, o que não equivale a uma única tentativa sem oráculo.

citacoes.trecho: We automatically synthesize programs using few-shot learning and OpenAI’s Codex transformer and execute them to solve course problems at 81% automatic accuracy.
Questions are given to Codex either as-is or by automatically adding minor context, as described below.
We add the text “write a program” before the question and focus on the Python programming language by placing the text within Pythonic triple quotes like a docstring.
For instance, we may add the Python library SymPy as context (see Figure 3 top panel 18.01), specifying that the program synthesized to solve the problem should use this package.
Zero-shot learning synthesizes a program from the original question or the automatically augmented question without examples.
citacoes.localizador: p. 3, Automatic Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Learning

citacoes.trecho: We take the most similar question and its corresponding code and use these as few-shot examples for the new question.
citacoes.localizador: p. 3, Automatic Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Learning

citacoes.trecho: If the generated code does not output the correct answer, we add another solved question–code pair, using the next similar solved question each time.
citacoes.localizador: p. 3, Automatic Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Learning

citacoes.trecho: We found that using up to five examples for few-shot learning works well in practice, increasing the total number of questions automatically solved from 71% using zero-shot learning to 81% using few-shot learning.
citacoes.localizador: pp. 3–4, Automatic Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Learning

citacoes.trecho: While 81% of the question is automatically solved by zero-shot and few-shot learning, 19% of the questions may require manual editing to be solved by Codex.
Question tidying primarily involves removing redundant information, breaking down long sentence structures into smaller components, and converting prompts into a programming format.
These special cases, which are among the remaining 19% of the questions, require interactively prompting Codex until reaching the desired visualizations.
Chain of thought (CoT) prompts for GPT-3 are implemented by adding the text “Let’s think step by step.” (7) after the few-shot questions and answers, and the new question.
Evaluations are considered correct if the printed output or the value returned by the generated program is the correct solution.
We fix all Codex’s hyperparameters to be the same for all solution and explanation experiments to yield deterministic and reproducible results.

We validate that our results are not merely overfitting training data by solving questions from a new Computational Linear Algebra course COMS3251 which is unavailable online and was unseen by Codex when trained.

There are a few different types of problems the model is incapable of solving: (1) any problem for which the question is in the form of an image or other non-text modality; (2) questions with solutions that require proofs; and (3) problems that are computationally intractable, such as factoring very large primes.
citacoes.localizador: p. 8, Types of Problems the Model Cannot Solve

tecnicas.nome_original: RING (multilingual repair engine; prompt com mensagem do compilador, seleção inteligente de few-shots e ranqueamento de candidatos)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 2 do PDF (contribuições); p. 3-4 do PDF (Approach, Figura 1); Tabela 1, p. 6 do PDF
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote comparado com o baseline Codex zero-shot (Tabela 1). O prompt do RING tem cabeçalho de instrução (Figura 1: «Fix ES Lint Errors in Javascript»), o código defeituoso (contexto), a mensagem de erro pré-processada do compilador/analisador (contexto), exemplos buggy-fixed recuperados do example bank por similaridade de diagnóstico (contexto e exemplos) e ranqueamento de vários candidatos pela média das log-probabilidades dos tokens (amostragem). Mecanismos acrescentados em relação ao baseline zero-shot: mensagem do compilador e exemplos recuperados; o ranqueamento não é contado como acrescentado porque a linha None/None das Tabelas 3-9 (configuração do RING sem localização nem transformação) tem valores idênticos aos do baseline Codex da Tabela 1, mas o estudo não declara explicitamente se o baseline usa o mesmo ranqueamento. A configuração do RING na Tabela 1 varia por linguagem (mensagem abstraída ou não; error vector ou message embedding) e é a de melhor desempenho escolhida pelos autores. Pacote híbrido: inclui temperatura 0,7 (decodificação, fora do escopo) informada só para os experimentos do RING. A decomposição em localização, transformação e ranqueamento é conceitual: o estudo não descreve etapas de LLM encadeadas, por isso não se registra `decomposicao`. O ganho do pacote não se atribui a um único ingrediente.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 3 do PDF (Fault Localization through Language Tooling, Figura 3); Tabelas 3-9, p. 12-13 do PDF
tecnicas.observacao: Mensagem de erro pré-processada do compilador ou analisador, com linha e coluna, incluída no prompt. O estudo não analisa o contraste com e sem a mensagem; a matriz de configurações (Tabelas 3-9, colunas Localization e Transformation) tem as condições Localization=None/Transformation=None e Localization=Compiler/Transformation=None, que diferem apenas nesse ingrediente (por exemplo, Tabela 3, Excel, P@1 0.60 e 0.70). A RQ2 avalia localização por outra medida (fração de localização correta, Figura 5), não por contrafactual de prompt. `amostragem` registrada porque as configurações das Tabelas 3-9 são do RING, que inclui ranqueamento.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 3 do PDF; p. 8 do PDF (Creating abstracted error message); Tabelas 3-9, p. 12-13 do PDF; texto p. 12 do PDF (Different Configurations of RING)
tecnicas.observacao: Variante da mensagem do compilador que remove a localização relatada e preserva o texto do erro. O estudo compara mensagem abstraída e não abstraída nas Tabelas 3-9 e comenta o contraste para Excel e PowerFx (p. 12). Em relação à mensagem completa, o ingrediente é a abstração (remoção de informação), registrada como variação de `contexto`.

tecnicas.nome_original: Smart selection of few-shots (Smart Shots / Transformation: Smart Selection), com as variantes error vector selection e message embedding selection
tecnicas.localizador: p. 3-4 do PDF (Code Transformation through Few-shot Learning, Figura 4); Tabela 2, p. 7 do PDF (RQ3); Tabelas 3-9, p. 12-13 do PDF
tecnicas.observacao: Recuperação de pares buggy-fixed do example bank por similaridade de diagnóstico: error vector selection (distância L2 entre vetores de contagem de categorias de erro; usada em Excel e JavaScript) ou message embedding selection (similaridade de cosseno entre embeddings das mensagens obtidos com CodeBert pré-treinado; usada nas demais linguagens). As duas variantes não são comparadas entre si: cada linguagem usa uma. Comparada com exemplos fixos pré-definidos na Tabela 2 (RQ3) e nas Tabelas 3-9; o ingrediente acrescentado em relação aos exemplos fixos é a recuperação (contexto). Leave-one-out sobre o benchmark; para C e Python, example bank formado a partir de 400 programas adicionais reparados pelo próprio RING sem seleção inteligente.

citacoes.trecho: We implement our approach in the RING system, which employs compiler (or diagnostic) messages, smart few-shot selection, and ranking of repair candidates to perform repair across varying languages.
Following this intuition, we include a preprocessed error message produced by the compiler or other static analyzers.
citacoes.localizador: p. 3 do PDF, Fault Localization through Language Tooling

citacoes.trecho: For languages where the error messaging may not be precise, particularly with regards to the error location reported, we found that a simple abstraction that removes the reported error location but preserves the error text worked well – we discuss how to create such an abstracted message in our discussion section.
citacoes.localizador: p. 3 do PDF, Fault Localization through Language Tooling

citacoes.trecho: Following the intuition that programs with similar mistakes have similar fixes, we select examples from a collection of buggy-fixed pairs based on error message similarity.
citacoes.localizador: p. 3 do PDF, Code Transformation through Few-shot Learning

citacoes.trecho: We then select programs from the example bank by minimizing the L2 distance between error vectors.
We use this description by embedding the compiler messages with a pretrained CodeBert (Feng et al. 2020) model and comparing embeddings based on cosine similarity.

We use a relatively simple (but effective) ranking strategy to order the candidate programs: averaging the log-probabilities of tokens selected during the decoding process and sort the candidates in descending order of their averages.
We also use zero-shot Codex as a baseline for all languages.
Smart selection is done via leave-one-out.
We run the best RING configuration (without smart selection) on these 400 programs and pick those that do not raise any diagnostics error.
We found that providing these arbitrary windows to Codex resulted in false edits, as the windows had syntax errors that were just an artifact of the windowing.
To mitigate this, we extracted the whole function (or whole file, if not in a function) that encompassed the originally buggy and the repaired code snippets.
Manual inspection of failures also revealed that RING performs fewer edits than required to match the ground truth.
We hypothesize that this may be a reflection of the (presumed) relative scarcity of PS commands in Codex’s training data.
In Javascript, RING is capable of generating the right repair but ranking needs to improve.

citacoes.trecho: Manual inspection revealed that Power Fx compiler messages tend to be imprecise, and using them to select examples can introduce some noise into the prompt.
In practice, this will be a very restrictive example bank that can potentially limit the number of successful repairs.

We kept a final set of 208 task pairs.
We introduce PowerShell commands as a new application for last-mile repair and collect a benchmark set of 200 PowerShell commands from StackOverflow, which we also release for future research.

O mesmo trecho cita que o Codex de base gera ocasionalmente código com defeitos.
Correspondências recuperadas obviamente incorretas podem entrar no prompt; o estudo aplica critérios de qualidade para evitá-las.

A melhoria do ajuste fino vem ao custo dos recursos computacionais necessários para ajustar o Codex; custo não quantificado (o estudo informa só o hardware e as épocas). citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we propose InferFix: a transformer-based program repair framework paired with a state-of-the-art static analyzer to fix critical security and performance bugs.
Our evaluation demonstrates that InferFix outperforms strong LLM baselines, with a top-1 accuracy of 65.6% for generating fixes in C# and 76.8% in Java.

we introduce a dedicated prompt augmentation technique for program repair task, which leverages dense retrieval from an external database of historic bugs and fixes, bug type annotations, and syntactic hierarchies across the entire source code file affected by a bug
In our approach we combine the benefits of both paradigms, by augmenting the prompts and then finetuning our model on the dataset of augmented prompts and predictions to get the best performance.

Given the baseline Codex model has been shown to occasionally predict insecure or buggy code [29], we prioritized finetuning it on a bug-free supervised dataset of bugs and fixes with contexts enriched via relevant program repair patterns from an external non-parametric memory.
For program repair, we introduce a prefix constructed of two answered prompts as, followed by the actual buggy code snippet [X], as shown in Figure 3.
Specifically, given a bug-free prefix, we run Codex model inference to complete the buggy code snippet, aiming to rewrite a program without bugs.
Fix a [bug type string] in the following code snippet: [snippet] In your response, output code snippet only.
The most basic prompt we can construct for the model is to provide the buggy method as input while expecting the model to generate the fix by outputting the fixed version of the given method.
In the following subsections, we will describe each prompt augmentation technique and quantify its impact on bug-fixing performance by adding features incrementally.
The simplest prompt augmentation step is to prepend a bug type annotation to a basic prompt consisting of a buggy method only.

We utilize the bug location information output by Infer in two ways: (i) we parse the source code file affected by the bug to extract a method which contains the buggy line, and (ii) we surround the buggy region with special sentinel <START_BUG> and <END_BUG> symbols.
Table 5 shows the effect of adding the eWASH syntax hierarchies and focal context in the prompt.
The resulting fixes are then prepended to the context with an instruction string // Structurally similar fix.

We apply quality criteria to avoid obviously incorrect matches: (i) retrieved fixes must be of the same bug type as the query, and (ii) impose a minimum similarity threshold between retrieved fixes and a query of 60%.
This improvement comes at a cost of computing resources necessary to finetune the Codex model, but provide an advantage of higher accuracy and cheaper inference as compared to few-shot Davinci.
However, there may be other candidate patches that correctly fix the bug using a different token sequence.
The performance gap between our approach and the best performing baseline (Finetuned Codex) is between 8.6% and 13% in absolute terms.
Each candidate patch is packaged as a separate Pull Request, which is individually validated.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote: descrição detalhada do Scientific Debugging em linguagem natural (instrucao) com vários exemplos por categoria (hipótese, predição, experimento, observação, conclusão; exemplos ilustrativos → exemplos), geração de hipótese/predição antes do experimento (raciocinio), laço hipotetizar-observar-concluir seguido de etapa de sugestão do patch (decomposicao), resultados reais de depurador/execução de teste devolvidos ao LLM (feedback), código da função defeituosa, teste, mensagem de erro e relatório de bug quando disponível (contexto), DSL de comandos REPLACE/ADD/DEL/RUN, script entre crases e sufixo de formato «full method, without comments» (restricoes). Contrafactual: AutoSD contra LLM-Base (prompt que pede o patch imediatamente) nas Tabelas 1 e 2. O sim vale para o pacote; o ganho não pode ser atribuído a um único mecanismo. Instrucao e contexto foram tratados como presentes também no LLM-Base (o LLM precisa receber o código defeituoso para corrigi-lo), por isso não constam como acrescentados; o estudo não detalha o conteúdo exato do prompt do LLM-Base (por exemplo, se inclui teste, mensagem de erro ou relatório de bug). Parâmetros de orçamento (s = 3 iterações; 10 patches por bug) estão em componentes_fora_escopo; o número de patches do LLM-Base não é declarado explicitamente.

riscos.descricao: Patches plausíveis podem ser incorretos e a explicação pode não ter relação com o patch: em BIP002 as hipóteses falharam (breakpoints não cobertos) e o patch gerado foi plausível mas incorreto.

A explicação gerada pode dar credibilidade a patches incorretos (raciocínio enganoso); em ARHE105, participantes aceitaram o raciocínio do AutoSD sem escrutínio e erraram. Risco de confiança indevida na revisão humana.
Quando as observações são previstas pelo LLM em vez de obtidas por execução real ('debugger hallucination'), o <DONE> deixa de indicar bom desempenho e menos execuções geram patch plausível.
Os dados de treinamento dos LLMs podem incluir partes dos dados de avaliação; o estudo constrói o ARHE para mitigar. Não há análise de contaminação para o Defects4J.
riscos.localizador: PDF p. 5, seções 4.1 e 4.2.1; p. 10, seção 6.1 (External Validity)

riscos.descricao: Invocações múltiplas do LLM e do depurador aumentam o tempo de reparo: o AutoSD pode levar cerca de cinco vezes mais tempo que o LLM-Base para gerar um patch; o estudo chama isso de custo adicional. Custo monetário ou em tokens não quantificado.

Falhas do processo de raciocínio: em 13 de 25 casos com todas as hipóteses rejeitadas, os breakpoints sugeridos nunca foram atingidos; outras falhas foram expressões de experimento inválidas (2/25) e múltiplos comandos print que causaram rejeição imprecisa de hipóteses (2/25).

citacoes.trecho: Inspired by the way developers interact with code when debugging, we propose Automated Scientific Debugging (AutoSD), a technique that given buggy code and a bug-revealing test, prompts large language models to automatically generate hypotheses, uses debuggers to actively interact with buggy code, and thus automatically reach conclusions prior to patch generation.
Our empirical analysis on three program repair benchmarks shows that AutoSD performs competitively with other program repair baselines, and that it can indicate when it is confident in its results.

To construct the initial prompt, as in the example presented in Figure 1 A, we first manually wrote a detailed description of Scientific Debugging that explains what hypotheses, predictions, experiments, observations, and conclusions are, along with multiple examples for each category, so that the LLM can generate an intelligible reasoning trace.

Regarding the DSL, the prompt specifies that the following commands are available: REPLACE(line, old_expr, new_expr) that changes an expression at line, ADD(line, new_expr) that adds a new statement above line, and DEL(line, old_expr) that allows deletion of an expression in a line.

On this description of scientific debugging, we add the bug-specific information: concretely, the buggy function/method, the test that reveals the bug, the error message when the bug is executed, and if available a bug report.

In addition to experiment commands, the prompt instructs to predict the <DEBUGGING DONE> token (<DONE> for short in the rest of the paper) if enough information to discern the patch has been gathered, so that we can gauge how confident AutoSD is in its patch.

The generated experiment script is passed to a background process based on traditional software engineering tools that provides real execution results back to the language model, so that we can ground the generation process of AutoSD on real results, and also build credibility for developer presentation.

When AutoSD has completed its interaction with the code, the conclusions to each of the hypotheses are assessed, and rejected hypotheses are automatically removed from the prompt prior to patch generation, as this empirically improved program repair performance in our experiments.

We thus seek to answer whether AutoSD achieves performance competitive to prior APR techniques, and when compared to prompting an LLM to immediately predict a fix (this baseline is referred to as LLM-Base in the rest of the paper).
The maximum iteration limit, s, is set to 3.
Furthermore, individual runs became much less likely to be plausible: while 73% of the individual AutoSD runs would yield a plausible patch, only 63% would when the debugger was ablated.

Finally, the generated explanation may occasionally lend credibility to incorrect patches; by allowing our technique to indicate its confidence in its output and demonstrating that confidence is correlated with correctness, we take the first steps to address this issue.
Meanwhile, for ARHE105 the participants who answered incorrectly accepted the reasoning of AutoSD without significant scrutiny.

Ultimately, while a fix is generated, the explanation has little connection to the patch, and as a result the human study participants rated the explanation as unhelpful; the patch itself is plausible but incorrect as well.

This is one of the most common failure causes - our analysis on 25 cases where all hypotheses were rejected revealed that in 13 of the 25 cases, breakpoints suggested by AutoSD were never hit, and consequently AutoSD could not get results for generated experiments.

First, to enable multi-step interaction with code, both the language model and debugger must be invoked multiple times, which increases the repair time of the technique; in our experiments, AutoSD could take about five times longer to generate a patch when compared to LLM-Base.

A particular concern when using large language models is that their training data may include segments of the evaluation data. To mitigate this issue, we newly constructed the ARHE dataset for repair and evaluated AutoSD on that benchmark.
To mitigate the impact of the first two concerns, we plan to make our implementation and repair results publicly available for scrutiny.

tecnicas.observacao: Prompt base adaptado de trabalho anterior [40]: pergunta se o programa tem defeito e pede o reparo, com o código-fonte do programa defeituoso inserido em [CODE] (contexto, D102). Linha de base de prompting das RQ1 e RQ2; não há condição sem o prompt base, por isso não é avaliada isoladamente. Também é a rodada 1 do diálogo da RQ3 (Figura 2, p. 7).

tecnicas.observacao: Template proposto pelo estudo a partir da categorização de perguntas reais do StackOverflow (Seção 4.1). Acrescenta ao prompt base a tarefa de aprendizado [X] e o conjunto de dados [Y] (contexto sobre a intenção do código) e o objetivo do reparo [Z] (instrução com objetivo explícito); mantém o código em [CODE] e remove a pergunta «Is the following program buggy?». O contraste com PT-B (mesmo benchmark, cinco requisições por consulta) é de pacote: PT-E difere de PT-B em mais de um ingrediente, e não há ablação de X, Y ou Z; o ganho não pode ser atribuído a um único ingrediente. Pacote só de prompting (não híbrido). Quando X, Y ou Z não estavam disponíveis, foram usadas variantes do template sem o elemento ausente (p. 6); o número de casos com cada variante e quem preencheu X/Y/Z não são informados.

Possível vazamento de dados: os casos do benchmark podem estar no conjunto de treinamento do ChatGPT e a saída ser fruto de memorização. O estudo não afirma contaminação efetiva.
A avaliação das respostas do ChatGPT foi feita manualmente e pode ser subjetiva ou conter equívocos (ameaça à validade).
Diferença entre a interface web do ChatGPT e a API usada nos experimentos (ameaça à validade); a repetição da RQ1 na interface mostrou «slight difference», não quantificada no texto.

citacoes.trecho: In particular, we split the debugging task into three steps, i.e., fault detection, fault localization, and program repair.
Prompt Template (Basic): Is the following program buggy? If so, please repair it. [CODE]
On top of the observation from real-world questions, we propose an enhanced prompt template (abbrev. PT-E) as follows:
Prompt Template (Enhanced): The following code is designed for a [X] problem trained on [Y].Please repair it in order to [Z]. [CODE]

where X describes the task (e.g., classification, regression), Y specifies the dataset (e.g., MNIST, ImageNet, numbers that follow the sine waves), and Z describes the objective (e.g., improve the accuracy) against the symptom.
Note that for the cases where the learning task/dataset/objective is unavailable, we use the variant templates as listed in Section 4.2.

In particular, for the cases that failed to be completely repaired in Section 4 (i.e., 18 cases), we first provide the fault locations using the following prompt template (Prompt Template (Locations), abbrev, PT-Loc).
(Round 3) Prompt Template (Locations) : The repair is wrong. Faults may happen in the following locations: [Loc]. Please repair it.
(Round 4) Prompt Template (IncR): The [Remaining_loc] is/are repaired incorrectly. Please repair it accordingly.
where the fault location information in PT-Loc is automatically filled in using the information provided by the benchmark [7], while the remaining locations in PT-IncR are filled after analysis.
We then integrate such failing information to ChatGPT by saying “The repair is wrong. For the input [1, 1], the output should be [0] instead of [1]. Please repair it again.”
It indicates that for DL program repair, providing the failing test cases may not be helpful.
We propose a few-shot prompt template as follows:
Compared with the human-written prompt (Reference), the meaning of two sentences are almost identical, which indicates the possibility to automate the prompt as discussed in RQ2.
We build a pipeline for our experiments using the latest ChatGPT API based on the gpt-3.5-turbo model released by OpenAI.
Due to the non-deterministic nature of ChatGPT, for each query, we run five independent requests by starting a new conversation every time on the API.
If the majority (≥ 3) of replies correctly report fault existence, we denote the result as a Yes; otherwise, No.
For ChatGPT, we put down the number of faults reported each round, and we use the best result among the five rounds for comparison.
To evaluate the automatic DL program repair ability of ChatGPT, we use a benchmark released by a recent study [7], which contains 58 buggy DL programs collected from StackOverflow and Github.
In the evaluation, we use the buggy programs collected from StackOverflow, because the programs in GitHub exceed the maximum input tokens.
While one should be careful with code refactoring and variable renaming, in case they cause a crash.
When asked to repair the program without an explicit repair goal, ChatGPT tends to focus on identifying outdated APIs and bad code smells.
It means that the repair could be invalid once newer version is released.
In addition, there are a few faults that are repaired correctly in the previous round but changed back to faulty in the next round.
Besides, ChatGPT is not able to execute the program at the current stage, even though a patch is provided by ChatGPT, a validation step is still needed.
Besides, ChatGPT’s replies are carried out manually, which may be subjective and misunderstandings.
To alleviate this threat, the cases used in the paper come along with StackOverflow post IDs.

Finally, since ChatGPT is trained on a large corpus of text data from the Internet (e.g., books, articles, open-source code repositories), it is possible that there is a data leakage problem, i.e., the cases in the benchmark were included in its training set, so the output is generated due to memorization.
This observation may partially alleviate the concern regarding such threat.
To avoid the difference between the ChatGPT website interface and the latest API, we repeat the experiment of RQ1 using the interface (Mar 14, 2023 Version).
One can avoid it by explicitly asking ChatGPT to return the complete repaired code.

Via further analysis, we found that among the 49 (72 - 23) escaped faults that belong to 18 cases, 16 of them (belonging to 7 cases) cannot be even detected, 32 of them (belonging to 11 cases) can be detected but cannot be correctly-localized.
With the best prior work, the performance of fault localization is still far less than satisfactory (only about 30%).

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote de dois prompts: (1) três exemplos <requirement, SCoT> mais instruções em itálico (objetivo e restrições: estrutura de entrada e saída e as três estruturas básicas sequência, ramificação e laço) para gerar o SCoT; (2) exemplos <requirement, SCoT, code> mais instrução para conferir o SCoT («Note that the solving process may contain errors») e gerar o código. Base de que deriva: CoT prompting (exemplos com raciocínio em linguagem natural, um passo). Acrescentados em relação ao CoT: instruções explícitas de objetivo e verificação (instrucao), formato estruturado do raciocínio com estruturas de programa e estrutura de E/S (restricoes) e pipeline de dois passos (decomposicao). A instrução de reconferir o SCoT é passo único, sem retorno de execução, e não foi classificada como feedback. Comparado com CoT, few-shot e zero-shot no mesmo modelo e benchmark (Tabela 2): o contraste é do pacote completo, que também difere em configurações de decodificação (segundo passo com temperatura 0; comprimento total igual ao do CoT), componente fora do escopo; trata-se, portanto, de pacote com diferenças de decodificação, e o ganho não se atribui a um único mecanismo.

citacoes.trecho: We apply SCoT prompting to two LLMs (i.e., ChatGPT and Codex) and evaluate it on three benchmarks (i.e., HumanEval, MBPP, and MBCPP).
(1) SCoT prompting outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline - CoT prompting by up to 13.79% in Pass@1.
SCoT prompting asks LLMs first to generate a SCoT and then output the final code.
Thus, we introduce three basic structures and constrain LLMs to use them to generate CoTs.
Next, the italic sentences are instructions for LLMs, which indicate the goal of LLMs and related constraints.
You should use three basic structures to build the solving process, including sequences, branches, and loops.
# Please check the above solving process and write a code based on it. Note that the solving process may contain errors.
Similarly, in SCoT prompting, the generated SCoT may contain noises (e.g., errors or missing steps).
First, as shown in Figure 4, we ask LLMs to double-check the SCoT and fix possible noises.
Second, SCoT prompting utilizes a two-step generation pipeline.
A prompt contains three examples by default.
Because HumanEval does not contain train data, we reuse examples from MBPP in HumanEval.
Previous work [1, 6, 7] found that standard Pass@k has high variance and proposed an unbiased Pass@k.
Zero-shot prompting [7] directly feeds the requirement into LLMs without examples.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [35] is a variant of few-shot prompting.
To ensure the fairness of comparison, all baselines and SCoT prompting have the same number of examples (i.e., three examples) and example seeds.
The maximum generated length of CoT prompting is 600 tokens.
The temperature is 0 and the maximum generated length is 300 tokens.
In terms of Pass@1, CoT prompting improves few-shot prompting by up to 2% in HumanEval, 7.51% in MBPP, and 3.79% in MBCPP.
In practice, people may write different examples, which makes the performance of SCoT prompting varies.
When removing basic structures, we use a CoT with an IO structure as the intermediate steps.
When removing the IO structure, the SCoT only contains a solving process with basic structures.
It is similar to SCoT prompting, but considers the pseudocode as intermediate steps.
CodeT does large-scale sampling and executes sampled programs on auto-generated test cases.
It is possible that the improvements come from the two-step pipeline.
It is possible that their training data contains the experimental benchmarks, leading to data leakage.
Thus, the reported relative improvements between baselines and our approach are credible.

citacoes.trecho: We propose a new paradigm to construct code prompts and successfully uncover social biases in code generation models.
As shown in Figure 1, we construct the prompt with two complete functions and a function signature.
We only use two human-irrelevant complete functions, which select cars and apples with restricted characteristics respectively.

Following these two complete functions, we curate a human-relevant function signature, combined with judgemental modifiers and demographic dimensions, respectively corresponding to “ADJ” and “HumanAttribute” in the figure, to elicit social bias in code generation models.
We mainly study the following aspects: the number of functions contained in the prompt, the relevancy of functions to humans, and the order of functions in the code prompt.
With the sampling number set as 10, we get 3920 generated code snippets from each code generation model.

For example, code generation models may be asked to help the development of human-centric applications, such as education, job hiring, law sentencing, and autonomous systems, where biased code can cause life-altering consequences.
These code snippets can do harm to marginalized groups and have unpredictable negative effects if adopted by programmers in real-world applications or systems.
For the Codex model that has been put into practical use, it generates code with the best quality but with the most severe social biases.
Compared with human evaluation, experimental results show that, though imperfect, the code classifier can be used as a code bias scorer.
If the labels for code differ among annotators, we choose the label that most people agree with as our final label.
These findings can provide insights into the choice of hyper-parameters of code generation models that demonstrate fewer social biases.
Pass@k is computed on the HumanEval benchmark [7], and the results are taken from corresponding papers.
We queried the OpenAI Davinci Codex API (code-davinci-002) to obtain results.
For example, −0.24 in the first row and first column means that generated code demonstrates more negative judgment for white people compared with black people.
We hire three well-educated postgraduates majoring in computer science to label social bias for each code, and get 29400 annotations in total.

citacoes.trecho: Leveraging these findings, we develop a set of prompting strategies and propose an AI integrated development workflow for embedded systems design, programming and debugging.
In these experiments, we specifically seek to test their performance with a single prompt and response.
In these experiments we provide zero additional context other than the prompt and used GPT-4 version 0314.

To develop an interface with LLMs we leverage the key observation that given an example format within prompts, all 3 of these language models can very reliably generate code to print data over serial.
Prompt engineering to provide LLMs with ample context is important to generating useful code.
First explain how to approach the task and then provide a program to accomplish it.
We find however that LLMs are also capable of automatically correcting their mistakes when error messages are copied back into the model as new prompts.
Generally a more specific prompt that details precisely how the behavior differs from what is desired will yield more relevant responses decreasing the number of queries required.
One powerful technique is to create prompts with example code and explain what you’d like the model to change.
We note that it is important to be explicit about what should be changed and what should be kept the same to prevent the model from making unprompted changes as shown in the following example prompt.
If the model fails multiple times to generate complete working code, try asking it to develop modular functions individually and integrate them into a complete program yourself.
Adding context of any user modifications to the generated code is important.
If GPT fails multiple times to fix an issue, it is often best to start over with a new chat.
If you find a bug that you know how to fix, fix it yourself.
We repeat this prompting for ten iterations with each model, and record the occurrence of specific and actionable improvements.

We verify this approach by prompting GPT-4 with a register table for a fictional temperature sensor IC (guaranteed not to be in the training data) and requesting pseudocode for a basic driver for this chip, and find GPT-4 produces code consistent with the register table and descriptions as shown in Figure 4 (see Appendix for full register table).
We perform a user study to evaluate our workflow guidelines and investigate the ability of LLMs to aid in hardware debugging.
Participants were timed and completed all four tasks in a random order and with varying levels of GPT-4: no access, access to GPT-4, and access to GPT-4 with our workflow guidelines.
We used a subset of the Latin square such that participants never had access to GPT-4 with our workflow guidelines before having access to GPT-4 alone.
Errors include identifying the incorrect I2C address from the SDO/SA0 pin voltage (38%) as well as hallucinating at least one of the register addresses or configuration values (100%).

While a human programmer working physically with these sensors may understand based on the sensor type what is desired, LLMs often subtly misinterpret tasks like this and can produce code that compiles and runs, but does something different than what the user intended.
In the context of embedded systems, we see this issue arise with models generating nonexistent pin numbers, register names, and library references.

Similarly, when queried to generate code and then requested to make changes to that same code, LLMs may make additional unnecessary and unprompted changes along with the requested updates which can easily go unnoticed.
This may be remedied through an understanding of the embedded software, by prompting the model to only make changes to specific lines or sections, or future automated tools to check for these errors.
We find another common error made by LLMs is confusing different open-source libraries and their versions.

While an inexperienced developer might simply implement the suggestions provided by a LLM and achieve a promising result, we again find that human evaluation is critical, since one suggestion, decreasing i2c speed, actually slightly increased the power draw of the system.
We note however that this particular sensor is available from numerous vendors and is also potentially well-represented in the training set.

We note that some of its explanations are direct copies of the datasheet, suggesting that this understanding of hardware components is at least partially due to datasheets being included in the training dataset.
This is particularly important in cases where embedded systems are used for mission-critical subsystems, where ownership and extensive verification of code can have significant safety implications.
We perform N=1000 measurements and use these to determine a threshold for “correct” outputs (e.g. within 10% of the reference).

While the best model only produced perfect end-to-end code on the most complex tasks 14% of the time (GPT-4, N=50 trials) these partially correct programs contained significant functional code, as well as detailed comments and explanation of how to correctly design the system.
In contrast, we find that GPT-4 is actually able to produce verifiable working code 16% of the time.

We find that our workflow improves productivity for all users and increases the success rate for building a LoRa environmental sensor from 25% to 100%, including for users with zero hardware or C/C++ experience.
In the Environmental Sensor task all 5 participants with GPT access and our workflow scored 100%, and half had little to no embedded systems experience.
Participants without GPT scored 25% on average.

The average perceived load for conditions in which participants had access to GPT and our workflow guidelines was lower than the perceived load when participants had access to GPT only (mean load 3.25 vs 3.83, t(38) = 1.49, p = 0.1), and also lower than the perceived load when participants had no access to GPT (mean load 3.25 vs 4.67, t(35) = 4.35, p << 0.01).

citacoes.trecho: In this experiment, we generated code from 1,081 prompts collected from existing code generation benchmarks [2], [19]–[22] and 70 prompts we created from questions posted on StackOverflow.
In light of this need, this paper describes FRANC, a lightweight, configurable, and model-agnostic framework to filter, rank, and repair code automatically generated by LLMs.
FRANC repairs code samples via Generated Knowledge Prompting (i.e., prompting for a task by incorporating knowledge or information [48]).
In this case, FRANC uses knowledge from the static analyzers to create the prompts.

FRANC uses the issue’s description and location detected by a static analyzer to craft a repair prompt using three different structures (P1, P2, and P3) and send it back to the code generation model to generate code again.
The prompt structure P1 adds source code comments after the code to be repaired in the format “Fix: At line « # », « error msg »\n Fixed Code:\n”, as shown in Listing 4 (lines 10-11).
The second prompt structure (P2) appends to the code to be repaired a comment followed by the original prompt.
For example, the repair prompt for the code in Listing 4 would include the lines 1–11 followed by lines 1-5 (i.e., the original prompt).
The third prompt repair structure (P3) only includes the code to be repaired up to the first line that has an issue, followed by the fix message.
For instance, while repairing the code in Listing 4, this prompt would only include lines 1–6 followed by lines 10–11.
Lastly, it is important to highlight that FRANC attempts to repair the output only once.
FRANC ranks all code snippets based on their quality score Q(ci) and presents the best one to the developer.
Thus, we investigate whether FRANC’s quality-based ranking performs better than the model’s original ranking.
We instructed each model to generate 10 suggestions for each prompt.
citacoes.localizador: p. 6 do PDF, Seção IV-B, Suggestion Inventory Creation

citacoes.trecho: Therefore, in this third phase, our framework inspects each snippet from the Suggestion Inventory and applies a set of rules to (a) remove unnecessary code from the snippet, and (b) check whether it is syntactically correct.
Although LLM-based code generation techniques may produce functionally correct code, they can contain code smells and vulnerabilities [7]–[9].
These code smells can introduce software maintenance problems.
Code generation models can output multiple suggestions for a single prompt, but not all suggestions are compilable [53].

Since this suggestion is not the top one recommended generated by the model as developers are biased towards the first suggestion they see [47], we need a lightweight ranking system to address the quality issues of the generated suggestions.

Conversely, LLMs were less capable of solving issues related to the Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm (CWE-327), Path Traversal (CWE-22), and Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource (CWE-732).
However, LLMs can hardly repair infinite loops, array indexing out of bounds, and useless control flow to next line.
Although FRANC adds an overhead, the extra time needed is less than 2 seconds (on average).
citacoes.localizador: p. 9 do PDF, quadro RQ4 Findings

citacoes.trecho: The Cohen’s kappa score of the inter-raters’ agreement is 0.815, which indicates a strong agreement between the raters [66].
A paired t-test comparing the NDCG@10 shows a statistically significant difference for both languages (p<0.0001).
In the end, we have 1,023 repair prompts (341 for each prompt repair structure).
For example, our results showed that without a static filter, no compilable suggestions were produced by InCoder (§ V-A).
For Python, the highest increase was from 0.3630 to 0.4671 for CodeGen 350M-mono (10% increase).
For Python, P2 is performing better except for GPT-3.5, though the difference between P2 and P1 is very close.
Thus, we acknowledge that our results may not generalize for other inference hyperparameters.

citacoes.trecho: This paper will delve into utilizing LLMs for code generation in private libraries, as they are widely employed in everyday programming.
This framework comprises two modules: APIFinder first retrieves potentially useful APIs from API documentation; and APICoder then leverages these retrieved APIs to generate private code.
Therefore, technically speaking, existing code generation models, such as Codex [14], InCoder [24], and CODEGEN [41], can be used directly as our APICoder by providing rich private API information.
Therefore, the baselines are all code generation models with No API setting, while we propose Oracle, TopK, and Human settings.
No API: no API is input to APICoder.
Oracle: the ground-truth APIs are input to APICoder.
TopK: The first K APIs retrieved by APIFinder are input to APICoder, where K ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5}.
Human: APIFinder offers the top 5 APIs for user selection (Figure 6), and the APIs chosen by a user are input to APICoder.
API Basic Only (B): the prompt only includes API basic consisting of API name, signature, and description.
API Examples Only (E): the prompt only includes API examples.
API Basic and Examples (BE): the prompt includes both API basic and examples.
In fact, we find that some components in API documentation, including API parameters and related APIs, significantly devastate the performance of LLMs.
If "None of the above" is selected, APICoder will prompt no APIs.
On the other hand, the majority of errors in these superior models are due to incorrect API usage, whereas subpar models fail to even invoke APIs.
When K exceeds 5, the performance of the small model CODEGEN 350M deteriorates across all benchmarks, while the large model Codex shows stability with no decline.

Moreover, to improve the robustness of CODEGENAPI, we incorporate noise APIs with a probability of 5% and shuffle these APIs in A, as the APIs returned by APIFinder may contain incorrect APIs and are unordered.

Despite our best efforts to modify public libraries into private ones by paraphrasing keywords and API documentation, there remains a potential risk to the validity and fairness of the private library evaluation.
Providing API examples to APICoder may introduce a minor bias in evaluating TorchDataEval, as the construction of TorchDataEval also refers to API examples in API documentation.
Unavoidably, our paper entails a heavy consumption of computational resources.
Considering potential privacy and security concerns, this remains a topic for future research.
As a result, our approach is relatively sensitive to the capabilities of the base model itself.

More importantly, all models in our experiments, including Codex and CODEGEN, are pre-trained on the GitHub corpus prior to the aforementioned release date, ensuring that the LLMs have no prior exposure to the library.
To provide APICoder with more accurate APIs, we design a pipeline that allows user engagement with APIFinder.

citacoes.trecho: This paper presents the first systematic empirical study on the threat of non-determinism of ChatGPT in code generation tasks.

This RQ compares the degree of non-determinism for different prompt engineering strategies (i.e., Chain-Of-Thought and requesting generated code as concise as possible) when using ChatGPT to generate code.
In particular, 1) we ask ChatGPT to generate Python code for each code generation task with zero-shot prompting; 2) we use the basic prompt design directly followed by programming task descriptions.
To guarantee that ChatGPT produces code rather than pure natural languages in its response, we augment the original coding problem description with an instruction to request for Python code.
To address this problem, we specify the format of the generated code into ‘Markdown’.
The first prompt is “Generate Python3 code (Markdown), make the code as concise as possible”.
This prompt aims to lead ChatGPT to generate short and concise programs, which may make the results more deterministic.

The second prompt is “Generate Chain-of-Thought steps of how to solve the problem first, and then generate Python3 code (Markdown)”, thereby demanding an initial conceptual explanation followed by the code.
Then, each prompt is followed by the code problem description.

When setting temperature=0, the code candidates generated from the Concise prompt are more deterministic than our Base prompt, while those code candidates generated from the CoT prompt suffer from higher randomness than our Base prompt.
citacoes.localizador: p. 20 do PDF (impressa 20), Resposta à RQ6

citacoes.trecho: Such non-determinism affects the correctness and consistency of the generated code, undermines developers’ trust in LLMs, and yields low reproducibility in LLM-based papers.
These results highlight that there is currently a significant threat to the validity of scientific conclusions.

Indeed, compared to other tasks of ChatGPT, such as question answering and text summarization, the non-determinism threat in code-related tasks is much more serious, because the inconsistency (especially semantic inconsistency) often indicates errors in the generated code [28].
The generated code also tends to be more buggy.
citacoes.localizador: p. 17 do PDF (impressa 17), Resposta à RQ4

citacoes.trecho: Unreliable and inconsistent code snippets can have significant negative effects on the process of software development, particularly in safety-critical applications where consistency and reliability are paramount [11, 30].
It may also undermine developers’ trust in LLMs when completely different suggestions are given at different times [62].
Overall, we observe that when temperature=0, ChatGPT has better determinism than the default configuration (temperature=1) for all three types of similarities.
However, setting the temperature to 0 does not completely avoid non-determinism.
To reduce the first threat, we checked our code twice, once during the experiment stage, and once during the record analysis stage.
To reduce the second threat, the two authors independently analyzed the experiment results and drew experimental conclusions separately.
We use single-threaded scripts to run the tests to ensure that the test cases are executed sequentially to avoid race conditions that may arise from concurrent executions.
For the HumanEval dataset, we evaluate our measurement on an external testset, EvalPlus [40].
To reduce the randomness caused by the non-determinism issue, researchers can report the average results, variance, or distribution from multiple requests.
In addition, using a prompt with detailed instructions, a clear structure, and concrete response requirements would help to reduce randomness in generated code.
In our study, we study the influence of temperature in RQ2 with three temperature values: 0, 1, and 1.5.
In RQ3, we set n=5 to investigate how the non-determinism of code candidates from the same request compares with those from different requests.
This parameter is strictly required, and in our case, we set this parameter to ‘gpt-3.5-turbo-0125’ or ‘gpt-4-0613’.
Although the benchmarks are very widely studied, their test suites can be inadequate.
Compared with the Base prompt and Concise prompt, the CoT prompt has a higher mean-variance (0.02), higher mean maximum difference (0.15), and a rather higher ratio of worst cases (1.82%).

Code candidates generated by the CoT prompt have a low mean LCS value (0.38) and high LED value (39.31), while those generated from the Concise prompt have a high mean LCS value (0.07) and low LED value (11.77).

For temperature=1, we can observe that GPT-4 is slightly more deterministic than GPT-3.5, with lower test pass rate variance, lower ratio of worst cases, lower OER and OER (no ex.), lower LCS, higher LED, and lower structural similarity under two settings.
When requesting by R1, the ratio of worst cases, where max diff is close to 0 (1.20%), and the OER and OER (no ex.) are higher than R2 and close to 1.

riscos.descricao: ICL e RAG acrescentam tokens de entrada ao prompt, o que pode ser inviável quando a informação contextual é grande e aumenta a sobrecarga computacional na inferência; no setup do estudo, o número de exemplos foi limitado por erros de falta de memória e ICL/RAG não foram executados no APPS (prompt acima de 2,048 tokens).
