riscos.descricao: Se o recuperador do RAG não identificar exemplos apropriados, pode injetar informação irrelevante ou enganosa no prompt e degradar o desempenho.
ICL e RAG dependem da seleção de exemplos representativos e são sensíveis ao desenho do prompt, o que, segundo os autores, pode resultar em menor eficácia que o ajuste fino.

Possível sobreposição entre exemplos de treino (fonte dos exemplos de ICL/RAG e dos dados de ajuste) e de teste; o estudo descreve controle só para o Conala curado. Não discute contaminação por pré-treinamento nem sobreposição no CodeAlpacaPy e no APPS; não afirma contaminação efetiva.

mitigacoes.descricao: No Conala curado, cada amostra de validação e teste contém ao menos uma função Python ausente do treino e exemplos do mesmo post do StackOverflow ficam em conjuntos diferentes; os autores afirmam garantir que nenhuma intenção de teste aparece no treino.
Para a ameaça de escolha de modelos, seleção de modelos de famílias, dados de pré-treinamento, objetivos e tamanhos diversos.
Para a ameaça de construto, uso de métricas difundidas e de EM@k sobre diferentes números de candidatos.

observacoes.descricao: O objeto do estudo é o ajuste fino eficiente em parâmetros (PEFT); ICL, RAG e o prompt zero-shot entram como linhas de base. Os resultados de PEFT, Full FT e QLoRA não são prompting e ficam fora de tecnicas e extracoes.

O contraste RAG contra ICL (Fig. 7; texto: CodeLlama-7B no Conala, 29.83 com ICL e 35.17 com RAG) é de prompting, mas envolve duas técnicas comparadoras e não técnica focal; por isso não entrou por cobertura.
Durante o ajuste fino, os tokens do template de instrução são ignorados na perda (valor -100), para o modelo focar na geração do código; componente do ajuste fino, não do prompting.
Todos os experimentos foram feitos com uma única GPU NVIDIA RTX A5000 de 24GB; código declarado público em https://github.com/martin-wey/peft-llm-code (não acessado nem validado nesta extração).
Os autores afirmam que a implementação de ICL é simples (seleção aleatória de exemplos com sementes diferentes), sem intenção de explorar todo o potencial do ICL.

citacoes.trecho: Throughout our study, we compare all the studied models on a Python code generation task.
Second, we seek to compare the effectiveness of LLMs tuned with these PEFT techniques against SLMs, ICL, and RAG.

The prompt is in the form of an instruction template, where “### Instruction:” and “### Response:” play the role of delimiting the instruction, i.e., natural language intent, and the answer, i.e., code generation.
These examples are randomly sampled from the corresponding training datasets and concatenated with the input prompt during inference.
At inference time, we retrieve up to 16 examples for Conala and 4 examples for CodeAlpacaPy, selecting those with instructions most similar to the test input.

In RQ3, we conduct a comparative study of the effectiveness of LoRA with ICL and RAG, a strong baseline that dynamically retrieves relevant examples by selecting those closest to the test instructions from the training set.
For Prompt tuning and Prefix tuning, we prepended a set of 20 trainable continuous virtual tokens to each input sample of the models and applied learning rates of 3e − 3 and 3e − 2.
One concerns the introduction of extra input tokens in the prompt, which may be infeasible when the contextual information is too large.
If the retrieval mechanism fails to identify appropriate examples, it can inject irrelevant or misleading information into the prompt, ultimately degrading performance.
However, these techniques comes with its own set of challenges, including the selection of representative examples and sensitivity to prompt design [37, 74, 90].
In practice, increasing the number of ICL/RAG examples at inference entails increased computational overhead as the token length of the prompt expands.
We do not compare LoRA and QLoRA with ICL and RAG for this dataset because they require increasing the prompt length beyond 2,048 tokens, which leads to out-of-memory errors.
In this curated version of the dataset, the authors ensured that each sample in the validation and test sets contained at least one Python function that does not appear in the training set.
Thus, we can guarantee that each natural intent in the test does not appear in the training set.
Instead, we opted for a simple implementation of ICL by selecting random few-shot examples using different seeds.

Furthermore, we note that for the more challenging CodeAlpacaPy datasets, RAG yields lower EM@10 compared to randomly selected examples using ICL, highlighting RAG’s limitations when problem complexity increases.
Most models achieve their best EM@10 scores when using three or four examples.
Models achieve peak effectiveness with eight and four examples for Conala and CodeAlpacaPy, respectively.

We show that all PEFT techniques studied in this paper significantly outperform full fine-tuning for SLMs like CodeGen-350M-mono and CodeT5+-770M on the Conala and CodeAlpacaPy datasets (see Table 3), highlighting the clear advantages of PEFT in these scenarios.

Under the same 24GB GPU memory limitation, the best LLM surpasses the best small model by 39.8%, 41.7%, and 47.1% (72.3%, 48.8%, and 9.1%) in EM@1, EM@10, and CodeBLEU concerning the Conala (CodeAlpacaPy) dataset, respectively.
Notably, QLoRA-4bit outperformed LoRA and QLoRA-8bit on the Conala and APPs datasets.

citacoes.trecho: Therefore, this result is best treated as a baseline when compared with other prompt types.
These prompts contain the full parsed context (including the imports, global variables classes, internal class functions, etc.), the summary, and the function signature, in that order.
These prompts have the same structure as the uncommented ones, but we add the context as a comment.

citacoes.trecho: These prompts contain the summary, the full (commented) parsed context, and the function signature, in that order.
citacoes.localizador: p. 6 do PDF, item 4 (Summary at Top)

citacoes.trecho: Following the instruction paradigm of some considered models, we test a version with the summary moved to the top, along with the text “# Here is an instruction. Complete the function using the required context”.
We use a mixture of our syntax solving algorithm and hand annotation to select precisely which objects within the context are necessary for the function to execute.
Using ChatGPT, we generated both “short” and “long” summaries, with the former being more concise and potentially omitting some details, and the latter providing more detail to reduce ambiguity.

citacoes.localizador: p. 6 do PDF, legenda da Tabela 4

citacoes.trecho: To accurately represent the performance of the LLM outputs, we implemented basic correction mechanisms to rectify minor syntax and style errors that did not impact functionality.
First, the use of closed-source LLMs, may introduce a degree of circularity in our methodology.
Despite our obfuscation step (including the ablation study in Appendix M), this circularity could potentially lead to inflated performance metrics and hinder the generalizability of our findings.
We partially mitigated this issue by including open-source models in the evaluation.
Moreover, the closed-source nature of some LLMs used in our study raises concerns about reproducibility and fairness in performance comparisons.
This bias could result in a dataset that is more easily solved by OpenAI GPT-like models, potentially skewing the performance evaluation.

To ensure system security and test reliability, we ran our tests in Docker environments using Amazon Web Services, coordinating tasks across multiple nodes to accelerate the process without compromising result validity.
The vast majority of the generated code samples tested encountered a syntax or runtime error without resulting in an output.
Note that for prompts that exceed the model’s context limit, this prompt is likely to fail.

riscos.descricao: Viés social (idade, gênero, região, educação, ocupação, raça) no código gerado para tarefas sensíveis, com possíveis decisões injustas em contratação, crédito e saúde. Não é cibersegurança.
riscos.localizador: p. 1 (impressa 1), resumo e introdução; p. 12-14, Tab. 4

riscos.descricao: Estratégias diretas de prompting podem aumentar o viés (por exemplo, few-shot no GPT-4: CBS geral de 59.88% para 68.56%); os autores supõem que o prompt longo com mais menções a atributos sensíveis confunda o modelo.
A mitigação pode alterar a funcionalidade do código: em verificação manual de 10 pares escolhidos aleatoriamente, 3 tiveram a funcionalidade alterada (estudo preliminar).
O código gerado e o CBS variam entre execuções e com a temperatura; CBS_U@K e CBS_I@K foram propostos por causa do não determinismo; mesmo com temperatura 0.0 o CBS não é zero.

A ampliação do pool de valores para eliminar falsos negativos aumenta o tempo de teste de 57.15s (texto; 57.16s na Tab. 14) para 3958.84s; o estudo trata como overhead e não a adota por padrão. Refere-se ao avaliador, não ao prompting.
O teste automatizado de viés tem falsos negativos (12 FN; recall de 92%) porque o pool de valores não cobre todos os casos (por exemplo, idades acima de 65).

citacoes.trecho: This paper presents a novel bias testing framework that is specifically designed for code generation tasks.

Moreover, we study five bias mitigation prompt strategies that are commonly used in current code generation scenarios, i.e., zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, and two Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts, with and without provided feedback-driven refinement.

Our evaluation results illustrate that using direct prompt engineering strategies has limited effectiveness in mitigating bias, but our test execution feedback can help to reduce the ratio of code biases to a large extent (e.g., from 59.88% to 4.79% for GPT-4).
Zero-shot | Prompt: Please avoid generating biased code. The protected attributes are age, gender, region, education, occupation, and race. Please avoid the code containing bias for these attributes.
One-shot | Prompt: Zero-shot + Example 1.
Few-shot | Prompt: One-shot + Example 2.
CoT1 | Prompt: Zero-shot + Please think step by step.
CoT2 | Prompt: CoT1 + Consider which attributes may cause bias, and then avoid using these attributes in the code.
Zero-shot | Prompt: Zero-Shot in Scenario 1 + Please correct the identified bias in the code based on the report log. + Feedback.
We require the code generation model for the first scenario to avoid generating biased code.
Based on this feedback information, we then construct prompts (as shown in Tab. 3) to require the code generation model to mitigate bias from their original generated code.

Scenario 1 requires first analyzing which bias attributes exist in the LLMs and then rewriting the source code to remove the identified bias attributes, which raises the question of whether the inferior results of Scenario 1 compared to Scenario 2 are due to the LLMs’ inability to detect bias behaviors in their own generated code.

As LLMs gain prevalence in software development, such biases can have far-reaching consequences, leading to unfair practices in hiring, biased lending decisions in finance, and skewed treatments in healthcare.
For example, for GPT-4, the overall CBS decreases from 59.88% to 36.23% for the zero shot learning prompt but increases to 68.56% for the few shot learning prompt.
The results show that 7 out of 10 code pairs have similar functionality, while the other three code pairs’ functionality has been changed.
They are proposed due to the non-determinism of LLMs [21] and are inspired by the ReCode’s multi-scenario robust evaluation metrics [22].
Specifically, the testing time increases from 57.15s to 3958.84s.
Finally, the recall of automated test case analysis increases from 92% to 100%.
To reduce the threat of randomness, we run each experiment five times and report the average results in Tab. 7 and 8.
Considering that Scenario 2 requires the code to be executable, we remove the few non-executable cases shown in Table 6 for both Scenario 1 and 2 for a fair comparison.
If any disagreements arise between the two participants, a third participant, who is a senior expert, will be involved to make a decision based on the findings of the previous two human participants.
The Cohen’s Kappa Coefficients are all above 0.9.

While the results in Scenario 1 show some changes compared to the direct LLM-generated code, they remain similar in some cases, suggesting that the decreased bias in Scenario 1 may be partially attributed to the change in the prompt.
During the inference, we set the temperature as 1.0 in our experiments.
For each different code generation prompt, we feed them into each code generation model to generate five code snippets to calculate metric scores.
Additionally, we include the recently released GPT-4 and GPT-4-turbo.

Then, when evaluating the education attribute, we observe that LLMs also exhibit higher bias behaviors. For example, Claude-instant-1, GPT-4-turbo, and GPT-4 obtain 31.44%, 32.63%, and 30.54% CBS in education attribute, and PALM-2-CodeChat-bison and GPT-4-turbo also achieve 8.68% and 24.85% CBS in education attribute.
Answer to RQ2.2: Automated bias testing can analyze the majority of the code generated by the LLMs we study. For example, it detects 173 out of 174 code biases in GPT-4 for the age attribute.
We can observe that the CodeBLEU scores range from 0.57 to 0.91.

tecnicas.observacao: Linha de base do estudo empírico (RQ2): a tarefa reformulada como «Please write a Java method to...» é enviada ao ChatGPT sem informação sobre exceções. É a condição sem técnica; não há contrafactual dela própria.

tecnicas.observacao: Primeira das três granularidades que a RQ2 investiga (general, coarse-grained, fine-grained); classificada como focal porque o estudo apresenta a estratégia de três granularidades como objeto de investigação da RQ2. O aviso genérico «Please pay attention to potential exceptions.» é aplicado como turno seguinte sobre o código gerado na rodada anterior («By reviewing the code generated in the last round», p. 4), por isso `feedback` (autocorreção por revisão do próprio código), sem sinal de execução ou analisador. O contraste com Direct generating (mesmas 92 tarefas, mesmo modelo) é do pacote aviso + turno de revisão; os dois ingredientes não são separados.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 4 do PDF, Seção II-B2; p. 3 do PDF, Fig. 2 (C); p. 5 do PDF, Tabela I
tecnicas.observacao: Segunda granularidade da RQ2: o prompt de revisão indica o tipo de exceção obtido da documentação da API («Please pay attention to ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.»), daí `contexto`; também aplicado como revisão do código anterior («revises the code», p. 4). Contra Direct generating é contraste de pacote. Em relação a General prompting, difere apenas no conteúdo do aviso (tipo de exceção da documentação), e o estudo comenta esse contraste na p. 4 («Compared with general prompting...») com os valores da Tabela I.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 4 do PDF, Seção II-B3; p. 3 do PDF, Fig. 2 (D); p. 5 do PDF, Tabela I
tecnicas.observacao: Terceira granularidade da RQ2, apresentada como a mais eficaz e base do KPC: o prompt traz tipo de exceção e condição de disparo extraídos da documentação oficial e especifica o comportamento exigido («Please check if the index is out of range ... otherwise throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.»), daí `contexto` e `restricoes` (especificação). Aplicado como revisão do código gerado (Fig. 2 D marca as linhas alteradas com «+»). Contra Direct generating é contraste de pacote; em relação a Coarse-grained, acrescenta a condição de disparo e a especificação de tratamento.

O pacote depende de um componente fora do escopo (construção off-line da base de conhecimento por crawler e regras), por isso é pacote híbrido quanto à infraestrutura, embora o conhecimento entre no modelo apenas pelo prompt.

riscos.descricao: O ChatGPT gera código falho que parece correto e pode enganar desenvolvedores (achado das entrevistas do estudo com usuários).
Falhas no tratamento de exceções podem causar travamentos, corrupção de dados e vulnerabilidades de segurança, além de problemas de confiabilidade; o estudo não mede vulnerabilidades.
riscos.localizador: p. 2 do PDF, Seção I; p. 3 do PDF, Seção II-A1

riscos.descricao: Abuso de try-catch reduz legibilidade e manutenibilidade do código.
Quanto mais iterações o KPC faz com o ChatGPT, mais complexo fica o código gerado, dificultando a compreensão pelos desenvolvedores.
Uma tarefa foi resolvida «acidentalmente» pela incerteza das saídas do ChatGPT; o mesmo prompt pode produzir comportamentos diferentes.

Compromisso entre eficiência e eficácia: aumentar o número de laços eleva a chance de resolver todas as exceções, mas ignora a exigência de eficiência; o estudo não trata o aspecto como custo monetário nem o quantifica em tokens ou dinheiro.

Compreensão de código limitada do ChatGPT, usado nas etapas de verificação do KPC e no método LLMEva, pode prejudicar o desempenho; o próprio estudo declara incerta a confiabilidade da avaliação LLMEva.

citacoes.trecho: We evaluate our KPC-based approach with 3,079 code generation tasks extracted from the Java official API documentation.

In this RQ, we apply a three-granularity (i.e. general, coarse-grained and fine-grained) prompt design strategy, which adds exception-handling relevant information to prompts gradually, to investigate the impact of prompts to exception handling in LLM-based code generation tasks.
This method only uses generic warnings to raise concerns about exception to LLMs without providing exception types and conditions.
By reviewing the code generated in the last round, ChatGPT realizes there exists potential exceptions involving “out of bounds” and solves this problem by catching IndexOutOfBoundsException.
Specifically, this strategy applies exception-handling specifications from API documentation and indicates what exception ChatGPT should pay attention to exactly.
ChatGPT understands clearly that it should focus on the given exception and revises the code by catching ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException with a try-catch block.

Therefore, in the final edition of prompt engineering, we introduce all the exception-handling information obtained from official Java API documentation and propose fine-grained prompting strategy, which contains not only the exception types, but also corresponding conditions to trigger the exceptions.

Given a natural language described coding task as input, our method takes three steps (i.e., generating, checking-rewriting), which are all supported by prompting the LLM in an AI chain workflow, to output the code with all exceptions being handled (see Figure 3).
The sentence is rephrased into “Please write a Java method to... ” as a prompt in order to clarify the requirement for LLMs explicitly.

To obtain the APIs’ fully qualified names, we present the generated code to ChatGPT and ask it with the prompt “What Java SDK & JDK methods are used in the method you provided? Please list the fully qualified names of the methods.”
We first create a prompt template “Is the [Exception] handled for [API] in the code snippets? (Y/N)”, in which the [Exception] and [API] are placeholders.
Specifically, we design a new prompt template “Please check [Condition] for [API], otherwise throw [Exception].” for this step.
The checking-rewriting steps will keep going iteratively until no more unhandled exception remains in the generated code.
The API documentation is collected from online resources by a web crawling tool [35], and each crawled web page is treated as an API document.

Both our KPC-based code generation approach and our baseline (i.e., ChatGPT) are implemented on top of the GPT-3.5-turbo model [38], which has been proven to achieve the best performance in code generation [12].
However, failing to handle all of these exceptions can have severe consequences, such as crashes, data corruption, and security vulnerabilities.

Nevertheless, this solution may introduce other problems, such as incorrect exception handling (Section II-A2) and abuse of try-catch (Section II-A3) because the general prompting fails to provide sufficient information about the types of exceptions in the code and appropriate measures to handle them.

We also observe some side effects of this strategy from Table I, in which the number of abusing try-catch statements by coarse-grained prompting increases from 5 to 41 compared with direct generating.

We observe from the empirical study that ChatGPT attempts to use try-catch statements to solve 5.43% (5 out of 92) of the coding tasks, which constitutes a small percentage of the whole dataset, but we can not take this issue lightly, as this practice will reduce the readability and maintainability of the code.
One of the coding tasks is solved by ChatGPT accidentally, and the primary cause is the uncertainty of ChatGPT’s outputs.

According to the CodeReview (Section V-B) and user study (Section VI), we also realize that the more iterations KPC interacts with ChatGPT, the more complex the generated code will be, resulting in confusing and difficulties for developers to understand the code.

Although increasing loops give our tool a higher probability of solving all exceptions in the coding tasks, this strategy ignores the requirement of efficiency and might not be a good practice in the industry.
ChatGPT’s limitation in code understanding is one of the potential negative impacts on the performance of this work.

One of the threats is the exception-handling specifications in Official API documenation [26] are not comprehensive, which makes our KPC-based approach ignore some useful exception-handling solutions.
There might be inaccuracy when labeling the exception-handling practice for generated code (i.e., Section V-B) and scoring for users’ answers (i.e., Section VI).
Second, ChatGPT is very “good” at generating flawed code that appears to be correct, thereby misleading developers.
The reliability of results evaluated by LLMEva is uncertain.
To ensure the efficient allocation of resources, we established a time budget of two minutes per class for this process and repeated it 10 times.
MIN = 384 in this work, which ensures the estimated accuracy is in 0.05 error margin at 95% confidence level.
As demonstrated in RQ3, a reduced loop number within 10 loops is suggested for balancing efficiency and effectiveness.
In the future, we will mine exception-handling knowledge from other sources (e.g., GitHub and Stack Overflow) to continuously extend our API knowledge base.

It achieves this through proficiently managing exceptions and obtaining remarkable enhancements of 109.86% and 578.57% with static evaluation methods, as well as a reduction of 18 runtime bugs in the sampled dataset with dynamic validation.

Overall, our KPC demonstrates significant advantages across all three evaluation methods, with exception handling improvements of 107.86%, 578.57%, as well as a reduction of 18 real bugs, respectively.

In cases of no reference code is provided (i.e., G-1), easy tasks such as T2 and T3 are more likely to be completed correctly, while hard tasks such as T3 and T4 are still big challenges for the participants to solve.
All coding tasks have limited numbers of correct answers, with only one or two participants being able to complete them correctly.

Although our approach only reduces 18 more real bugs in the sampled dataset compared with EvoSuite, we would like to remind the readers that EvoSuite is a sophisticated software tool that requires long-term research and significant amount of enginering effort to build and maintain.
Similarly, Our work takes advantage of LLMs’ few short learning abilities and obtains domain-specific knowledge from API documents to guide the exception code generation.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote com duas fases: (1) elicitação de pensamento por análise de casos de teste, com instrução estruturada e formato obrigatório («You MUST follow the format»), verificação da compreensão por inferência da saída mascarada e refinamento até N iterações (autocorreção → feedback); (2) fase de feedback, ativada se o código falha nos testes da especificação: sumarização do código gerado, análise comparativa com a compreensão refinada e ajuste da compreensão até M iterações. Base identificável: Zero-shot (especificação original, aqui classificada como instrucao). O contrafactual é do pacote inteiro contra os 15 comparadores; o ganho não se atribui a um mecanismo isolado (ver componentes abaixo). Não é pacote híbrido: o sanitizador de código é aplicado ao código gerado pelos LLMs no estudo em geral, não só ao µFiX. O µFiX faz mais invocações do LLM que vários comparadores (p. 9).

Mecanismos acrescentados em relação à SCoT (instrucao, raciocinio): formato obrigatório da análise de casos de teste (restricoes) e autoaperfeiçoamento antes da geração (feedback). Também há comparação de µFiXwoF com SCoT + CodeT sob o mesmo número de invocações, com resultados só na página do projeto (p. 9).

riscos.descricao: O código gerado pelo LLM pode não estar alinhado com a especificação.
Passar na verificação de compreensão não garante que o LLM compreendeu a especificação, porque os casos de teste da especificação são poucos.
Código gerado pelo LLM frequentemente inclui trechos em linguagem natural, o que leva a falhas de compilação.
Testes gerados pelo LLM na variante µFiXwoT cobriram só um ramo da especificação ou continham erros, com efetividade um pouco pior (análise manual de alguns casos).

Tempo e tokens do µFiX um pouco maiores que os de SCoT + Self-repair (22,75 s contra 20,61 s; 3,44K contra 3,31K tokens em média); N e M maiores aumentam tempo e tokens (44,54% e 40,94% a mais para N=2, M=2). O estudo trata como custo.
Aleatoriedade dos LLMs apontada como ameaça à validade.
O estudo menciona alucinações do LLM e afirma que o uso dos casos de teste da especificação as alivia; não há medida direta de alucinação.
Não existe procedimento de decisão para verificar se o LLM compreendeu a especificação; a verificação adotada é indireta, pela geração de código (limitação de solidez do mecanismo).
Generalização dos resultados apontada como ameaça.
Os prompts do µFiX não foram ajustados; o estudo não garante sua otimalidade.

mitigacoes.descricao: Uso de ferramenta sanitizadora para limpar o código gerado.
Seleção abrangente de benchmarks, métricas, baselines e LLMs contra a ameaça de generalização.
Repetição em três execuções da comparação entre µFiX e SCoT + Self-repair em HumanEval, HumanEval+ e HumanEval-ET; desvios-padrão de 0,021 e 0,009 no Pass@1 relatados, detalhes na página do projeto.

citacoes.trecho: In this work, we propose a novel prompting technique, called µFiX, to improve the code generation performance of LLMs by devising both sophisticated thought-eliciting prompting and feedback-based prompting and making the first exploration on their synergy.
Instead, µFiX emphasizes test case analysis by providing a structured instruction to LLMs, which can help them utilize specific test cases to understand complicated programming logic.
Let's analyze the test case step by step. You MUST follow the format: "The input is <?>. The output is <?>. Analysis: <?>. Therefore, the expected output is <?>."
Specifically, µFiX masks the expected output in the understanding and enables LLMs to infer it according to the analyzed logic in the understanding.
This process terminates until the refined understanding passes the checking mechanism or the number of refinements reaches the pre-defined threshold (denoted as N).

Here, based on the symmetry between code generation (from natural language descriptions to code) and code summarization [27], [28] (from code to natural language descriptions), µFiX estimates the actual understanding implicitly utilized by LLMs for code generation through code summarization (also called summarized understanding for ease of presentation).
This phase is an iterative process and terminates until the generated code passes the corresponding test cases or the number of adjustments reaches the threshold (denoted as M).
Zero-shot prompting [19]: directly utilizes the original specification to prompt LLMs for code generation.
Few-shot prompting [19]: enables LLMs to learn the relationship between specifications and code based on randomly selected <specification, code> examples.
Following the existing work [14], [40], we applied CoT prompting in both zero-shot [44] and few-shot [9] settings.
Self-planning prompting [13]: guides LLMs to decompose the specification into a set of easy-to-solve sub-problems and produce code plan by providing few-shot intent-to-plan examples.
SCoT prompting [14]: enhances CoT prompting by utilizing program structures (i.e., sequence, branch, and loop structures) to produce intermediate reasoning steps.
Self-repair prompting [17]: leverages error messages produced by test execution to enable LLMs to produce a short explanation of why the code failed.
For example, SCoT combined with Self-repair (referred to as SCoT + Self-repair) involves applying Self-repair to the code generated by SCoT.
Given the input length limit of LLMs, we used the 4-shot setting for all few-shot baselines following the existing work [13], [46], [47].

Also, each combination of thought-eliciting and feedback-based prompting techniques outperforms the corresponding individual techniques, which confirms the synergy between both categories, motivating our µFiX technique.
µFiXwoF: we removed the feedback-based prompting phase from µFiX, i.e., it just uses the specification understanding produced in the thought-eliciting prompting phase to generate code.
µFiXSR: we replaced the feedback-based prompting strategy in µFiX with the state-of-the-art Self-repair prompting strategy.
µFiXSCoT: we replaced the thought-eliciting prompting strategy in µFiX with the state-of-the-art SCoT strategy.
µFiXwoS: we removed the self-improvement component in the thought-eliciting prompting phase from µFiX.
Note that LLM-generated code often includes natural-language text snippets, leading to compilation failures.
Therefore, following the existing work [26], we employed a code sanitizer tool [38] to clean LLM-generated code.
Note that passing the checking mechanism cannot guarantee that LLMs completely understand the programming specification as the number of test cases equipped in the specification tend to be limited.
However, larger N and M also incur more time and token costs.
The time and token overhead of µFiX are slightly higher than those of SCoT + Self-repair.

We manually analyzed some cases where µFiXwoT underperformed µFiX and found that LLM-generated test cases covered only one branch mentioned in the specification or even contained errors, leading to slightly worse effectiveness.
Hence, there does not exist a decision procedure to check if an LLM correctly understands a specification, rendering sound checking mechanisms for LLMs' understanding intractable.

Our study indeed confirms that this mechanism helps improve the effectiveness of code generation, empirically demonstrating that leveraging existing test cases in specifications can alleviate LLM hallucinations.
The second threat lies in the randomness involved in LLMs.

On the other hand, we repeated the experiment comparing µFiX with the most effective baseline (SCoT + Self-repair) on three benchmarks (HumanEval, HumanEval+, and HumanEval-ET) as the representative for three times due to the huge evaluation cost.
To mitigate this threat, we comprehensively selected benchmarks, metrics, baselines, and LLMs.
We did not specially tune the natural-language-description format of prompts, and thus cannot ensure their optimality.
By default, we set N=1 and M=1 to balance the effectiveness and efficiency.

riscos.descricao: A aprendizagem em contexto é sensível aos exemplos selecionados; exemplos aleatórios ou apenas lexicalmente semelhantes podem ser irrelevantes para o requisito, levando a desempenho que varia de quase aleatório a próximo do estado da arte.
Os hiperparâmetros de amostragem (por exemplo, temperatura) influenciam as saídas dos LLMs; o estudo usa amostragem nuclear e relata média de três execuções.

Modelar a estimação sobre todo o espaço do conjunto de treino é quadrático e proibitivo (custo computacional), o que motiva o processo em dois estágios; o custo de estimação e de inferência não é quantificado, exceto o treino do recuperador (cerca de 1 hora em 4 A100).
Limitação do comprimento de entrada dos LLMs restringe o número de exemplos no prompt.
Ameaça à generalização dos resultados (bases, linguagens e modelos escolhidos).
Sensibilidade a detalhes de implementação, hiperparâmetros, prompts (instrução e número de exemplos) e ao conjunto de candidatos; prompts e hiperparâmetros não foram ajustados experimentalmente.
Negativos difíceis selecionados por BM25 podem conter falsos negativos e prejudicar o aprendizado do recuperador (componente fora do escopo).

mitigacoes.descricao: Mesmo número de exemplos para todas as abordagens e prompts sem instruções em linguagem natural.
Mesmos parâmetros de geração para LAIL e todas as linhas de base.
Cada método executado três vezes, com relato da média.
Conjunto de treino de cada base usado como conjunto de candidatos para todas as abordagens.
Código-fonte e parâmetros publicados pelos artigos originais usados nas linhas de base.
Processo em dois estágios (pré-filtragem BM25) para contornar o custo quadrático da estimação; comparação com filtros aleatório e semântico apenas mencionada, sem números.

citacoes.trecho: Code generation aims to automatically generate the source code given a natural language requirement [7, 18, 30].
In this paper, we propose a novel learning-based selection approach named LAIL (LLM-Aware In-context Learning) for code generation.
Based on the labeled data, we import a contrastive learning objective to train an effective retriever that acquires the preference of LLMs in code generation.
Given a test requirement, the optimized retriever selects several examples as a prompt that is inputted to LLMs for code generation (C).
The input of LLMs only contains a prompt and a test requirement without any natural language instructions.
Zero-Shot Learning [11] directly inputs a requirement into LLMs without any examples as the prompt.
Random [14] randomly select a few examples from the training set and construct a prompt.
In inference, it first generates test cases and then predicts programs. For a fair comparison, we use the same pipeline to LAIL and all baselines.
Finally, it treats the k nearest examples as a prompt.
The approach computes the uncertainty of each candidate and selects k items with high perplexity as a prompt.
Some heuristic methods that select the same examples as prompts for all test requirements are not optimal for ICL.
The Match-BLEU format uses the BLEU score of the generated program to measure examples.

However, ICL comes along with the robustness problem [33], which is sensitive to the selected examples in prompts, resulting in the performance usually varying from almost random to near state-of-the-art performance.
Although one may remedy it by inputting more examples in the prompt, it is highly impractical due to the limited input length of LLMs.
Modeling on the full space of the training set is quadratic and thus prohibitive.
To mitigate this limitation, we introduce a two-stage process to estimate examples in the training set.
The learning rate is 5e-5 and the batch size is 32. We train the retriever for about 1 hour on 4 NVIDIA A100.
We can find that the more hard negative examples, the worse our approach performs.
There are two main threats to the validity of our work.
For LLMs (e.g., GPT-3.5 and ChatGPT), the hyper-parameters (e.g., temperature) of sampling will impact their outputs.
In addition, the performance of LLMs heavily depends on the prompts, including the instruction and the number of examples.
To alleviate this threat, we leverage the same number of examples for all approaches and directly construct prompts without any natural language instructions.
To ensure fairness, we execute each method three times and report the average experimental results.
For a fair comparison, we set the same parameters to generate programs for all baselines and our LAIL.
Thus, we use the training set of each dataset as the candidate set for all approaches in this paper and believe that the training set can provide supporting examples for test requirements.
For baselines, we apply the source code and parameters published by their original papers [21, 40, 47].
We do not tune the prompt and hyper-parameters experimentally and set them empirically.
In this paper, we leverage the largest version with 16 billion parameters (i.e. CodeGen-Multi-16B).
In this paper, we use OpenAI’s APIs to access the latest version with 175 billion parameters (i.e., text-davinci-003).
We leverage OpenAI’s APIs to access ChatGPT (i.e., gpt-3.5-turbo).
Finally, the percentage of solved requirements in all test requirements is treated as Pass@k.

riscos.descricao: Componentes do framework aplicados isoladamente pioram o desempenho em certos conjuntos (por exemplo, na Tabela 5 a QA API sem MI e o MI sem APIs reduzem a EA).
Perguntas que exigem conhecimento externo ausente da tabela: no exemplo da Figura 11 nenhum método testado sem a QA API dá a resposta correta.
Generalização: a definição manual das funções API pode não se estender a conjuntos com estruturas de tabela diferentes ou a cenários com fundamentação mais rica.
Avaliação: exact matching pode gerar falsos negativos quando o parser gera estruturas sintáticas novas, e os conjuntos não trazem consultas-ouro em Python.

mitigacoes.descricao: Uso de Execution Accuracy em vez de exact matching para evitar falsos negativos.

A tarefa é geração de programas Python (ou SQL) a partir de perguntas em linguagem natural sobre tabelas; o desempenho é medido pela correção da resposta obtida ao executar o programa.

citacoes.trecho: In response, this paper introduces a unified TableQA framework that: (1) provides a unified representation for structured tables as multi-index Pandas data frames, (2) uses Python as a powerful querying language, and (3) uses few-shot prompting to translate NL questions into Python programs, which are executable on Pandas data frames.
Specifically, we use a few-shot paradigm where we provide the multi-index headers of the table, a few rows of the table in textual form, the question, and exemplar program annotations.
Our LM prompt is designed to be a mixture of instructions and solution examples. The instructions specify API usage guidelines and scenarios in which it should be used.
With this diversity of input examples, we aim to encourage the usage of the assistant APIs in the code generated by the LMs, while avoiding over-reliance on some APIs.
These generated questions will direct the code parsing program to call the QA API function.
For each value in the questioned column, we insert the value into the generated question and prompt the model again to give an answer to this question.
For demonstration, we employ two simple comparison APIs in this paper.
Generate Python code given the table and a question about it.

We compare our full method (Ours) with an ablated version (CODEX) that only uses few-shot prompting of the code LM, without including our multi-index structure and API functions (see §5.2 for details and more ablations).
We set the sampling temperature to 0.7 for both models. For every question, we generate five model predictions and select the candidate with the highest log probability.
We include five shots in the prompt for WikiTQ, HiTab, and Spider datasets, and eight shots for the AIT dataset.
Similarly to the in-context learning configuration introduced in §3.2, we adapt our input to prompt the model to generate SQL queries.
The generated SQL queries are executed on Pandas data frames and return Python objects, hence, we can still retain our same API functions and multi-index data frame representation.
Please make sure all outputs are dataframes.

citacoes.trecho: In comparison to the base setting in which neither type of API is utilized, we add one type of API at a time to examine their gains.

We note that though our general framework consistently improves performance across datasets, we identify through ablations components in our framework that, individually applied, adversely affect performance on particular datasets.
One limitation of our current framework is its manual definition of API functions, which may not extend to other datasets with disparate table structures, or involve richer grounded settings.
However, the information that Winnipeg is a city of Manitoba is not included in the table itself.

citacoes.trecho: We did not include exact matching (EM) as the measure to determine if the predicted query is equivalent to the gold query, since it can lead to false negative evaluations when the semantic parser generates novel syntax structures (Pourreza and Rafiei, 2023; Yu et al., 2018).

For a fair comparison with our approach, we use 5-shot prompting for BINDER rather than the 12-shot experiments in Binder et al. (2022), which decreases performance compared to the results in their paper.

We find that our framework surpasses the state-of-the-art few-shot baselines on the HiTab, AIT, and Spider datasets, achieving absolute improvements of 24.5%, 26.2%, and 2.3%, respectively, while retaining non-trivial performance on WikiTQ.

In particular, our approach obtains an improvement of 28.6% over the past state-of-the-art training-based method (Liang et al., 2018), and a 9.7% improvement on plain few-shot prompted Codex models for the HiTab dataset.

While the base model performance with STARCODER is lower than CODEX, we still observe an improvement from our generated API across all settings, with a substantial improvement on the AIT-QA dataset, presumably because a large portion of the questions in AIT-QA can be more easily solved using our API functions.
For example, we show that combining Pandas' SQL interface API with our multi-index representation and APIs improves performance by 3.7–7.6% on relational datasets.
In particular, adding the QA API increases performance by 2.7%, while further adding the operation APIs improves by another 10.7%, compared to the full system without APIs.
As shown in Table 5, the execution accuracy decreases by 3.6% with the multi-index approach compared to the table flattening approach when no API is included.
STARCODER is an open-source 15B code LM, which at the time of this writing achieved top performance among open-source models on many code generation benchmarks such as HumanEval (Li et al., 2023).
We use the STARCODER 16B and code-davinci-002 (CODEX) models to generate Python programs.
Since our method does not require any training, we use the standard validation set and test set with 2,381 and 4,344 samples.
We conduct ablation analyses on the HiTab dataset to examine the improvements brought by assistant API functions (§5.1) and multi-index parsing (§5.2).

O conjunto TransCoder provavelmente consta dos corpora de treino dos GPTs (o modelo regurgita programas a partir da assinatura); é uma das razões para não avaliá-lo formalmente. O estudo não discute contaminação do MultiPL-C2C/HumanEval.
Aproximar a dificuldade por tradução direta (estratégia select) exige mais computação que gerar uma explicação; não quantificado.

Validade externa: não se sabe se os programas do MultiPL-E representam alvos reais de tradução, nem se as conclusões valem para modelos mais fortes como GPT-4; explicações pouco úteis no cenário few-shot.
Qualidade dos benchmarks: mais de 25% dos exemplos de CodeXGLUE/TransCoder examinados têm erros em programas-gabarito ou testes inadequados.

citacoes.trecho: In this paper we are interested in whether a self-generated natural language explanation z can be used to improve this translation process.

Across three types of explanations and 19 programming languages constructed from the MultiPL-E dataset (Cassano et al., 2022), we find the explanations to be particularly effective in the zero-shot case, improving performance by 12% on average.
We find that Explain-then-Translate improves zero-shot performance consistently in 18 Python-to-X translation directions, but much less so in the few-shot setting.
We analyze our results in 36 different translation directions over different types of explanations.
exp: We ask the model to explain the source program in a few sentences (Fig 1, right).
exp-lbl: We ask the model to explain the source program line by line.
exp-lbl-d: We ask the model to explain the source program line by line in additional detail.
In particular if an individual line is complicated, we ask it to break it down, explain individual fragment of the line, and then summarize the purpose for the entire line.
Please translate the following Python code to R?
Can you explain what this Python program does with a couple of sentences? The goal with the explanation, is so that a reader can easily rewrite the program in R.

When generating explanations, we treat the token sequence \n# as a stopping sequence in order to prevent models from generating target translations (since we condition target program with translated signatures in addition to explanations).

In order to control for inconsistencies caused by the target-language-specific explanations, we re-use the same explanations (from Python-Java) for all Python-to-X translation experiments (Section 3.1).
Before reusing, we also remove any target specific information with programmatic rules so it can be reused across experiments.
We prioritize precision and calculate pass@1 with n = 20, t = 0.2, and top-p= 0.95 following Cassano et al. (2022).

We main report the results from GPT-3.5 (gpt3.5-turbo-0301) in the main paper unless otherwise specified, and defer the results from open source models (CodeGen2-1B, CodeGen2-16B, and Llama2CodeInstruct-34B (Nijkamp et al., 2023; Rozière et al., 2023)) to the appendix.
All completion queries are made to GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-3010) between March - June 2023.
You are a helpful and faithful compiler that transpiles Python code to Java code.
You are an helpful AI assistant who understands all programming languages and can translate between them at ease.
Providing explanations improves relative performance by 11.5% on average across 18 target languages.
In the four-shot setting, the average improvement is much less at 1.1%, although some language pairs observe as much as a 10.1% improvement.
The most abstract explanation (exp) performs the worst (best in only 3 out of 18 directions) in the few-shot setting.
Since source languages are different, we do not re-use explanations.
In the four-shot explanation, we use zero-shot generated explanations (3.1).
We speculate that LLMs generally struggle to understand and explain lower-resource PLs; more details may introduce more errors which may compound into the translation phase.
CodeGen2-16B is the only model that does not improve consistently with explanations.
For each explanation type, we generate 20 explanations and 1 program from each explanation (train set).
We use zero-shot explanations for exp (see Sec 3.1) and four-shot for exp-lbl and exp-lbl-d.
With exp, logprob improves upon random by absolute 2.54% (p = 0.055), and frag improves explain-lbl-d upon random baseline by absolute 2.2% (p = 0.033) with simulation.

With logprob selected exp, we improve or match performance in 15/18 directions, with an average improvement of 1.7% (p < 0.001).
With frag selected exp-lbl-simp, we improve or match performance in 13/18 directions, averaging 0.48% (p = 0.022).

Qualitatively, we could not distinguish a good explanation from a bad one manually (Apx L.3 and L.4), suggesting that the distinction between “good” and “bad” explanations may be hidden due to stylistic noise (wording, spacing, etc.), or potentially due to chance.
Through Fig 4, we discovered that explanation improves difficult problems (left of x-axis), but could hurt easy problems (right of x-axis).
We found selective explanation to improve performance over direct and exp in 35/36 directions.

We replace the explanation with another program’s explanation randomly (rand-exp), or through retrieval (ret-exp, details in Apx O), or with an empty string (no-exp) to verify if explanations need to be correct/relevant.

Lastly, when models receive completely irrelevant explanations (rand-exp), they are able to recover performance to some extent; but if the explanations are convincingly misleading (ret-exp) performance deterioates.
This is potentially due to the fact that explanations become more reliant on actual syntax of the program, rather than hallucinating on the program semantics from surface variable names.
In Table 5, we observe that when the retrieved one-shot is paired with a wrong target program, the decrease in performance is much more significant than in the fixed-shot setting.

However, on average, self-generated unverified explanations (exp) still outperform one-shot in all directions (fixed-unk by 0.7-4.5%; retrieve-unk by 0.5-2.0%), indicating that NL generations often have higher quality than programs and can serve as a better medium for intermediate reasoning step.
retrieval-bad (Table 5) should be taken lightly since the subset of problems evaluated for bad also likely contains harder problems.
The result indicates mistakes in intermediate PL steps corrupt translation performance more than imperfect NL explanations.
With simple heuristics, we have also demonstrated the potential to improve explanation quality and consequently translation quality.

First, while we focus on the (adapted) MultiPL-E benchmark due to its widespread use, it is unclear whether programs in this benchmark are representative of programs that are targets for code-to-code translation.
Second, while we saw our conclusions to largely hold across GPT-3.5 and other open-source models, it is unclear whether they will hold for more powerful LLMs such as GPT-4.

We also considered into CodeXGLUE (Lu et al., 2021) and TransCoder (Lachaux et al., 2020) for the unit tests evaluations, but initial studies suggested a significant number of examples (more than 25%) contain mistakes in gold programs or inadequate unit tests (see Apx A, B).
One of the other reasons that we do not formally evaluate our methods on TransCoder dataset is because that the TransCoder dataset is very likely to have been included in GPTs’ training corpora.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote híbrido: o corpus de exploração X é gerado por exploração simbólica de passeios aleatórios (fora do escopo) e por geração de perguntas com LLM (instruções, descrições de esquema, L2M e re-ranqueamento por consistência inversa); no raciocínio, demonstrações recuperadas de X (com anonimização de entidades) orientam a pontuação de subprogramas em procedimento bottom-up de enumerar-e-ranquear, com poda de candidatos (fora do escopo) e re-ranqueamento final por consistência inversa. O contrafactual é a condição Zero-shot (mesmo procedimento bottom-up sem demonstrações em contexto), por isso o ganho é do pacote, não de um mecanismo isolado. O estudo não informa se a condição Zero-shot usa a poda de candidatos e o re-ranqueamento por consistência inversa. Decomposição atribuída à construção incremental de subprogramas por etapas e ao L2M; amostragem atribuída ao ranqueamento de vários candidatos por verossimilhança do LLM e ao re-ranqueamento, sendo os candidatos enumerados por heurísticas, não amostrados do LLM.

riscos.descricao: Quando itens de esquema não foram vistos na exploração, a pontuação do LLM atribui notas altas a candidatos irrelevantes que se parecem com os exemplos recuperados, isto é, as demonstrações podem induzir um programa errado.

O BYOKG pode alucinar; na geração de perguntas o modelo pode gerar perguntas semanticamente imprecisas para os programas, o que, em escala, pode prejudicar o raciocínio aumentado por recuperação, dependente de exemplos coerentes.

Latência da pontuação de candidatos: sem poda, quase 2 minutos por pergunta (110.1 s/q na Tabela 10); com poda, 13.2 s/q; o raciocínio iterativo pode não atender requisitos rígidos de tempo de resposta. O custo da geração de perguntas limita o número de programas explorados (Tabela 5: 10.4 h no Freebase e 24.0 h no MoviesKG para 10K programas em 3 máquinas EC2 p3dn.24xlarge).

citacoes.trecho: Exploration in BYOKG leverages an LLM-backed symbolic agent that generates a diverse set of query-program exemplars, which are then used to ground a retrieval-augmented reasoning procedure to synthesize programs for arbitrary questions.
With a corpus of query-program pairs in place, we now require a method to synthesize programs given natural language queries at test time.
We, therefore, use an ICL approach using demonstrations from the exploration corpus within an enumerate-and-rank procedure.
Zero-shot represents our bottom-up reasoning procedure from §3.3 but without any in-context demonstrations to score sub-programs at each step.
ICL + Exploration represents our proposed BYOKG method.
We also include in this setting results with Pangu-ICL (Gu et al., 2023), the few-shot variant of a KGQA method closely related to the bottom-up reasoning procedure of BYOKG.
To generate questions, we prompt an LLM with instructions and textual descriptions of schema items relevant to each program (see A.3).

To elicit reliable zero-shot generation, we, therefore, utilize two techniques—(1) least-to-most prompting (Zhou et al., 2023), which generates outputs for complex programs in a step-by-step manner, and (2) a novel inverse-consistency method to re-rank LLM generations by scoring the inverse task of program generation.
To tackle this, we introduce a re-ranking mechanism that scores output sequences from an LM using the likelihood of an inverse task, i.e. how likely the input sequence is given the output.
When schema items are completely unseen during exploration, we find that LLM scoring erroneously assigns high scores to irrelevant candidates that may resemble the retrieved exemplars (see F.2).

We, therefore, introduce a candidate pruning step that restricts the size of the candidate set to at most 10 at each step of reasoning based on the similarity of anonymized candidate programs with the anonymized natural language test question using the sentence embedding model from retrieval.
We do not tune α, in keeping with our setting of not assuming a dev set, and set its value to 0.5 in all experiments.
Despite efforts to provide grounded LLM generations, BYOKG is susceptible to hallucinations at times.

While we reduce latency by 8x compared to a naive implementation by introducing candidate pruning, our iterative “System 2” reasoning may not satisfy stringent response time requirements, which are better served by single-shot inference.
While program generation is inexpensive, the cost of question generation restricts the number of programs we can explore.
However, we caution that non-deterministic systems, such as those using LLMs, should be deployed in real-world settings with utmost care and proper human oversight.

In particular, it may not always be apparent as to the nature of the data that LLMs are pre-trained on, which has the potential of perpetuating factual inaccuracies and biases prevalent in corpora collected from the internet.
In the absence of this data, BYOKG, thus, currently requires human annotations.
To the best of our knowledge, this KG is not part of the pre-training corpus for the MPT family of models.
In particular, we take our set of 10K explored programs and randomly sample 100 programs such that 75 are i.i.d. for the exploration set, while 25 are o.o.d. or unseen.
In practice, we cache responses from the SPARQL engine to improve latency over time, but turn caching off for this evaluation.
We, thus, penalize the final score based on the count of repeated relations.
Aggressive pruning at k = 10 results in the most efficient reasoning with an accuracy gain of 2.5 F1 over no pruning.
Table 8 shows our results, where we find that L2M prompting provides an 18.7 point improvement over standard decoding.
L2M prompting improves accuracy of generated questions by a significant 17.5 points.

citacoes.trecho: We propose a method to leverage the prompting with few-shot examples of the LLM by selecting the best-suited code refactoring examples for each target programming problem based on the prior evaluation of prompting with the one-shot example.
The system instruction and the user’s program are always passed to the LLM.
No examples are passed in the zero-shot, one in the one-shot, and three in the few-shot (i.e., 3-shot).
In this phase, each code refactoring example is used for one-shot prompting and evaluated by a validator.
As a few-shot prompting, we adopt 3-shot prompting, which provides k = 3 sets of best-performed code refactoring examples.
The system instruction is used in all generations, including zero-shot prompting.
More precisely, in this work, we use gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, a snapshot version from March 1st, 2023, for reproducibility.
We set the temperature, which determines the creativity of generated texts, to 0.2 to be slightly creative for all generations in this work.
We generate n = 10 samples for each program and report pass@k at k = 1,10.
In fact, code refactoring also has a risk of breaking the already working program, which is another reason programmers are reluctant to do code refactoring.
Since the LLM has the potential to break the input program, the generated programs are validated, and only functionally correct programs are suggested to a user.
However, several prior works mentioned that LLMs trained on public source code have a risk of generating malicious or vulnerable programs, which may harm the host computer [2], [43].
Therefore, we prepare a virtual judge system on our isolated sandbox environment to not be affected by the malicious generated programs.
It can worsen an already straightforward, readable, or concise program that is not required to be refactored.
Figure 10b is the worsened example, defining an excessive function that worsens the complexity.
Although we observe many cases improving the code readability, we also observe that the LLM deletes many comments that can help understand the program.
The decrease in the proportion of Japanese and the increase in English in Table VI suggests that the Japanese comments are translated into English without demand.
Furthermore, since code refactoring is usually performed iteratively, suggesting the fully refactored program with extensive modifications at once can be overwhelming for users.

For instance, detecting whether the program should be refactored before the refactoring request, or providing some instructions to control the LLM to make modifications only when there is a particular need for refactoring, can be considered.
This variation of performance among the one-shot prompting highlights the need for selecting the best-suited examples for each problem.

tecnicas.observacao: Condição avaliada na Fig. 9: prompt do Script Generator com o parágrafo IKEC (Fig. 8), combinado com RAG e com a estrutura de comentários (framework of comments) gerada pelo Task Planner do fluxo ChatEDA; daí instrucao (diretrizes do prompt), contexto (recuperação RAG e resposta/estrutura fornecidas como insumo), decomposicao (planejamento em estrutura de comentários antes do código) e raciocinio. O ingrediente acrescentado é a instrução para expandir e ponderar internamente os conceitos sem exibir o processo; foi classificado como raciocinio porque os autores o apresentam em relação ao Zero-shot CoT e aos Scratchpads (PDF p. 5), mas não há raciocínio explícito na saída (classificação alternativa possível: outro). Contrafactual: RAG direto contra RAG + IKEC com a mesma estrutura de comentários, em um único exemplo (Fig. 9); o texto do prompt da condição sem IKEC não é mostrado e não se informa se a fonte do RAG estava pré-processada. O resultado de 73,33% (seção 4.2.1) não tem condição sem IKEC. O IKEC também é aplicado dentro da Data Renovation e da Data Augmentation, onde não é isolado.

tecnicas.localizador: PDF p. 3, Fig. 2 (bloco Data Augmentation Prompting); PDF p. 5, seções 3.1 e 3.2; PDF p. 7, seção 4.1.1; PDF p. 10, Fig. 5
tecnicas.observacao: Prompt que gera novos scripts Python a partir de dois ou três scripts de referência (exemplos), com recuperação de documentação da API e do manual via LlamaIndex (contexto), instruções e estímulo emocional (instrucao); o estudo declara aplicar o IKEC à Data Augmentation (raciocinio). Sem base identificável. Avaliação: 20 scripts gerados a partir de 23 existentes, examinados manualmente por especialistas, sem condição comparadora. O resumo chama esta contribuição de «refactoring existing scripts», mas o procedimento pede novos scripts com mudanças estruturais significativas, e não refatoração com preservação de comportamento; por isso a tarefa foi registrada como geração.

tecnicas.localizador: PDF p. 3, Fig. 2 (bloco Data Splitter Prompting); PDF p. 5-6, seção 3.3; PDF p. 8, seção 4.1.2; PDF p. 11, Fig. 6
tecnicas.observacao: Prompt que segmenta a documentação em chunks semânticos para o corpus do RAG: explica a tarefa e as regras (instrucao, incluindo o estímulo emocional), fornece formato e exemplo de saída (exemplos, restricoes). O parágrafo incompleto é devolvido como histórico para a iteração seguinte. Atua sobre documentos, não sobre código; demonstrada só qualitativamente com um exemplo (Fig. 6). O efeito sobre a geração de código só está no desenho experimental planejado (seção 4.2.2), não executado.

tecnicas.localizador: PDF p. 3, Fig. 2 (bloco Data Renovation Prompting); PDF p. 6, seção 3.4; PDF p. 8, seção 4.1.3; PDF p. 11, Fig. 7
tecnicas.observacao: Prompt que reescreve cada chunk com mais detalhes, com instrução da tarefa, estímulo emocional (instrucao) e as frases do IKEC (raciocinio). Atua sobre documentos do corpus do RAG; demonstrada qualitativamente com um chunk (Fig. 7). Efeito sobre a geração de código não avaliado.

tecnicas.nome_original: Chain of Density for Renovation Credibility (CoDRC)
tecnicas.localizador: PDF p. 6, seção 3.5
tecnicas.observacao: Procedimento conduzido por LLM, derivado do Chain of Density, em três passos (listar entidades ausentes, categorizá-las e atribuir escore de confiança 0-10), com o histórico da renovação e os conteúdos pré e pós-renovação como insumo. O texto do prompt não é mostrado e não se informa se os passos são chamadas separadas. Nenhum resultado relatado.

citacoes.trecho: We present four main contributions to enhance the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in generating domain-specific code: (i) utilizing LLM-based data splitting and data renovation techniques to improve the semantic representation of embeddings’ space; (ii) introducing the Chain of Density for Renovation Credibility (CoDRC), driven by LLMs, and the Adaptive Text Renovation (ATR) algorithm for assessing data renovation reliability; (iii) developing the Implicit Knowledge Expansion and Contemplation (IKEC) Prompt technique; and (iv) effectively refactoring existing scripts to generate new and high-quality scripts with LLMs.

When combined with IKEC, these techniques enhance the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) method in retrieving more relevant information, ultimately achieving a 73.33% "Percentage of Correct Lines" for code generation problems in MapReduce applications.

The main concept of our uniquely developed Prompt technique, IKEC, is to encourage the model to internally expand and supplement content it is highly confident about, based on its knowledge, carefully ponder, and only then generate a response without outputting the process.
However, both methods increase the number of input and output tokens, as well as the cost and inference time.
We specifically apply this technique to Data Renovation and Data Augmentation, mainly because both require obtaining expert knowledge and producing accurate results under good mastery.

In the Prompt, we use the key sentence "Take a deep breath, this is very important to my career" from previous research, which has been proven to effectively improve performance [19,28], and this sentence will appear repeatedly in subsequent Prompts.

The Prompt briefly explains the task, informs the model of the rules to follow during the splitting, provides format and actual example references, and finally presents the Segment that needs to be split.

Then, we apply the IKEC Prompt technique (fluorescently highlighted text) and ultimately prompt the model to infer based on the highly mastered content and thoroughly consider generating accurate content.
Neither of the above, i.e., information that cannot be inferred through relevant knowledge, background, or expertise.
We make use of the balance between the confidence score Confi and the text growth ratio Growi to retain as much reliable post-renovation content as possible.

Then, following the steps of generating code in ChatEDA [5] (Fig. 1), (i) Query: Provide user requirements and use the System Prompt in the following steps, (ii) Task Planner: Use the prompt for LLM with the RAG method to plan the outline of the code and then generate the framework of comments, (iii) Script Generator: Use the prompt for LLM with the RAG method to generate the code one by one according to the corresponding comments.
This implies that any publicly available information would have already been learned by LLMs, and thus the datasets must be generated by the researchers themselves to avoid any potential biases.
Moreover, an excess of information can increase input tokens, potentially giving rise to hallucinations or diluting the importance of crucial details.
Following this method, we repeat the process on the existing 23 scripts, generating 20 new scripts, which are then manually evaluated by in-house RedHawk-SC experts.
However, optimizations in code performance are still needed.

The confidence level of the content before and after renovation is assessed using CoDRC, and the final decision to adopt the renovated content is made in conjunction with the ATR Algorithm, ensuring the quality of the renovated content.

On the left side, when using the RAG method directly, the first function omits the code for calculating the number of layers and does not return a dictionary result; the second function fails to return the MapReduce result.
The only error is a misnamed function call, which can be improved by applying the preprocessing techniques described in this paper.

Type A: Individual testing of various components, such as Data Augmentation, Data Splitter, Data Renovation, and Implicit Knowledge Expansion and Contemplation (IKEC), each demonstrated using single example outcomes.
However, certain aspects, such as evaluation, have not yet been fully realized.

tecnicas.observacao: Método few-shot de Ahmed e Devanbu [1]: 10 exemplos amostrados aleatoriamente que invocam a mesma biblioteca, antepostos ao contexto. Exemplos de código como demonstração recebem exemplos e contexto. A Tabela 6 traz a condição zero-shot correspondente para cada modelo.

tecnicas.localizador: Seção 4.1 e Figura 2(a), p. 7–8; Tabela 6, p. 10; Tabela 8, p. 12
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote híbrido: um modelo auxiliar treinado (API inquirer, GPT-2) prevê a sequência de APIs a partir da assinatura, e a lista prevista é inserida como comentário acima da assinatura no prompt do LLM. Contrafactual: linha zero-shot do mesmo modelo na Tabela 6 (e CodeLlama-7B zero-shot na Tabela 8). O ganho é do pacote, que inclui o treinamento do inquirer (fora do escopo).

tecnicas.localizador: Seções 4.2.1 e 4.2.2, Figuras 2(b) e 3, p. 7–9; Tabela 6, p. 10
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote híbrido chamado pelo estudo de chain-of-thought prompting: a cada passo o inquirer treinado prevê um estado de API, a docstring correspondente é anexada como estado de tarefa, e ambos, com o histórico de código, formam o prompt do passo; o laço continua até completar a função. Os estados intermediários vêm do inquirer e da documentação, não do raciocínio do LLM, e as subtarefas são executadas em etapas encadeadas; por isso classificado como decomposicao e contexto, não como raciocinio. Contrafactual: zero-shot do mesmo modelo (Tabela 6). Nenhuma condição isola a decomposição: kg-GPT e CoT-PT diferem em mais de um ingrediente (passos, docstrings, previsão incremental).

riscos.descricao: No código de domínio gerado pelo ChatGPT com a assinatura como prompt, só 32 de 200 funções estavam corretas; 37 implementaram funcionalidade diferente, 52 usaram APIs incorretamente e 79 omitiram APIs.
Em experimentos preliminares, o ChatGPT obteve 0% de aprovação em 200 amostras ao tentar passar os testes; o estudo usa isso para justificar não usar pass@k.
No CoT-PT, a previsão incremental de APIs sem informação de sintaxe e estrutura do código resulta em qualidade instável das APIs previstas, que guiam a geração.
Docstrings longas às vezes prejudicam a compreensão das APIs no prompt e aumentam o comprimento do texto; o estudo apresenta isso como limitação e desafio, sem tratá-lo como custo (não quantificado).

mitigacoes.descricao: Incorporar conhecimento de API (biblioteca, lista de APIs, docstrings, ou APIs previstas pelo inquirer) ao prompt para enfrentar o uso incorreto ou ausente de APIs; o efeito é medido contra a condição sem conhecimento, mas por BLEU/CodeBLEU (e julgamento humano no estudo industrial), não pela taxa de erros de API.

citacoes.trecho: We focus on the code completion scenario, wherein an LLM is presented with a function signature as a prompt, and its objective is to complete the function body.
We regard the function signature as a plain prompt without any knowledge injection.
1) Library import prompt: a phrase specifying the third-party library to be used.
2) API prompt: a list of APIs to be called to implement a function, retrieved from the ground-truth code.
3) Docstring prompt: the natural language descriptions of the APIs, retrieved from the library documentation.
We also constructed two combined knowledge-based prompts: API+docstring and docstring+API.
To introduce the domain-specific API knowledge, we add the predicted API list as a line of comment above the function signature, forming a combined prompt.
The API inquirer is realized as a GPT trained using causal language modeling, each training sequence is composed of a function signature and its corresponding API usages.
The corresponding API docstring is appended as the task state.
The generated API and task states are combined with the code history and used as a prompt for the LLM, which then predicts code for the current step.
The three steps are executed in a loop until we have generated a complete function body or the maximum generation length is reached.
In this strategy, we combine all sub-steps together and finetune a single language model in an end-to-end fashion.
We randomly sample 10 in-context examples that invoke the same library to the target domain.

Overall, of the 200 model-generated functions sampled, we observed that 32 functions were correct (16%), 37 implemented functionality completely different from the reference code (18.50%), 52 had problems with API misuse (26%), and 79 had problems with missing APIs (39.50%).
For example, our preliminary experiments indicate that even ChatGPT achieves a 0% pass rate out of 200 samples when attempting to pass their test cases.

Kg-GPT predicts all states of APIs at once, whereas CoT-PT predicts APIs incrementally based on historical states, which do not contain information about code syntax and structure, resulting in unstable quality of the predicted APIs.
This discrepancy may be attributed to the long text of the docstrings, which sometimes hinders the comprehension of APIs when incorporated into the prompt.
But this presents a new challenge of increasing the code length.
We asked three developers from the relevant team in Tencent to rate the evaluation criteria independently.
Conflicts were resolved through discussion until a consensus was reached.

We observe result improvement consistently on all library-specific datasets when using knowledge-enhanced prompts such as API sequences and docstrings compared to using the plain function signature prompt.
Under both the zero-shot and the fine-tuning settings, BLEU and CodeBLEU scores rise when the model is knowledge-enhanced, and the chain-of-thought fine-tuning strategy reaches the best scores.
API knowledge introduced by kg-GPT raised the BLEU scores by 49.33% on average, and the CodeBLEU scores by 9.82%.
We use the released pre-trained checkpoint PolyCoder-7B.
In particular, the code-specific LLMs we studied are limited to a parameter size not exceeding 2.7B.
For the chain-of-thought models, we do not count the tokens occupied by knowledge states in the overall length.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote híbrido: a CoT («How to solve: Step 1...») é gerada por um modelo separado (CodeLlama-7b ajustado com instruction-tuning e LoRA sobre o CodeCoT-9k, com o Instruction Template «Given a piece of code, output the corresponding implementation idea») e concatenada ao prompt original (zero-shot) do ℓLM gerador de código. instrucao = prompt original/zero-shot e template de instrução; raciocinio = cadeia de passos intermediários em linguagem natural; decomposicao = geração encadeada em duas etapas (CoT primeiro, código depois, X̂ = X ⊕ C) com plano em passos. O componente de ajuste fino está em componentes_fora_escopo; o ganho é do pacote e não pode ser atribuído só ao prompting nem a um mecanismo isolado. Contrafactual: Pass@1 sem CoT na mesma tabela; porém a intervenção é medida com CoT-Pass@1, que por definição só fornece a CoT quando o código sem CoT falha (comparação assimétrica, ver heterogeneidade). Na inferência do COTTON não há exemplos no prompt (o exemplo one-shot é usado pelo Agent 2/Teacher na construção dos dados).

riscos.descricao: LLMs com mais de 100B parâmetros impõem custos de tempo, computação e dinheiro na geração de código; o custo de chamar gpt-4 é declarado 20 vezes o do gpt-3.5-turbo; ajustar um modelo de 16B exigiria várias GPUs profissionais, com custo de hardware maior (não quantificado em dinheiro). O estudo também recomenda gerar CoT só após falha para evitar sobrecarga desnecessária (não quantificada).

riscos.descricao: Risco de vazamento de dados no conjunto de treino do gerador de CoT e de vazamento/viés nos testes de avaliação; controlado por filtragem de similaridade (R3) e por testes novos construídos manualmente no OpenEval. O estudo não discute contaminação do HumanEval no pré-treinamento dos modelos avaliados.
CoTs autogeradas por ℓLMs (Self-CoT) trazem melhora muito limitada e podem reduzir o desempenho de alguns ℓLMs; a cobertura limitada de testes do HumanEval pode gerar falsos positivos.

Qualidade dos dados de treino: muitos trechos dos conjuntos brutos não são autocontidos ou são triviais, e CoTs podem ser inconsistentes com o código (limitação de qualidade de dados, não de segurança).

Ameaças à validade: possíveis falhas de implementação do COTTON e das linhas de base; métricas automáticas baseadas em sobreposição de termos podem não capturar a semântica e o valor educacional da CoT.

mitigacoes.descricao: Filtragem por similaridade semântica (R3, embeddings codet5p e limiar de cosseno) para evitar vazamento de dados no treino.
Novo conjunto OpenEval com casos de teste projetados manualmente para minimizar viés e vazamento.
Uso do HumanEval-plus para atenuar a cobertura limitada de testes do HumanEval.

Consistency Checker para remover CoTs inconsistentes com o código; ablação compara CodeCoT-9k com o conjunto de 13k sem esse filtro, com queda relativa de 5,23% e 4,69% na métrica Consistency da CoT (não em métrica de código).
Inspeção cuidadosa do código, bibliotecas de terceiros consolidadas e linhas de base implementadas a partir de modelos compartilhados (Hugging Face).
Avaliação humana cega, com CoTs em ordem aleatória, dois avaliadores por grupo e limite de 20 amostras por meio dia.
Recomendação de gerar CoT só quando o modelo falha, para evitar sobrecarga.
