citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we investigate a new approach to adapt LLMs to program repair.
Based on this insight, we designed D4C, a straightforward prompting framework for APR.
To align LLM’s inference objective with its pre-trained completion objective, we adopt a one-shot prompting strategy.

As shown in Fig. 4, once the buggy function is identified, D4C will automated extract (1) documents or comments that describe the general purpose of the function and its input-output data types, (2) the inputs and expected outputs of the failed test cases, and (3) error messages from executing those failed test cases.

Following this, D4C integrates the bug report into a complete prompt, which is carefully designed to include a concise role-play system instruction (e.g., You are an AI debugger ...) and a fixed example consisting of a handcrafted bug report and its refined program.
This one-shot ICL also allows us to restrict the output format of the LLM to a refined function rather than other common output formats related to APR (e.g., unit diff patch [67]).
Furthermore, we adopt a much smaller sampling number of 10, as the inference budgets (fee, time, etc.) for LLMs are much larger than traditional methods.
To control a moderated randomness of text generation, we follow the previous work and set the randomness hyper-parameter, temperature, as 1.0.
In our implementation, we also carefully modified the system instructions to adapt to each output setting.

For the generated patches by Report-Hunk, as we do not provide a specific location to modify and cannot precisely determine where the generated patch should be applied, we instruct Mixtral-MoE to help us to automatically apply the generated patches to the original buggy program before patch validation.
w/o Document: D4C without including the program documents or function comments in the prompt.
w/o Test: D4C without including inputs and expected outputs of the failed test cases in the prompt.
w/o Message: D4C without including error message from the failed tests in the prompt.
- Pure: D4C without including any guidance like mask or artifacts to identify bugs in the prompt, i.e., an aligned LLM.
Since some of the baselines are not open-sourced, we cannot re-run them to reproduce the result.
Specifically, for baselines, the perfect buggy hunks within the buggy function is provided, while for D4C, only the buggy function is provided.
Since it contains data from previous versions of open-source projects where most code models have been trained on, it faces the threat of data leakage.
Since DebugBench is not exposed to the threat of data leakage, we use it for our insight validation (RQ2).
Table V shows that D4C generates a total of 210 plausible patches but 30 are incorrect with respect to the human patches.
To mitigate the potential bias in the manual analysis, two authors independently confirm the patch correctness.
Moreover, as LLM’s inference overhead and time cost is much higher than traditional APR tools, using LLM to generate patches for all given hunks may result in huge resource waste.
Given OpenAI’s pricing of $0.01 per 1,000 input tokens and $0.03 per 1,000 output tokens [76], the average cost per patch is $0.023 ($0.021 for resolved bugs and $0.024 for unresolved bugs).
Generating 10 patches per bug results in a total cost of $0.23 for the entire dataset.
Thus, there is a labor cost of manually validating the correctness of plausible patches beyond the token cost of patch generation.

As the effectiveness of the model may vary in different settings, our results may not generalize beyond the studied settings and other programming languages beyond the supported ones in Defects4J and DebugBench.
We mitigate this threat by reusing configurations in prior work, and widely used benchmarks.
Therefore, we decide to release our experimental results for public verification.

Thus, D4C can subsequently verify all 10 patches without involving significant waste of effort on incorrect patches (within 5 minutes), rather than suffering from a time-consuming process of verifying hundreds of patches (up to 5 hours [18], [25], [26], [30], [70]).
However, D4C requires running tests only up to 10 minutes per bug, with a timeout of 1min per patch.

This is because D4C only needs to generate at most 10 patches during decoding (i.e., beam search), which is significantly less than the sampling number of existing methods (i.e., over hundreds of sampling).
For Defects4J, the average input prompt length is 1,386.84 tokens overall, with 1,325.68 for resolved bugs and 1,369.72 for unresolved bugs.
In terms of sample size, we notice that a sample size of 10 is the optimal setting to allow D4C to find the correct patches.
Despite this, GPT-4 with the completion objective still fixes more bugs (414 vs 408) on DebugBench than GPT-4 with the infilling objective and masked hunk (“Mask-Hunk” in Table IV).
This paper is not aimed at proposing D4C as a new APR technique, but rather to introduce a new mindset or paradigm for better harnessing LLMs in APR in the future.

citacoes.trecho: We also investigated whether fixing the identified quality issues in the benchmarks’ prompts affects a model’s performance.
Fixing all these issues in the benchmarks can lead to a better performance for Python code generation, but not a significant improvement was observed for Java code generation.
Since a prompt can have more than one quality issue, the authors first fixed the issues one by one by creating a modified prompt version that does not contain one particular type of problem.
Subsequently, they created a new prompt version that fixed all the quality issues in the prompt.
To mitigate subjectivity when fixing issues, the senior author, who has over 10 years of experience, checked the modification and updated the prompts in multiple rounds of discussions.
We set k to 1, 3, and 10 and generated n = 20 outputs for each prompt.
To better understand how each quality issue may affect an LLM’s performance, we created prompts that fixed one issue at a time and prompts that fixed all issues.
Prompts with incorrect examples of input/output pairs give inaccurate contextual information to the model.
When fixing incorrect input/output pair examples (Q.I.5) we noticed that the pass@1 improved for CodeGen and StarCoder.
While we observed cases where fixing one (or all) issues in a prompt increased a model’s pass@k, there was not a consistent trend across models and languages.
Fixing spelling and grammatical issues and having the standard JavaDoc and Docstring style can perform similarly to original prompts.
citacoes.localizador: PDF p. 7, quadro RQ3 Summary of Findings

citacoes.trecho: We also found evidence that GPT-3.5-Turbo and CodeGen-2.5 models may have data contamination issues.
This indicates that test set contamination issues are present in the CodeGen-2.5 model.
As the prompts were modified by us, they would not be a part of the training set, though they are similar to the original prompts.
Hence, a model can perform better on the existing evaluation dataset but may not perform well in real-world software due to hallucinations [55].
Evaluation benchmarks with quality issues can provide a false sense of performance.
One of the possible solutions is uploading the evaluation set in a binary format [57].
As we used only HumanEval datasets in RQ3 and it contained only a subset of the found issues in RQ2, the results may not be generalized for other benchmarks and with different issues.

tecnicas.observacao: Prompt único aplicado a todos os modelos avaliados no conjunto proposto (60 problemas). Conteúdo conferido na Figura 1: papel ('You are an expert Python programmer'), palavras-chave (problem, variables, options), descrição da tarefa e duas regras (usar os nomes de variáveis dados; retornar a string das opções) → instrucao e restricoes; um exemplo resolvido com código (one-shot) → exemplos; instrução final de devolver só código Python, sem comentários adicionais → restricoes. Apesar do nome 'Chain-of-Thought', a Figura 1 não contém instrução de raciocínio passo a passo nem pede explicação antes do código (pede o contrário), por isso `raciocinio` não foi atribuído. Não há prompt base identificável nem condição sem o prompt: todos os modelos do conjunto proposto recebem o mesmo prompt, e as comparações do estudo são entre modelos e níveis de quantização. O prompt foi adaptado ao template de chat de cada modelo (papéis e tokens especiais), sem alteração declarada do conteúdo.

tecnicas.nome_original: Prompt used to generate Python code for the databases: HumanEval and EvalPlus (0-shot)

O estudo não o apresenta como proposta nem como linha de base de outra técnica; o rótulo `componente` é o mais próximo entre os disponíveis, mas não há pacote com ablação. Não é comparável ao prompt CoT/one-shot porque é aplicado a outros conjuntos de dados, com outra formulação de entrada; por isso não há contraste entre os dois prompts.

citacoes.trecho: To assess the performance of CPU-friendly models in generating Python code, we employ semi-manual evaluation.
In addition to that, we improve the performance of these models by proposing a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022b) prompt that specifically guides the model into the problem solving.
The prompt specifies the model’s role, the keywords it needs to focus on, and describes the target task.
Then, a single example is provided to validate the process (one-shot inference).
Finally, the prompt mentions that the goal is to have only one solving function, without any additional explanations or comments.
Figure 1 displays the complete prompt we propose as the input for each evaluated model.
Provide only Python code, do not include any additional comments.
citacoes.localizador: Figura 1 (Proposed Prompt), p. 17 do PDF (p. 15 impressa)

citacoes.trecho: You are an expert Python programmer. You will be provided with Python code that requires your completion.
The primary weakness observed in the llama-2-coder-7 models is a flaw in their background knowledge.
Additionally, there are numerous irrelevant comments unrelated to the prompt that indicate the models’ tendency to hallucinate.
For instance, the model references nonexistent NumPy functions or incorrectly attributes SciPy functions to the NumPy library.
This model often complicates code generation by adding unnecessary explanations to nearly every line and failing to maintain proper indentation, making the code difficult to copy and paste.
Although it adheres to the variable names specified in the prompt, it frequently introduces errors when using new variables.
However, LLMs’ substantial computational and memory requirements often make them inaccessible to users with limited resources.
In addition, even when LLMs are freely accessible, there is a risk of privacy leakage (Wu et al., 2023).
Our experience shows that the model occasionally assigns a score of 0 when a 0.5 is more appropriate.
First, we double-checked the scores assigned by GPT-3.5-Turbo to code generated by the quantized models using test cases from our dataset.
However, we manually review the code assigned scores of 0 and 0.5.
To ensure a fair comparison with the scores reported on the EvalPlus Leaderboard, we used the greedy search decoding algorithm to generate code outputs.
After receiving the LM’s response, we perform postprocessing to extract only the generated Python code, as some LMs may include unnecessary text.
We will make our dataset and prompts publicly available to support further research.

citacoes.trecho: This paper presents a preliminary evaluation of GPT-4-Vision, a state-of-the-art deep learning model, and its capabilities in transforming Unified Modeling Language (UML) class diagrams into fully operating Java class files.
In our study, we used exported images of 18 class diagrams comprising 10 single-class and 8 multi-class diagrams.
We used 3 different prompts for each input, and we manually evaluated the results.
Since this study aimed not to optimize textual prompts but to assess the code-generating capabilities of GPT-4-Vision, we conducted our experiment using relatively simple prompts.
However, we defined 3 levels of granularity for our prompts:
The prompt did not include any information about the project, classes, or functional details.
In this case, we used the following prompt: “Create Java source code from the image!”
The prompt concisely summarized the program represented by the given diagram.

An example prompt is as follows: “This is a really simple application where we have classes for books, reading, and bookshelf, and also got an exception for reading too fast. Create Java source code from the image! Try to implement the logic of these methods.”
The prompt detailed the program’s purpose shown on the diagram in natural language.
We created an evaluation strategy to evaluate all of the generated class files manually.
To ensure objective evaluation, unit tests will be utilized in the future.

We would like to emphasize that this is the result of a manual evaluation, in which we accepted any non-empty and non-skeleton implementation as a valid implementation to avoid making subjective decisions on when a source code can be considered correct.
The production of unit tests with adequate code coverage for an objective evaluation is ongoing.
In some instances, the scores achieved by the second prompt are higher than those obtained with the third prompt.
Nonetheless, there are occasions where the model autonomously omits methods that are present in the diagram.
This issue can likely be resolved by fine-tuning the textual instructions in the prompt.
We observed that the visibility modifiers indicated on diagrams (denoted by “+”, “-”, “#” symbols) are rarely considered by the model.
In one such instance, the GPT generated an interface source code for a traditional class (its data members were transformed to abstract methods in this case).
Furthermore, the GPT introduced a non-existent relationship with this interface class.
We believe this issue could be resolved by fine-tuning our prompts, which we will definitely do in the future.
Additionally, we observed that the detail of the given textual prompt can influence the model’s performance.

citacoes.trecho: Specifically, UniTrans first crafts a series of test cases for target programs with the assistance of source programs.
Afterward, UniTrans further (iteratively) repairs incorrectly translated programs prompted by test case execution results.
In experiments, we adopt a one-shot learning setting to make every LLM understand more about the task and only evaluate their first outputs.
Particularly, we instruct LLMs to generate 10 candidate inputs for each inference, explicitly stating the requirement that inputs need to be differentiated.
Hence, LLMs can leverage the above prompt to augment the code translation with extra test case information (Step 6).
Afterward, the extracted information can be embedded into the Repair Prompts, facilitating LLMs to fix corresponding error programs and refine the translation (Step 9-10).
Iteratively repairing error programs can fix more bugs but also bring the risk of degeneration.
citacoes.localizador: p. 18 do PDF (impressa 71:18), resposta à RQ6

citacoes.trecho: Incorporating more test cases indeed offers a more extensive vision to LLMs to translate code, but it also brings redundancies and distracts LLMs.
citacoes.localizador: p. 16 do PDF (impressa 71:16), resposta à RQ4

citacoes.trecho: One threat to the internal validity comes from the potential data leakage of LLMs, which means there may be some overlaps between the training set of LLMs and the testing set used in this work.
Besides, endlessly repairing incurs extra unaffordable time costs.

It should be noted that even though each translated program can be evaluated with more than one test case, we only feed the first failed case for repair due to the restriction of the prompt token length.
However, the dataset is flawed, as we mentioned in Section 5.1, and manually cleaning the dataset may not eliminate all noises or errors.
To do this, we curated 82 C++ codes manually written by some undergraduate students.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote híbrido: além de prompting (papel e objetivos → instrucao; especificação, código, logs, padrão Verilog-2001 e conhecimento de erros → contexto; exemplos de código RTL e exemplos da Tabela 1 → exemplos; self-planning → decomposicao; iteração com logs de compilador e simulador → feedback; agente depurador e agente avaliador → multiagente; restrições de estrutura e formato de saída na Figura 7 → restricoes; repositório de candidatos com seleção do código de maior nota → amostragem), inclui configuração de temperatura, possível ajuste fino («SFT»), testbench gerado por script Python, rollback por contagem de linhas e limite de 10 iterações (ver componentes_fora_escopo). Contrafactuais na Tabela 3: GPT-x+MEIC contra GPT-x na forma padrão e contra GPT-x+Knowledge, para GPT-3.5 e GPT-4. Os acrescentados foram contados em relação a GPT-x+Knowledge, que o estudo trata como «knowledge only» (MEIC inclui o conhecimento); não é informado se self-planning e role prompting (descritos na Seção 3.2, «Tuning Method», com os prompts da Figura 3) também estão na condição +Knowledge, por isso decomposicao não foi contada como acrescentada. O ganho do pacote não pode ser atribuído a um mecanismo isolado.

tecnicas.nome_original: Domain-specific knowledge (+Knowledge; descrito pelo estudo como fine-tuning por instruções de sistema e conhecimento nos prompts)
tecnicas.localizador: PDF p. 3 (Seção 3.2, «Domain-specific knowledge»); p. 7 (Tabela 3, colunas GPT-3.5+Knowledge e GPT-4+Knowledge); p. 8 (RQ3)
tecnicas.observacao: Componente do sistema proposto (Seção 3.2) avaliado na Tabela 3 com e sem conhecimento (GPT-x+Knowledge contra GPT-x), mantido o modelo. O conhecimento reúne instruções de sistema (instrucao), padrão Verilog-2001, conhecimento de erros e dados de depuração (contexto) e exemplos de código RTL e exemplos de forma esperada e inesperada da Tabela 1 (exemplos); por reunir vários ingredientes, o isolamento é do pacote de conhecimento. Ambiguidade: o estudo chama o procedimento de fine-tuning (nota 2 remete ao guia de fine-tuning da OpenAI; a Figura 2 rotula «SFT»), mas a Seção 3.2 descreve o fornecimento de informação «through the prompts»; não é possível determinar se houve alteração de pesos. O prompt da forma padrão não é descrito, por isso não se pode excluir que ela já contivesse instrução ou contexto.

componentes_fora_escopo.descricao: O estudo afirma usar agentes «fine-tuned» (contribuições, Figura 2 com rótulo «SFT», nota 2 com o guia de fine-tuning da OpenAI), mas a Seção 3.2 descreve o procedimento como fornecimento de instruções e conhecimento pelos prompts. Infraestrutura de verificação: casos de teste gerados com a biblioteca Random do Python e convertidos para testbench Verilog por script; asserções SystemVerilog inseridas no código; simulação automatizada no ModelSim. Gera os logs usados como feedback, mas não é prompting.
Regra que dispara o rollback quando há redução significativa de linhas ou código ausente, independentemente do agente avaliador; repositório que salva cada versão com seus logs.
Pós-processamento que limpa a resposta do LLM e extrai apenas o bloco de código para a iteração seguinte.
Limite de 10 iterações, definido pela experiência dos autores.

metricas.definicao: Proporção de instâncias com erro cuja versão corrigida passa em todos os casos de teste do testbench (Equação 1), em percentual; todos os FR são média de 10 experimentos repetidos.

Tempo entre o recebimento dos arquivos de projeto e a saída do código final, em segundos, com decomposição em simulação, depuração, avaliação e transmissão; comparado ao tempo de engenheiros humanos (speedup).

linguagens.uso: código transformado para inserir asserções na detecção de erros funcionais

riscos.descricao: Situações inesperadas chamadas de alucinação, como o LLM retornar código incompleto; iterações baseadas nessas saídas comprometem o resultado.

O LLM pode modificar partes corretas do código e introduzir novos erros, de modo que iterações são gastas corrigindo erros criados pelo próprio LLM; com temperatura mais alta, a correção de erros sintáticos pode introduzir alterações que geram novos erros, raramente corrigidos depois.
Incertezas e desempenho instável das saídas de LLM, que o estudo trata com a abordagem iterativa e com baixa temperatura no agente avaliador.
Limitação declarada: apesar da melhora geral, houve desempenho menor que o dos modelos na forma padrão em certos testes, e nenhum modelo cobre todos os cenários de depuração.

mitigacoes.descricao: Agente avaliador e mecanismo de rollback para tratar código incompleto ou novos erros, retomando o código de maior nota.
Temperatura baixa (0,1) no agente avaliador para reduzir a incerteza da pontuação qualitativa.
Instrução para não alterar drasticamente a estrutura do código, para evitar novos problemas.
Limpeza e extração do código da resposta para impedir que conteúdo irrelevante entre nas iterações seguintes.
Casos de teste do testbench escritos em Python para mitigar erros de causa comum entre o DUT e o testbench.
FR calculado como média de 10 experimentos repetidos.

citacoes.trecho: This work introduces a novel framework, Make Each Iteration Count (MEIC), which contrasts with traditional one-shot LLM-based debugging methods that heavily rely on prompt engineering, model tuning, and model training.
An iterative framework: MEIC integrates RTL toolchain (e.g., compilers and simulators), with two LLM agents, and a code repository.

Dual LLM deployment: MEIC employs a fine-tuned debug agent that identifies and attempts to correct syntax and function errors, followed by an LLM scoring agent that assesses the quality of RTL candidates derived from the debug agent.
We acknowledged that fine-tuning’s definitions are various in different LLMs.
Based on this property, we fine-tuned the LLM by supplying relevant information as system-level instructions and incorporating domain knowledge through the prompts [12, 27, 32, 39, 47].

To facilitate the interpretation and correction of Verilog code, we incorporated the Verilog-2001 standard [33] into the knowledge, along with a number of RTL code examples (e.g., HDLBits [44], Verilog-G [35], RTL Coding Guidelines [29], etc.) and the error knowledge (in Table 1).
To further improve the performance of the LLMs in code generation and debugging, we utilised advanced prompt engineering techniques, e.g., self-planning and role prompting as described in [18, 25].

The use of self-planning helps the LLMs to break down a complex task into several planned steps and the use of role prompting enables more relevant and contextually appropriate responses, allowing structured and relevant LLM responses.
Please offer necessary steps to debug the design module code. Then try to achieve the debugging.
If the agent does not generate the correct code in the current iteration, the next iteration will be performed using the highest-scored code from the previous iterations.
Do not drastically change the structure of code.
If the assessed score falls below a predefined threshold, a rollback mechanism is activated to revert the design code to the most recent comparable and simulatable version.
For example, the LLM may return incomplete code.

Also, the LLM can inadvertently modify both erroneous and correct portions of the code, leading to a situation where most of the iterations are spent addressing new errors introduced by the LLM itself.
To further mitigate the uncertainty of the qualitative scoring, a low temperature is configured to the scorer agent.
To mitigate common-cause errors between the DUT and the testbench, we developed the test cases in the testbench using Python.
Unless otherwise stated, we used the GPT-4 Turbo model as our default LLM agent for both debugging and scoring.
It is worth noting that all FR presented in this paper are calculated based on the average of 10 repeated experiments.
While attempting to rectify a syntax error, the agent with a higher temperature may inadvertently introduce alterations that result in the generation of new errors.

In addition, despite prompt engineering, model tuning, and model training bringing overall improvement to the model performance, decreased performance was observed in certain tests compared to the models in their standard forms.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote de quatro agentes de prompting (Retrieval, Planning, Coding, Debugging) com travessia dinâmica guiada por escores de confiança dos planos. Comparado com Direct Prompting e outras técnicas na Tabela 2; o ganho sobre Direct é do pacote e não autoriza atribuí-lo a um único mecanismo. Mecanismos: papéis de agentes que interagem (multiagente); exemplos autogerados com código e plano, à maneira do analogical prompting (exemplos); planos passo a passo executados pelos agentes seguintes (decomposicao); k planos com escore de confiança ordenados e percorridos (amostragem); depuração iterativa com teste nas sample I/O (feedback); «Let's think step by step» nos prompts de código e depuração (raciocinio); formato XML e restrições de resposta (restricoes). O tutorial de algoritmo gerado pelo próprio LLM (Retrieval Agent) não é recuperação externa e não foi codificado como contexto. Não é pacote híbrido: não há componente fora do escopo descrito. Parâmetros k (exemplares autogerados) e t (tentativas de depuração): k = t = 5 no HumanEval e k = t = 3 nos demais (p. 5).

riscos.descricao: Casos de teste incorretos gerados por IA podem levar a código errado em abordagens de autorreflexão; o estudo observa que 8% das falhas no HumanEval e 15% no MBPP decorrem de testes incorretos gerados por IA (denominador não especificado).
A dependência de poucas sample I/O para depuração pode não cobrir todo o espectro de casos de teste.

Desempenho reduzido em problemas mais difíceis e em categorias como Combinatorics, Constructive, Number Theory, Divide and Conquer e DP; inspeção manual de cinco problemas de DP mostrou má interpretação do problema e escolha de abordagens gulosas ou de força bruta.

O MapCoder gera muitos tokens, o que pode ser desafio em ambientes com recursos limitados; quantificado na Tabela 8 (média de 16,7 chamadas de API e 21,25 mil tokens contra 1 chamada e 0,64 mil tokens do Direct Prompting). O aumento de k e t eleva o tempo, não quantificado.
Executar código gerado por máquina envolve riscos potenciais; o estudo recomenda executá-lo em sandbox. Trata-se de segurança operacional da execução, não de vulnerabilidades do código gerado.

Possível vazamento de casos de teste ocultos no prompt ao fornecer, no MBPP, um caso do MBPP-ET como sample I/O; o estudo descreve controle de exclusividade mútua. O estudo não discute contaminação no pré-treinamento.

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we introduce a new approach to code generation tasks leveraging the multi-agent prompting that uniquely replicates the full cycle of program synthesis as observed in human developers.
Our framework, MapCoder, consists of four LLM agents specifically designed to emulate the stages of this cycle: recalling relevant examples, planning, code generation, and debugging.
Instead, we leverage the LLM agent itself, instructing it to generate such problems.
To help the generation steps in the following agents with the utility information for each plan, our designed prompt for the planning agent asks the LLM to generate both plans and a confidence score.
Finally, the Debugging Agent utilizes sample I/O from the problem description to rectify bugs in the generated code.
These plans are sorted, and the highest-scoring one is sent to the Coding Agent.
Direct Prompting instructs language models to generate code without explicit guidance, relying on their inherent capabilities of LLM.
Test case generation is equally challenging as code generation (Pacheco et al., 2007), and incorrect test cases can lead to erroneous code.
Among the limitations of our work, firstly, MapCoder generates a large number of tokens, which may pose challenges in resource-constrained environments.
Although sample I/Os provide valuable insights for LLMs' code generation, their limited number may not always capture the full spectrum of possible test cases.
Another important concern is that while running machine-generated code, it is advisable to run it inside a sandbox to avoid any potential risks.
Importantly, this removed test-case is carefully selected to ensure mutual exclusivity from the hidden test sets in MBPP and MBPP-ET.

Manual inspection of five DP category problems reveals occasional misinterpretation of problems, attempts to solve using greedy or brute-force approaches, and struggles with accurate DP table construction when recognizing the need for a DP solution.
Our findings (Table 7) reveal that higher k, t is proportionate performance gain at the expense of time.

Furthermore, we observe that the Debugging Agent has the most significant impact on the pipeline, as evidenced by a performance drop of 17.5% when excluding this agent exclusively, and an avg performance drop of 24.83% in all cases.

citacoes.trecho: AnalogCoder is an LLM-based agent that interprets task descriptions in natural language to automatically generate Python code, representing functionally correct analog circuits.
Our approach to prompt engineering encompasses three main aspects: (1) programming language selection, (2) in-context learning [37], and (3) Chain-of-Thought [38].
Therefore, to mitigate this limitation, we directly prompt the LLM to generate executable Python code compatible with the PySpice library.
Furthermore, we integrate in-context learning [37] to enhance circuit design, providing a detailed example of a two-stage amplifier with active and resistor loads as one-shot learning [42].
All design tasks are distinct from the provided example to maintain evaluation fairness.
Additionally, the Chain-of-Thought strategy [38] involves prompting the LLM to generate a detailed design plan, including necessary components and their interconnections.
For any errors occurring in these checks, the relevant error information is returned to the LLM, which then regenerates a circuit design.
Due to limitations in the LLMs’ code repair capabilities, we allow up to three code generations, which means up to two retries.
This method also helps identify the optimal bias voltage, increasing the success rate of the design.
If a circuit task has been successfully completed multiple times, store the optimal circuit design based on the key specification, such as gain.
In composite circuit design, the task description is used to formulate a query prompt, enabling the retrieval of the requisite subcircuit tools by LLMs.
Cross-validation techniques [50] are applied to ensure that tasks used in fine-tuning were excluded from the testing set.
All LLMs, except GPT-4o, have been enhanced by prompt engineering, design flow feedback, and the circuit tool library.
To ensure a fair comparison and highlight the tool library’s impact, we applied our strategies across all LLMs but specifically excluded the circuit tool library from GPT-4o to isolate its effects.
Specifically, “GPT-3.5 (SPICE)” refers to the GPT-3.5 in which the LLM is prompted to generate SPICE codes rather than Python.
The variants “GPT-3.5 (w/o context)” and “GPT-3.5 (w/o CoT)” explore the impact on performance when omitting in-context information and Chain-of-Thought reasoning from the prompts, respectively.
Furthermore, “GPT-3.5 (w/o flow)” indicates a setup in which our proposed design flow was not utilized, and only the first generated codes were applied for functional testing.
The findings consistently show that removing these components leads to a decrease in design performance.
‘GPT-3.5 (w/o context)’ disregards the context example in the prompt, meaning that a demonstrative design question and answer should not be provided.

citacoes.trecho: It can be observed that even the slightest discrepancy can render a circuit non-functional.
If a design is not achieved within this limit, the LLM’s further attempts are unlikely to succeed, and token consumption continues to rise.
The number of design attempts for composite circuits has been limited to two because they involve more complex and challenging fixes and have high generation costs.
Currently, LLMs lack the capability to design highly complex analog circuits, but future advancements may address this.
Additionally, their use is constrained by costs and the availability of computational resources.
As LLMs improve, there is a risk of AI replacing parts of human roles, a challenge common to all projects involving LLMs.
When employing LLMs for inference, we set temperature= 0.5 and top_p= 1.0 in all models to generate varied results in each trial.
As a result, the outcomes post-fine-tuning may exhibit instability.
Considering the overall costs, we have decided to implement our AnalogCoder based on GPT-4o.
The number of trials in our experiment was determined by considering factors such as financial costs and computational resources.

citacoes.trecho: In the domain of code generation, self-debugging is crucial.
It allows LLMs to refine their generated code based on execution feedback.
In this work, we propose LEDEX, a training framework that significantly improves the self-debugging capability of LLMs.

Compared with directly asking for a refined solution (referred to as “Code Refinement” in the feedback block), asking LLMs to provide an explanation of the wrong solution and then refine it in a chain-of-thought manner (referred to as “Code Explanation and Refinement” in the feedback block) helps it to better understand the unit test feedback and increases the success rate of providing refined solutions (details in Appendix A.1).

We evaluate two prompting strategies for querying LLMs to perform code refinement: one where the LLMs directly generate the refinement (Figure 5 (3.1)), and another where they first explain why the code is incorrect before generating the refinement (Figure 5 (3.2)).
Generally, LLMs that first explain the incorrect code are more likely to generate accurate refinements.
For the generation of the initial solutions, the models sample 100 solutions per task in the benchmarks (temperature set to 0.8), which are run against the provided test cases.
For every incorrect solution that fails any test case, we let the models sample one refinement (and one explanation).
The improvements from SFT are compared to direct prompting, while the improvements from RL are relative to SFT.
The prompting approach does not work for this example, and the prompted StarCoder generates a hallucinated explanation and simply repeats the wrong solution.
Actually, such simple repeats of wrong solutions are very common when using the prompting approach, which supports our motivation to train LLM to self-debug.
Yet, the refinement from CodeLlama-13B is not fully correct, as “(x, y, z) == ((int)x, (int)y, (int)z)” is not equivalent to checking if these numbers are integers.
As LLMs may provide wrong explanations or refinements, we cannot blindly take them as training data.
Thus, we verify the refinements by running them against the test cases again, and only those passing all the test cases are considered correct refinements.
On the MBPP+ and HumanEval+ benchmarks, which feature more rigorous test cases, respectively [26], we observe even greater improvements from RL training on the CodeLlama models.

Additionally, our current experiments only use two types of prompts for enabling LLMs to self-debug: one that directly asks for refinement and another that first asks for an explanation of the wrong code followed by refinement.

riscos.descricao: O desempenho na geração em nível de repositório é insatisfatório; na inspeção manual de falhas, os LLMs têm dificuldade em compreender contextos longos e heterogêneos e deixam de usar dependências disponíveis, sobretudo entre arquivos. O maior Pass@1 impresso é 53.04 (gpt-4, Local File (Infilling)).

riscos.descricao: Risco de vazamento de dados: repositórios usados para construir o DevEval podem estar nos dados de treinamento dos LLMs. O estudo julga o impacto leve; não afirma contaminação efetiva.

Viés de medição do Recall@k: por Python ser dinamicamente tipado, algumas dependências só são determinadas em tempo de execução e podem escapar ao parser estático, o que pode levar a Recall@k menor que o valor real (risco de validade da métrica, não do código gerado).
riscos.localizador: Seção 5, «The bias of Recall@k», p. 9 do PDF; seção 9, limitação 2, p. 10

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we present CatCoder, a novel code generation framework designed for statically typed programming languages.
Specifically, it leverages static analyzers to extract type dependencies and merges this information with retrieved code to create comprehensive prompts for LLMs.
You are given a blank {Java|Rust} function with type context, referential code snippet and docstrings.
To construct a prompt, we follow the context format in previous work [32, 40, 53], and fill the CONTEXT field by concatenating the type context and the retrieved code chunks.
These examples often perform semantically related or symmetric operations and thus provide reusable implementation patterns.
As the CONTEXT field is the only variable, we compare our approach with methods that fill different contexts in the prompt.
In this case, all natural language descriptions are given, but the CONTEXT field in Fig. 4 is left empty.
We extract code before the function to be generated and put it in the CONTEXT field.
We adopt their idea and implement this baseline for Java and Rust based on our retrieval pipeline.
From the second iteration, it uses the previously generated code for retrieval.
(2) -CR: Relevant Code Retrieval is removed.
(3) -TC: Type Context Extraction is removed.

When provided with only the in-file context for such a task, an LLM may hallucinate and produce code that appears plausible but fails to compile or execute correctly within the project (e.g., misusing an API or referencing an undefined identifier).
In such cases, the absence of type context increases the risk of hallucination, such as referencing non-existent methods or fields.
The retriever may still return incomplete or even misleading context.
This example illustrates that function code generation is inherently complex, and the effective use of repository context does not always guarantee correctness.
Therefore, a limitation is that CatCoder may produce incomplete type context when the repository heavily relies on dynamic features.
In large repositories, the full dependency graph can become vast, making the resulting type context too long to fit in an LLM’s context window.
For evaluation on the benchmarks, the ground truth code in the repositories is removed during retrieval to prevent leakage.
In future work, possible research attempts include investigating the data leakage problem of the benchmarks.
To control the randomness of the generated code [17], we set the temperature to 0.6 and the nucleus sampling [24] parameter (top_p) to 0.7.
Significant latencies would negate the advantages of automated assistance and lead to user frustration.
As shown in Table 8, the measured cold start time is 38.8 seconds, with the Relevant Code Retrieval component as the main bottleneck.
To some extent, the type context in CatCoder helps mitigate this limitation by supplying accessible API information that the LLM can cross-reference, as illustrated in Section 5.1.2.
Therefore, in practice, we constrain the scope of type context creation to the direct neighbors of the initial types in the graph.
This is due to CatCoder’s caching mechanism, which stores intermediate data, including embedding vectors of code chunks and intermediate states of the static analyzer.
Notably, the scores of CatCoder and RepoCoder are very close, with RepoCoder even slightly outperforming CatCoder in CodeBLEU.
On the Java benchmark, CatCoder achieves a relative improvement of up to 17.35% in pass@k, whereas on Rust, the maximum relative improvement is 6.68%.
In detail, for the -CR variant, the compile@k and pass@k scores decrease by up to 19.43% and 38.35%, respectively, on the Java benchmark, and by up to 46.24% and 56.03% on the Rust benchmark.

citacoes.trecho: We conduct an initial evaluation of different LLMs and their variants, including zero-shot code generation, in-context learning (ICL), and Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods.
This paper addresses this gap by introducing a comprehensive evaluation framework designed specifically for assessing LLM performance in VHDL code generation task.
prompt: Commented problem statement concatenated with function/entity declaration.
In-Context Learning: We leverage the in-context learning ability of LLMs by placing “training” data into a prompt preceding each test prompt.
We experiment with “Codellama-70b-instruct” model under ICL setup with k=5 examples due to the limits on the context length.
In our work, we finetune CodeGen2.5 using the LoRA implementation from HuggingFace PEFT [20] and the 8-bit AdamW from bitsandbytes [21].
Our experiments with in-context learning (ICL) show marginal performance improvement for Codellama-70b-instruct and Granite-20b-instruct models.
This suggests potential for further improvement by incorporating more meaningful code snippets into the context, but challenges remain due to context length limits and VHDL verbosity.
These testbenches, while useful, may not cover all critical scenarios and might not be exhaustive or sufficient for all problem sets.
The problem sets and their solutions are self-contained, lacking real-life design complexities.
To mitigate potential benchmark leakage issues [19], where evaluation data is inadvertently used for model training, we reframe problem statements to prevent direct reuse.

Lastly, despite efforts to prevent benchmark leakage as explained in Section II-B, we cannot guarantee that the problem sets and code were not part of the original training set of the LLMs evaluated, given the scale of their training data.
It is essential to ensure that the number of generated samples n is sufficiently large to yield low variance estimates for Pass@k, as suggested in the literature.
To systematically evaluate the generated code, we prioritize two primary goals: ensuring syntactic correctness and validating functional correctness through self-verifying testbenches.
The dataset will be published soon after getting clearance.

Na análise de falhas da própria abordagem, o LLM produz refatorações erradas quando a refatoração é complicada (ordem dos elementos alterada em list-comprehension; sequência não aritmética tratada como aritmética em star-in-func-call).

citacoes.trecho: Inspired by the motivating examples in Section 2, we propose a hybrid approach based on LLMs to refactor non-idiomatic code with Pythonic idioms.
Finally, we design prompts to instruct LLMs to abstract and idiomatize code, and then invoke ARIs from the ARI library to rewrite non-idiomatic code into the idiomatic code.

Then two authors discuss their results and give the final description of abstracting code (<prompt>) and three examples of original non-idiomatic code and the corresponding abstract non-idiomatic code for each Pythonic idiom (<examples>).
The idiomatization module consists of three steps: abstracting code, idiomatizing code and rewriting code.

The second (Prompt-LLM) is to directly call the LLM to find code pairs for any given method code for each Pythonic idiom to illustrate the capability of LLM and the strengths of our proposed approach using LLM.
Then two authors discuss their results and give the final prompt and three examples for each Pythonic idiom.
Since the success of ChatGPT, the LLM our approach and baselines use are state-of-the-art of GPT-3.5-turbo [2].
And we set temperature to 0 to make the outputs mostly deterministic.
Following the retrieval of the generated Python code, authors manually validate its correctness.
It occurs in identifying refactorable non-idiomatic code but wrongly refactoring it, resulting in inconsistency in code behavior before and after refactoring.
This non-deterministic nature can inadvertently lead to the oversight of refactorable non-idiomatic code [6, 17, 52].
The idiomatic code is wrong because the order of elements is different from the non-idiomatic code.

citacoes.trecho: It is expensive for LLMs to handle so many codes and is difficult to make sure the non-idiomatic code is not missing and is correct from unrelated code in a given Python code.
Currently, our approach only supports syntactically correct Python code, as it requires parsing the code into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).

Prior studies [6, 17, 51, 52] have shown that employing Pythonic idioms may yield benefits, such as code conciseness and improved performance, but it can also have drawbacks, including potential impacts on code readability and performance degradation.
The one internal threat is inaccuracy when evaluating the correctness of benchmark in Section 4.
The Cohen's Kappa values [46] of nine groups for their annotation results all exceeded 0.75 (substantial agreement).
To mitigate this threat, our experimented methods of benchmark are from previous research [53], representing an unbiased benchmark for our research.

For the precision, although RIdiom exhibits a slight advantage in precision (with differences ranging from 0.8% to 6.2%) for eight of the idioms, our approach consistently achieves over 93.8% precision for each idiom.
We define a TP as a code pair detected by an approach is in the benchmark.

riscos.descricao: Erros de compilação ligados a herança, encapsulamento e herança ilegal, interpretados como compreensão insuficiente das restrições sintáticas e semânticas do contexto.
Erros de completude: o modelo ignora o código a completar e deixa o corpo do método vazio, associados pelo estudo a ignorar informação no meio de contextos longos; mais frequentes no WizardCoder.

Falhas de teste dominadas por AssertionFailedError (50,75%) e IllegalArgumentException (25,88%), com casos de não seguimento da documentação e de implementação trivial feita só para compilar. Denominador das porcentagens (exceções em projetos gerados) não informado em número absoluto.

riscos.descricao: Limitação de contextos longos: o modelo pode não processar o esqueleto completo do projeto no Maximum Context.
Possível contaminação: modelos que viram o código canônico no treinamento poderiam ter escores exagerados; o estudo considera a preocupação menor por os projetos terem sido mantidos confidenciais.
Variação de desempenho decorrente da engenharia de prompt: um prompt melhor projetado poderia gerar melhor desempenho (ameaça à validade).
Generalização limitada a outros modelos (só cinco LLMs, por limites de tempo e hardware) e influência da qualidade das descrições em linguagem natural sobre a geração (ameaças à validade).

mitigacoes.descricao: Projetos e soluções canônicas mantidos confidenciais pelos estudantes por integridade acadêmica, para reduzir a ameaça de contaminação.
Verificação dos projetos, leitura do retorno dos estudantes e ajuste das descrições para reduzir confusão e ambiguidade.
Template de prompt baseado em prática comum, para atenuar a ameaça de variação por engenharia de prompt.
Seleção de modelos de famílias diferentes como representantes, para atenuar a ameaça à generalização.
Soluções canônicas preparadas por programador experiente, validadas por outros programadores e revisadas por mais de 200 estudantes; testes construídos manualmente cobrindo os conceitos exercitados.

citacoes.trecho: In particular, we design three context settings (i.e., maximum/minimum/selected context) in prompting, adopt five synthesis strategies (i.e., holistic, independent, incremental, and its two variants), and evaluate the synthesized projects at two evaluation granularities (i.e., class-wise and test-wise) using three metrics (i.e., Completion@k, Compilation@k, and Pass@k).
Following the common practice of prompting LLMs [9, 28], the prompt template consists of two parts: a system message to initialize the model, and an instruction to state the purpose of the task.
You are a helpful Java programmer who writes the project based on the following context.
A straightforward context is to feed the entire project skeleton to LLMs, providing as much information as possible, i.e., the Maximum Context setting.
With this context size, 53.3% of the contexts are truncated, and the truncated characters account for 42.9% of the total characters.
Opposite to the maximum context, it is natural to use only the class to be completed, i.e., Minimum Context.
In addition, to minimize the input tokens while maintaining the context as informative as possible, we only include the method signatures in the related class, excluding the method body.
Independent Synthesis: each method is synthesized independently without being affected by other generated methods.
Holistic Synthesis: all the methods in a class are synthesized in one pass by LLMs.
Incremental Synthesis: methods in a class are generated one by one in a specific order.
Different from prior work [28], in addition to considering sequential the order to synthesize methods, we also consider the reverse and random orders.
We used the selected context setting and exercised three synthesis strategies (Section 3.1.2) to generate the entire project.
We fix the synthesis strategy as holistic because it performs the best in RQ1.
Due to the space limitation, we only show the impact of DeepSeek-Coder-6.7b on Completion/Compilation/Pass@1 and @5.
We used nucleus sampling [37] in line with recent works [20, 28, 48, 58], where five solution samples were randomly generated with a temperature of 0.2 [23].
Among the three synthesis strategies, holistic synthesis yielded a better performance across all LLMs against three metrics at two granularities on JavaBench.
The selected context is the best setting on JavaBench, resulting in 70.92% (class-wise) Pass@1.
Providing too much or too little context has a negative impact on project-level code generation.
Compilation errors indicate that LLMs have an insufficient understanding of the syntactic and semantic constraints provided by the context.
A completion error happens when LLMs ignore the code to be completed and leave the method body blank.
Among them, AssertionFailedError happens the most frequently (50.75%), followed by IllegatlAugumentException (25.88%).
This implementation is evidently a placeholder meant solely to pass compilation.
Note that due to the limitation of long input contexts, it is possible that an LLM fails to digest the entire project skeleton.
Students are required to keep the course assignments and canonical solutions confidential for academic integrity, which reduces the data contamination [33] threat to our benchmark.
LLMs having seen the canonical code during training could lead to exaggerated scores, known as data contamination [33].
However, the projects in JavaBench were kept confidential (Section 2.2.1), thus having minor concerns.

Since choosing one best-performing prompt is challenging [44], and a well-designed prompt could yield better performance, so we follow the common practice of prompting LLMs [9] to design the prompt template, trying to alleviate this threat.
In this study, we only studied five LLMs due to time and hardware limits, so the conclusion may not be able to generalize to other LLMs.
To alleviate this threat, we carefully checked the subjects in JavaBench, scanned students’ feedback, and adjusted the descriptions to mitigate confusion and ambiguity.

First, we noticed that regarding project-level Java programming, LLMs are far behind undergraduate students (no project can be correctly completed by any studied LLMs, and at most 41.17% Pass@5 in a more relaxed evaluation).
The best LLMs under the best setting only reach a 41.7% Pass@5 in test-wise granularity (Section 4.1), compared with 90.93% achieved by undergraduate students under a stricter evaluation.

Overall, the average Completion/Compilation/Pass@5 under holistic strategy across all LLMs are 97.21%(+5.48%), 84.43%(+12.10%), 84.43%(+13.51%) at the class-wise granularity; 94.21%(+5.48%), 51.23%(+16.28%), 48.24%(+20.84%) at the test-wise granularity.
The best average test-wise Pass@5 in JavaBench is 48.24%.
The four projects have similar scales, with 89 to 125 functions spreading across 23 to 30 Java classes.
The difficulty of all projects is similar, with an average of 90.96 to 95.41.
From the lower part of Figure 5, the red dashed line outperforms the other two lines, with an advantage of 6% (86.07% - 80%) in the reversed order.

riscos.descricao: CodeLlama-34b gerou instruções novas (alucinações), o que impediu a avaliação; o modelo foi excluído dos resultados.

Os modelos erram com preposições espaciais, formas geométricas/objetos reais e anáforas; limitações listadas: localizações fora das dimensões da grade, falha em instruções na perspectiva do agente e dificuldade com abstrações do diálogo.

riscos.descricao: Execução direta de código gerado com conteúdo nocivo poderia afetar o sistema inteiro; também a extensão do estudo simulado para agentes no mundo real pode levar a consequências incorretas (segurança operacional, não cibersegurança).
Código gerado pode favorecer certos estilos e prejudicar a portabilidade; a complexidade do código gerado pode dificultar refinamento e reúso pelo usuário final.

Validade da avaliação: 23.3% dos turnos contêm erros do builder no ground truth (place seguido de pick), o que penaliza o modelo; instruções subespecificadas impedem correspondência de 100% com o ground truth.

citacoes.trecho: Leveraging LLMs’ in-context learning abilities, we use few-shot prompting techniques, that significantly improve performance over baseline methods.
Taking advantage of the code-generation capabilities of LLMs, we model the action prediction task as a code-generation task.
This is followed by dynamically adapted in-context examples suitable to the current turn instruction from the training set.
The top three turns and their corresponding builder actions are selected as in-context examples.
Adopting the approach recommended by Song et al. (2023), we use adaptive prompts, dynamically retrieving examples from the training set that are similar to the current test instruction.
You are an expert at interpreting natural language instructions and translating them into specific actions for placing colored blocks within a 3D grid.
You should only use these specified functions and not create any hypothetical functions.
Stick to the given format. Think step by step.
Consequently, we use the prompt featuring all components with three in-context examples to ensure the best performance.

However, the results were not sat- isfactory because the generated response contained new instructions generated by model (hallucinations) and it was impossible to evaluate the closeness of the resulting generation to the ground truth, and hence this model is excluded from the experimental results.
Moreover, it’s crucial to ensure LLM-generated responses are free from harmful code, as their direct execution could impact the entire system.
Another concern is the potential complexity of LLM-generated code, which can hinder end-user refinement and reuse.
However, the pre-trained LLMs, which inherit biases from their training data, may lead to code that favors certain styles and neglects others, hindering code portability.
(iv) Since the study is carried out in a simulated world, extending it to real-world agents may lead to incorrect consequences..

In the test set, 75.42% of the utterances include a spatial preposition, but the model correctly generates code for only 26.03% of them, highlighting significant challenges in interpreting spatial prepositions and a need for improvement.
These inaccuracies in the ground truth lead to lower evaluation scores, as the model is penalized for errors that are not indicative of its true performance.

tecnicas.observacao: Framework de agentes em quatro fases: Analyzer (modelagem de ameaças com Stepwise Solution Blueprint e hipóteses de vulnerabilidade H), Coder (geração condicionada a H com diretiva defense-in-depth), Tester (suíte de testes funcionais e adversariais sob restrição de assinatura) e Executor/Repairer (refinamento em ciclo fechado com feedback de execução). O isolamento é do pacote completo contra Greedy e CoT (mesmo backbone, temperatura 0); o ganho não pode ser atribuído a um único mecanismo. O Executor executa código, ingrediente classificado como feedback; o pacote não inclui componentes fora do escopo além das configurações comuns de decodificação e orçamento. As linhas de base de prompting não recebem iterações de reparo, de modo que o número de chamadas ao modelo difere (não quantificado). No reparo de código inseguro (RQ5), o Analyzer recebe o código inseguro como insumo (contexto, presente também nas linhas de base desse cenário) e a etapa inicial de geração é omitida. Os textos dos prompts não são reproduzidos no artigo.

tecnicas.observacao: Ablação w/o Threat Modeling remove só a Fase I. Além do raciocínio sobre superfície de ataque, a fase acrescenta o plano por etapas (blueprint) e as restrições específicas de vulnerabilidade (H), mas as categorias decomposicao e restricoes permanecem na variante ablada (fases encadeadas e restrição de assinatura do Tester), por isso só raciocinio é listado como categoria acrescentada. A remoção da Fase I também retira as hipóteses H que condicionam as Fases II e III; o contraste cobre a fase e seu uso a jusante. Mecanismos listados são os do pacote completo (condição com o componente).

riscos.descricao: Endurecimento de segurança por verificações excessivamente restritivas pode degradar a utilidade; o estudo separa F-Pass@1 e S-Pass@1 para detectar esse efeito.

Hipóteses de vulnerabilidade e testes de refinamento gerados por LLM podem conter erros que se propagam no pipeline; testes sintetizados podem ser fracos, mal especificados ou produzir casos hallucinated-green.
riscos.localizador: p. 19 do PDF (impressa ISSTA068:19), Seção 7; p. 16, Seção 6.4

riscos.descricao: Os testes de segurança executáveis do benchmark não caracterizam todas as variantes de exploração e podem não detectar vulnerabilidades sofisticadas, dependentes de contexto ou sem falha; resultados podem não generalizar para outras linguagens ou repositórios.

Pipelines de agentes exigem mais chamadas ao modelo e etapas de execução que a geração de passo único, com latência e custo de inferência adicionais; uso de tokens e custo computacional podem diferir entre os métodos de agentes. Não quantificado.

Taxas absolutas de sucesso continuam limitadas, especialmente no reparo em SecEvalBase; os autores afirmam que o reparo automatizado exige validação independente e supervisão humana e que o SecAwareCoder é um framework de pesquisa, não defesa pronta para produção.

citacoes.trecho: Building on CodeSecEval, we propose SecAwareCoder, an agent-based framework that shifts code generation toward secure-by-construction synthesis.

RQ5 evaluates whether SecAwareCoder remains effective beyond generation, when the model is provided with an insecure implementation and must repair it to satisfy both functional and security requirements.
SecAwareCoder consists of four main phases: (1) Task-Adaptive Threat Modeling, (2) Constraint-Guided Code Generation, (3) Security-Aware Test Generation, and (4) Closed-Loop Self-Refinement.
Rather than guessing potential flaws, the agent first constructs a Stepwise Solution Blueprint for the given problem, a structured plan that outlines the algorithmic steps without syntactic details.

Unlike standard generation that conditions primarily on the functional description, our agent is additionally conditioned on H, which provides vulnerability-specific constraints and mitigation directives.
citacoes.localizador: p. 10 do PDF (impressa ISSTA068:10), Seção 4.3 (H em notação caligráfica no original)

citacoes.trecho: Concretely, we provide a defense-in-depth directive and inject the mitigation strategies into the synthesis context, encouraging the model to integrate security controls (e.g., input validation, parameterized execution, and boundary checks) directly into the program logic.
A Repairer agent then uses this differentiated feedback to iteratively refine the solution.
Greedy generates a single solution by selecting the token with the highest probability at each step.
CoT [33] prompts the model to generate intermediate reasoning steps prior to code synthesis, leveraging the model’s latent logic to improve performance.

The framework consists of three agents: a Coding Agent responsible for code generation, a Static Analyzer Agent responsible for identifying vulnerabilities, and a Fuzzing Agent responsible for performing mutation-based dynamic testing to detect runtime errors.
For AutoSafeCoder and SecAwareCoder, we use the same backbone, decoding configuration, and maximum number of repair iterations.
To eliminate variance associated with random sampling and ensure a deterministic comparison, we set the temperature to 0 for all LLM generations.
For the agent-based frameworks (AutoSafeCoder and SecAwareCoder), we permit a maximum of two repair iterations following the initial generation.

Specifically, we compare SecAwareCoder (Full) against two variants: (i) w/o Threat Modeling, which removes Phase I (Task-Adaptive Threat Modeling), and (ii) w/o Test+Refine, which removes Phase III+IV (Security-Aware Test Generation and Closed-Loop Self-Refinement).
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for program synthesis, yet they often generate code that is functionally plausible but insecure.

Across baselines, we observe a clear gap between functionality and security: S-Pass@1 is consistently much lower than F-Pass@1, indicating that passing benign functional tests is substantially easier than satisfying vulnerability-targeted security checks.

This separation allows us to determine whether a method improves vulnerability-targeted security-test performance by introducing overly restrictive checks that degrade utility, or whether it achieves functional correctness while remaining vulnerable under adversarial inputs.

SecAwareCoder relies on LLM-generated vulnerability hypotheses and executable refinement tests, so errors in threat localization, mitigation reasoning, or test construction may propagate through the pipeline.
Synthesized tests may also be weak, incorrectly specified, or insufficiently diverse, potentially missing relevant exploit patterns or producing hallucinated-green cases.

Moreover, although its executable security tests cover representative and deterministic attack patterns, they cannot exhaustively characterize all exploit variants and may miss sophisticated, context-dependent, or non-crashing vulnerabilities.
Agent-based pipelines require more model calls and execution steps than single-shot generation, resulting in additional latency and inference cost.
Although we use the same backbone, decoding configuration, and repair-iteration limit for the compared agent-based methods, their internal token usage and computational costs may differ.
This shows that dependable automated vulnerability repair still requires independent validation and human oversight.

SecAwareCoder should therefore be regarded as a research framework rather than a production-ready defense, and its outputs still require independent testing, complementary security analysis, and human review.

Such signals are often noisy and incomplete: static rules can produce both false positives and false negatives, while crash-oriented fuzzing yields sparse, non-deterministic feedback and may miss semantic, non-crashing vulnerabilities.

Moreover, some benchmarks explicitly reveal the intended mitigation in the task description or prompt, which can turn security into a form of instruction following and inflate measured robustness without reflecting a model’s ability to infer and apply defenses from the vulnerability context.

Prompt-based methods can be brittle because their effectiveness depends on retrieval quality, prompt composition, and exemplar relevance, and they may not provide comprehensive task-specific coverage of security-critical regions.
(1) The Problem is clear and unambiguous, specifies well-defined expected behavior, and does not disclose the targeted vulnerability type or provide explicit mitigation guidance.

tecnicas.nome_original: LLM-driven program repair framework (Proposed Framework with RAG)
tecnicas.localizador: Seção III-A e Fig. 2, p. 3 do PDF; Seção III-B e Figs. 3 e 5, p. 4; Fig. 11 (Apêndice II), p. 8; Tabela II, p. 5; Fig. 6, p. 6 (páginas sem numeração impressa)
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote híbrido: pré-processamento com o LLM para detectar erros potenciais, scripts tradicionais de reparo (fora do escopo), reparo com RAG (templates de correção com mensagem de erro, exemplo de violação, orientação e exemplos de correção), reparo iterativo com a mensagem de erro do compilador HLS e, depois, otimização de largura de bits, verificação de equivalência e otimização PPA. Mecanismos da condição de reparo: papel de especialista e diretrizes (instrucao); código completo, erros do compilador e orientação do manual (contexto); exemplos de violação e de correção nos templates (exemplos); reparo iterativo guiado pelo erro de compilação (feedback); etapas encadeadas pré-processamento → reparo (decomposicao); pedido de código completo sem outras palavras (restricoes). Contrafactual de pacote: o framework contra «GPT-4 Turbo directly» (Tabela II, Fig. 6); o ganho não se atribui a um ingrediente isolado. Os mecanismos acrescentados são incertos porque o prompt do baseline não é descrito; não se sabe se o baseline recebia as mensagens de erro e as cinco consultas por instância («In each instance, the LLM was queried five times...», p. 5), por isso feedback e restricoes não constam como acrescentados.

tecnicas.localizador: Seção III-A item 2, p. 3 do PDF; Seção III-B e Fig. 3, p. 4; Fig. 6 e texto, p. 6
tecnicas.observacao: Componente do sistema proposto. O estudo compara o framework com «GPT joint scripts (ablation experiments without RAG)» na Fig. 6 (rótulo da legenda: «GPT-4 Turbo with Scripts»). O estudo chama a condição de ablação sem RAG, mas não descreve se ela preserva o pré-processamento com LLM e o reparo iterativo; o rótulo sugere apenas GPT-4 Turbo com scripts. Se outros ingredientes também faltarem, o contraste não seria de ingrediente único. Recuperação por similaridade (sentence transformer) de templates com orientação do manual (contexto) e exemplos de violação e correção (exemplos).

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we propose an automated LLM-driven C/C++ program repair framework for HLS, which employs an LLM-based search and iterative repair process to eliminate HLS-incompatible errors while enhancing hardware performance.
However, due to the limited training of LLMs considering hardware and software simultaneously, hallucinations may occur during program repair using LLMs, leading to compilation failures.
Besides, using LLMs for iterative repair also incurs a high cost.
These templates are matched through an embedding retrieval mechanism to enhance the quality of input prompts for LLMs, which leads to a 23.33% increase in the repair pass rate.

Since the compiler may not be able to detect all errors in a single compilation, the common HLS-incompatible errors, along with the complete program, are fed into LLM to detect other potential errors.
citacoes.localizador: Seção III-A item 1, p. 3 do PDF

citacoes.trecho: A repair library containing correction templates for HLS is manually established, which is built with human guidance and from the official documentation of HLS tools.
citacoes.localizador: Seção III-A item 2, p. 3 do PDF

citacoes.trecho: If the compilation of C_Ref fails, the error message will be fed back to the LLM for iterative repair.
citacoes.localizador: Seção III-A item 2, p. 3 do PDF

citacoes.trecho: LLMs are prone to producing hallucinations, especially in the interdisciplinary field such as HLS that requires both software and hardware knowledge.
After synthesizing the HLS-C program into a corresponding RTL code, the C-RTL co-simulation is performed for equivalence verification.
citacoes.localizador: Seção III-A item 4, p. 3 do PDF

citacoes.trecho: Each template integrates the error message from the compiler log, a violation example, corresponding guidance context, and correction examples extracted from the manual of the HLS tool.
This technique sends the C/C++ code, corresponding task scenarios, and the descriptions of input data to the LLM as prompts.
To minimize the repair cost of using LLMs, we first use traditional HLS repair scripts, which run efficiently on the local CPU to repair the HLS-incompatible errors in the regular C/C++ program.

The most suitable optimization strategies will be matched via a similarity search, such as a sentence transformer [28], and then integrated into the prompts, utilizing the LLM’s in-context learning capabilities to generate an optimized program.
In each instance, the LLM was queried five times to repair the program based on the errors reported by the HLS tool.
Fig. 6 compares the simulation pass rate of the proposed framework with those using GPT-4 Turbo directly and GPT joint scripts (ablation experiments without RAG) for program repair, respectively.
According to this comparison, pre-repairing simple errors with scripts locally can significantly reduce the overall repair costs of only using the LLM by 21.56% on average.
System Prompt: You are an expert in repairing the High-Level Synthesis (HLS) incompatible errors in the regular C/C++ program.
Please provide a completely corrected HLS-compatible C++ code, no other words.

citacoes.trecho: In this study, we investigate the impact of different prompting techniques on the security of code generated from NL instructions by LLMs.
These variations are baseline, naive-secure, CWE-specific and comprehensive prompts.
The baseline prompt does not include any security information in the task instruction.

Following the recommendation from [52], we utilized the trigger phrase ’Let’s think step by step’, along with explicit demand to generate secure code in the remaining part of the prompt as shown in Table 2.
Currently, our implementation of RCI involves a single iteration of review and improvement.
We employed the persona of a "software security expert" to prompt LLMs towards generating security-conscious code.
Our findings reaffirm the fact that LLM-generated code contains a large number of security weaknesses mainly related to CWE-78, CWE-259, CWE-94, and CWE-330.
However, this approach can be expensive due to the iterative nature of the process.
However, GPT-4 (gpt-4-1105-preview) was trained on data up to April 2023, suggesting a slight risk of leakage since the GitHub repository predates this one.
The average similarity score obtained for all the code generated using RCI technique and the secure implementation present in the LLMSecEval dataset is 0.075.
Since this study exclusively relied on API interactions, there is no risk of indirect data leakage.
The validity analysis of code responses generated by all LLMs was conducted by a single author, potentially introducing biases in the evaluation process.
We also note that the responses generated by the LLMs were not subjected to a randomness check.
Some specific security weaknesses may have gone undetected.
Code snippets with incomplete logic were removed from our security analysis in the code validity analysis step.
However, it is noteworthy that in many cases, the actual implementation within these methods remains unaltered, despite the suggestive ’secure’ prefixes in the method names.
We obtained a Kappa value of 0.87 averaged over the results of 7 prompting techniques from the 3 LLMs.
To facilitate the maximum reproducibility of our results, we set the value of the temperature parameter to 0.0.
Static analysis tools like Bandit and CodeQL seem to be able to detect the issues that LLMs may overlook (such as CWE-259, CWE-94, CWE-78).

riscos.descricao: Vazamento direto: os benchmarks HumanEval e MBPP são amplamente replicados (todo prompt do HumanEval aparece em buscas no GitHub, mínimo de 43 ocorrências) e os LLMs modernos podem ter sido treinados com esses dados de avaliação.

Filtros de descontaminação baseados em correspondência superficial (n-gramas, hashing) têm baixa revocação para código; o vazamento também pode ocorrer incrementalmente quando o uso real de modelos via API, que inclui avaliações de terceiros, é anotado para treino futuro.
Vazamento indireto por dados sintéticos de treino (evol-instruct, Starcoder2-Instruct), com alta similaridade entre prompts desses conjuntos e prompts do HumanEval/MBPP.
riscos.localizador: p. 3, seção 3.2, Fig. 2 e Tabelas 3 e 5 (p. 7 e p. 9)

riscos.descricao: Sobreajuste aos conjuntos de teste durante a seleção de modelos ou checkpoints, que o estudo inclui entre as fontes de contaminação.
O próprio LBPP pode sofrer vazamento futuro após sua liberação pública; os autores reconhecem que esse vazamento não poderá ser controlado.
Validade da avaliação: escores em HumanEval/MBPP podem distorcer a percepção do desempenho em uso real, e os rankings de modelos mudam entre esses benchmarks e o LBPP.

mitigacoes.descricao: Construção do LBPP por anotadores com experiência em programação competitiva: problemas novos, não resolvidos por um modelo interno forte no laço, sem cópia de fontes da web ou de LLMs, verificação manual de que os prompts não são facilmente encontrados na web, revisão adicional (cerca de um terço das propostas desqualificadas) e revisão manual final pelos autores. O estudo apresenta evidência indireta (menor similaridade com conjuntos sintéticos na Fig. 2; LBPP inalterado após ajuste fino com evol-instruct), mas não mede o efeito do procedimento contra uma condição controlada sem ele.
Liberação do LBPP como substituto ou complemento dos conjuntos de avaliação atuais, para avaliar LLMs em cenário livre de contaminação.

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we consider contamination by code generation test sets, in particular in their use in modern large language models.

We discuss three possible sources of such contamination and show findings supporting each of them: (i) direct data leakage, (ii) indirect data leakage through the use of synthetic data and (iii) overfitting to evaluation sets during model selection.
To address this, we release LBPP: an uncontaminated new benchmark of 161 prompts with their associated Python solutions.
LBPP is a dataset of 161 code completion problems in the style of HumanEval.
All prompts include evaluation unit tests, with a median of 4 tests per example.
Table 2: Pass@1 results across popular models for zero-shot HumanEval, MBPP and LBPP.
All models perform worse on LBPP than either existing benchmark.
Rankings between models change between HumanEval and LBPP, contrasting to Riddell et al. (2021).
Notably, leading models for HumanEval and MBPP perform up to 43% and 27% poorer on LBPP respectively.
In Section 4, we observe that SOTA models on HumanEval perform up to 43% worse on LBPP.

A condição avaliada pelos modelos-alvo é o problema concatenado à lista de restrições (x ⊕ C_t, Eq. 1, p. 5) com o mesmo prompt de resolução de problemas do Apêndice D, que traz papel e diretrizes (instrucao) e restrições de formato da saída (restricoes); a técnica acrescenta a proibição explícita de técnicas de programação («DO NOT use the following techniques»). Na construção do conjunto (modelo de aumento GPT-4), o estudo também usa um único fio de conversa com as interações anteriores e um prompt de detecção de técnicas que escolhe a próxima restrição (p. 4); o estudo não informa que esse histórico entra no prompt dos modelos-alvo na avaliação. Os resultados são relatados por estado (rodada de negação: Tabela 3, Figuras 4, 5 e 7). O estado 0 não tem restrições, mas nos estados seguintes o problema e o critério de correção mudam (seguimento das restrições entra na métrica convergente) e o número de problemas diminui (Tabela 1, p. 5); o estudo não apresenta condição comparável sem a técnica, e os estados funcionam como níveis do benchmark.

riscos.descricao: Apesar de recentes, os problemas do NeoCoder podem ser expostos a futuros LLMs no pré-treinamento; o estudo também levanta a hipótese de que o Llama3 foi pré-treinado em problemas e soluções humanas do Codeforces, o que explicaria seu desempenho convergente superior ao GPT-4 em t = 0. Contaminação efetiva não é verificada.

Ao pressionar humanos ou LLMs a buscar soluções mais criativas (mais restrições), há grande probabilidade de erros e de cópia de soluções anteriores; o estudo descreve um trade-off entre qualidade e novidade da solução.

Respostas alucinadas podem ter alta H-criatividade, mas frequentemente carecem de correção e de seguimento das restrições; LLMs com capacidade de raciocínio insuficiente tendem a inventar soluções novas independentemente da qualidade diante de problemas incomuns.

citacoes.trecho: In our experiments, we apply DENIAL PROMPTING on Codeforces, a challenging Text-to-Code task where model solutions can be automatically verified and allows comparison to substantial historical human solutions.

We introduce DENIAL PROMPTING which pushes LLMs to develop more creative solutions to a given problem by incrementally imposing new constraints on the previous solution, compelling LLMs to adopt new strategies.
Finally, we update the problem x to x⊕τ1 which explicitly prohibits the use of the technique τ1 and update constraint list C0 to C1 = {τ1}.
We apply the same problem-solving prompt in both DENIAL PROMPTING and the benchmarking process.
