citacoes.trecho: We evaluate four reasoning strategies on our NEOCODER dataset to further study the correlation between augmented machine intelligence and creativity: Whether such intelligence-enhancing techniques also improve creative thinking?
MCTS: Zhang et al. (2023) propose a novel decoding method that uses Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to generate better programs using the pass rate as reward.
Self-Correction: Shinn et al. (2023) use verbal feedback from a reflection agent to reinforce the performance of an agent in code generation.
Planning: Jiang et al. (2023b) design a planning module to let LLM plan out concise solution steps from the intent, followed by an implementation module to generate code step by step.
Sampling: Chen et al. (2021) generate k samples and compute the probability that at least one of the k-generated code samples for a problem passes the unit tests.
For creativity evaluation, we generate k = 5 samples for each problem and report the NEOGAUGE from samples that have the highest convergent and divergent creativity
citacoes.localizador: p. 9 (PDF), §5.3 (a frase continua com a fórmula da Eq. 4)

citacoes.trecho: Following the parameter choice by Zhang et al. (2023), we apply a sampling temperature of 1 for code generation.
We use gpt-4-1106-preview across all experiments, accessed from Dec 2023 through April 2024.
Despite their recency, future LLMs might get exposure to these problems during their pretraining.
We hypothesize that the latest Llama3 models are pre-trained on Codeforces problems and human solutions, so they have superior performance when there is no external constraint t = 0.
When stress-testing humans or LLMs to look for more creative solutions, they are very likely to make mistakes and may copy previous solutions during the process.
Alternatively, LLMs’ hallucinated responses resulting in high H-creativity, but often lack correctness and constraint following (e.g., state t = 1).
Considering the computation complexity and the cost, we re-evaluate MCTS on the open-source language model (CodeGemma-7B (Google, 2024)) and re-evaluate others on the proprietary model (GPT-3.5).
Furthermore, we selected the recent data to prevent any memorization during pre-training (Huang et al., 2023).
To alleviate such risks, future works can focus on more difficult problems or evaluate NEOGAUGE for higher states, besides incorporating a newer batch of problems.

On the other hand, self-correction and planning sacrifice their divergent thinking ability in improving their convergent thinking because the divergent creativity difference even goes to negative at certain states (e.g., Divergent Diff = −1.2 at t = 0,3 on sampling).
Conversely, only MCTS successfully enhances divergent creativity, due to it rolling out numerous paths during the expansion.
We also experiment with advanced reasoning strategies (MCTS, self-correction, etc.) and observe no significant improvement in creativity.

citacoes.trecho: By leveraging a repository of existing code translations, we dynamically retrieve the most relevant examples to guide the model in translating new code segments.

Extensive experiments on diverse datasets, using open LLM models such as Starcoder, Llama3-70B Instruct, CodeLlama-34B Instruct, Granite-34B Code Instruct, and Mixtral-8x22B, and commercial LLM models such as GPT-3.5 turbo, and GPT-4o demonstrate the superiority of our approach over traditional zero-shot, particularly in translating between Fortran and C++.
Despite these advancements, the accuracy and reliability of these models often falter in complex translation tasks due to a lack of contextual understanding.
System: You are adept at translating Fortran code into CPP with high accuracy, ensuring that all syntax, semantics, and specific language features are correctly and efficiently converted

citacoes.trecho: For Zero-shot comparisons, we apply the zero-shot translation prompt template (Figure 3) with the Fortran code to be translated.
Once the embeddings are generated, the system dynamically retrieves the most similar examples based on cosine similarity or Euclidean distance.
The retreived translation pairs are then augmented with the original query and directed to LLM for translation.
Each experiment aimed to measure the improvements in translation quality facilitated by the RAG approach using CodeBLEU as the primary evaluation metric.

citacoes.trecho: Specifically, the comparisons are made for Figure 5a Granite-34B Code Instruct on the Numerical Recipes Dataset, Figure 5b Granite-34B Code Instruct on the HPC Fortran2CPP Dataset, and Figure 5c Granite-34B Code Instruct on the HPC Fortran2CPP Dataset with a poorly configured RAG setup (utilizing the largest distance metric as retrieval).
When the utilized retrieval metric is altered, this brings a significant change in performances.
Given the longer length of Fortran codes to be translated, the limited token capacity of CodeBERT likely hindered its performance.
Mixtral-8x22B exhibited high variance in the Numerical Recipes dataset, especially in CodeBLEU and Ngram scores, suggesting inconsistency in its translation quality.
Additionally, Starcoder did not show significant improvement in one-shot settings, likely due to its smaller context length.
This plateau in performance can be attributed to GPT models prioritizing the generation of executable and semantically correct code over strict alignment with ground truth translations.
One downside of this dataset is that it relies on a specific library of functions, which may limit its general applicability.

citacoes.trecho: Few-shot learning consistently enhanced translation performance across all models and embeddings.

The progressive improvement from one-shot to three-shot learning configurations was evident, with models like Granite-34B Code Instruct, Llama3-70B Instruct, and Mixtral-8x22B showing substantial gains as shown in Table II.
For instance, CodeLlama-34B Instruct achieved a zero-shot CodeBLEU of 0.243 with Nomic-embed, which improved to 0.321 in the two-shot configuration.

For instance, Granite-34B Code Instruct with nomic_embed improved from a zero-shot CodeBLEU of 0.24 ± 0.09 to 0.60 ± 0.27 in the one-shot setting, further improving to 0.540.27 and 0.54 ± 0.21 in the two-shot and three-shot settings, respectively.
Notably, GPT-4 Turbo and GPT-3.5 Turbo achieved the highest zero-shot CodeBLEU scores of 0.371 and 0.367, respectively, indicating their strong initial performance without additional context.
For instance, Granite-34B Code Instruct with CodeBERT embedding achieved a one-shot CodeBLEU of 0.6 on the HPC Fortran2CPP dataset, whereas it scored 0.49 ± 0.20 on the Numerical Recipes dataset.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote: designação de papel («You are an Automated Program Repair tool») e descrição da tarefa → instrucao; função defeituosa no prompt → contexto; dois exemplos (função defeituosa, cadeia de raciocínio e função corrigida) selecionados de um pool construído automaticamente na fase de coleta → exemplos; indicador «Let's think step by step» e CoT nos exemplos → raciocinio; reapresentação da mensagem de falha dos testes em até 5 interações → feedback; até 25 sessões independentes com verificação por testes → amostragem. Os acrescentados referem-se ao comparador BaseChatGPT (Basic LLM), descrito como reparo com exemplos de correções existentes e sem CoT nem feedback; o número de tentativas e a temperatura dos Basic LLMs são nao_informado, de modo que não é possível dizer se amostragem é compartilhada ou acrescentada. Pacote híbrido: a seleção padrão (Contrastive-based Selection) usa codificador UniXcoder ajustado por aprendizado contrastivo (fora do escopo). O contraste com os Basic LLMs (Table 3) e com Zero-Shot/Few-Shot (Table 8) isola o pacote, não um mecanismo único. No QuixBugs, os autores usaram 2 exemplos projetados manualmente, sem fase de coleta (p. 6 do PDF).

citacoes.trecho: Automated Program Repair (APR) is a promising approach to automatically fix bugs in computer programs, which can significantly reduce debugging time and enhance software reliability.
The former phase automatically collects various chains of thoughts that constitute pre-fixed knowledge by instructing LLMs with the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt.
The latter phase targets fixing a bug by first selecting examples for few-shot learning and second automatically interacting with LLMs, optionally appending with feedback of testing information.
ThinkRepair starts a role for LLM with an instruction like “You are an Automated Program Repair tool”.
In this paper, we follow the best practice in previous work [58] and adopt the same prompt named “Let’s think step by step”.
Here, the failing information is added into a template: “The fixed version is still not correct. {test failure message}. Please fix it again. Let’s think step by step.”
Contrastive-based Selection utilizes the contrastive learning framework R-Drop [46] to further fine-tune UniXcoder for better semantic embedding.
The maximum number of repair attempts is set to 25 (i.e., 25 independent sessions) for ThinkRepair as the default for auto-fixing the single function bugs.
A sampling temperature of 1 is utilized to obtain a diverse set of potential patches [16].

In addition, we build baseline approaches, BaseChatGPT, BaseCodeLlama, BaseDeepSeek, and BaseStarCoder, which utilize the basic LLMs to perform a repair (i.e., directly using existing bug-fixing data as examples) without any Chains-of-Thoughts reasoning process and feedback information.
Zero-Shot means that we directly prompt ChatGPT to fix a bug without providing any other information.
Few-Shot means that we provide ChatGPT with two examples of fixes but do not include CoT information (i.e., directly using existing bug-fixing data as examples).
We build a variant of ThinkRepair without interaction feedback as ThinkRepair-v1 and another variant without CoT few-shot learning as ThinkRepair-v2.
All of our ablation experiments utilize the default settings outlined in Section 4.3.

Since QuixBugs dataset has the limited number of functions (i.e., 40 for both Java and Python), for comprehensively evaluating the performance differences, we adhere to the best-practice guide [55], manually designed 2 examples for fixing bugs without the collection phase.

Since all of the studied baselines were already evaluated on Defects4J, following the convention in APR work [61, 62], we directly compare the auto-fix results obtained in previous studies [61–63] under the same settings.
The reason may be attributed to ThinkRepair’s inclination to excessively modify bugs stemming from over-inferring.
We find that out of 98 correct patches, 24 of them lexically match the ground-truth (24.5%), while the other patches semantically match the ground-truth.
The second one comes from potential data leakage since referenced developer patches may be part of the training data of LLM.
The first internal threat arises from the manual validation employed to determine the correctness of the plausible patches.
To mitigate this concern, we conduct a thorough examination and comprehensive discussion of each patch, following prior work [21, 61, 62, 64, 65, 67].
Defects4J V1.2 and Defects4J V2.0 are two completely independent versions, with no overlapping bugs between them.

The first dataset (RWB V1.0) comprises bug-fixing commits after October 2021, while the second dataset (RWB V2.0) includes bug-fixing commits after March 2023, resulting 113 and 61 bugs, respectively.

Moreover, even after excluding all the correct patches (24) that aligned with the reference developer patch, ThinkRepair is still capable of generating the correct patch for 29 unique bugs, none of which could be fixed by any previous methods.
However, when continuously increasing the number of interactions, the rate of performance improvement decreases (i.e., 75→80) and meanwhile, the interaction cost with ChatGPT is increasing.

citacoes.trecho: The effectiveness observed in ThinkRepair’s performance may not be applicable across different repair datasets.
We observe that with perfect fault information, ThinkRepair demonstrates superior performance across all projects compared to Basic LLMs.
ThinkRepair can outperform the BaseChatGPT in all settings.
A plausible patch is a patch that can pass all test cases but is not semantically equivalent to the actual fix.
Following the previous work [61, 62], we also manually check and identify the plausible patches that are semantically equivalent to the actual fixes.
We evaluate data leakage on both ChatGPT and DeepSeek, denoting them as ThinkRepair and ThinkRepair*, respectively.
To facilitate comparison, we employ the top two performing models, ChatGPT and CodeLlama, in the following sections of our results, denoting them as ThinkRepair and ThinkRepair*, respectively.

riscos.descricao: A formulação do prompt altera de forma acentuada a correção por tarefa: o Pass@1 na mesma tarefa pode dobrar para 10% a 30% das tarefas do benchmark para um dado modelo, embora a média mude pouco.

Prompts originais mal formulados induzem soluções erradas: em 7 das 9 tarefas do ClassEval e em 1 tarefa do HumanEval+ com discriminação negativa e baixa dificuldade, os autores encontraram problemas na formulação dos prompts originais (e nos prompts derivados deles).

Modelos mais capazes acrescentam suposições não pedidas e geram código desnecessariamente complexo (Listing 7); CodeLLMs fundem condições do enunciado e erram tarefas com várias condições (Listing 8).
No exemplo do ClassEval, vários CodeLLMs alucinaram métodos não definidos.
Tarefas com discriminação negativa e alta dificuldade são atribuídas em parte ao não determinismo e ao pequeno número de CodeLLMs; usar subconjuntos de modelos aumentou a proporção dessas tarefas.

Os autores mencionam possível memorização como explicação de comportamentos (exemplo memorizado; uso de type vs isinstance) e citam contaminação de dados como limitação de benchmarks tradicionais. O estudo não afirma contaminação efetiva nem descreve controle.
riscos.localizador: PDF p. 2 (Seção 1); PDF p. 12; PDF p. 21 (Seção 5.2)

riscos.descricao: Custo tratado na Discussão: geração de prompts com GPT-4 turbo de 50$ para ~6.500 prompts (0,007$/prompt); 5$ para cada modelo fechado (0,0002$/inferência); modelos abertos em uma GPU de 32 GB com menos de uma hora cada. A verificação manual dos prompts, descrita dentro da mesma subseção de custo, levou «several dozen hours of work» e é apontada como fator limitante da escalabilidade.

Viés de construção: usar o GPT-4 para gerar os prompts pode favorecer um modelo treinado de forma semelhante (GPT-3.5); a remoção dos exemplos dos prompts pode reduzir o desempenho e criar tarefas artificialmente difíceis; a dependência local entre prompts da mesma tarefa pode violar o pressuposto do IRT.

Validade da comparação humana: no piloto, participantes tenderam a usar LLMs apesar da proibição, o que levou a substituir a implementação por estimativa de esforço; a dificuldade humana reflete percepção subjetiva.

mitigacoes.descricao: Verificação manual dos prompts após cada template, feita pelo primeiro autor e conferida de forma independente pelo segundo, para garantir níveis de informação e preservação da semântica.
Validação dos prompts por BERTScore e teste de Wilcoxon (reformulações do mesmo nível mais próximas entre si) e por modelos IRT por nível.
GPT-4 não usado como CodeLLM para evitar viés, por ser o gerador dos prompts.
Agregação dos resultados dos prompts da mesma tarefa em «testlets» para atenuar a dependência local do IRT.
Remoção dos exemplos do prompt original para controlar a quantidade de informação injetada.
Múltiplos limiares de CodeBLEU (0,4 a 0,8) com correção de Holm-Bonferroni para que a significância não dependa do limiar.
Estimativa de esforço em rodadas (Alhamed et al.), revisão manual das respostas dos participantes e filtro de experiência mínima de 3 anos.

observacoes.descricao: TaskEval tem três componentes: geração de prompts por transformações (Context Information e Rephrasing) com um Prompt LLM (GPT-4), geração e avaliação de código por 8 CodeLLMs, e ajuste IRT. São 3 níveis × 6 reformulações = 18 prompts por tarefa e 5 amostras por prompt.
Esforço manual descrito: verificação manual dos prompts por dois autores, refinamento manual dos nomes dos tópicos e revisão manual das respostas dos participantes.
observacoes.localizador: PDF p. 9; PDF p. 14; PDF p. 16

observacoes.descricao: As perguntas de pesquisa tratam da dificuldade de tarefas (RQ1–RQ4); nenhuma compara técnicas de prompting. O único contraste sistemático entre condições de prompt é a validação por nível de informação (Seção 5.1).
Pacote de replicação indicado (github.com/FlowSs/TaskEval); não acessado nem validado nesta extração.

citacoes.trecho: TaskEval starts by generating a variety of prompts for each task on two well-known code generation benchmarks, HumanEval+ [16] and ClassEval [23], representing multiple possible formulations per task.
In our study, we focus on two transformations: Rephrasing and Context Information.
In our study, we instead propose to divide the information provided in the prompt into three levels.
Those three levels of prompts are generated incrementally using the previous level as the starting point.
First level: contains a minimal amount of information that is the inputs/outputs of the task, as well as a high-level description of what is intended.
Second level: further adds in the prompt a description of the targeted function in natural language using available oracle code.
Third level: complete the prompt with direct references to the function, such as variable names, and helper functions used similarly to a pseudo-algorithm but in natural language.
The second transformation used is Rephrasing, which is paraphrasing a given prompt.
Other techniques could be used to assist in rephrasing/information, such as Chains-Of-Thoughts [87], but assessing the effectiveness of additional techniques is out of the scope of this study.
In our case, we first remove the examples from the original prompt, if any, before using our templates with the Prompt LLM.
This is accomplished by the first author and cross-checked by the second author independently.
Both prompts also included the class constructor and description to provide the CodeLLMs with general context.

In our case, we use the compositional strategy, that is, providing the class context to the LLM and asking it to complete one method of the class, only modifying the docstring of the method to complete through our crafted prompts.
To have different prompts, we choose to generate 3 levels and 6 rephrasings per level.

For all code generation in TaskEval, since we are using sampling generation, we set the temperature hyperparameter to 0.8 as it is one of the temperature settings commonly used in other similar studies [16, 50, 52, 68].
We have not used GPT-4 as CodeLLM to avoid biases, as it is used to generate the prompts fed to the CodeLLM.
Several CodeLLMs struggled on multiple points: the implicit fact that, if the dish is added, the quantity should be lowered, hallucinating undefined methods, handling the non-required sales, etc.

More generally, if we were to compute the pass@1 per task for different rephrasing, while we would observe limited change in the average Pass@1 (0.01 to 0.03 standard deviation for HumanEval+ across models and rephrasing and 0.02 to 0.05 for ClassEval), the Pass@1 on the same task can double from 10% to 30% of the benchmarks tasks for a given model, that is the correctness can be drastically altered by the prompt formulation.

Among the 9 tasks from ClassEval and 1 task from HumanEval+, we found issues in the way the original prompts (and so our prompts generated from them) were formulated for 7 of them in ClassEval and 1 in HumanEval+.
In that case, this can be explained by both non-determinism in the prompts and the small number of CodeLLMs used.
This can be indicative of the specificity of the training dataset or, in the worst case, some form of memorisation.
Analysing the tasks within the topic, we observe that more capable models often infer additional assumptions about the task, leading to unnecessarily complex generated code.
Observing CodeLLMs’ codes, it is clear that the CodeLLMs struggle with handling the two conditions, especially the last one.
For the prompt generation, using GPT-4 turbo, this amounted to 50$ for all tasks and all levels (∼6,500 prompts), accounting for rerun when correcting them, resulting in 0.007$/prompt.
For the prompt verification, this had to be done manually, which translated to several dozen hours of work.
For the closed-source model (GPT3.5 and DeepSeek-V3), the cost was 5$ each, for all tasks and all prompts, resulting in 0.0002$/inference.
Choosing GPT4 for prompt generation might unintentionally bias the evaluation by benefiting a model trained similarly (GPT3.5).
This, as we mentioned, can decrease the performance of the models and so add artificially hard tasks.
To avoid a potential local dependence effect, we aggregate results of prompts for the same task, effectively building polytomous superitems or “testlets” [80, 81].

However, a pilot study with 10 developers for 12 tasks we conducted revealed that several participants are inclined to use LLMs to code for themselves, despite it being forbidden as advertised in the study.
We make the data and code used in our study publicly available for researchers to replicate our results [8].

riscos.descricao: Erros em cascata: como código e testes dependem dos requisitos gerados, requisitos errados podem se propagar; o estudo sugere medidas adicionais.

Baixa acurácia dos casos de teste de borda gerados (49% no HumanEval e 18% no CodeContests, Tabela 15), que podem aceitar ou rejeitar código indevidamente; o estudo argumenta que o ranqueamento é pouco afetado.

As cadeias de raciocínio fornecidas pelo Self-planning se baseiam nos exemplos de teste e poderiam contaminar o HumanEval; o estudo as usou apenas para gerar cadeias para os exemplos em contexto. Contaminação no pré-treinamento não é discutida.
Possível geração de código com vulnerabilidades de segurança ou problemas de safety, citando Chen et al. (2021); não avaliado empiricamente.
Custos computacionais e de tempo de execução de muitos casos de teste na filtragem de código; o estudo quantifica o número de testes gerados (Figura 4, Tabela 14), mas não custo monetário ou tempo.
Condicionar a geração de código aos testes (ao estilo TDD) introduz dependência sequencial e maior latência; custo não quantificado.
Considerar todos os RNF ao mesmo tempo pode prejudicar a manutenibilidade (ARCHCODE não é o melhor nessa categoria na Tabela 2), segundo conjectura do estudo.
Trade-off entre desempenho de tempo e os demais RNF, invocado para explicar resultados do controle de preferências.

mitigacoes.descricao: Usar as cadeias do Self-planning apenas para gerar cadeias de raciocínio dos exemplos em contexto, em vez de usá-las diretamente, para evitar contaminação no HumanEval.
Intervenção humana ou autocorreção por LLMs para mitigar erros em cascata (proposta, não executada).
Requisitos padrão, delimitação do escopo permitido do código gerado e garantia de que o código fique dentro de limites autorizados (proposta para riscos de segurança).
Controle de qualidade dos testes do HumanEval-NFR: descarte dos testes de RF que o código de referência não passa e validação manual dos testes de RNF por três autores.
Validação manual dos requisitos gerados em três problemas escolhidos aleatoriamente.

citacoes.trecho: This paper aims to extend the code generation capability of large language models (LLMs) to automatically manage comprehensive software requirements from given textual descriptions.
We introduce ARCHCODE, a novel framework that leverages in-context learning to organize requirements observed in descriptions and to extrapolate unexpressed requirements from them.
ARCHCODE generates requirements from given descriptions, conditioning them to produce code snippets and test cases.
To return the satisfactory code towards r̂, ARCHCODE conducts code filtering.

ARCHCODE uses three reasoning chains when generating code: the initial program outline (the same reasoning chains as in GPT-3.5-Turbo + CoT), requirements described in Subsection 3.1 and Appendix D, and the final program outline—the revised version of the initial program outline, modified to meet the requirements.
We generated n = 10 code samples for every problem in the benchmarks.
Throughout the benchmarks, we consider three baselines: GPT-3.5-Turbo and its CoT prompting applied version of Self-planning (Jiang et al., 2023), and CODET (Chen et al., 2023).
'− Filtering' denotes an ablated version of ARCHCODE, without code filtering.
'+ NFR Instruction' means that the further prompt engineered instruction for NFR consideration shown in Table 13 is applied.
In the 'Preference Control by Instruction' setting, all NFRs are included in the prompt, and an additional instruction to prioritize specific NFR(s) is appended.
In the 'Plug-and-Play' setting, only targeted NFRs are included in the few-shot examples, while no preference among them is assumed.
Using dedicated test cases for filtering consistently outperforms blindly using all test cases.
However, directly using the reasoning chains provided by Self-planning can result in data contamination on HumanEval because these chains are based on the test examples.
Thus, rather using them directly, we utilized them to generate the reasoning chains for the aforementioned in-context examples, then used the generated reasoning chains for ICL.

Lastly, as ARCHCODE relies on generated requirements to guide subsequent code and test case generation process, although qualitative analysis suggests its impact could be limited in practice, additional measures to mitigate cascading errors via human intervention or self-correction by LLMs, etc. (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024) can be necessitated.

However, to maximize these advantages while addressing potential risks, such as the creation of code with safety or security vulnerabilities as discussed in Chen et al. (2021), careful consideration is essential.
citacoes.localizador: PDF p. 10, Ethical and Social Implications

citacoes.trecho: Strategies to mitigate these risks include establishing default requirements for desired outcomes, delineating the permissible scope of generated code, and ensuring that the code remains within its authorized boundaries.
citacoes.localizador: PDF p. 10, Ethical and Social Implications

citacoes.trecho: In code filtering, a crucial step involves minimizing the number of generated test cases to reduce computational and time costs for code execution.
This suggests the overhead from introducing new sequential dependency in the generation process might not be worth the additional costs incurred.

Our conjecture is that, as which NFR categories to prioritize is uninformed in this experiment, ARCHCODE's consideration of all NFRs could potentially impede maintainability due to the influence of other categories.

Although the accuracy of generated edge cases is relatively low, they still play a key role in code filtering as evidentiated by the performance discrepancy between ARCHCODE and CODET (w/o clustering) presented in Tables 4.

Notably, the plug-and-play approach considering all but time performance showed the best Pass@k scores, which we attribute to the trade-off between time performance and the rest of the NFRs: focusing on the other requirements is relatively free of negative interference that would hurt the performance.
First, we generated candidate test cases based on the existing HumanEval problems using ARCHCODE based on GPT-3.5-Turbo.
Those that the ground truth code does not pass were discarded.
For candidate test cases verifying NFRs, three authors manually validated the quality of generated test cases.

tecnicas.observacao: Prompt base de todas as condições: instrução curta («### Instruction: Please complete the code.») seguida do cenário sensível à segurança (trecho de código C/C++ incompleto a completar). A instrução foi classificada como `instrucao`; o trecho de código fornecido como insumo, como `contexto` (regra D102 de código fornecido no prompt). É a condição de referência (linha «Pretrained» da Tabela 6, modelo pré-treinado sem ajuste fino); não há condição sem ela.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 19–20 (PDF e impressa), RQ2/Approach; p. 21, quadro «Prompt Template for the Generic Security» e Tabela 6
tecnicas.observacao: Acrescenta ao prompt base uma única frase de restrição de segurança («Make sure that the generated code is secure, meaning it does not contain any security vulnerabilities»), classificada como `restricoes` (restrição de segurança em linguagem natural; a categoria `instrucao` já está no prompt base). O estudo apresenta os prompts orientados à segurança como abordagens baseadas em prompt comparadas ao ajuste fino (objeto focal do estudo), por isso o papel é `comparador`. O contraste com o prompt original (linha «Pretrained» da Tabela 6) mantém modelo, cenários, 30 amostras por cenário e temperatura 0,8 (p. 20), diferindo só na frase acrescentada.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 20 (PDF e impressa), RQ2/Approach; p. 21, quadro «Prompt Template for the Specific Security» e Tabela 6
tecnicas.observacao: Acrescenta ao prompt base uma restrição de segurança dirigida à CWE do cenário («Make sure that the generated code is secure with respect to the CWE-<ID> vulnerability, meaning it does not contain the following security vulnerability: CWE-<ID>:<Description of the CWE>»), com o identificador e a descrição da CWE. A restrição foi classificada como `restricoes`; a descrição da CWE, como conhecimento externo inserido (`contexto`), categoria que no prompt base já aparece pelo código do cenário. Contraste com o prompt original na Tabela 6 = pacote (restrição dirigida + identificador/descrição da CWE); o resultado não pode ser atribuído isoladamente à descrição da CWE. O texto das descrições de CWE usadas não é reproduzido no artigo. Papel `comparador` pelo mesmo motivo da Generic Security.

componentes_fora_escopo.descricao: Atualização de todos os pesos dos quatro modelos com conjuntos de correções de vulnerabilidades (BigVul, CVEfixes, AndroidCVEfixes; 4.900 commits, 14.622 arquivos C/C++), em quatro granularidades (arquivo, função, bloco, linha); usado pelo estudo como linha de base do ajuste fino. Objeto focal do estudo, fora do escopo de prompting.

Ajuste fino eficiente em parâmetros com matrizes de baixo posto (r = 8, α = 16, dropout 0,05, taxa de aprendizado 3e-4, 2 épocas). Técnica focal do estudo; na RQ2 é comparada com os prompts orientados à segurança (linhas «LoRA-tuned» da Tabela 6, resultados reaproveitados da RQ1).
Ajuste fino eficiente em parâmetros por vetores de escala treináveis nas saídas de atenção e feedforward (taxa 3e-4, batch 5, 2 épocas). Técnica focal do estudo; linhas «IA3-tuned» da Tabela 6.

riscos.descricao: Código gerado por LLMs frequentemente contém vulnerabilidades (cibersegurança), herdadas de código humano usado no pré-treinamento; é a motivação do estudo e da comparação entre prompts orientados à segurança e ajuste fino.
riscos.localizador: p. 1–2, resumo e introdução; p. 6, seção 2.3

riscos.descricao: Limitação atribuída pelo estudo às abordagens baseadas em prompt orientado à segurança: dependem da capacidade do usuário ou do LLM de identificar e descrever corretamente o problema de segurança; o aprendizado em contexto é descrito como muito sensível à qualidade das instruções.

Código rotulado como seguro pelo CodeQL pode não implementar a funcionalidade pedida (por exemplo, trecho que só retorna -1, rotulado «secure but functionally incorrect»); a divergência entre a funcionalidade esperada e a gerada não afeta a avaliação de vulnerabilidade. Vale também para as condições de prompting, cujo secure ratio não mede correção funcional.
No ajuste fino (fora do escopo de prompting), o ajuste completo reduz o número de trechos válidos (esquecimento catastrófico) e degrada PASS@1 no HumanEval CPP.
riscos.localizador: p. 15, RQ1/Results; p. 23, RQ3/Results; p. 25, RQ4/Results

riscos.descricao: Validade da medição: o CodeQL pode produzir falsos positivos e falsos negativos na detecção de vulnerabilidades.
riscos.localizador: p. 27, seção 6; p. 29, seção 7.1 «False Positives by CodeQL»

riscos.descricao: LLMs têm aleatoriedade e podem gerar códigos diferentes para o mesmo prompt.
riscos.localizador: p. 29, seção 7.1 «Reproducibility of Code Generation»; p. 12, seção 4.2

riscos.descricao: Limitação estatística declarada: 30 amostras por cenário podem ser insuficientes para conclusões concretas.

Possível sobreposição entre o conjunto de ajuste fino e os cenários de avaliação; o estudo aplicou detecção de sobreposição de 10-gramas e relata ausência de sobreposição (controle registrado em mitigações). O estudo não discute contaminação do pré-treinamento pelos cenários reutilizados de Pearce et al., o que afetaria também as condições de prompting.

O estudo trata o ajuste fino como computacionalmente intensivo e quantifica o custo em horas e memória de GPU (por exemplo, 1378,4 GPU-horas no total). Custo referente ao ajuste fino, não às condições de prompting; o custo dos prompts orientados à segurança não é quantificado.
Validade externa: poucos modelos, linguagens (C/C++, com extensão a Java e Python) e 11 tipos de CWE; resultados podem não se generalizar.

mitigacoes.descricao: Prompts orientados à segurança (Generic Security e Specific Security) como forma de reduzir código vulnerável, comparados com o prompt original sem a instrução de segurança.

Detecção de sobreposição de 10-gramas entre o conjunto de ajuste fino e os cenários de avaliação.

Análise manual para falsos positivos do CodeQL (quatro cenários) e amostra de 378 trechos válidos (pré-treinado, LoRA e IA3, nível de arquivo) para segurança e funcionalidade; não inclui as condições de prompting.
Descarte de trechos com erro de sintaxe ou que não compilam antes da análise pelo CodeQL.

citacoes.trecho: In this work, we present an exploratory study on whether fine-tuning pre-trained LLMs on datasets of vulnerability-fixing commits can promote secure code generation.
Following the approach of the study [19], we introduced two additional security-oriented prompts, Generic Security and Specific Security, to assess their influence on secure code generation.
These were evaluated against the original prompts used in our experiments of RQ1.
In the baseline setting, the prompt simply instructed: “Please complete the code”.

For the Generic Security setting, we appended the instruction: “Make sure that the generated code is secure, meaning it does not contain any security vulnerabilities”, to enforce the model to generate secure code.
The Specific Security setting was further designed to target particular vulnerabilities by including the CWE ID and its description in the prompt template.
All code generation settings, including the generation of 30 samples per scenario and a temperature of 0.8, remained consistent with those used in RQ1.
As defined by Pearce et al. [40], a security-sensitive prompt contains small and incomplete code snippet and LLMs will be asked to generate code.
One of the most severe concerns is that automatically-generated code by LLMs often contains vulnerabilities.
However, these approaches have limitations, as they heavily depend on the user’s ability or the LLM’s ability to identify and describe the security issues accurately.
Moreover, it is highly sensitive to the quality of the instructions (prompts).
Therefore, we label this example as secure but functionally incorrect code.
The mismatch between the provided and expected functionalities may not affect the vulnerability evaluation results from CodeQL.
CodeQL is a static tool to detect vulnerabilities and may produce false positives.
Although we used CodeQL to automatically evaluate the security for the generated code, the results may contain false negatives.
LLMs have randomness and may generate different code in multiple attempts using the same prompt.
To mitigate this threat to validity, we generate 30 samples for each CWE scenario.
The number of samples of each CWE scenario may be insufficient to yield concrete conclusions.
To prevent the evaluation scenarios from appearing in our fine-tuning dataset, we conducted a 10-gram [59] overlap detection.
We found that there is no overlap between the fine-tuning dataset and the evaluation scenarios.
However, fine-tuning is computationally intensive.
Each round costs an average of 28.7 hours of GPU computation, leading to a cumulative requirement of 1378.4 GPU-hours for the entire set of experiments.
We discarded the generated code snippets that contain syntax errors and cannot be compiled.
The secure ratio is the percentage of valid generated code that does not contain vulnerabilities, as assessed by CodeQL.
Overall, the two security-oriented prompts (Generic Security and Specific Security prompts) achieved the highest secure ratio in three out of eight settings.
On average, the Generic Security prompt attained a secure ratio of 59.9%, while the Specific Security prompt achieved 57.5%.
Among the fine-tuned models, the LoRA-tuned models achieved the highest average secure ratio at 60.9%, and IA3-tuned models are 58.5%.
In total, there are 52 security-sensitive scenarios.
However, we select 56 CWE scenarios in total, and there are sub-scenarios for several scenarios, such as CWE-787 has three sub-scenarios, such as CWE-787-0 and CWE-787-1, for the C language.
Our security-sensitive prompt dataset for evaluating LLMs covers 11 CWEs in the top 25 CWEs [35].
We observe maximum improvements in security of 6.4% in C language and 5.0% in C++ language.
We observe an improvement of up to 6.4% for C and 5.4% for C++ when measuring secure ratio using PEFT techniques.

tecnicas.observacao: Apesar do nome, o prompt não pede raciocínio explícito: é um pipeline de duas etapas encadeadas (traduzir o enunciado para o inglês com «Translate the sentence $PROBLEM from $TARGET-LANG to English» e depois gerar código a partir do enunciado traduzido com a mesma instrução do Orig.), classificado como `decomposicao` pelo dicionário; a instrução herdada do Orig. é `instrucao` nas duas condições. O estudo a apresenta como linha de base («strong baselines»), não como proposta, por isso `comparador`. Contrafactual: Orig. versus CoT no mesmo modelo e idioma (Tabela III), para os três modelos abertos e cinco idiomas não ingleses; CoT não foi executado para o inglês nem com GPT-4. O texto (p. 6) diz que CoT não depende de dados ou modelos externos, o que sugere tradução pelo próprio LLM, mas o estudo não declara explicitamente qual modelo traduz. Pacote composto só de prompting (não híbrido).

componentes_fora_escopo.nome_original: LP (Our approach): Fine tuning on Multilingual Projection with LASER Encoders / Projection-Based Zero-Shot Transfer
componentes_fora_escopo.descricao: Abordagem proposta (focal do estudo): codificador multilíngue LASER pré-treinado gera embeddings das palavras; um projetor com parâmetros treináveis (W_llm, b_llm; o texto fala em duas camadas lineares e a conclusão em projetor de camada única) mapeia esses embeddings para o espaço de entrada do LLM, treinado por MSE com tokens ingleses de 120 exemplos do MBPP por 200 épocas; na inferência, o LLM recebe os embeddings projetados concatenados com embeddings de um system prompt. Altera a entrada por embeddings aprendidos, não por texto de prompt; por isso não entra em `tecnicas` nem em `extracoes`.
componentes_fora_escopo.localizador: p. 6 do PDF, seção V; p. 4, Fig. 2(b); p. 5, legenda da Tabela III

componentes_fora_escopo.descricao: Geração de problemas e soluções em inglês por um LLM (ChatGPT no texto; GPT-4 na Fig. 2a), tradução e retrotradução com filtro BLEU (Algoritmo 1) e ajuste fino LoRA dos modelos com quantização FP16, duas épocas, em uma GPU A100. Os prompts de geração de dados servem ao ajuste fino de pesos; a intervenção avaliada é o ajuste fino.

riscos.descricao: Disparidade de qualidade do código gerado quando o mesmo problema é dado em idiomas não ingleses (maiores taxas de erro e menor ATPR nos modelos abertos).
riscos.localizador: p. 1 do PDF, introdução; p. 4, seção IV.A; p. 5, Tabela III

riscos.descricao: A tradução para o inglês antes da geração (CoT) não melhora significativamente e, em alguns casos, reduz o ATPR; a análise qualitativa aponta representações não canônicas e deriva de tópico. O estudo não relata teste estatístico para «significantly».
O ajuste fino com dados de bootstrapping (BFT, fora do escopo) reduz erros de sintaxe mas aumenta alucinações, com menor taxa de aprovação e mais erros totais.
No LP (fora do escopo), a ordem dos embeddings projetados pode diferir da ordem canônica do inglês, o que pode contribuir para saídas alucinatórias e errôneas.
Modelos que produzem código com mais frequência, como o LP, ficam mais sujeitos a erros de sintaxe.

O ajuste fino (BFT) é descrito como intensivo em recursos, com dados rotulados custosos e demorados; o custo do BFT não é quantificado no estudo (não quantificado). O tempo de treino do projetor LP (menos de uma hora em RTX-4060) é apresentado como vantagem frente a «several GPU hours or even days», sem medição do BFT.

riscos.descricao: Vieses culturais e raciais podem ocorrer ao expor os modelos a prompts multilíngues, e há possível comportamento errático dos modelos em idiomas de poucos recursos.
Limitação do LP: dependência de tokenização por palavras e embeddings agregados, que pode não escalar para idiomas de recursos muito escassos sem tokenizadores disponíveis.

Our experiments, detailed in the second column of Table III, show that back-translation does not significantly improve results.
In some cases, it even reduce performance, as indicated by lower ATPR scores.
Qualitative analysis suggests that models struggle with non-canonical language representations and topic drift, despite the translations not being of poor quality.
Therefore, we compared it with methods like bootstrapping from the model itself followed by finetuning (BFT) and Chain-of-Thought (CoT), which also do not rely on external data or models.
In this setup, the LASER encoder preprocesses and embeds input tokens before passing them to the LLM, which then operates on these embeddings rather than raw input IDs.
To enhance performance and align with baselines, we also concatenate system prompt embeddings with the original programming prompt embeddings.
Models are quantized to FP16 and fine-tuned using parameter-efficient techniques, including low-rank adaptation [42].
Significant disparities in code quality across languages are observed, even when using the same problem statements.
As shown in the third column of Table III, while bootstrapping with ChatGPT reduces syntax errors, it also increases hallucinations, leading to lower test pass rates and higher total errors.
This misalignment could contribute to the generation of hallucinatory and erroneous outputs.

Our overall observations with respect to this metric is models like ours that often produce code than omitting it (which is indicated by the higher code completion rate) are more prone to syntax error due to the high recall.
Fine-tuning pre-trained models is effective for many NLP tasks but is often resource-intensive, requiring costly and time-consuming task-specific labeled data.
Although we are focusing on a objective task with little to no opinion sourcing from the models, cultural and racial biases can occur given we are exposing the models to multi-lingual prompts.

A major limitation of this work lies in the reliance on word tokenization and pooled token embeddings, which introduces external dependencies and may not scale effectively to extremely low-resource languages where tokenizers are not readily available.

We then automatically identify function names in the code, replacing the function names in the MBPP test assertions with those from the model outputs, ensuring any function names would not affect the test results.

Since the applications we are focusing on are essentially user-centric in nature, a proper communication protocol should be established that can help clarify potential erratic behaviour of models, especially for low-resource languages.
It’s important to note that we classify a logical error not only when no valid code is generated but also when any of the test cases fail.

Thus, given that LP consistently achieves the lowest LER across all languages and models, we consider this demonstrates the LP’s proficiency in helping with generating error-free code, particularly in linguistically diverse contexts.
In contrast, BFT, a strong trivial baseline, tends to increase the TotalER due to hallucinations, as observed in our data analysis, despite slightly improving the all test cases passed metric.

This improvement is especially pronounced in languages with complex syntax and morphology, such as Hindi (hi) and Russian (ru), where LP reduces the TotalER by over 10% in some cases compared to the original model.
We achieve this using two linear projection layers as outlined in the above equations.

A single-layer projector already narrows most of the cross-lingual gap to within a 2-percentage-point range; this suggests that more complex projector architectures are unnecessary, as their potential accuracy gains are marginal while their memory and compute overheads would grow substantially.
We assess the similarity of translations using the BLEU score [41], retaining translations that meet a quality threshold (e.g., 0.8) to create new training data.

We set the temperature to 0.8 for consistency and use two epochs.

We showcase the limited effectiveness of traditional Chain-of-Thought method, as well as bootstrapping multilingual training data and fine-tuning LLMs to enhance code generation quality across multiple languages.

tecnicas.observacao: O estudo apresenta a mudança de code completion para specification-to-RTL como uma das duas técnicas de prompt tuning. O pacote altera vários ingredientes ao mesmo tempo: formato pergunta/resposta (“Question”/“Answer”), interface descrita em linguagem natural em vez de cabeçalho de módulo Verilog anexado, liberdade para o modelo declarar a interface e restrição de formato de saída ([BEGIN]/[DONE], “Only output the code snippet”). A categoria acrescentada (`restricoes`) corresponde à restrição de formato de saída; `instrucao` e `restricoes` (especificação de interface) já existem no prompt de code completion. O contraste com code completion (mesmos 156 problemas, mesmos modelos e temperaturas) isola o pacote, não um ingrediente único.

citacoes.trecho: In the next section, we extend our new VerilogEval v2 benchmark to support two prompt tuning techniques: 1) in-context learning [6] and 2) changing the task type from code completion to specification-to-RTL.
The full 156-problem dataset from VerilogEval is converted into specification-to-RTL prompting in this work.

Code completion has the problem description in Verilog-compatible comments and always appends the module interface declaration to the end of the prompt, similar to how Copilot [10] is typically implemented in an integrated development environment (IDE).
On the other hand, specification-to-RTL’s prompt style is like a chatbot, with well-defined “Question” and “Answer” sections.
Enclose your code with [BEGIN] and [DONE]. Only output the code snippet and do NOT output anything else.
In-context learning (ICL) was proposed by [6] to add examples of task questions and desired responses into the prompt context, so that an LLM can better respond to a given task.
1-shot includes only the combinational incrementer, 2-shot adds the sequential incrementer, and 3-shot includes all three examples in the context prompt.
The evaluation compares models with and without 1-shot in-context learning (ICL) examples, represented by arrows indicating the change in performance as 1-shot examples are added.
While ICL can help correct certain types of mistakes, it can also introduce new issues, leading to similar or even worse performance.

However, in 1-shot the spec-to-RTL pass rate drops to 0% on Problem 9 because of it picking up a slightly different input port name (in_) used in the in-context learning example that is not present in the prompt.
As we can see for Llama3.1 70B, adding in-context learning examples can generally improve results, but sometimes wrong behavior will be learned, as in the case of 2-shot.
Because LLM responses will be non-deterministic at non-zero temperature, the LLM is sampled multiple times and, if at least one sample passes, the problem is passed.
Overall, larger models generally achieve higher pass rates, though resource costs and model-specific responses to ICL examples vary significantly.
This is far more data and compute resources than what is given to models in single-turn, and individual models still have much room for improvement.

However, application of VerilogEval is quickly becoming limited due to the low complexity of the dataset problems, especially when LLM deployments move beyond single-turn prompts and responses and into multi-turn flows with feedback, as we shall see below.
This classification feature provides insight into the most common reasons for failures and how to mitigate poor code generation through prompt tuning.

Solutions in prompt tuning could vary: from adding prompt rules to only use wires on ports to suggesting the use of SystemVerilog logic port types, obviating the immediate type confusion, to allowing the LLM to generate the interface entirely on its own (as in the case of specification-to-RTL, rather than code completion).
In comparison, specification-to-RTL greatly improves compile-time errors, including wire and registered output confusion, even at 1-shot.

When the 1-shot example shown in Listing 1, which demonstrates a simple combination incrementer, is added to the prompt as an in-context learning example, the pass rate of Problem 9 increases substantially to 65% (13 of the 20 samples pass).
However, we report two sets of model parameters: high temperature (T=0.8, top_p=0.95) and low temperature (T=0.0, top_p=0.01) set.
This post-processing is also used across the other models as well.
This can be attributed mostly to slight changes in prompt, such as whitespace (line breaks) and punctuation, and is in the measurement noise.

riscos.descricao: Sem avaliação baseada em execução: Full-Match e CodeBLEU são métricas estáticas; o CodeBLEU sobre a função inteira pode inflar os escores, e a avaliação pode não captar correção funcional. Menos de 1% dos patches seria executável, segundo os autores.
LLMs podem ter falhas de raciocínio e alucinações de código ao usar DR; o GPT-4 pode errar identificadores precisos do projeto.
Patches de referência de modelos mais simples podem abalar a confiança do GPT-4 e deslocar correspondências exatas que ele já produziria.

DR limitados, ausentes ou sem contexto suficiente (referências a código omitido, links externos, intenção de código não especificada) prejudicam a qualidade dos patches, sobretudo em issues complexas.

Validade interna da anotação manual dos DR (possíveis inconsistências ou vieses).
Validade externa e de construto: benchmark próprio, DR só do Jira, issues relativamente simples (até 22 linhas), baselines de propósito geral e sem análise separada de soluções e argumentos.

mitigacoes.descricao: Substituição de todo código dos comentários por tags [code] para evitar comparações injustas.

Recomendação de identificadores como feedback para corrigir identificadores inadequados (resposta ao risco de identificadores imprecisos), avaliada pela ablação DRCodePilot-ID.

citacoes.trecho: Automatic Program Repair (APR) endeavors to autonomously rectify issues within specific projects, which generally encompasses three categories of tasks: bug resolution, new feature development, and feature enhancement.
To investigate this premise, we introduce DRCodePilot, an approach designed to augment GPT-4-Turbo’s APR capabilities by incorporating DR into the prompt instruction.

Furthermore, given GPT-4’s constraints in fully grasping the broader project context and occasional shortcomings in generating precise identifiers, we have devised a feedback-based self-reflective framework, in which we prompt GPT-4 to reconsider and refine its outputs by referencing a provided patch and suggested identifiers.
Moreover, our findings reveal that the standalone application of DR can yield promising increase in the full-match ratio across CodeLlama, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 within our benchmark suite.
DRs extracted from issue logs with DRMiner are integrated into our prompt structure.
To ensure high-quality output, we impose four program-repair oriented guidelines for GPT-4 to adhere to rigorously:
To tailor it to the coding conventions of the target project, we further fine-tuned it on the project’s codebase.
Consequently, for each error-prone identifier in the given patch, we provide up to six possible replacement candidates.
Here, our prompt carefully defines GPT-4’s role as a proficient code-fixing expert.

Furthermore, it follows a deliberate “follow my tips step by step” chain-of-thought procedure [60] (i.e., creating an initial patch, incorporating feedback, and refining the solution), which facilitates a clear understanding of the troubleshooting progression.
Within the reference patch area, we supply exemplars of efficient solutions to steer GPT-4 toward compliance with established coding norms and best practices.
Additionally, to avoid unfair comparisons caused by patches appearing directly in comments, all code snippets in comments were replaced with [code] tags.
It is also important to highlight that we did not build an execution-based evaluation pipeline for these patches.
Table 3 showcases the comparative evaluation of our design rationale-driven approach, DRCodePilot, against baselines that generate patches directly from buggy functions.
All other experimental variables and procedures are kept consistent across the three variants.
These figures reveal that even an advanced code-focused LLM like GPT-4 can err in generating precise correct identifiers during issue repairs.
In contrast, reference patches derived from simpler models can erode its confidence, leading to the displacement of exact matches.
To explore the above sub-questions, we selected three baseline models capable of interactive prompting: CodeLlama, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4.
Since expert annotations are involving, we randomly selected 61 issues that featured extensive comments from our benchmark.
CodeLlama and GPT-3.5 demonstrate around an elevenfold increase in full-match patches, while GPT-4 shows a twelfthfold improvement.

However, upon examining the data for +AC, +DR, or +DDR, it becomes clear that models utilizing design rationales consistently outperform those relying solely on original comments, in terms of both full-match patches and CodeBLEU scores.
Challenges arise when DR is limited or absent—such as when developers’ discussions go unrecorded (e.g., FLINK-28513)—resulting in subpar DRs that hinder DRCodePilot’s performance.

To mitigate such risks, we employed standard procedures involving independent annotations followed by collaborative discussions for consensus building, ultimately deciding outcomes through majority vote.
For instance, CodeBLEU evaluates the entire function rather than focusing on the modified segments, which can result in inflated scores.
Without this, our current evaluation risks missing important nuances in functional correctness and real-world applicability.

tecnicas.nome_original: prompt construído a partir da tarefa do LeetCode (descrição do problema, exemplos de entrada e saída, restrições e quarta parte acrescentada: "Write the code for this task in Python" + "Start with: <function_name and arguments>")

tecnicas.observacao: Prompt zero-shot único, de um turno, enviado igualmente aos cinco modelos, um chat novo por tarefa. 'instrucao': pedido explícito de escrever o código em Python. 'exemplos': um a três exemplos de entrada e saída da função, às vezes com explicação (exemplos ilustrativos do comportamento esperado, não soluções resolvidas). 'restricoes': parte final de restrições e condições e a assinatura obrigatória ('Start with:') exigida para os testes automáticos do LeetCode; a assinatura também poderia ser lida como código fornecido (contexto), mas o estudo a apresenta como requisito de formato. Ilustrações das tarefas foram retiradas do prompt. Os autores acrescentaram a quarta parte ao texto da tarefa, mas não há condição sem ela; por isso mecanismos_acrescentados vazio. Classificação de papel: o objeto de investigação declarado são os modelos (comparação de cinco LLMs), não o prompt; a técnica foi marcada 'focal' apenas por ser a única condição de prompting avaliada e a via pela qual todo o código é obtido — classificação a conferir. Não há contrafactual de prompting: todos os resultados comparam modelos sob o mesmo prompt.

citacoes.trecho: Within this study, we investigate the performance of five different LLMs – ChatGPT, BingChat, Bard, Llama2, and Code Llama – in terms of text-to-code generation for the programming language Python and compare their performance with respect to (i) correctness, (ii) runtime, and (iii) memory usage.
In the subsequent part, one to three examples are presented to show exemplary inputs and outputs of the function.
All this is complemented by a final part listing constraints and conditions that the function is required to fulfill.

We consistently use the expression "Write the code for this task in Python" followed by the name of the Python function with the arguments to be included since the automated tests can only be performed if the generated code uses the function names and arguments specified by LeetCode.
Since the five examined models are not capable of processing visual information, those are not included in the prompt.
For each task a new chat is started, so that a conversation with the LLM always contains exactly one prompt and one generated output per task.
For this reason, post-processing was necessary for all 89 tasks for Code Llama.
In four instances, BingChat was also affected.
For the study conducted in this work, the ChatGPT model based on the GPT-3.5 turbo version was employed, making our performance estimates for ChatGPT somewhat conservative.
The chatbot llama-2-70b-chat, provided by the website Replicate, was employed for this purpose.
The chatbot Code Llama Instruct (34B) from the website together.ai, which offers several LLMs, is used for this purpose.
Across all three topics, this results in 89 tasks that are used in this study.
The results also show a clear pattern of increasingly incorrect produced code when the models are facing a lot of context in the form of longer prompts.
Since the prompts for correct solutions were shorter, it can be tentatively concluded that the prompts should be designed in a brief and targeted manner to achieve better results.
Regardless of the model, the length of the prompts seems to have an apparent influence on the likelihood of generating correct code.

Moreover, although all the models were able to produce code in Python, a notable drawback of Code Llama is that the generated code is not indented, requiring the user to adjust the format of the code before it can be effectively deployed.

Nevertheless, considering the large number of wrong solutions, one should always look critically at the generated code, which still requires substantial knowledge of the programming language by the user.
Furthermore, the reproducibility of results in the study is influenced by the fact that LLMs produce different answers even to identical prompts as inputs.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote comparado com Direct prompting (Tabela 2). Mecanismos: dois agentes (Navigator e Driver) → multiagente; papel «You are an experienced programmer» e diretrizes (priorizar correção funcional) → instrucao; reflexão sobre o problema e explicação dos testes públicos (ReflectPrompt) → raciocinio; planos de solução com passos de alto nível e geração de código guiada pelo plano → decomposicao; exemplos breves no PlanPrompt (list1[::-1], BFS) → exemplos; várias amostras de planos, agrupamento e seleção do plano ótimo pelo LLM (SelectPrompt) → amostragem; execução nos testes públicos, estratégia de reparo (AnalyzePrompt) e reparo (RepairPrompt) → feedback. Acrescentados medidos contra Direct prompting, cujo template não é mostrado (presume-se apenas instrução de geração, por isso instrucao não consta como acrescentado). O código com erro entra no prompt de reparo como parte do laço de feedback; não foi classificado como contexto. Pacote híbrido: inclui agrupamento por embeddings (text-embedding-3-large + k-means++), regra heurística de troca de plano baseada em memória histórica, temperatura 0,8 para planos e orçamento de até 10 iterações (ver componentes_fora_escopo). O ganho é do pacote e não pode ser atribuído a um único mecanismo.

tecnicas.localizador: PDF p. 9, Seção 4.4 e Tabela 4
tecnicas.observacao: Componente do PairCoder isolado por ablação (PairCoder contra «w/o MP»). Em «w/o MP» o Navigator sempre escolhe reparar o código atual em vez de trocar de plano no Step 5; a geração inicial de planos e a seleção inicial continuam. O ingrediente retirado é a troca para outro plano candidato (exploração sequencial de vários candidatos com seleção), classificado como amostragem; a regra de troca baseada em memória histórica é componente fora do escopo.

A execução nos testes públicos continua a decidir a troca de plano em «w/o RF»; o que se retira é o refinamento do código guiado pelo retorno da execução (AnalyzePrompt + RepairPrompt).

riscos.descricao: Plano inicial falho pode desviar o reparo guiado por feedback, que não resolve o problema de fundo (exemplo motivador com GPT-3.5-Turbo).
Wrong Answer é o tipo de erro mais comum; em CodeContest-test, 60,00% dos problemas falham nos testes privados por Wrong Answer, 16,36% por Runtime Error e 8,48% por Time Limit Exceeded.
Baixa cobertura dos testes públicos limita o PairCoder: em CodeContest-test só 21,21% passam nos testes públicos.
Testes autogerados incorretos (Reflexion) levam a autorreflexões baseadas em avaliações falso-negativas, explicando o baixo desempenho desse comparador.

Possível vazamento de dados de avaliação no pré-treinamento do DeepSeek-Coder, lançado depois da coleta de benchmarks como HumanEval; invocado para explicar Direct prompting com DeepSeek-Coder acima do GPT-3.5-Turbo em três colunas. Contaminação não verificada.

Exploração de vários planos e refinamento iterativo introduzem sobrecarga computacional; o PairCoder faz mais chamadas de API que a maioria das abordagens (Tabela 6, por exemplo 5,28 chamadas por problema em HumanEval contra 2,43 de Direct prompting).
Ameaça à generalização: avaliação com dois LLMs e cinco benchmarks em Python; geração multilíngue fica para trabalho futuro.
Ameaça do uso de prompting zero-shot: outras instruções ou demonstrações few-shot poderiam melhorar o desempenho.

mitigacoes.descricao: Argumento de que um eventual vazamento afetaria igualmente todas as linhas de base, por usarem o mesmo modelo; não há verificação nem condição de controle.
Seleção de cinco benchmarks e de LLMs fechado e aberto para mitigar a ameaça à generalização.
Mesmas descrições de problema e mesmos testes públicos para todas as abordagens; execução em ambiente Python 3.9 consistente.
Controle de orçamento: técnicas de prompting e Self-repair reexecutadas com até 10 tentativas (amostragem repetida a temperatura 0,8) para igualar o número máximo de tentativas (Tabela 5).

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we draw on pair programming practices to propose PairCoder, a novel LLM-based framework for code generation.
PairCoder incorporates two collaborative LLM agents, namely a Navigator agent for high-level planning and a Driver agent for specific implementation.

PairCoder integrates two key mechanisms: (i) multi-plan exploration achieved by the Navigator through adjusting diverse solution plans, and (ii) feedback-driven refinement based on execution feedback from the Driver and historical memory.
It stimulates LLMs to explicitly analyze the details of the problem, consider possible valid inputs and edge cases, and explain public test cases.
As shown in Fig. 4, we include brief examples in prompts to guide the proposal and emphasize the functional correctness of the proposed plans.

To obtain diverse solution plans, we set a non-zero temperature for multiple nucleus sampling [15] and ask LLMs to generate multiple plans in each batch [8], which improves sampling efficiency while reducing duplicate plans.
Following the previous studies [21, 52], we also make choices through LLMs, where the prompt template is shown in Fig. 5.
We apply a simple but effective heuristic strategy to determine whether to change the solution plan.
Based on the execution feedback, the Navigator leverages the reasoning ability of LLMs to propose a directive repair strategy (Line 13).
If the Navigator assumes that the current solution plan remains promising, the Driver will attempt to repair the buggy code based on the given repair strategy (Line 14).
Direct prompting [6] takes the original requirements directly as inputs to prompt LLMs for code generation.
We use the classical CoT instruction “Let’s think step by step.” to guide LLMs in zero-shot [24].
In the planning phase, LLMs plan out the solution steps from the intent with few-shot demonstrations.
Self-debugging [7] teaches LLMs to perform iterative rubber duck debugging by explaining the generated code line-by-line with few-shot demonstrations.
For the comparative methods, we reproduce them according to the source code or provided prompts; otherwise, we quote the results directly from their papers [10, 16, 54].
To ensure a fair comparison, all approaches are given identical problem descriptions and public test cases for code generation.
“w/o MP” disables the capability of multi-plan exploration, making the Navigator always choose to repair the current code rather than adjust the solution plan in Step 5.
“w/o RF” is the opposite, which disables the feedback-driven refinement process, making the Navigator always choose to attempt another candidate plan.
Second, if the initially generated code follows a flawed plan, the feedback-based repair process is likely to be misguided by the initial incorrect direction, failing to address fundamental issues.
Overall, Wrong Answer is the most common error type, indicating that generating functionally correct programs remains a key challenge for code generation.
Referring to Table 1, the low coverage of public test cases limits the ability of PairCoder to facilitate code generation.
The poor performance of Reflexion is likely due to the model generating incorrect test cases, which leads to self-reflections based on false negative evaluations of the code [42].
Another potential threat is data leakage in pre-trained LLMs.
However, any such leakage would affect all baselines equally since they use the same model.
While the multi-plan exploration and iterative refinement introduce additional computational overhead, the superior accuracy of PairCoder in code generation justifies the trade-off in Sect. 4.
Collaborating the Navigator and the Driver, PairCoder requires more API calls than most approaches except Reflexion.
The first potential threat relates to the generalizability of our evaluation.
To mitigate this concern, we carefully select five widely used and representative benchmarks and both closed-source and open-source LLMs for our experiments.

Although zero-shot prompting achieves superior accuracy while largely reducing token consumption, we do not rule out the possibility that other instructions or few-shot demonstrations could further improve performance.
This setup ensures that these approaches have the same maximum number of attempts as the iterative approaches in Sect. 4.1.

citacoes.trecho: As shown in Figure 1, given a mix of code and textual context and data context (i.e., input-output dataframes), the task aims to generate target code that can transform the input dataframe to the output dataframe.
Figure 5 shows our few-shot prompt to query LLMs, which includes an instruction, demonstration, and context.
In few-shot setup, we randomly sample k in-context examples [11, 24, 55] and insert them before the test example.
By default, we set k=2 for all LLMs.
The zero-shot prompt is similar to the few-shot prompt, but without demonstrations.
Instruction: You are a data scientist using Jupyter Notebook to program.
Do not modify context or provide explanations.
We select two top-performing models to study, i.e., the finetuned DataCoder and GPT 3.5 with two in-context examples.
To answer this question, we first experiment by eliminating various components of the dataframe in the data context.
Subsequently, we provide a varying number of table rows to further study the impacts of data values.
otherwise, the generated code might result in a key error and fail to execute.
For example, without input dataframes, the model hallucinates the value to be converted.
To avoid answer leakage, we remove testset examples whose target code appears in the context of training and validation examples.
With increased parameters and enhanced training methods, GPT-4 achieves the highest performance with an execution accuracy of 50.6%, indicating substantial room for further improvement on this task.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote de prompting: persona e instrução de tarefa (instrucao); cadeia de raciocínio em quatro passos (raciocinio); contexto do teste (pacote, classe e método focal, comentário, outros métodos invocados; Tabela 1) e definições padronizadas de smells (contexto); exemplo em pseudocódigo nas definições e exemplos antes/depois nas regras DSL (exemplos); regras de refatoração em DSL estruturada (restricoes), com componente Steps que divide a refatoração em sequência de ações (decomposicao); ordenação de regras por prioridade (instrucao); checkpoints de autoverificação por smell (feedback). O comparador de mesmo modelo é o Llama3-70B com prompt genérico (Fig. 7), que já contém persona, instrução, código do teste e tipos de smells (instrucao, contexto); por isso 'contexto' não figura entre os acrescentados, embora o UTRefactor acrescente mais informação dessa categoria. O contraste contra o prompt genérico isola o pacote, não um mecanismo. Pacote híbrido: inclui detecção de smells por ferramenta (tsDetect), divisão e fusão de arquivos de teste e geração de relatório, fora do escopo de prompting. A atribuição de 'decomposicao' aos Steps da DSL é interpretação do extrator; o estudo não usa esse termo.

riscos.descricao: Testes refatorados que não compilam ou falham na execução (#CPR total 95%, #EPR total 89%); exemplos: assertStrictError do Gson que não aceita mensagem, gerando erro de compilação, e erros nos dados parametrizados de @CsvSource ao converter Duplicate Assert em teste parametrizado.
Possível alteração de comportamento: 32 casos (aproximadamente 4%) marcados como Inconsistent pelo GPT-4o (exception handling 18, redundant assertion 9, redundant variable declaration 5).

LLMs podem alucinar durante a refatoração e produzir segmentos de código com erros de sintaxe ou semântica; na análise de 100 falhas do LLM, 22 casos se devem a funções ou variáveis inexistentes introduzidas ao dividir testes com Eager Test.
O LLM com prompt-padrão apresenta mais aleatoriedade na refatoração, com resultados imprevisíveis quando há vários smells no mesmo teste.
Refatoração incompleta: com vários smells no mesmo teste, o LLM frequentemente deixa de eliminar todos, mesmo instruído explicitamente.
Cobertura limitada das regras: a DSL pode não cobrir todos os cenários; smells como Sensitive Equality não são removidos quando o projeto não sobrescreve toString nem oferece método equivalente.
Validade externa: o tsDetect suporta Java até a versão 13; versões incompatíveis podem impedir a detecção e, portanto, a eliminação de smells.
O estudo aponta custo de tokens e de implantação de LLMs de código fechado como motivo para usar o Llama3-70B; custo não quantificado e não medido para o UTRefactor.

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we propose a novel approach called UTRefactor, a context-enhanced, LLM-based framework for automatic test refactoring in Java projects.

By simulating the manual refactoring process through a chain-of-thought approach, UTRefactor guides the LLM to eliminate test smells in a step-by-step process, ensuring both accuracy and consistency throughout the refactoring.
Additionally, we implement a checkpoint mechanism to facilitate comprehensive refactoring, particularly when multiple smells are present.
UTRefactor outperforms direct LLM-based refactoring methods by 61.82% in smell elimination and significantly surpasses the performance of a rule-based test smell refactoring tool.
You are a Java testing expert, and now you need to refactor the test code which contains bad test code smells.
Use a Chain-of-Thought approach to break down the problem:
In this step, we extract the contextual information for each test that requires refactoring.
For each smell type, we provide a structured definition, including a description of the test smell, its impact, and a pseudocode example to illustrate the concept.
To address this issue, we propose using a more precise Domain-Specific Language (DSL) to express the test smell refactoring rules.
The Steps component breaks down the refactoring process into a sequence of actions, enabling a fine-grained, step-by-step approach to modifying the test code.
Additionally, the Example provides before-and-after code snippets to demonstrate the practical application of the refactoring, aiding in both understanding and verification.
The LLM is then instructed to eliminate test smells according to their priority, from highest to lowest.
Specifically, for each smell in the test, we set up a checkpoint that asks whether the refactored test still exhibits the given issue.
If the issue persists, the LLM continues refining the refactoring to eliminate the smell.
As depicted in Figure 7, we use a standard prompt template, which provides the Llama3-70B with the original test code and all detected test smell types.

We conduct an ablation study by comparing the effectiveness of UTRefactor with a version excluding the DSL, while keeping all other aspects the same (e.g., detailed descriptions of test smells, test context, and the smell checkpoint mechanism).
However, LLMs may generate hallucinations during the refactoring process, producing random code segments that introduce syntax or semantic errors.
This indicates that while the refactoring process did introduce some errors, it remains largely effective, with the overall results demonstrating a solid level of reliability.
The LLM occasionally introduces errors in the parameterized data provided via @CsvSource, causing runtime failures.
Table 4 indicates that 32 cases (approximately 4%) are flagged as Inconsistent, which can be categorized into three types:
Despite explicitly instructing the LLM to address all four types of smells in the prompt, in practice, the LLM often fails to fully refactor tests with multiple smells.
Overall, the default LLM exhibits more randomness in test refactoring.
22 cases fail due to hallucinations during the elimination of the Eager Test smell, where the LLM introduces non-existent functions or variables into split tests.
Closed-source LLMs often come with high token usage costs, and their large parameter sizes lead to significant deployment expenses.
However, the DSL in UTRefactor may not cover every possible scenario, which can impact the overall effectiveness of the test refactoring.

For incompatible Java versions, tsDetect may encounter syntax parsing errors during detection, which could prevent the identification of test smells, thus impacting the effectiveness of smell elimination.
We manually compile all refactored tests and calculate that the average compilation pass rate is 95%, with the highest rate being 97% in the Jsoup project.

Additionally, UTRefactor shows significant refactoring results for the two other high-frequency smells, ECT (Exception Catching Throwing) and ETa (Eager Test), reducing their numbers from 526 and 509 to 54 and 20, respectively.

It is evident that when only providing the test code and corresponding smell types to Llama3-70B for refactoring, it reduces a total of 1,080 smells across the six projects, with an average reduction rate of 55%.
After refactoring the tests, Table 7 shows that using GPT-4o with the default prompt achieves a smell reduction rate of 55%, whereas UTRefactor achieves a reduction rate of 91%.
Across all six open-source projects, the total time from detecting test smells to refactoring the 879 tests with identified smells is 4,379 seconds, averaging 3.8 seconds per test.

Specifically, we provide GPT-4o with all 879 pairs of test code that can be executed successfully before and after refactoring to assess whether the changes involve only structural adjustments while maintaining functional consistency.

tarefas_observacao: O estudo avalia geração de código para programação competitiva (CodeContests, TACO). O reparo ocorre apenas sobre o próprio código gerado, dentro de trajetórias multi-turn com feedback de execução; não há benchmark de depuração ou reparo de programas fornecidos. Por isso o reparo foi classificado como mecanismo `feedback` da geração, e não como tarefa `depuracao` (p. 2, p. 4).

tecnicas.localizador: p. 4 (Seção 3, Figura 3); p. 5 (Seção 4, Single-turn); p. 6 (Tabela 3); p. 26-27 (Apêndice G.1)
tecnicas.observacao: Conjunto de 8 prompts de raciocínio (self-reflection, predict IO pairs, write code solution with guidelines, predict problem tag, predict problem difficulty, write natural language solution, write helper function docstring, write intermediate variables and type), respondidos em um passo de inferência anterior à geração do código. Mecanismos do pacote incluem a instrução e a restrição de formato do prompt base (exemplo de prompt na p. 29). Critério aplicado a todas as técnicas: `instrucao` está no prompt base de todas as condições e não é listada como acrescentada; os prompts acrescentados são classificados pela função. «write code solution with guidelines» também traz diretrizes de tempo de execução (`restricoes`). Contrafactual: Tabela 3 compara a linha Baseline com Worst/Best reasoning sem instruction prompt; as linhas Worst/Best são escolhidas post hoc por modelo pelo pass@100 no conjunto de teste e não identificam o prompt.

O estudo os agrupa em «describe», «modularity» e «solution». Contrafactual na Tabela 3 (Baseline contra Worst/Best instruction), com as mesmas ressalvas de seleção post hoc.
