riscos.descricao: Prompts de CoT podem piorar o desempenho quando o modelo não segue as instruções ou propõe plano subótimo, em geral força bruta que não cumpre o limite de tempo; o prompt «weak solution» pode enviesar para força bruta irrecuperável; e o código gerado pode ignorar as variáveis intermediárias definidas no raciocínio.
Multi-turn sozinho traz ganhos modestos e às vezes fica abaixo do single-turn com o mesmo orçamento de amostras, sobretudo em modelos menores.

Feedback de execução mais detalhado induz comportamento exploratório menor (maior similaridade entre códigos consecutivos), o que o estudo associa à menor diversidade dos programas e a quedas de desempenho com orçamentos grandes.

Soluções multi-turn exigem várias chamadas ao LLM e, portanto, custo maior; pass@k ignora o custo computacional. O estudo controla o número de tentativas de código com pass n@k, mas não quantifica tokens, dinheiro ou tempo das técnicas de prompting (não quantificado); reconhece que uma comparação mais justa consideraria tokens de entrada e saída.

Sobreposição não nula entre CodeContests/train e TACO test e entre TACO train e TACO test (problemas quase idênticos com URLs diferentes). O estudo não discute contaminação no pré-treinamento dos modelos avaliados.

mitigacoes.descricao: Uso de pass n@k em vez de pass@k para comparar single-turn e multi-turn com o mesmo número de amostras de código.
Descontaminação das trajetórias do CodeContests/train contra o TACO test (288 problemas detectados) antes do RFT.
Pré-seleção dos prompts em pequena escala (pass@10) com 500 exemplos do conjunto de treino do CodeContests, disjunto do teste.
Exclusão dos prompts de CoT na comparação de granularidades de feedback, para isolar o efeito do tipo de feedback.

observacoes.descricao: Avaliação em regime zero-shot; o enunciado do problema inclui exemplos de entrada e saída do próprio benchmark, que não foram classificados como mecanismo `exemplos`.
Os reasoning prompts exigem um passo adicional de inferência, que o estudo não conta como turno adicional por comparar o número de tentativas de código.

Análises comportamentais: similaridade entre códigos consecutivos por tipo de feedback (Figura 6) e antes/depois do RFT (Figura 8); fração de texto não código (Tabela 11) e relação entre tokens de raciocínio e pass@1 (Figura 22), que o estudo diz invalidar a hipótese de que mais tokens não código correlacionam com melhor desempenho.

citacoes.trecho: After systematically decomposing reasoning, instruction, and execution feedback prompts, we conduct an extensive grid search on the competitive programming benchmarks CodeContests and TACO for multiple LLM families and sizes (Llama 3.0 and 3.1, 8B, 70B, 405B, and GPT-4o).
Finally, we integrate execution feedback from intermediate solutions to allow for code repair.

As CoT can intervene at different times in code generation, we categorize reasoning prompts (NL → NL) that elicit understanding of the problem before code generation, and instruction prompts (NL → Code) that guide the code output to enhance readability and modularity.
We thus evaluate several types of feedback, ranging in granularity:
Our grid search comprises 8 reasoning prompts and 6 instruction prompts, detailed in Appendix G.
We also introduce the CoT-retry setup, which allows for adaptive inference budget based on problem difficulty.
If the first solution fails on more challenging problems, we prompt the LLM with a combination of execution feedback and a reasoning prompt.
We do not include CoT prompts in this feedback comparison to isolate the effect of different feedback types.
For Llama 3.0 models, simply extending the single turn reasoning and instruction prompts to the multi-turn setting yields superior performance (reported as "Multi-turn CoT" in Table 1).
CoT-retry only reasons when the first attempt fails and therefore works best across Llama 3.1 models for all sampling sizes and benchmarks ("Multi-turn CoT" in Table 1).
If the first code generation is incorrect, we add an instruction prompt, "write code solution with guidelines," to separate problem-solving and code writing.
This prompt is fixed to "Give it another try" throughout the whole paper.
CoT makes performance worse if the model fails to follow the instructions or makes the LLM propose a sub-optimal plan.
Sub-optimal plans are usually brute force approaches to solve the problem which do not fit the time limits constraint (see Appendix H for an example).

The weak solution prompt, although effective when done correctly as shown by its high performance across models, can bias the model towards a brute force approach that it is unable to recover from as shown below in Example 1 and Example 2.
The multi-turn setting alone brings modest gains and is sometimes worse than its single-turn counterpart under equal sampling budgets.
We show that this can be attributed to reduced diversity of generated programs which results in performance drops for large sample budgets.
In multi-turn settings, solutions are obtained via several generations (i.e., LLM calls) and hence at a higher cost, rendering these two setups not directly comparable (Kapoor et al., 2024).
In this study, we opt to measure performance via pass n@k (Li et al., 2022) rather than pass@k for a fair comparison of techniques.

Although a maximally fair comparison (at the cost of complexity) should account for total input and output tokens (Olausson et al., 2024) as well as model size (Hassid et al., 2024), we believe pass n@k, which stresses the number of code attempts, constitutes a simple yet superior alternative to pass@k.
We found that there is a non-zero overlapping between CodeContests training set and TACO test set.
We also find that there are non-zero overlaps between TACO training set and test set.
To determine this list, we ran experiments at a small scale (pass@10) with over 30 prompts on 500 examples sampled from the CodeContest training set.
Meta Llama 3.0 and 3.1 series are open-weight, and gpt-4o-2024-05-13 (GPT-4o in the paper) are available through OpenAI API.
Given the code contest problem and your self-reflection on the problem, your goal is to write a valid Python code with stdio that correctly solves the problem.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote em duas etapas encadeadas: o GPT-4o recebe o problema e gera o tipo MBTI e uma descrição detalhada da personalidade (Personality Generation Prompt); essa descrição é inserida no prompt de geração de código, que pede ao LLM que atue como programador com essa personalidade (instrucao, persona). A etapa encadeada foi classificada como decomposicao (etapas encadeadas). O prompt de código também especifica o nome da função («The function name should be <Function>»), classificado como restricoes. O comparador «Direct» pede ao LLM que gere código como programador, mas seu texto não é mostrado; por isso não se sabe se contém a especificação do nome da função, e restricoes não foi listada como acrescentada. O contraste MBTI × Direct (Tabela 2) isola o pacote, não um ingrediente. Ingredientes do pacote são isolados em parte por RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 e apêndices B e C (ver entradas próprias).

riscos.descricao: O estudo reconhece o não determinismo dos LLMs na geração de código e, por isso, executa cada LLM três vezes por conjunto e relata a média; não relata variância nem dispersão entre execuções.

O estudo admite que, em tarefas fáceis (HumanEval+), a orientação por personalidade pode trazer melhoria limitada ou pequena queda de pass rate; a Tabela 2 mostra quedas para GPT-4o, DeepSeek-Coder V2 e CodeLlama em HumanEval+ e/ou APPS.

O estudo trata o consumo de recursos como custo: uma rodada no MBPP Sanitized (direto, sugestão de personalidade e geração guiada) consome 0,35M tokens, cerca de US$ 1,75 com GPT-4o; modelos locais exigem 11,5 h (Llama 3.1) e 1,5 h (CodeLlama) de GPU A800. O estudo considera o custo eficiente; o custo adicional da etapa de geração de personalidade, separado do prompting direto, não é quantificado.

mitigacoes.descricao: Três execuções por LLM e conjunto, com média do pass rate, para lidar com o não determinismo.
Pass@5 e Pass@10 relatados como complemento para reforçar a robustez das conclusões no MBPP Sanitized (cinco modelos).

baseline: Direct (prompting direto como programador), executado nos sete modelos e quatro conjuntos; Three-shot e CoT executados no MBPP Sanitized.

citacoes.trecho: Our results show that personality guidance significantly enhances code generation accuracy, with improved pass rates in 23 out of 28 LLM-dataset combinations.
For a given coding task, we prompt GPT-4o, an advanced LLM for general text understanding, to generate an appropriate personality type most suited for solving the task.
In our approach, GPT-4o generates both the MBTI type and a detailed description tailored to the coding task.
We prompt the LLM to take on the role of a programmer with the specified MBTI personality, providing a detailed description of that personality, and then it generates the code to solve the task.
Please generate a function as a programmer with the following MBTI description: <Personality>

Specifically, for each LLM on each dataset, we evaluate two approaches: directly prompting the LLM to generate code as a programmer (the “Direct” row) and using the personality-guided method (the “MBTI” row).
This RQ investigates whether the effectiveness of personality-guided code generation can be further enhanced by combining it with existing prompting strategies.

For few-shot learning, we use a three-shot approach, a widely adopted setting in the code generation literature (Zheng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023); for CoT, we prompt the LLM to think step by step (Wei et al., 2022).
You should first write a rough problem-solving process, and then output the final code. Don't give usage of the code, just the code.

To address this, in this RQ, we evaluate whether providing a detailed description alongside the MBTI type yields better results than using a shorter prompt that only indicates the MBTI type (e.g., INTJ).
For each approach, Qwen-Long is prompted to take on the role of a uniform MBTI personality across all coding tasks.
The results indicate that using the general template results in a pass rate of 65.5%, significantly lower than the 80.8% achieved by our default approach.
We use the same experimental setup and prompts as those used for MBTI prompting, with the only change being the personality model, which is switched to the Big Five Personality.
Using the representative MBPP Sanitized dataset, we prompted the LLM to adopt the role of a programmer with the specified S/N property for each task.
This RQ evaluates this setting by comparing it to a setting where the code-generation LLM is also used for personality generation.

Considering the non-determinism of LLMs in code generation(Ouyang et al., 2025), to ensure the reliability of our results, we run each LLM on each dataset three times and report the average pass rate as the final outcome.
It is reasonable that on easier tasks, where models already perform well (as seen with HumanEval+), personality guidance may offer limited improvement, or in some cases, a slight decrease.

Regarding computational costs, using the representative MBPP Sanitized dataset (427 tasks), one experiment round, including direct prompting, personality suggestion, and personality-guided code generation, consumes 0.35M tokens, costing about $1.75 with GPT-4o ($0.004 per task).
The results of Pass@5 and Pass@10 are the same as the conclusions about MBPP Sanitized in RQ1, which help strengthen the robustness of the findings.
In contrast, APPS is the most challenging, with no LLM achieving a pass rate above 40%.
In 11 combinations, the improvement exceeds 5%, and in 5 combinations, it surpasses 10%.

Three-shot + Personality outperforms the personality-guided approach in only three of the seven LLMs, while CoT + Personality achieves better results in five of the seven LLMs, with improvements ranging from 3.8% to 12.9%.

We select the MBPP Sanitized dataset for this experiment, as it shows the most significant improvement with our personality-guided approach, making it an ideal candidate to explore potential further gains.
First, the personality traits examined are limited to the MBTI framework.

tecnicas.observacao: Sistema multiagente com agentes de recuperação, planejamento, codificação, depuração e validação. Mecanismos: papéis de agentes (multiagente, instrucao); RAG com documentação e amostras de código ST validadas (contexto, exemplos); prompt one-shot e dicas de sintaxe (exemplos, instrucao); regras e restrições de domínio e templates de patch (restricoes); CoT na depuração e na geração de propriedades (raciocinio); planos em formato de autômato executados por etapas e pipeline compilação-verificação (decomposicao); N planos gerados e ranqueados, usados em sequência (amostragem); retorno do compilador e do verificador formal ao agente de depuração (feedback). Pacote híbrido: inclui ferramentas que não são prompting (compilador, verificadores formais nuXmv/PLCverif/CBMC, modelo de embeddings, LoRAs no CodeLlama 34B). Comparado apenas com sistemas alternativos (LLM4PLC, ChatDev), sem condição com o mesmo modelo e sem o framework (por exemplo, prompting direto); por isso não há contrafactual da técnica. mecanismos_acrescentados vazio: o comparador LLM4PLC não é prompt base de que o Agents4PLC derive.

Ferramenta de geração de especificações formais com CoT para usuários que não conseguem definir propriedades.

citacoes.trecho: To address these challenges, this paper introduces Agents4PLC, a novel framework that not only automates PLC code generation but also includes code-level verification through an LLM-based multi-agent system.

We further enhance our ‘agents’ specifically for industrial control systems by incorporating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), advanced prompt engineering techniques, and Chain-of-Thought strategies.
Evaluation against the benchmark demonstrates that Agents4PLC significantly outperforms previous methods, achieving superior results across a series of increasingly rigorous metrics.
The Planning Agent receives the user input and the information retrieved by the retrieval agent, based on which it generates actionable plans using a structured automata-like format.
The planning agent ranks these plans, which later will get executed sequentially, based on their ranking, help identify the most suitable solution.
By utilizing a RAG block, the agent accesses a comprehensive database of PLC documentation and validated ST code samples.
These prompts encapsulate domain-specific rules and constraints, to guide the Coding Agent to follow the compiler requirements and the predefined validation criteria.
The fixing employs a structured patch generation process, utilizing a step-by-step Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methodology that analyzes the origin of error code, its info and description respectively.
Employing previously generated patches in a self-RAG context can improve the effectiveness of repair, capitalizing on the wealth of information contained in the generated outputs.
Otherwise, the above workflow will iterate until it exceeds a predefined loop threshold, where the planning agent provides another plan for code generation.
We investigate the effects of three significant enhancements: syntax hints in prompts, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and one-shot prompting on the ST code generation process.
Intermediate Configuration without RAG: The framework utilizing one-shot prompting and syntax hints, but excluding RAG.
Intermediate Configuration without Syntax hint: The framework utilizing simple one-shot prompting and RAG, but excluding syntax hints.
Baseline Configuration: The foundational setup with zero-shot prompting and no supplementary aids (syntax hints and RAG).
We compare the framework’s performance when both components are disabled, effectively operating without CoT reasoning and patch templates.
Note that LLM4PLC is designed to be a half-automated framework with human interactions, we write an extra automation program to drive the components of the LLM4PLC framework.
Code generated by LLMs often exhibits considerable uncertainty and may sometimes fail to compile or meet specified requirements [45].

Functional verification is crucial for PLC code, ensuring that the generated ST code can accurately and reliably implement the intended control logic and operations in real-world applications, thereby preventing equipment failures or production interruptions due to logical errors or unforeseen circumstances.
One primary challenge with LLM-guided verification is the potential of inconsistencies between the original ST code and the translated version used for formal verification.

Also, automatically translated code may lead to state explosion, a common problem in model checking where the state space grows exponentially, making verification computationally expensive or infeasible.
However, it is also worth noting that despite explicitly prompting the ChatDev framework to generate ST code, it occasionally produces code in unrelated languages, such as Python or C++.
These methods significantly enhance the framework’s ability to handle complex problems, but when not carefully designed, they may interfere with the reasoning process on simpler tasks.

To address these, we integrate advanced translation-based verification tools like PLCverif, which has been optimized for translating ST code into SMV or CBMC formats for model checking and bounded model checking (BMC), and may help alleviate the problem of state explosion.
As a result, the current experiments may not fully capture the effectiveness of the debugging agent.

tecnicas.observacao: O objeto investigado (RQ1) é a língua natural do prompt: a docstring do HumanEval traduzida para 203 outras línguas, com o mesmo modelo, o mesmo template e as mesmas 164 tarefas. Não é uma técnica de engenharia de prompt no sentido usual; a categoria `outro` descreve a variação da língua natural do enunciado (incluindo a qualidade da tradução, que varia por língua e por classe, p. 4–5). Os mecanismos `instrucao` e `restricoes` são herdados do template de cada modelo (por exemplo, Claude3.5: instrução de sistema «Write a Python Code snippet for the following» e exigência de bloco de código; GPT4o/GPT3.5: papel de sistema e exigência de bloco de código Python; Aya: só o prompt), e o texto do template permanece em inglês. Os prompts do HumanEval contêm declaração de função e exemplos opcionais na docstring (Figura 3, p. 4), mas o estudo não descreve exatamente o que compõe mHumanEval[i] nem trata esses elementos como ingrediente; por isso `exemplos` e `contexto` não foram atribuídos (registrado como incerteza). O contraste inglês × outra língua é analisado pelo próprio estudo (RQ1, conclusão p. 8), mantidos modelo, template e tarefas; a tradução, porém, altera simultaneamente a língua e possivelmente o conteúdo (erros de tradução, p. 7–8 e Apêndice H.1), de modo que o efeito é da língua do prompt tal como traduzida, não da língua isoladamente da qualidade da tradução.

riscos.descricao: Código que resolve a tarefa errada por compreensão equivocada do problema, porque termos traduzidos não preservam o significado (exemplo: «prime number» em zulu interpretado como dígitos significativos).
Erros de compilação porque o código contém palavras-chave e identificadores na língua do prompt (Aya; exemplo em rundi).
Código sem sentido, às vezes em outra linguagem que não Python, especialmente com prompts não ingleses (DeepSeek-Coder e WizardCoder).

Segurança operacional da execução do código gerado (laços infinitos, gerenciamento de memória, travamento do sistema); não se trata de cibersegurança. O estudo afirma que nenhum modelo produziu código malicioso.

citacoes.trecho: RQ1: How do the code generation capabilities of LLMs vary when prompts are provided in English, or other high-, mid-, and low-resource NLs?
For translation, we only consider the docstrings (enclosed in triple quotes).
By computing the mean of the two metrics for each prompt, we select the candidate with the highest score.
We follow the standard prompt templates for each LLM.
We use simple RegEx commands to extract these blocks, and evaluate them locally in batches using Python's subprocess library, focusing exclusively on the Pass@1 metric.
However, a significant number of errors arise from misunderstandings of the problem, resulting in code that addresses incorrect tasks.
Furthermore, the Aya model often uses identifiers or keywords from different languages, leading to compilation errors (Appendix H.2).
A recurring problem with DeepSeek-Coder and WizardCoder is the generation of nonsensical code, sometimes not even in Python, especially when prompted in a non-English language (Appendix H.3).
LLMs generally demonstrate optimal performance when prompted in English.
Given the benchmark's extensive 33,456 prompts, the evaluation process is exceedingly costly.
To ensure safety and reliability, we recommend executing code generated using prompts from mHumanEval in a contained virtual environment.
This precaution helps prevent potential issues related to infinite execution loops and memory management.
The max_tokens parameter is set to 1000, and the temperature is maintained at 0.7.
We observe that GPT-4o and DeepSeek-Coder achieve strong results in Classes 4 and 5, with scores consistently exceeding 0.85 in Python, Java, and C++.

tecnicas.observacao: Método proposto de compressão de DocString em quatro etapas (pré-processamento com remoção de quebras de linha, tabulações e stop words filtradas por similaridade semântica > 0,999; ordenação de tokens por importância calculada com CodeGPT-py-adapted; espaço de busca Top-N com n-gramas; restrição de similaridade de cosseno dos logits do primeiro token >= tau = 0,999). O prompt base é a assinatura mais a DocString, em geração zero-shot (instrucao); a busca automática pela versão comprimida da DocString foi classificada como otimizacao_prompt. O contrafactual é o pacote completo (ShortenDoc) contra a DocString original sem compressão ('None', Tabela 3) e contra outros compressores na mesma taxa; o ganho ou perda é do pacote, não de uma etapa isolada. O estudo não descreve se as DocStrings dos conjuntos contêm exemplos de entrada e saída; por isso exemplos não foi atribuído.

Contrafactual: Tabela 1 compara a DocString original (coluna 0) com a compressão a 10%, 20%, 30% e 40%.

riscos.descricao: Com taxas de compressão maiores, os métodos existentes reduzem o Pass@1 porque podem remover informação semântica necessária para gerar código correto; no BigCodeBench a maioria dos modelos perde Pass@1 já após a compressão.

Ao migrar as DocStrings comprimidas em Python para C++, Go, Java e JavaScript, o Pass@1 do ShortenDoc nem sempre alcança o da DocString original; os autores atribuem a queda ao modelo base CodeGPT treinado para Python.

Parte da informação removida pelo ShortenDoc é redundante com o nome do método; quando o nome é genérico ('foo'), o Pass@1 do ShortenDoc cai, o que torna a compressão dependente da qualidade dos nomes.

A compressão acrescenta sobrecarga: cerca de 2 s por DocString, FLOPs adicionais (entre parênteses na Tabela 4) e 0,23 GB de memória de GPU para o modelo base; o estudo trata essa sobrecarga como modesta. A economia financeira com APIs é argumentada com cálculo hipotético e não quantificada experimentalmente.
Ameaça interna: possíveis erros de implementação do ShortenDoc e das linhas de base.

Ameaça externa: a avaliação multilíngue usa traduções de um único conjunto (HumanEval-X), o que pode limitar a generalização; tau = 0,999 foi escolhido só no CodeHarmony e pode não ser ótimo para os demais conjuntos.

Modelos proprietários têm custo de API e atualizações frequentes de versão que podem afetar a estabilidade e a reprodutibilidade dos resultados; o tempo de geração por API pode variar com a carga do servidor.

mitigacoes.descricao: Busca gulosa e hiperparâmetros iguais para todos os modelos.
Mesma taxa de compressão para todos os métodos dentro de cada conjunto, para comparação justa.
Inspeção do código do ShortenDoc e uso de bibliotecas maduras contra erros de implementação.
Linhas de base executadas a partir do código aberto original ou reimplementadas conforme os estudos originais.
No estudo com humanos: DocStrings anônimas e em ordem aleatória, consulta à Internet permitida e carga de trabalho limitada.

baseline: DocString original sem compressão (None/Original) e, nas mesmas taxas, Random, Selective_Context e LLMLingua2, todos executados pelo estudo.

citacoes.trecho: In our study, we propose a novel compression method, ShortenDoc, dedicated to DocString compression for code generation.

Our experiments on six code generation datasets, five open-source LLMs (1B to 10B parameters) and one closed-source LLM GPT-4o confirm that ShortenDoc achieves 25–40% compression while preserving the quality of generated code, outperforming other baseline methods at similar compression levels.
Our empirical study show that the state-of-the-art prompt compression methods achieve only about 10% reduction, as further reductions would cause significant performance degradation.
In this section, we conduct an empirical study to explore the applicability of existing prompt compression methods to code generation tasks.
We explore two state-of-the-art prompt compression methods: Selective_Context [22] and LLMLingua2 [37].
Additionally, we introduce the Random method as a baseline.
Our approach consists of four main stages: Step 1: Pre-processing, Step 2: Token Importance Sort, Step 3: Search Space Construction, and Step 4: Constraint Definition.
Compression is performed only for those tokens where the similarity metric exceeds a threshold of 0.999, ensuring the preservation of DocString’s semantic integrity.
Tokens are iteratively compressed until the constraint is no longer satisfied.
In addition, we employ Greedy Search as the inference strategy for all models.

To test this, we conducted controlled experiments where we systematically removed these characters from the DocStrings and compared the model’s Pass@1 score against a control group where these elements were retained.
Our experiments involved removing stop words from DocStrings to assess if the model’s Pass@1 score would change.
This suggests that existing compression methods, while removing more information, may also remove semantic information that is critical for the model to generate correct code.
Notably, on the BigCodeBench dataset, most models show a decrease in Pass@1 scores after compression.

At the same time, we observe a slight degradation in Pass@1 scores when directly migrating the compressed DocStrings obtained in RQ1 (Python) to other programming languages such as C++, Go, Java and JavaScript.
This finding suggests that a portion of the information compressed by ShortenDoc is redundant with the information already present in the method name.
The time overhead introduced by ShortenDoc’s compression process is relatively modest, averaging around 2 seconds per DocString.
The first internal threat is the possibility of implementation errors in ShortenDoc.
To alleviate this, we conducted a thorough code inspection of the implementation and utilized mature libraries.
To mitigate this threat, we implemented all baselines by running their open-source code directly or reimplementing them according to the original studies.
The reliance on translated versions of a single dataset, rather than naturally occurring code in different languages, might limit the generalizability of our findings.
While proprietary models such as GPT-4 might offer superior performance, their high API costs and frequent version updates could impact the stability and reproducibility of our results.
To ensure a fair comparison, we apply the same compression ratio to all methods within each dataset.
To maintain the quality of the human evaluation, the compressed DocStrings were presented in random order, ensuring that the evaluators were unaware of which method generated the DocString.

O encadeamento rascunho→tradução→compilação/teste não foi classificado como decomposicao porque o rascunho é produzido por substituição de padrões sem LLM e a compilação/teste é manual. O tempo do desenvolvedor (Figura 5) foi medido apenas com o CodeScribe, variando o modelo; não há condição sem o pacote no mesmo estudo. A afirmação de 2-3 arquivos/dia antes da ferramenta e 10-12 depois (p. 5) é comparação histórica sem descrição de condições, não condição contrafactual comparável. Pacote híbrido: inclui pré-processamento determinístico, classes FArray e escolha de modelo fora do escopo.

riscos.descricao: A saída da IA generativa não tem correção garantida, o que mantém necessária a intervenção manual (revisão e teste).

Conversão incorreta da função de instrução zab2 por todos os modelos avaliados (como array multidimensional no GPT-3.5 Turbo, com inconsistências de uso no GPT-4o) e conversão incompleta da variável Fcc pelo Mistral-7B, exigindo intervenção manual.

Conversão entre indexação a partir de 1 (Fortran) e a partir de 0 (C++) apontada como um dos aspectos mais propensos a erro; sem rascunho, os LLMs introduziam tipos de dados errôneos ou redefiniam estruturas existentes.

Sem orientação, os LLMs geravam código periférico para funções externas ou programas principais de exemplo; o Mistral-7B alucinou a interface Fortran copiando código do target.f; com as anotações RAG, o LLM ainda alucina ocasionalmente apesar de informado sobre as funções externas.

Tempo de revisão e teste do desenvolvedor tratado pelos autores como sobrecarga e custo do desenvolvedor ('developer costs'), quantificado em minutos para um arquivo na Figura 5; modelos GPT exigem compra de créditos de API (custo monetário não quantificado).

mitigacoes.descricao: Anotações RAG no rascunho informando funções externas (with-function-context), comparadas com o rascunho sem elas; efeito relatado só qualitativamente e como inconsistente.

citacoes.trecho: However, because the output of GenAI cannot be guaranteed to be correct, manual intervention remains necessary.
In the process, we developed a tool, CodeScribe, which combines prompt engineering with user supervision to establish an efficient process for code conversion.
It uses chat completion as a prompting technique to generate desired coding output from GenAI models.
This template outlines code conversion rules and includes an example representing a set of files that follow a similar pattern.
Using the chat template as a seed prompt, CodeScribe appends the source and draft files and triggers the LLM to complete the code conversion.
Any errors found during compilation are addressed manually by the developer or sent for regeneration by updating the seed prompt.

Blue steps indicate tasks handled by CodeScribe, such as project indexing, draft generation, and LLM-driven translations, while red steps indicate manual activities, including chat template generation, code review, and verification.

For instance, when prompted to translate a subroutine that references external functions, the LLM would often extrapolate code for these external functions or even provide a main program example to demonstrate functionality.
To mitigate such hallucinations, we developed the Index command to capture a detailed structural map of the source code using YAML files.
Without a preliminary draft, LLMs frequently introduced erroneous data types or redefined existing structures, leading to incoherence in generated C++ code.

Additionally, comments embedded in the draft help prevent common hallucinations, such as re-declaring functions or subroutines already defined elsewhere, by clearly indicating these constructs in advance.
The LLM is instructed to produce output for the C++ source and the corresponding Fortran-C interface, enclosing them within <csource>...</csource> and <fsource>...</fsource>.
The conversion process initially averaged 2-3 files per day before the development of the tool. After the tool was implemented, developer productivity increased to 10-12 files per day.
We utilized five models for the code conversion task: CodeLlama-7B, Mistral-7B, CodeLlama-34B, GPT-4o, and GPT-3.5 Turbo, each with distinct architectures, parameter counts, and capabilities.
All models operated under a maximum token limit of 4096, with CodeLlama and Mistral models utilizing a maximum batch size of 8 and default values for temperature and top-p parameters.
However, it hallucinated the Fortran interface by copying code directly from the target.f file and, like CodeLlama-7B, failed to convert the statement function zab2.
Converting between 1-based and 0-based indexing is one of the most error-prone aspects of translating between these languages, especially when it impacts index values and array bounds.
To mitigate this, we often batch the translation, review, and testing of multiple files simultaneously, optimizing the overall process and helping manage developer costs more effectively.
To evaluate its effectiveness in code translation, we applied RAG elements within CodeScribe, specifically during the Draft command.
While the RAG-enhanced draft file annotations improve accuracy, the results are inconsistent, as the LLM occasionally hallucinates despite being explicitly informed of the use of external functions.
Our evaluations demonstrate that CodeScribe reduces the developer time required for code conversion and testing, showcasing its potential to enhance productivity in scientific computing projects.

citacoes.trecho: Specifically, we formulate the Interaction-to-Code task and establish the Interaction2Code benchmark, encompassing 127 unique webpages and 374 distinct interactions across 15 webpage types and 31 interaction categories.

To address these limitations, we propose four enhancement strategies: Interactive Element Highlighting, Failure-aware Prompting (FAP), Visual Saliency Enhancement, and Visual-Textual Descriptions Combination, all aiming at improving MLLMs’ performance on the Interaction-to-Code task.
You are a web developer proficient in HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Combine HTML, CSS and JavaScript codes into one file and respond the codes only:

For the CoT prompt [53], we use the instruction “let’s think step by step” and design three intermediate steps: analyze the interaction effects, locate the interactive elements, and implement the interaction.
For the Mark prompt, we use red bounding boxes to highlight the interaction area, prompting MLLMs to focus on the interactive parts.
FAP incorporates the failure example into the prompt and tell MLLMs to avoid these types of failures (as shown in Figure 5 ).
Based on failure types, we propose FAP to stimulate the self-criticism ability of MLLM, thereby avoiding problems that may occur in the Interaction-to-Code task.
Table VI shows the results of the FAP methods, we can find that Failure-aware Prompt can improve the performance of the Interaction-to-Code task on all models.
By cropping the image to increase the proportion of the interactive part, VSE makes the model to better perceive the interaction area.
Although increasing magnification may result in some UI areas being cut off, this can be effectively addressed through a two-step generation approach:
We observe that: when the magnification factor is set to 1, all evaluation metrics yield values of 0, indicating the unsuccessful interaction generation.
To investigate the impact of different input signals, we conduct experiments on GPT-4o using 10 randomly selected webpages from failure cases.
We evaluate three settings: visual input only (V), textual description only (T), and combined visual-textual input (V+T).
The results are in Table V, which shows that MLLMs are prone to make 10 types of failure (Limitation 2).
To confirm that MLLMs are not “cheating” by recognizing and reciting the original webpage code, we compute the BLEU [45] score between the generated and original webpage HTML.
As webpages become more complex with numerous interactions, the input context expands, potentially exceeding the context window constraints of MLLMs (e.g., 128K tokens for GPT-4o).
Nevertheless, this limitation can be mitigated by employing iterative generation, progressively producing interactions for a webpage over multiple rounds.

The benchmark we collect does not include back-end code; we cannot verify the generation effect of such interactions, but we believe our work is an important step toward generating interactive websites.
Both CoT and Mark prompts improve model performance compared to direct prompting, with the Mark prompt showing superior results.

citacoes.trecho: To fill this gap, in this paper, we conduct an empirical study to investigate the potential of LLMs in automated software refactoring, focusing on the identification of refactoring opportunities and the recommendation of refactoring solutions.
To answer RQ1-1, we designed the first prompt template P1. It specifies the role of the large language model, the task, and the source code to be refactored.
Besides all the information specified in P1, P2 also specifies the requested refactoring type.
As a developer, imagine your team leader requests you to review a piece of code to identify potential refactoring opportunities.
Rename method refactorings are frequently employed to modify low-quality identifiers to improve readability.
It specifies the role of the large language model, the task, the code entities that should be refactored, and the requested refactoring type as well as its explanation.

To this end, we retrieve similar refactoring patterns from the history of the subject projects to serve as contextual cues, instructing the LLMs to understand the necessary background knowledge for each refactoring subcategory.
Notably, for each refactoring subcategory, we designed a unique strategy to narrow the search space, noted as Search Space Limitation.
In the example illustrated in Fig. 6, the search space was limited from the entire document to a single method because the method name is only associated with the functionality of its method body.

In this study, we employ the latest GPT-4 [5] (called GPT for short in the rest of this paper) and Gemini-1.0 Pro [3] (called Gemini for short) as the evaluated large language models because they represent the state of the art in this area [45, 56].

However, 13 out of the 176 solutions suggested by ChatGPT and 9 out of the 137 solutions suggested by Gemini were unsafe in that they either changed the functionality of the source code or introduced syntax errors, which indicate the risk of LLM-based refactoring.
Among such 22=13+9 buggy solutions, 18 results in semantic changes and 4 results in syntax errors.
Notably, in this paper, the hallucinations refer to instances where LLM-driven refactorings result in syntax errors or change the intended behavior of the code.
The existing datasets might have been utilized to train the selected LLMs.
Notably, we only mined refactorings from commits submitted after April 2023 because GPT’s training data extends up to this date [5], while Gemini’s training data extends to February 2023 [3].
A threat to statistical validity is the inherent randomness of LLMs’ predictions.
To minimize this threat, we sampled 20 examples from different subject projects for each type of refactoring to reduce potential statistical bias.
The first limitation is that the detect-and-reapply tactic may reapply some safe but profitless refactorings.
However, developers may not know exactly the expected refactoring subcategories in advance.
Finally, we only investigated within-document refactorings because of the length limitation posed by LLMs on their input and output.

Our evaluation results on the 22 cases suggested that RefactoringMirror was effective in that it successfully reapplied most (94.3%=33/35) of the conducted refactorings whereas all bugs introduced by the large language models have been avoided.
RefactoringMirror then reapplied all detected refactorings, and 32 out of the 33 refactorings had been reapplied successfully.
In case of inconsistent validation, we simply discarded the case and turned to the next one.
All participants rated independently, and they reached a high consistency by achieving a Fleiss’ kappa coefficient [36] of 0.82.
To mitigate this limitation, we propose an interactive tactic where both the outputs of RefactoringMirror and the modifications made by LLMs are presented to users.

Explicitly specifying the expected refactoring types improved the success rate of GPT on all types of refactoring opportunities whereas it only improved Gemini on four out of the nine categories of refactoring opportunities, i.e., extract method, rename attribute, rename method, and rename parameter.
Our findings suggest that with proper prompts, LLMs have the potential to identify 86.1% of the refactoring opportunities with high accuracy.
In total, GPT and Gemini suggested 10 and 6 refactoring solutions respectively that changed the functionality of the involved source code.
In total, GPT and Gemini suggested 3 and 1 such kind of unsafe solutions.
Gemini achieved a comparable accuracy of 64.9%=61/94.
In the previous research questions (RQs), we observe that GPT consistently outperformed Gemini across all types of refactorings and in both prompt settings.

Consequently, it remains unclear to what extent developers can benefit from LLM-based refactoring concerning the effect (i.e., quality improvement caused by conducted refactorings) and the cost (e.g., human cost and computational expense) compared against the state of the art.

citacoes.trecho: Specifically, InterCode and our evaluation use C# as the programming language for code generation.
In total, we obtain 172 programming tasks for example-based code generation: 24 of these tasks are from CodeHunt, and 148 are from HumanEval.
The prompt at this stage includes four parts: an instruction stating that I/O examples describe the requirement, a set of I/O examples, using statements, and the function signature.

In addition to the information contained in the first prompt, the feedback prompt at this stage also introduces (1) the instruction that indicates that the previously provided I/O examples do not describe the functionality completely; (2) the supplementary I/O examples where the previously generated code cannot produce the expected outputs.
During the iterations, this new prompt is presented to the LLM along with the history of previous conversations.

To evaluate the influence of natural-language descriptions, we evaluate the LLMs on prompts combining I/O examples with two different granularities (i.e., full descriptions and keywords) of natural-language descriptions, and then calculate their pass@5 score.

Unlike full descriptions, the keywords for each target functionality point out only the general direction but do not tell the details (e.g., for the full description “return x+17”, the keyword is “Arithmetic Operation”).

The preliminary experiment compares the original manually designed prompt with three variants: COT (Chain of Thought) [72], Persona (assigning a specific role with its perspective to LLMs) [66], and Few-shot Learning [7].
For sub-objective2 (i.e., implement the target functionality), the score under the original prompt is overall higher than that under all three other prompt variants.
The illustrations of each prompt variant and the results can be found in our project website [18].
Llama-2-7b-chat tends to perform input matching, directly generating conditional statements from the I/O examples without inferring input-output relationships.
The most frequent error is “fail in the given tests”, indicating that as the number of iteration rounds increases, the LLMs struggle to generate code that satisfies all the given I/O examples.
The evaluation takes pass@k as the primary metric, which mainly concerns correctness but does not fully reflect code quality, such as readability and maintainability.
(3) Tool Reliability: in our evaluation framework, due to the discrepancies in the C# versions supported by tools, in very few cases, correct code can be determined as failures after compilation.
To mitigate this threat, we manually check and correct the compilation results as thoroughly as possible.
To cope with the possible bias introduced by random sampling, we prepare five sets of randomly sampled I/O examples for each programming task for the beginning of executions.

Different from most code-generation benchmarks, InterCode sets a default function name (i.e., Puzzle) for all programming tasks to avoid revealing the target functionalities through their function names.
Furthermore, the framework also employs a structural test generator [8, 20, 56, 61] to check the generated code, aiming to reduce false positives caused by incomplete tests.
To mitigate this threat, we involve multiple researchers to conduct the result analysis and cross-validation.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote completo: prompt inicial estruturado (definição da tarefa e papéis → instrucao; requisitos de formato de entrada/saída e descrição da regra de projeto → restricoes; guia passo a passo em subtarefas → decomposicao; dois exemplos de layout com localizações de DRV → exemplos), dois agentes LLM (Planner e Programmer) em group chat (multiagente; fases de planejamento e codificação, categoria decomposicao já presente no prompt base), funções de ferramenta com VLM que analisam imagens da regra e dos layouts e devolvem texto ao Planner (contexto) e função DRC Code Evaluation que executa o código no conjunto de layouts e devolve relatório de desempenho para depuração iterativa (feedback). Comparador: standard prompting com o mesmo prompt da Figura 6, sem feedback de ferramentas (p. 7). O contraste DRC-Coder × standard prompting isola o pacote, não um mecanismo individual. O estudo afirma configuração zero-shot no sentido de não fornecer exemplos de código (p. 4); os exemplos de layout com DRVs foram classificados como exemplos de entrada/saída. O pacote usa VLM (GPT-4o) para interpretar imagens; o estudo declara não haver ajuste fino (p. 6).

Ablação: variante multi-agent w/o vision capability mantém Planner e Programmer sem essas funções (Tabela 2), comparada pelo estudo com o DRC-Coder completo (Tabela 1, GPT-4o). As duas funções são retiradas juntas; não há isolamento de cada uma.

Não há ablação que retire só esse componente; a única condição sem feedback é o standard prompting, que também não tem Planner nem análise visual (contraste de pacote). O estudo mostra apenas a evolução por rodada no estudo de caso da regra M0.S.1 (Figura 11) e o número de iterações por regra (Tabela 1).

riscos.descricao: Alucinação de um único agente LLM em codificação DRC complexa e alucinação induzida por contextos longos, que leva a limitar o relatório de DRVs.
Falsos positivos e falsos negativos de DRVs produzidos pelo código gerado, isto é, verificador DRC que não reproduz o relatório da ferramenta comercial.
Limite de comprimento de contexto dos LLMs impede reportar todos os DRVs no relatório de feedback.

mitigacoes.descricao: Divisão da tarefa entre dois agentes especializados (Planner e Programmer) para melhorar o raciocínio e reduzir alucinação. O efeito é medido por P/R/F1 na ablação single-agent (Tabela 2) contra o sistema completo (Tabela 1); alucinação não é medida diretamente.

Função DRC Code Evaluation com feedback de falsos positivos e negativos para depuração automática. Só comparada como parte do pacote contra standard prompting, sem condição que retire apenas o feedback.
Relatar apenas DRVs com distâncias x, y únicas para contornar o limite de contexto e a alucinação em contextos longos.

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we present DRC-Coder, a multi-agent framework with vision capabilities for automated DRC code generation.
We also design an auto-evaluation function for LLMs to enable DRC code debugging.
By assigning two LLMs with different roles to handle each sub-task, we enhance the LLM reasoning ability and reduce the potential hallucination of LLMs in solving complex DRC coding with one agent.
This could help LLM to effectively avoid false positives and negatives of DRVs produced by the generated code.
To make DRC-Coder more applicable when facing new technology node, our code generation is under a zero-shot setting, i.e., no example codes are provided during generation.

The fix part contains: (1) A task definition for developing a Python function to identify DRVs in layout data. (2) The requirements that formally states the input and output format of the function. (3) A step-by-step guide that decomposes coding problem into subtasks for the Planner and Programmer.

The DR dependent part has: (1) The target design rule description from foundry document. (2) Layout examples with metal information and corresponding DRV locations to provide concrete cases for analysis.
Note that we randomly select two layout examples that has the target DRVs from our dataset to construct the prompt.
This multi-agent approach decomposes the DRC process into planning and coding phases, allowing each agent to focus on its specialized task to enhance overall system performance.
In detail, this function executes our generated code on cell layouts in the dataset and directly compares the code output with the golden DRC reports of the commercial tool.
We cannot report all the DRVs due to context length limitation of LLMs and the potential hallucination problem of LLMs triggered by long contexts.
Planner and Programmer agents, along with the VLMs embedded in two tool functions, are powered by GPT-4o [12] using the OpenAI API version 2024-05-13.
Our evaluation dataset, generated as described in Section 3, comprises 207 standard cell layouts and covers 7 distinct design rules, as illustrated in Table 1.
Thus, the main baseline is set to the standard prompting, which using prompt in Figure 6 to directly generate the code without tool function feedback.

We set two variants of DRC-Coder as other baselines for abalation study: (1) single-agent with vision capability: Only use Programmer to directly generate code and (2) multi-agent without vision capability: Keep Planner and Programmer but without Foundry Rule and Layout DRV Analysis.
This inconsistency shows the limitations of conventional prompting when dealing with the intricate DRC.

citacoes.trecho: In this study, we present two key findings: (1) retrieving examples whose presented algorithmic plans can be referenced for generating the desired behavior significantly improves generation accuracy, and (2) converting code into pseudocode effectively captures such algorithmic plans, enhancing retrieval quality even when the source and the target PLs are different.

Based on these findings, we propose Plan-as-query Example Retrieval for few-shot prompting in Code generation (PERC), a novel framework that utilizes algorithmic plans to identify and retrieve effective examples.

First, it drafts a plan for the given problem to form an expanded query, which is used to retrieve examples that were projected to plan space in indexing time. Then, the retrieved examples and their plans are integrated into a reasoning chain to generate a revised plan and the final code.
We use generated pseudocode as intermediate reasoning steps for code generation (Jiang et al., 2024).

When the target programming language differs from that of example code c, we replace c with generated code ĉ in the target language, where the LLM generates ĉ using the in-context example shown in Appendix D:

We compared our method against several established baselines to highlight the effectiveness of PERC: 1) w/o Examples generates code directly without using few-shot examples, 2) Random Selection uses a randomly chosen, then fixed set of examples, 3) Problem-As-Query Retrieval retrieves examples based on problem-problem similarity, 4) CEDAR (Nashid et al., 2023) uses code-code similarity, and 5) RepoCoder (Zhang et al., 2023) expands the query with predicted code.

In all few-shot prompting-based code generation experiments, ICL was performed using an inference chain consisting of problem description, pseudocode, and code. To ensure fair comparison of retrieval methods, the code was replaced with code converted to the target PL, as done in PERC's approach.
For a fair comparison, we also used this retriever for the RepoCoder baseline as well, which originally used a sparse bag-of-words model.
Table 6 shows such conversion is crucial, as syntax, APIs, and other elements specific to the source PL may inadvertently influence the generation and lead to performance degradation.

tecnicas.observacao: Proposta do estudo: laço CEGIS em que o LLM recebe, em zero-shot, a descrição da IPA, a suíte de testes e um esboço do programa em que as linhas apontadas pela localização de falhas baseada em MaxSAT (CFaults) são substituídas por @ HOLE @; se o programa falha, um contraexemplo da suíte de testes é devolvido ao LLM. Comparação de pacote com De-TS (prompt básico sem localização de falhas e sem contraexemplo), na mesma Tabela 2. Pacote híbrido: as lacunas do esboço resultam de uma ferramenta formal de localização de falhas, que não é prompting (ver componentes_fora_escopo); o ganho do pacote não se atribui a um ingrediente isolado. Mecanismos: instrução («Complete all the '@ HOLES N @'...»), contexto (descrição da IPA e código do aluno fornecido como esboço, com informação de localização de falhas), restricoes (suíte de testes como especificação; «Code only. Provide no explanation.»), feedback (contraexemplo após falha nos testes). A suíte de testes foi classificada como especificação (restricoes), não como exemplos resolvidos.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 4 (Prompts: «two different types of prompts»), p. 6 (Tabela 2, colunas De-TS e FIXME_De-TS)
tecnicas.observacao: Um dos dois tipos de prompt que o estudo usa para incorporar a localização de falhas (formulação própria avaliada em colunas separadas da Tabela 2); cada linha apontada pela ferramenta de localização é marcada com /* FIXME */ e o primeiro comando muda para «Fix all buggy lines with '/* FIXME */' comments in the buggy program below.». Contrafactual: FIXME_De-TS contra De-TS, que diferem apenas nas anotações e no comando. O ingrediente acrescentado é informação de localização de falhas sobre o código fornecido (contexto, categoria já presente no prompt base). A anotação deriva de ferramenta formal (CFaults), fora do escopo de prompting. Também avaliada com contraexemplo (FIXME_De-TS-CE contra De-TS-CE).

Contrafactual: Sk_De-TS contra De-TS e Sk_De-TS-CE contra De-TS-CE (Tabela 2), além de Sk_De-TS-CE-CPA/RI contra De-TS-CE-CPA/RI. O ingrediente acrescentado é informação de localização de falhas sobre o código fornecido (contexto, categoria já presente no prompt base).

riscos.descricao: LLMs, embora rápidos, frequentemente produzem correções incorretas.

Reparos por LLM tendem a reescrever extensamente o programa em vez de ajustes mínimos, gerando correções mais invasivas e dificultando a aprendizagem do aluno (risco pedagógico, não de cibersegurança).

Com a implementação de referência no prompt, os LLMs copiam o programa correto, ignorando a instrução de não fazê-lo; 442 dos 876 programas reparados pelo Granite em Sk_De-TS-CE-RI têm TED zero em relação à implementação de referência.
Aprendizado few-shot pode levar a correções maiores que o necessário (afirmação da introdução, não testada no estudo).

Modelos fechados como o ChatGPT são apresentados como proibitivos em custo, e modelos muito grandes (por exemplo, 70B) exigem recursos computacionais significativos e demoram mais a responder; não quantificado.
Preocupação com a privacidade de dados dos alunos no uso de modelos fechados (privacidade, não segurança de código).

Instrução no prompt para não copiar a implementação de referência («Do not copy this program»); não há condição com e sem essa instrução.
Instrução para modificar o código o mínimo possível («Modify the code as little as possible.»); não há condição com e sem essa instrução.

Análise separada das configurações com e sem implementação de referência e uso do distance score para penalizar cópia da implementação de referência (procedimento de análise, não intervenção comparada).

Componentes do sistema: gerador de prompts, LLM, módulo Decider que executa a suíte de testes e escolhe o contraexemplo, e localizador de falhas CFaults (Figura 1). O localizador pode ser substituído por outras ferramentas, segundo os autores.

Análises adicionais sem extração: Tabela 4 (subconjunto em que CLARA falha) e Tabela 5 (quartis de complexidade ciclomática, calculada com lizard) comparam LLMs, cada um na sua melhor configuração, e não técnicas de prompting; a Figura 2 compara TED do Granite com e sem implementação de referência em escala logarítmica, sem valores numéricos legíveis.

citacoes.trecho: Our method uses MaxSAT-based fault localization to identify buggy parts of a program, then presents the LLM with a program sketch devoid of these buggy statements.
If the suggested program is incorrect, a counterexample from the test suite is fed back to the LLM for revised synthesis.

Our experiments on 1,431 incorrect student programs show that our counterexample guided approach, using MaxSAT-based bug-free program sketches, significantly improves the repair capabilities of all six evaluated LLMS.
This method allows LLMS to repair more programs and produce smaller fixes, outperforming other configurations and state-of-the-art symbolic program repair tools.
Basic prompts are the simplest prompts that can be fed to an LLM without additional computation, including all the programming assignment's basic information.
Fix all semantic bugs in the buggy program below. Modify the code as little as possible. Do not provide any explanation.
FIXME annotated prompts are prompts where each buggy line identified by the fault localization tool is marked with a /* FIXME */ comment.

In the second type of prompt, to address program repair as a string completion problem, we evaluated the use of prompts where the buggy program is replaced by an incomplete program (program sketch), with each line identified as buggy by our fault localization module replaced by a hole.

This new prompt indicates that the LLM's previous suggestion to fix the buggy program was incorrect and provides a counterexample (i.e., an IO test) where the suggested fixed program produces an incorrect output.

The reference implementation can be either the lecturer's implementation for the same IPA or the closest correct program based on the programs' Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) from a previously submitted student program, determined by Tree Edit Distance (TED) values (Orvalho, Janota, and Manquinho 2022a).
citacoes.localizador: p. 7 (texto sobre a parte inferior da Tabela 2)

citacoes.trecho: Hence, symbolic approaches demand an excessive amount of time to produce an answer, and LLMS, while fast, often produce incorrect fixes.
This tends to lead to more invasive fixes, making it harder for students to learn from their mistakes.
If the lecturer's reference implementation shown in Listing 2 is suggested as a reference in the prompt, both LLMS simply copy the correct program, ignoring instructions not to do so.
Notably, 442 of these repaired programs exhibit a TED value of zero between the reference implementation and the fixed program, indicating that GRANITE is replicating the reference implementation.
Nonetheless, few-shot learning can lead to larger fixes than necessary, as it is based on a limited number of examples.
Firstly, closed-access models like Chat-GPT are cost-prohibitive and raise concerns over student data privacy.
To address this, we separately analyzed configurations that include and exclude access to a reference implementation.
This score aims to identify and penalize LLMS that replace the buggy program with the reference implementation rather than fixing it.
We employ MaxSAT-based Fault Localization to guide and minimize LLMS' patches to incorrect programs by feeding them bug-free program sketches;

citacoes.trecho: To address these issues, we propose Tree-of-Code (ToC), a self-growing framework that generates nodes through self-supervision, incorporating prompt and model exploration in a GT-free setting.
Experiments on two datasets with ten popular zero-shot LLMs show that ToC boosts accuracy by nearly 20% over CodeAct with fewer than 1/4 turns.
LLMs are prompted to first analyze and break down the problem, generate reasoning-based thoughts for solving it, and then produce the complete code that reflects and executes that reasoning.
As long as execution fails, self-reflection continues iteratively, generating next-layer new nodes.
The breadth-first search (BFS) strategy is applied, with each parent node branching into M = 3 child nodes.
At the instruction level, prompts are randomly selected from a diverse pool, created through self-evolution and human crafting.
At the system level, different LLMs from our list, introduced in Section 4.1, are explored randomly with a consistent temperature setting of 0.1.
Specifically, we used ten LLMs to generate ten diverse prompts through prompt evolution from the root prompt (see Appendix A).
Once valid outputs from successfully executed nodes are collected, the same LLM makes the final decision by performing a majority vote and summarization to determine the most likely answer.

Thus, to maintain end-to-end flow, we introduce two functions: a general res_handler, which defines a prompt to generate results that meet the prompt requirements for final summarization, and a specific next_action for web tasks, which decides the next action from a given set of possible browsing actions based on the page content, visited URLs, and task query.
At each turn, you should first provide your step-by-step thinking for solving the task, for example: <thought> I need to print "hello world!"</thought>.
Ensure the code matches the fn_signature and input-output formats for proper execution.
Based on the provided chat history, reflect on the code and its execution.
ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) combines reasoning and action in a dynamic, step-by-step interaction, providing a flexible approach to task-solving.
CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024) utilizes a block of code as the LLM agent's action, enabling more efficient multi-turn interactions.
However, CodeAct greedily generates the next action's code block by relying on fragmented thoughts, resulting in inconsistency and accumulative hallucination.
Moreover, as the number of turns increases, repeatedly integrating prior thoughts causes context overload, heightening model hallucinations (Ji et al., 2023), increasing computational cost.

Note that the process supervision relies solely on the node's execution success or failure, rather than on the specific content executed (whether correct or incorrect), which would require pre-known labels.
This label is weak but available, simple, and useful—unlike pre-known GT or correctness judgments.
In such cases, it cannot provide a complete final solution.
While our framework provides a solid foundation inspired by human problem-solving, it uses a basic reflection mechanism, relying on execution feedback alone.
Ablation results in Table 4 confirm the effectiveness of prompt exploration.
We also record the average number of output words for the API cost evaluation.

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we introduce DomainCodeBench, a multi-domain code generation benchmark designed to systematically evaluate LLMs across 12 software application domains and 15 programming languages.
The Function signature field is included as part of the prompt provided to the LLM, specifying input and output of the target function to guide code generation.
Besides, to better showcase LLMs’ code generation performance, we combine the docstring and function signature in accordance with the characteristics of the task’s corresponding programming language.

In this experiment, we adopt a standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline to retrieve code snippets from the repository that are likely highly similar to the target code (referred to as Similar Context in Table 7).

In this experiment, we directly extract the oracle project dependency context from the ground truth and provide these code snippets that the target function depends on (referred to as Dependency Context in Table 7) to the LLM to explore the upper bound of the model’s performance when given sufficient and accurate project dependency context information.

Since most existing repository-level code generation methods do not involve the mining of domain-specific information, we directly extract the third-party library API information required by the target function (referred to as API Context in Table 7) from the ground truth and provide it as domain-specific input for the model.
The values in Table 7 are computed by subtracting the performance of the LLMs using the basic prompt from that of the LLMs using the basic prompt with additional information.
These similar code snippets provide a good example for the LLMs, helping the model more directly generate code that meets domain-specific requirements.
Following prior work [45], we set the temperature to 0.4 and top-p to 0.95.
To mitigate randomness of model generation, the experimental results presented in this paper are obtained by conducting three repeated experiments and averaging the results.

Finding 6: During generating domain-specific code, LLMs often struggle to generate correct code due to insufficient understanding of project-specific context, such as dependencies and defined functions, leading to errors like misusing APIs or accessing undefined interfaces.

Although this metric reflects the accuracy of LLM-generated results from various aspects, it does not fully capture whether the generated code can execute correctly or pass the corresponding test cases.
The first external threat is that DomainCodeBench contains data from GitHub before 2023, which may have already been included in the training datasets of the evaluated models.

To mitigate this risk, we provide each task instance in DomainCodeBench with a manually annotated docstring, avoiding the use of docstrings from online code repositories to prevent LLMs from directly associating training data with the programming tasks in DomainCodeBench.
The inherent randomness in LLM generation may make it difficult to accurately reveal the models’ code generation performance in specific domains.
To mitigate this threat, we repeat each experiment three times and take the average result to reduce the impact of model uncertainty.
We ultimately choose the prompt template that yields the best results after testing several options.
This is unexpected because the accuracy of similar context retrieved through search is generally limited, making it difficult to recall all the dependency information needed by the model.
(3) Contextual enhancement: we show that augmenting prompts with domain-specific knowledge improves performance by around 38.17%, providing actionable insights for performance optimization.
As shown in Table 3, DeepSeekCoder-33B ranks 4th on HumanEval yet achieves top performance in most application domains.

Among these models, only DeepSeekCoder-33B exceeds 50 CodeBLEU score (blockchain domain), with even SOTA closed-source LLMs like GPT-4 demonstrating moderate domain-specific performance (≤ 46.33 CodeBLEU).

When we feed these three types of additional information (API context, dependency context, and similar context) to LLMs separately, the performance of domain-specific code generation improves to some extent in each case.

Com a técnica Packages indicando pacote local ou desconhecido, o LLM tentou importar funções inexistentes (inspeção manual de cinco prompts).
O modelo de frase inicial da técnica Packages causou erros de uso de pacotes errados (sensibilidade à formulação do prompt).
O código gerado pode não cobrir casos-limite complexos que a solução humana trata e que os testes do CoderEval podem não cobrir.
Few-shot e assinatura, que mais favorecem a correção, geram funções com mais code smells e maior complexidade; o estudo descreve um trade-off entre correção e manutenibilidade.

citacoes.trecho: In this study, we introduce CodePromptEval, a dataset of 7072 prompts designed to evaluate five prompt techniques (few-shot, persona, chain-of-thought, function signature, list of packages) and their effect on the correctness, similarity, and quality of complete functions generated by three LLMs (GPT-4o, Llama3, and Mistral).

We follow a full factorial experiment design and evaluate the code generation functionality of LLMs by varying two levels (present/absent) of five factors in a prompt, that is, the five prompt techniques: (1) few-shot learning, (2) Chain-of-Thought (CoT), (3) persona, (4) function signature, and (5) the list of packages.
Instead, we use zero-shot as a baseline for prompt technique comparisons.
We use two input-output examples explained in natural language.
We apply Zero-shot-CoT [26] to isolate the impact of CoT from the few-shot prompt technique.
For the persona, we use the role of a software developer who focuses on practices and standards that software developers follow.
Signature is a line of code that includes the signature of the function to generate.
Packages is a list of libraries and files that exist in the environment in which the code runs.
We also append a constraint at the beginning of each prompt to ensure that the output has a block of Python code with a self-contained function.
Our findings also indicate that sometimes the addition of more information in the prompt leads to worse performance.
We found that when the prompt indicated the use of a package that is local or unfamiliar to the LLM, the LLM hallucinated and attempted to import non-existent functions from the specified packages.

In general, we observe that prompts that apply the few-shot and signature prompt techniques generate functions with more code smells and, more specifically, warning and error code smells compared to other prompts.
Finally, since we used recent LLMs, they may have been trained on the same open-source GitHub code we used.
To reduce this risk, we avoided code-focused models like Codex and CodeLlama, which are known to be trained specifically on GitHub data.
We found that for all models, 85% of the generated functions had a maximum similarity score below 0.4, and none were higher than 0.7.
We run all 7072 prompts on the selected LLMs three times to account for the non-deterministic nature of LLMs.

We observed similar behavior when experimenting with the template “The function uses the following packages” for the packages prompt technique and found that it caused errors related to using the wrong packages.
In addition, the manual creation of few-shot examples for our dataset may have introduced a degree of subjectivity.
Regarding internal validity, we acknowledge that LLMs can be sensitive to format or structure of the prompt [51], or even the order of the few-shot examples [21].

However, a more negative interpretation may also be that the generated code does not cover some complex corner cases that human-written solutions account for (which may not be covered by CoderEval tests).

citacoes.trecho: Recently, the use of large language models (LLMs) for Verilog code generation has attracted great research interest to enable hardware design automation.

Given a user prompt, i.e., instructions for Verilog code generation (CodeGen), it will be fed into a CoT prompting model to translate the vanilla user prompt into a refined CoT prompt, which can mitigate symbolic hallucinations.

As countermeasures against the hallucination taxonomy, HAVEN integrates three techniques, i.e., symbolic interpretation based CoT (SI-CoT) to mitigate symbolic hallucination, while fine-tuning the CodeGen-LLM with knowledge enhanced dataset (K-dataset) and logical enhanced dataset (L-dataset) against knowledge- and logical-hallucinations respectively.
By using a structured prompt template, CoT prompting model maintains the integrity of the original instruction while ensuring the symbolic logic is clearly communicated.
citacoes.localizador: p. 3 do PDF, Seção III-B, item 2

citacoes.trecho: If the module header is missing, CoT prompting model appends an appropriate module header to define the module name, inputs and outputs, standardizing the instruction.
citacoes.localizador: p. 3 do PDF, Seção III-B, item 3

citacoes.trecho: Vanilla+CoT: Base LLMs fine-tuned by vanilla dataset, then prompted by SI-CoT instructions.
Solely adopting SI-CoT improve the Pass@1 and Pass@5 by 3.6% and 6.6% on average, while fine-tuning LLMs with KL-dataset improves these metrics by 12.3 % and 8.7% on average.
They may produce syntax, functional or logical errors that do not match the expectation of HDL engineers.
Hallucination [11] in language models refers to the generation of incorrect or misleading information not grounded in reality.
This verification step ensures erroneous or incomplete pairs are filtered out.

tecnicas.nome_original: RETESTER (chain-of-thought (CoT) prompts for refactoring-preserving transformations; mutation prompt template of Table V)
tecnicas.localizador: Resumo, p. 1; Seção III-E e Tabela V, p. 6; Seção V-B e Tabela IX, p. 8-9 do PDF
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote completo: extração few-shot dos programas de entrada (Tabela I, dois exemplos manuais), extração one-shot da informação de refatoração e do template (Tabela III), e prompt de mutação (Tabela V) com definição da refatoração (contexto), template de estrutura do programa (contexto), característica propensa a erro (instrução), etapas numeradas e exigências de sintaxe, versão do JDK e formato (restrições). 'raciocinio' registra a inspiração em CoT declarada pelo estudo; a Tabela V não pede explicação explícita, e sim etapas sequenciais (também 'decomposicao'), e o pipeline encadeia extração e mutação. O contraste de pacote é com a linha de base de Gligoric et al. replicada com LLM (Tabela IX), que não faz mutação: é pacote híbrido, pois inclui filtragem por compilador JVM e teste diferencial manual nos IDEs, e o modelo usado na linha de base não é informado. Mecanismos acrescentados vazios: a linha de base não é um prompt base do qual RETESTER derive.

tecnicas.nome_original: Input program structure template (in the mutation prompt)
tecnicas.localizador: Seção V-D (RQ4), p. 9; Tabela VII (linhas Template = Y/N), p. 8; Fig. 5, p. 10 do PDF
tecnicas.observacao: Ablação (RQ4): o template é substituído pelo programa de entrada real no prompt da Tabela V, mantidas as demais configurações. Mecanismos listados são os da condição completa (Template = Y). Nenhuma categoria é acrescentada em relação à condição sem template, porque as duas fornecem código ao prompt ('contexto'): o template é uma abstração do programa, e a troca é de conteúdo dentro da mesma categoria.

tecnicas.localizador: Seção V-D, p. 9; Tabela VII, p. 8 do PDF

O estudo compara as três características entre si e cada uma com a linha de base de Gligoric et al., mas não executa condição sem característica; a linha de base difere em mais de um ingrediente. O estudo chama as configurações de componentes do seu instrumento, não de técnicas distintas.

tecnicas.nome_original: Gligoric et al. [18] testing approach replicated with an LLM (LLM proposes refactoring operations for each input program)

O prompt não é impresso e o modelo não é nomeado nesta seção; mecanismos inferidos da descrição (instrução e programa fornecido). A abordagem original de Gligoric et al. aplica refatorações em projetos reais, não em programas de relatórios de bug.

Our prompt design is inspired by chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, where instead of directly generating the final output, the prompt asks the model to finish task by breaking down the problem into sequential steps.
You need to generate the variant according to the Input Program Structure Template, it is {Template}.
For example, to reduce the uncompilable variants, we require the generated variants should conformance with specific JDK version.
For this study, we modified the mutation prompts in Table V by substituting the template information with details from the actual input program.
Except for these modifications to the mutation prompts, all other experimental settings remained unchanged.

Specifically, for each program, the LLM is instructed to suggest ten possible refactoring operations, mirroring the number of transformations we have predetermined for each category, such as “Lambda”.
Specifically, the prompt to extract input program from bug report is in Table I, we manually constructed two examples in order to instruct the LLM.
Meanwhile, by parsing the bug reports, we let LLM acts in a chain-of-thought way.
We adopt one-shot-learning for this step.
The model type is gpt-4o-mini with the default settings [45] and the knowledge cut-off date is Oct 2023.
Given that our tool leverages a large language model (LLM), it inherently generates variants that may contain syntax errors [47], [48].

However, the refactoring engine in ECLIPSE requires syntax-error-free input programs, otherwise refactoring operations cannot be performed, we subsequently filter the uncompilable variants using a JVM compiler.

This happens because the method to be refactored in the input program is mutated to a static method in variants, however, one of the preconditions to perform “Make static” refactoring is that the method to be refactored should not already been static [49], thus leading to eight variants cannot applying “Make static” refactoring.

Those two differential results were produced because the default configurations for “Make static” refactoring are slightly different in those two refactoring engines as described above, thus leading to two false positive.

Only two input programs have been incorrectly extracted because the input programs are incomplete code snippets only contain few lines of code and deeply interleaved with the natural language descriptions.
The internal threat to validity mainly lies in our manual classification and labeling of refactoring engine bugs, which may have subjective bias or errors.
As our dataset and our approach only focus on Java input programs generation, the findings may not generalize for other programming languages beyond Java.
To ensure the reliability and objectivity of the manual process, two annotators independently refactor each variant in the IDEs according to the reproduce procedures in the seed bug reports.
As each oracle violation may indicate potential bugs in refactoring engines, we manually verify all violations.
Before submitting the issues, we search in the corresponding bug-tracking systems of the target IDEs to avoid submitting duplicate reports.
Particularly, the Cohen’s Kappa coefficient was nearly 70% for the first 10% bug reports labeling results, thus we conducted a training session about labeling.
For ECLIPSE, there are three overlap bugs when testing “Inline method” refactoring with and without input program template during mutation stage, thus leading to 15 unique new bugs.
Without performing mutation on the input program, Gligoric’s approach fails to find any bugs using the same set of seed input programs as our approach.
