citacoes.trecho: The Qwen verifier achieves an accuracy of 42%, which is close to random performance in distinguishing correct and incorrect responses.
This indicates that small-scale Qwen fails to provide effective feedback, thereby harming rather than improving the initial response.
However, despite employing a costly verifier with relatively high accuracy, the results in Table 1 show only a marginal 5% gain over simple prompting.
The prompts were designed and implemented based on the manuscript, with Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) using a 3-shot prompting for both feedback generation and correction.
I have some code. Can you give one suggestion to improve the solution to the problem. Don’t fix the code, just give one suggestion.
We use a sampling temperature of 0.7 and set the number of generation to 20.
2. Think step by step to verify if the statement satisfies each of the constraints.
There might be an error in the code above because of a lack of understanding of the question. Please correct the error, if any, and rewrite the solution. Only output the final correct Python program!
This is further supported by Figure 2, where Qwen2.5-1.5B shows minimal changes (edit distance ≤ 0.05) in 93% of cases when the second response is incorrect, compared to only 32% for Gemini.
Specifically, we propose an online reinforcement learning objective that trains the model to confidently maintain correct outputs while progressively correcting incorrect outputs as turns proceed.
During inference, we use greedy decoding to ensure reproducibility.
KodCode is curated to exclude data from MBPP, HumanEval, and ODEX.
The results suggest that using boost models as the backbone in our experiments has minimal impact.

tecnicas.localizador: Resumo, p. 1; Seção III-E-2, p. 4; Seção III-F-3, Fig. 2, p. 5; Algoritmo 1, p. 6; Seção IV-C, p. 8-9; Tabela III, p. 10 do PDF
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote: prompt inicial zero-shot ('Please complete the Python function'), teste do código com casos gerados pelo GPT-4o e, para o código que falha, prompt de regeneração ('The previously generated code is incorrect...') com a exigência de valores diferentes para as cinco métricas de complexidade mais influentes (Shapley), até 5 iterações. 'feedback': regeneração guiada pela falha nos testes gerados e por valores de métricas calculados por analisador; 'restricoes': a exigência de que o código tenha valores diferentes nessas métricas restringe uma característica do código. Mecanismos acrescentados em relação ao prompt base zero-shot (Iteração 0). Contraste de pacote: Iteração 0 (zero-shot, 'first baseline') contra Iteração 5. É pacote híbrido: inclui regressão logística com valores de Shapley para escolher as métricas, cálculo das métricas (Radon e funções próprias) e geração de testes pelo GPT-4o, que não são prompting. O ingrediente 'métricas de complexidade no feedback' é isolado à parte pela segunda linha de base (ver componente). A descrição da função (assinatura e docstring) faz parte da especificação da tarefa em todas as condições e não foi contada como 'contexto'.

Contraste de pacote: Iteração 0 das linhas Reflexion contra Iteração 5; o ingrediente de complexidade é isolado pela linha branca Reflexion sem métricas. citacoes.trecho: Building on these findings, we propose an iterative feedback method, where LLMs are prompted to generate correct code based on complexity metrics from previous failed outputs.

Experiment results show that our approach makes notable improvements, particularly with a smaller LLM (GPT-3.5 Turbo), where, e.g., Pass@1 increased by 35.71% compared to the baseline’s improvement of 12.5% on the HumanEval dataset.
The study expands experiments to BigCodeBench and integrates the method with the Reflexion code generation agent, leading to Pass@1 improvements of 20% (GPT-4o) and 23.07% (GPT-o3 mini).

tecnicas.nome_original: test-time scaling strategy / Iterative Test-Time Scaling for RTL Coding (ScaleRTL†)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 2 do PDF (contribuições; Seção III); p. 3–4 do PDF (Seção III-B; Algoritmo 1); p. 4 do PDF (Seção IV-A-c, Model Inference); p. 5 do PDF (Tabela 2; Seção IV-C); p. 9 do PDF (Apêndice B; Tabela 5)
tecnicas.observacao: Técnica de prompting proposta pelo estudo, aplicada sobre o modelo ajustado ScaleRTL-32B. Quando a solução não passa no testbench (Algoritmo 1, linha 6: IsCorrect(S)), a solução após o delimitador «</think>» é descartada e o delimitador é substituído por um prompt corretivo («Wait, my reasoning must be incorrect. Let’s check the reasoning rules: {Reasoning Rules}. Wait, I did not follow the rules. Let’s try again.»), e o traço é reenviado ao modelo para continuar o raciocínio; o processo é iterativo (até T iterações; no experimento, duas passagens adicionais). Mecanismos do pacote: instrucao (especificação em linguagem natural herdada da inferência padrão e regras gerais de RTL em linguagem natural no prompt corretivo), raciocinio (o prompt corretivo pede revisão e extensão do raciocínio) e feedback (nova iteração condicionada à falha no testbench; o prompt corretivo não inclui o conteúdo do resultado do teste, só é acionado pela falha). Comparador executado: ScaleRTL-32B com inferência padrão (Tabela 2, Tabela 5, Figura 3). Pacote híbrido: além do prompt corretivo, a condição ScaleRTL† tem passagens adicionais com limites de tokens maiores (32,768 e 49,152 contra 16,384 na inferência inicial), componente de orçamento fora do escopo; o ganho da Tabela 2 é do pacote e não pode ser atribuído só ao prompt corretivo nem às regras. O estudo não informa se o testbench usado em IsCorrect é o mesmo da avaliação.

tecnicas.nome_original: {Reasoning Rules} (general RTL coding rules no prompt corretivo)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 4 do PDF (Seção III-B); p. 9 do PDF (Apêndice B; Figura 7)
tecnicas.observacao: Regras gerais de codificação RTL geradas offline por prompt ao Claude3.7-Sonnet (Figura 7, até três regras por resposta) e inseridas no prompt corretivo; exemplo impresso: «Carefully implement output signals based on their timing requirements». Diretrizes em linguagem natural → instrucao, categoria já presente na condição base (especificação zero-shot), por isso sem mecanismo acrescentado em nível de categoria. O Apêndice B afirma que as regras servem como «effective hints», mas não há condição do prompt corretivo sem regras; a contribuição das regras não é isolada. citacoes.trecho: We evaluate model performance on two representative RTL code generation benchmarks: VerilogEval [19] and RTLLM [23], which are designed to assess RTL code generation from natural language specifications.
For test-time scaling, we introduce a novel iterative approach that extends the model’s reasoning process through rethinking and self-correction, leading to more accurate final solutions.

If the solution fails to pass the testbench, the end-of-reasoning token delimiter “</think>” is then replaced with a corrective prompt: “Wait, my reasoning must be incorrect. Let’s check the reasoning rules: {Reasoning Rules}. Wait, I did not follow the rules. Let’s try again.”
The {Reasoning Rules} are generated offline and consist of general RTL coding guidelines, such as “Carefully implement output signals based on their timing requirements”.

For ScaleRTL†, we apply two additional inference passes per test problem using our test-time scaling strategy, as discussed in Section III-B.
The first pass uses a token limit of 32,768, and the second extends it to 49,152.
We use vLLM [17] with bf16 precision, a tensor parallelism factor of 4, a temperature of 0.2, and an initial token limit of 16,384.
As introduced in s1 [25], a straightforward approach to test-time scaling is to append a “Wait” token at the end of the reasoning trace to prompt the model to continue its reasoning process.
As a result, this simple trick often reproduces the original code solution generated by ScaleRTL and fails to correct any errors.
However, the model may still follow flawed reasoning paths, leading to solutions that fail to pass the testbench.
We develop an automated method to generate these general rules by prompting Claude3.7-Sonnet with the text shown in Figure 7.

To enable ScaleRTL to rethink and self-correct earlier reasoning steps, we find that incorporating general RTL coding rules into the corrective prompt serves as effective hints, encouraging the model to generate longer chain-of-thought reasoning traces during test-time scaling.

citacoes.trecho: We obtain the ScaleRTL model by fine-tuning DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on our curated CoT dataset containing 3.5B tokens shown in Table 1.
To prevent data contamination of downstream RTL benchmarks, we compute the Jaccard similarity between each collected code sample and the golden solutions in the benchmarks.
We discard any script whose similarity score exceeds 0.8 with respect to any golden reference.
We ensure that our CoT dataset contains no specification or code overlapping with existing RTL benchmarks, thereby avoiding any data contamination.

For more recent foundation models such as DeepSeek-R1 and Claude3.7-Sonnet, we intentionally exclude them from our main comparisons, as their training data cutoff dates postdate the release of RTL benchmarks.
It is likely that these models have been exposed to benchmark data during pre-training.
As a result, it is highly likely that their training corpora contain benchmark-related information, which may lead to overestimated performance on these evaluation sets.
A model that lacks such capabilities risks overfitting to narrow RTL coding problems in those benchmarks and may fail when applied to more open-ended or unfamiliar design challenges.

Notably, VerilogEval consists of two subsets: VerilogEval-Human, which contains 156 manually adapted problem descriptions from the HDLBits platform, and VerilogEval-Machine, which includes 143 descriptions automatically generated by GPT-3.5.
We choose n = 10 in this work.
In addition to the standard pass@k metric used for all baselines, we also report the pass rate, which measures whether a problem can be solved at least once within n = 10 trials.
Finally, the performance gap between ScaleRTL and ScaleRTL† confirms that test-time scaling plays a critical in accurate RTL code generation.
For instance, although CraftRTL-70B is significantly larger, it still underperforms compared to our 32B ScaleRTL model across all benchmarks.
Experimental results show that our models achieve substantial accuracy improvements over all baselines on two well-established RTL benchmarks: VerilogEval [19] and RTLLM [23].
Specifically, our best model improves pass@1 over the strongest prior RTL-specific baseline by up to 10.7% on VerilogEval and 11.7% on RTLLM.
To this end, we analyze the performance of five ScaleRTL variants across three benchmarks: VerilogEval-Machine, VerilogEval-Human, and RTLLM.

Specifically, we suppress its reasoning in the middle by replacing the keyword “Wait” with the delimiter “</think>,” which signals the end of reasoning and forces the model to directly output the RTL solution.

citacoes.trecho: To this end we propose an evaluation pipeline for LLM code generation with a focus on measuring sensitivity to prompt augmentations, completely agnostic to a specific programming tasks and LLMs, and thus widely applicable.
We apply three augmentation methods to the prompts: keyboard typos, synonyms, and paraphrasing.
This method attempts to simulate typos that a human can make while typing text on a keyboard.
Paraphrasing uses the translation capabilities of LLMs (i.e., Gemini) to paraphrase the prompt.
These reference outputs serve as ground truth representations of the model’s behavior on the original task specification.
To ensure all requests produce valid code, we added prefixes and postfixes, unaltered and ignored in the analysis, that stressed to the LLM that each request represents a coding task.
To reduce stochasticity of the results, we repeated each request to a LLM 5 times and recorded all responses, and we have also set the temperature of all models to 0.
Importantly, we do not evaluate correctness of generated code, and specifically focus on deviations between the codes generated from the original and altered prompts.
While temperature is considered to be the main parameter that gauges how random the output of a LLM is, even setting temperature to 0 does not guarantee fully deterministic results.
Llama 3.3 and Claude 3 Haiku, on the other hand, exhibit higher instability for unaltered prompts, again with temperature set to 0.
Unfortunately the most commonly circulated LeetCode tasks are included in the training data of most modern LLMs, which means they achieve almost 100% correct performance on these problems.
Matching their publication dates and official training cut-off dates of the LLMs we used, we have high confidence these tasks were not used in the training data for LLM models we evaluated.

Not only do we observe high variance for even unaltered prompts (only 0.7 similarity between generated code outputs), we can also confirm that code similarity drops below 0.5 TSED after only 10% of the prompt is modified, suggesting high sensitivity to these modifications.

Even on its own structural variability matters: users providing similar prompts may receive dramatically different implementations, affecting code review, maintenance, and trust, even when the code is functionally equivalent.
As mentioned before, TSED measures structural similarity, not functional equivalence, creating potential construct validity issues.
Structural variability poses real challenges for users who must understand, debug, and maintain different implementations.
We have also used multiple LLM providers in all our experiments to show how our method can be applied to different models.

The setup of the experiment was to instruct the LLM to adopt each persona in turn and to paraphrase a provided prompt, using their background and assumed knowledge to inform the language they use to describe the task and to add any details that they consider relevant.
We then randomly sampled one of these prompts for each persona and input it into the user interface of ChatGPT and Claude to generate the code.
The code generated by each persona on the three tasks and two models (ChatGPT and Claude) was evaluated observationally for trends.
We used all male personas in order to isolate whether programming experience influences prompt development and the resulting code without influence from gender bias in the training set of the LLM.

Using the framework from El-Assady et al. [9], we can see from the visualisation in Figure 4 the relative number of entities that are common between the prompts generated by the different personas by the thickness of the lines connecting the persona names in the visualisation.

This resulted in large differences in the generated code, with the most dramatic being no code generated when it asked for “the computer to write up a set of financial reports” for the accounting report generation task, which provided a set of instructions for how the user could send the reports in and it would then process them without providing a code implementation.

Specifically, the mean BERT score was 98.0%, with all 26532 recorded evaluations scoring above 91.0%, suggesting potential range restriction and ceiling effects that could negatively impact our experiments were they to use this metric [28].
A lower Sacre BLEU metric value indicates higher diversity.

The test revealed a statistically significant effect of augmentation rate on code similarity (p < 0.001 for keyboard typos and synonyms, p < 0.02 for paraphrasings), indicating a strong relationship between augmentation rate and LLM code generation sensitivity.

The test showed significant (p < 0.001 for keyboard typos and p < 0.02 for synonyms) difference in the distribution of sensitivity increases across three datasets, supporting the generalizability of our pipeline for a variety of programming tasks.

tecnicas.observacao: Framework proposto: Program Repair Module (agente de teste e agente de patch, com prompts de tarefa, contexto da issue, feedback de execução iterativo via ReAct, localização hierárquica, várias amostras de patch e seleção final por LLM) mais Memory Module (memória episódica com demonstrações recuperadas por BM25 e memória semântica com insights resumidos e atualizados por ADD/EDIT/REMOVE e anexados ao prompt de tarefa). Mecanismos: instrucao (prompt de tarefa com papel, requisitos e insights como diretrizes); restricoes (formato estrito do patch, requisitos do script de teste); contexto (descrição da issue, estrutura do repositório, conteúdo de arquivos, linhas localizadas, demonstrações recuperadas); exemplos (demonstrações como exemplos em contexto); raciocinio (fase FIX ANALYSIS antes da implementação; ReAct); decomposicao (encadeamento geração de teste → localização → geração de patch → validação); feedback (resultados de execução da tentativa anterior); multiagente (agentes de teste e de patch que colaboram); amostragem (vários patches candidatos e seleção por LLM); otimizacao_prompt (atualização automática dos insights da memória semântica, que o estudo chama de «lightweight auto-prompting technique»). Pacote híbrido: inclui recuperação BM25, execução de testes e ferramentas, e componentes fora do escopo (fallback para o4-mini, temperatura alta). Na Tabela 1 é comparado com sistemas externos cujos resultados foram copiados de leaderboard ou artigos; não existe condição «sem ExpeRepair» com o mesmo restante do sistema, por isso nao/nenhum para o framework inteiro. As ablações isolam módulos (ver Memory Module, Episodic Memory e Semantic Memory).

tecnicas.observacao: Contrafactual de pacote: ExpeRepair completo contra «w/o Memory Module», que remove as duas memórias e trata cada issue isoladamente, com Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Ingredientes acrescentados: demonstrações recuperadas (contexto e exemplos) e insights anexados ao prompt de tarefa (instrucao) mantidos por resumo e atualização automática (otimizacao_prompt); contexto e instrucao já existem no prompt base por outros ingredientes. O sim do pacote não autoriza atribuir o ganho a uma das memórias isoladamente. O pacote inclui recuperação BM25 e o limite de 15 insights.

citacoes.trecho: We propose ExpeRepair, a novel LLM-based program repair framework inspired by the dual-memory systems of human cognition, where episodic and semantic memory synergistically support learning and decision-making.
It further enhances adaptability through dynamic prompt composition, integrating both memory types to replace static prompts with context-aware, experience-driven prompts.
The repair module orchestrates a test agent and a patch agent, which collaboratively perform test generation, patch generation, and patch validation for each issue.
The retrieved demonstrations are then incorporated into the agent’s prompts as in-context examples, offering concrete precedents for constructing accurate reproduction scripts or patches.
This mechanism, effectively serving as a lightweight auto-prompting technique [36, 37, 45], incrementally improves repair effectiveness by guiding agents with accumulated semantic experience.
Write the patch using the strict format specified below:
citacoes.localizador: p. 6 do PDF, Prompt for Patch Generation

citacoes.trecho: In each iteration, we perform multiple samplings with a high temperature to generate diverse candidate patches.
Then, we pass candidate patches and their corresponding test results to the LLM, which selects the final patch based on criteria such as correctness and adherence to best practices.

This is because we empirically observed that reproduction scripts typically focus narrowly on the specific symptoms described in the issue, leading to false positives where patches pass limited tests but fail in broader contexts.
o4-mini is invoked only in rare fallback cases (less than 1% of total LLM calls) when temporary API unavailability occurs, following a practice similar to SpecRover [35].
For baselines, we directly use the reported results either from the official leaderboard or from the tool’s official paper/repository.
citacoes.localizador: p. 11 do PDF, legenda da Tabela 1

citacoes.trecho: Unless otherwise specified, all experiments use Claude 3.5 Sonnet as the foundation model.
Dense retrieval occasionally returns semantically related yet causally different issues.
Figure 2 shows that variants without REMOVE consistently underperform, as accumulated insights can saturate the prompt context and introduce noise.
At the same time, issues solved exclusively by DARS highlight a limitation of ExpeRepair: its effectiveness drops when relevant prior experience is unavailable.
This raises the risk that evaluation results reflect prior exposure rather than genuine generalization.
To mitigate this concern, we avoid long-standing APR benchmarks (e.g., Defects4J [22]), which are more likely to have been included in model training corpora.
Our evaluation is limited to open-source projects implemented in Python, constraining our ability to demonstrate cross-language effectiveness.

tecnicas.observacao: Sistema multiagente sobre GPT-4o (AutoGen) com quatro módulos: compreensão e raciocínio iterativos (sumarização, decomposição em subfunções, dicionário estruturado de informações revisado por um Verifier), codificação progressiva com otimização de prompt (pseudocódigo → Python → C++, Coder e Verifier, Prompt Optimizer Agent), reflexão adaptativa (Analysis Agent e Reflection Agent com quatro ações, inclusive pedido de intervenção humana) e otimização de código para HLS (Code Optimizer Agent com diretrizes extraídas do tutorial da ferramenta). O contrafactual de pacote é a linha de base Single-Shot (documento inteiro e geração do RTL em uma tentativa), executada pelo estudo. Pacote híbrido: inclui conversão C++ → RTL pela ferramenta comercial Stratus HLS, substituição de subfunções por regra, pré-processamento do PDF (PyPDF e capturas de tela) e intervenções humanas quando a reflexão escala o problema; o ganho é do pacote e não pode ser atribuído a um único mecanismo. Mecanismos acrescentados registrados por ingrediente em relação ao Single-Shot, que já contém instrução e o documento de especificação como contexto. A comparação com a linha de base Human mede substituição de trabalho humano, não um ingrediente de prompting.

Os prompts, o número de pessoas, sua experiência e a forma de contar intervenções não são descritos (nao_informado). Os valores da Tabela I são aproximados («∼20»). tecnicas.observacao: Três etapas: Summarization Agent (resumos por seção → contexto), Decomposer Agent (subfunções → decomposição) e Information Augmentation, em que o Description Agent organiza um dicionário estruturado (entradas, saídas, funcionalidade, referências ao documento → restrições de formato) revisado por um Verifier (feedback entre agentes). A Fig. 3 mostra também um Understanding Agent. Ablação W/o Understand: o documento inteiro vai direto ao módulo de codificação, mantidos os demais módulos. As três etapas internas não são isoladas entre si. Contexto, feedback e multiagente também existem em outros módulos; aqui são registrados por serem ingredientes que o módulo acrescenta (resumos e dicionário; ciclo Description Agent–Verifier).

tecnicas.localizador: p. 4 do PDF (Seção IV-C; Fig. 3); p. 5 do PDF (Seção V-A, Baselines (4); Seção V-C; Tabela I, colunas Naive Coding e Spec2RTL-Agent); p. 6 do PDF (Fig. 5)
tecnicas.observacao: Módulo que reúne as duas técnicas Progressive Coding e Prompt Optimization. Ablação Naive Coding: substitui o módulo por um módulo C++ ingênuo que gera o C++ de cada subfunção com as informações fornecidas, sem melhorias iterativas nem otimizações; os demais módulos permanecem. As duas técnicas são retiradas juntas, por isso o contrafactual vale para o módulo e não para cada uma.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 4 do PDF (Seção IV-C, Progressive Coding; Fig. 3)
tecnicas.observacao: Geração sequencial de pseudocódigo, Python e C++ por subfunção, com o código de nível mais alto como referência para o de nível mais baixo (contexto; representações intermediárias encadeadas → decomposição). Um Coder redige e um Verifier avalia, sugerindo revisões ou regeneração (feedback, multiagente); o Verifier deriva casos de teste do documento ou do código de nível mais alto, ou faz autovalidação contra a especificação. Só é retirada junto com Prompt Optimization (Naive Coding); sem contrafactual próprio.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 4 do PDF (Seção IV-C, Prompt Optimization); p. 6 do PDF (Seção V-E, Prompt Optimization; Fig. 5)
tecnicas.observacao: O agente analisa o registro de implementação da subfunção, extrai aprendizados e refina o prompt do Coder (Fig. 5: prompt de papel «You are a python coder» acrescido de dicas sobre formato e dimensão de entradas e saídas). A Fig. 5 é ilustração qualitativa de um caso (AddRoundKey()), sem medida. Só é retirada junto com Progressive Coding (Naive Coding); sem contrafactual próprio.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 4 do PDF (Seção IV-D; Fig. 3); p. 5 do PDF (Seção V-A, Baselines (5); Seção V-C; Tabela I, colunas W/o Reflection e Spec2RTL-Agent); p. 6 do PDF (Fig. 6)

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we address this gap by proposing an LLM agent system, termed Spec2RTL-Agent, designed to directly process complex specification documentation and generate corresponding RTL code implementations, advancing LLM-based RTL code generation toward more realistic application settings.

We evaluate Spec2RTL-Agent on a benchmark of three specification documents, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating accurate RTL code with as much as 75% fewer human interventions compared to existing approaches.

These results underscore Spec2RTL-Agent’s role as the first fully automated multi-agent system for RTL generation from unstructured specification documents, reducing the reliance on human effort and expertise in hardware design.
Notably, Spec2RTL-Agent achieves as much as 75% fewer human interventions compared to existing methods.

A Summarization Agent is employed to generate concise summaries for each section of the document, thereby simplifying the initial comprehension process and reducing the complexity for further processing.
A Decomposer Agent receives both the summarized data and the original document, tasked with organizing the target implementation into a sequence of implementable sub-functions.

The Description Agent uses the original document, the summaries provided, and specific sub-function requirements as inputs to collate and format the necessary information into a structured dictionary.
The Verifier then reviews this dictionary, providing feedback to enhance the quality and accuracy of the information.
The process involves sequentially generating pseudocode, Python, and C++ code.

citacoes.trecho: This often results in scenarios where a newly implemented sub-function fails to pass test cases due to errors in previously implemented sub-functions.
An Analysis Agent first reviews the entire generation trajectory to summarize the completed work and propose potential areas where errors may reside.
If the error source remains unclear, the agent escalates the issue for human intervention, summarizing the situation and requesting guidance on corrective measures.
This agent adapts the C++ code to meet the HLS tool’s constraints based on guidelines extracted from the tutorial of this HLS tool.
(1) Single-Shot: The entire specification document is input into an LLM, which is tasked with generating the target RTL in a single attempt.
(2) Human: Mirroring approaches like that in [7], a human handles the understanding and reflection phases while delegating code implementation to an LLM based on provided instructions.
(3) W/o Understand: This variation of our pipeline omits the iterative understanding and reasoning module, directly feeding the entire document into the coding module to complete the implementation.
(4) Naive Coding: This configuration removes the progressive coding and prompt optimization module, replacing it with a naive C++ coding module.
(5) W/o Reflection: This configuration bypasses the adaptive reflection module.
In our study, we use GPT-4o [43] as the core architecture for all agents, with agent interactions and tool usage managed via the AutoGen framework [26].

citacoes.trecho: The Single-Shot approach, which directly prompts LLMs to generate implementations, failed in all three test cases, underscoring the complexity of the task.
Specifically, Spec2RTL-Agent reduced human interventions by approximately 75%, easing the burden of RTL implementation and enhancing development efficiency.
Compared to W/o Reflection and Naive Coding, our full Spec2RTL-Agent reduced human interventions by 51.9% and 31.6%, and coding iterations by 47.8% and 31.0%, respectively.
These results confirm the effectiveness of each module in improving code accuracy.

Em relação à condição sem taxonomia, a única categoria nova é 'exemplos': 'contexto' já está no prompt base (código fornecido), e a taxonomia acrescenta conteúdo dentro dessa categoria; 'restricoes' está nas duas condições (tabela de cinco colunas sem Scenario ID). O contraste é com e sem a taxonomia, com o mesmo modelo, os mesmos 25 trechos e a mesma temperatura; o formato de saída também muda (coluna Scenario ID), e a taxonomia junta conhecimento descritivo e exemplos de código, de modo que o ganho não pode ser repartido entre 'contexto' e 'exemplos'. citacoes.trecho: This taxonomy, along with the original Python source code, is provided as input to an LLM, which is then tasked with identifying instances of migration scenarios in the code and suggesting appropriate refactoring solutions.
For each code sample, we conducted two independent interactions with the same LLM: one where the full migration taxonomy was included as context, and one where it was omitted.

When the taxonomy was included, the prompt additionally required the model to reference the corresponding scenario identifier or indicate with an ”*” if no match was found, indicating the model found a migration scenario not present in the taxonomy.
To standardize the model outputs and facilitate comparison, we instructed the LLM to return its migration suggestions in a structured markdown table format.
Line numbers were pre-inserted in the code through an automated preprocessing step to improve referential clarity in the output.
All experiments were conducted using OpenAI’s gpt-4-0613 model via the chat.completions API endpoint, with a temperature setting of 0.1 and default values for all other parameters.
No chain-of-thought prompting, function calling, or external tools were used.

As such, we assume the model had access to documentation up to Qiskit versions 0.46, 1.0, and possibly 2.0 at the time of training, which introduces an uncontrollable variable discussed later in the discussion.
The review process was performed independently without formal inter-rater reliability measures, though all scores were cross-checked for consistency.
In the remaining 3 non-refactoring cases, the model produced incorrect migration suggestions (false positives).
The taxonomy-assisted model produced 40 incorrect or misleading changes (false positives), compared to 61 incorrect suggestions without the taxonomy.

For example, in cases involving deprecated module imports, the model occasionally suggested their direct removal without considering their subsequent usage within the code, when a proper replacement would have been more appropriate.
As a result, we observed occasional inconsistencies, such as the reuse of placeholder variables copied verbatim from the taxonomy examples.
Thus, we created a taxonomy targeting version 0.46 using ChatGPT 4.1.
The results were refined and manually verified by experts in quantum computing programming.
The were a total of 50 invocations to the model, two per each of the 25 code snippets.
citacoes.localizador: Legenda da Fig. 1, p. 3 do PDF

citacoes.trecho: We test these prompting strategies under the added stressor of Qiskit version drift and demonstrate that their effectiveness degrades in the absence of domain adaptation—highlighting new boundary conditions for prompt engineering in quantum code tasks.
In contrast to approaches like RAG, our study operates in a static, zero-shot setting.
However, the impact of taxonomy quality on model performance was not quantitatively assessed in this study and warrants further investigation.

The model failed to detect or provide incorrect suggestions on 31 lines that required refactoring when guided by the taxonomy, while it missed 52 of such lines in the absence of the taxonomy (false negatives).

citacoes.trecho: Through this research, we aim to evaluate the capability of LLMs in generating syntactically and logically accurate LaTeX code (which we refer to as accurate LaTeX code generation or simply LaTeX generation) and analyse the main types of errors they encounter.
We evaluate popular open and closed-source LLMs on TeXpert by computing the success rate across three difficulty classes
For each sample across the three difficulty levels in TeXpert, we provide the LLM with a prompt containing task instructions for LaTeX code generation (provided in Figure 5 in Appendix B).
You are a helpful LaTeX code assistant.
Your main job is to produce syntactically correct and logically accurate LaTeX code based on instructions given as TASK INSTRUCTIONS.
Make sure to follow each and every small instruction given in the task instructions.
Do not give any output other than the LaTeX code, please!
During generation, model parameters were set to predetermined values to ensure deterministic outputs, as detailed in Table 11 in Appendix B.
Rule-based extraction techniques are used to extract the LaTeX code from the response.

We then evaluate each LLM’s response with GPT-4o as a judge, using a predefined evaluation prompt (refer to Figure 4 in Appendix B) to compute success rates and classify error types (described in Table 7 in Appendix B).
The evaluation prompt was iteratively refined through manual spot checks of evaluation outputs, focusing on clarity, correctness, and alignment with evaluation criteria.
For the hard set, we also provide manually generated and verified LaTeX code as a reference during evaluation, to help identify all requirements of the task.
To mitigate potential evaluation bias from using the same model family as the judge, we use DeepSeek v3 as an evaluator for GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini.
We use the OpenAI Python SDK to access the models via API, specifying seed=1234 and n=1 along with the parameter values listed in Table 11, to ensure maximum determinism in responses.
Due to limited configurable parameters, only temperature=0.0, top_p=1, and max_tokens=8096 were explicitly set, with all other settings left at their defaults.

With a focus on a small but high-quality dataset, we manually verify every row across all three classes in our dataset to ensure clear LaTeX generation requirements and consistency with the difficulty constraints.

We curate a structured benchmark dataset containing natural language instructions for generating LaTeX code for various elements of scientific content using a combination of manual effort and LLM-based command generation.
Our dataset consists of a total of 440 high-quality samples, organised by difficulty.
Even models that perform highly on other benchmarks like GPT-4o and Mistral Large fail to achieve over 80% and 60% accuracy in simple and average sets, respectively.
Accuracy across the Simple and Average sets remains consistent across models, however, models show a dramatic performance cliff on hard tasks, with Claude and Gemini completely failing.
This demonstrates the potential of open-source models to provide powerful yet cost-effective alternatives.
Logical errors consistently account for the majority of issues across LLMs, highlighting struggles to fully satisfy task requirements.

In all the cases we analysed, the most pronounced errors across all model variants were focused on missed instructions and wrong structural placement, especially in GPT-4o-mini and all open-source models.

GPT-4o has the lowest share of missing packages, showing encouraging signs that more inclusive training data might mitigate this issue, although Codestral’s minimal package error rate also suggests potential for alternative approaches to reduce them further.

Additionally, the use of non-standard or incompatible packages, especially in DeepSeek and Mistral models, is concerning and may point to LLMs hallucinating or making up packages to fill reasoning gaps.
The Hard set’s restricted size of 40 samples is a possible challenge in the generalisability of our findings.

Using our dataset to fine-tune models and reduce logical and package errors in LaTeX-based tasks is another straightforward extension to our work, along with checking advanced prompting structures for performance improvements.

The prompts used during experimentation to evaluate responses using GPT-4o/DeepSeek v3 as a judge and to generate LaTeX code using natural language instructions and are given in Figures 4 and 4 respectively.

citacoes.trecho: This paper benchmarks LLMs for PennyLane-based quantum code generation using real-world challenges from the Quantum Hackathon (QHack).
We introduce QHackBench, a novel benchmark dataset derived from QHack competitions, and evaluate model performance under vanilla prompting and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

Results indicate that RAG-enhanced models, supplemented with an augmented PennyLane dataset, approximately generate similar results as the standard prompting, particularly in complex quantum algorithms.
Additionally, we introduce a multi-agent evaluation pipeline that iteratively refines incorrect solutions, further enhancing execution success rates.

To foster further research, we commit to publicly releasing QHackBench, along with our evaluation framework and experimental results, enabling continued advancements in AI-assisted quantum programming.

Our study shows that while RAG improves accuracy in specific cases, such as reducing hallucinated API calls and refining circuit structures, current foundation models still face significant limitations in generating reliable quantum code.
In this study, we report only binary outcomes—each challenge is either solved correctly or not.
Furthermore, integrating a multi-agent refinement pipeline further improved the execution success rate significantly.
By leveraging PennyLang, LLMs can access previously solved quantum problems, reducing API hallucinations and improving functional correctness in PennyLane programming [22].

To analyze the effectiveness of RAG, we evaluate multiple LLMs, including GPT-4o mini (RAG and non-RAG) and GPT-o3 Mini (RAG and non-RAG), allowing a direct comparison between retrieval-enhanced responses and baseline prompting.
Once the solutions are generated, we employ an automated execution system that runs the code in an isolated environment, verifying functional validity and correctness against predefined test cases.
Base query. The QHack challenge description and template are provided to LLMs (GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7, ...) for initial code generation.

citacoes.trecho: This retrieved knowledge is appended to the model prompt, improving accuracy and reducing hallucinations.
Construct prompt: P = system_prompt + S + Q
Validation & Correction Agent (GPT-o3-Mini): Executes the generated code, analyzes errors from execution logs, and iteratively refines the solution through self-reasoning and debugging.
If RAG is enabled, the retrieved context from the PennyLang dataset is also included in the updated query to enhance code corrections.

This process is repeated iteratively, with a maximum of five refinement attempts, ensuring that the solution is progressively improved until it successfully passes all test cases or reaches the retry limit.
We curated a dataset comprising 49 unique QHack challenges from 2023-2024 [26], [27].
Single-agent generation. A “builder” LLM receives the challenge and must solve it in at most five attempts, with or without RAG.
Multi-agent refinement. A validator LLM inspects failing runs and reformulates the query; the builder then regenerates code.
Using RAG, the validator performs a ChromaDB vector search (MMR, top-k=3) over the PennyLang corpus and injects the most relevant code chunks into the follow-up query.
Pass@k: Probability of obtaining a correct solution within the first k attempts.
Execution Success Rate: Percentage of solutions that execute without runtime errors.
Correction Efficiency: Average number of iterations needed for successful code refinement.

citacoes.trecho: This case highlights how RAG can degrade performance when irrelevant context misleads the model, demonstrating the importance of retrieval quality and fallback strategies.
(1) Even with RAG, models frequently produce hallucinated APIs and incorrect quantum circuits, revealing a lack of domain-specific understanding despite access to documentation.
(2) Binary pass@k fails to capture semantic errors; many outputs are syntactically correct but fail at runtime due to flawed quantum logic.
Comparing vanilla prompting, RAG, and a simple multi-agent refinement method, we find that RAG boosts correctness, while the multi-agent approach improves execution success via iterative reasoning.
Evaluations on GPT-4o, GPT-o3-Mini, and DeepSeek-V3 highlight both capabilities and limitations in quantum programming, demonstrating the promise of agent-based techniques in this domain.

citacoes.trecho: This study systematically evaluates the performance of several common CoT techniques in APR tasks and proposes an innovative framework T3, which integrates the powerful reasoning capabilities of LLMs with tree search, effectively improving the precision of generating candidate repair solutions.
T3 decomposes the reasoning process for generating candidate patches into four stages: sample retrieval, cause analysis, repair plan generation, and patch generation.
The top-n results, selected based on cross-tree consistency and voting mechanisms, are then used for further processing.

This paper introduces a novel repair method that achieves substantial improvements over previous approaches; specifically, it improves repair accuracy by 11.20% and 9.90% compared to methods based on CoT reasoning.
These limitations hinder the generation of innovative solutions, increase the risk of entering infinite feedback loops, and ultimately constrain further advancements in repair efficiency.
Custom prompt templates based on four common CoT variants were designed, and experiments were conducted to comparatively analyze their effectiveness in this domain.
“Analogical Reasoning” [14] encourages the generation of examples analogous to the original problem, solving these examples first to inform the final solution.
To retrieve code examples similar to the target program snippet Ptarget, we employ the BM25 algorithm.
To improve the reliability of error cause selection, we introduce a self-consistency mechanism.
Unlike prior work [31], which applies self-consistency for patch selection, we leverage this mechanism to filter and rank error causes.

To ensure the reliability of our results, each program in every experimental group is tested with 30 generated samples, and the temperature parameter is set to 0.7 to mitigate the influence of randomness.

Given that previous experiments conducted by Toufique Ahmed [31] were based on the deprecated code-davinci-002 model, we uniformly select the widely used gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4o-mini to eliminate the impact of foundational model discrepancies on repair performance.
To ensure reproducibility, we use the version gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 and gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18

Additionally, we compare our approach with several advanced techniques, including CoT [28], Tree-of-Thought prompt [12], Plan-and-Solve [13], and Analogical Reasoning [14], to provide a comprehensive evaluation.
Specifically, the data for S-C and S-C+BM25 are sourced from [31], while the data for NatGen are obtained from [33].
In contrast, Analogical Reasoning shows markedly lower performance (31.40% on B2Fs, 15.70% on B2Fm), likely due to its dependence on potentially mismatched example retrievals.
This implies that, for complex tasks, the T3 model employs a variety of reasoning pathways to augment overall repair efficacy, notwithstanding a compromise in consistency during patch generation.
Since the retrieval module is consistently used across all control groups, we do not perform ablation on it.
CoT performs even less satisfactorily, as it not only fails to fix the primary error but also modifies correct parts of the target program.
Both methods generate repair patches in a single step, sometimes resolving the issue but often introducing unnecessary modifications to unrelated parts of the program.

tecnicas.nome_original: layered knowledge injection framework (Layered/Hierarchical Knowledge Injection)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 1 (resumo), p. 2 (contribuições), p. 3 (Seção III e Fig. 2), p. 7 (Tabela II) do PDF
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote proposto: prompt CoT com formato de saída restrito (código entre crases triplas, sem explicações), mais contexto injetado em três camadas sucessivas (Bug, Repository e Project Knowledge). Mecanismos herdados do prompt base (Bug Knowledge Layer): instrucao, raciocinio (CoT), restricoes (formato), contexto (fatos do bug). Acrescentados em relação a essa base: contexto (repositório, documentação recuperada), exemplos (histórico de issues resolvidas, do qual o agente de QA extrai estratégias e alterações de código de correções anteriores) e outro (escalonamento progressivo: só os bugs cujo patch falha nos testes recebem o prompt da camada seguinte; o estudo não informa que o patch anterior ou o resultado dos testes volte ao modelo, por isso não foi classificado como feedback). Contrafactual de pacote: a Bug Knowledge Layer (rodada no corpus inteiro e declarada linha de base das camadas seguintes) contra o pacote completo (linha Project Knowledge Layer da Tabela II, resultado cumulativo). Ressalvas: o resultado do pacote é cumulativo entre até três rodadas de 10 respostas por bug não resolvido, enquanto a linha de base tem uma rodada; o ganho é do pacote e não pode ser atribuído a um mecanismo isolado. O pacote inclui componentes fora do escopo (recuperação densa com embeddings e FAISS, análise estática, mineração de co-mudanças, agente de QA com GPT-4o-mini e localização perfeita de falhas): pacote híbrido. O contraste com «All Knowledge Layers at Once» isola o escalonamento (ver técnica própria). A comparação com Parasaram et al. usa números de outro artigo e não é comparador executado.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 3 (Seção III), p. 4 (Seções III-B e III-C, RQ1), p. 5 (GitHub Description), p. 7 (Tabela II) do PDF

Prompt com CoT e formato restrito. Não há condição sem esse contexto (por exemplo, prompt só com a função defeituosa) executada no estudo; por isso sem contrafactual.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 5 (RQ2: Co-occurring Files, Structural Dependencies, Latest Changes), p. 7 (Tabela II e resultados da RQ2), p. 8 (Tabela III) do PDF
tecnicas.observacao: Acrescenta à camada de bug as dependências estruturais (funções e classes chamadas e chamadoras, via AST e Jedi, limitadas aos arquivos co-modificados) e o commit mais recente na função defeituosa; os arquivos co-modificados não entram diretamente no prompt. Aplicada só aos bugs não resolvidos na camada anterior (107 para Llama 3.3 e 117 para GPT-4o-mini): contribuição cumulativa por rodada, sem condição comparável sem a camada no mesmo conjunto de bugs com igual número de tentativas.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 5 (RQ3: Documentation, Issue Resolution History), p. 8 (resultados da RQ3, Tabela III), p. 7 (Tabela II) do PDF
tecnicas.observacao: Acrescenta trechos de documentação recuperados por similaridade e resumidos por um agente de QA (LangChain) e insights de issues resolvidas anteriores ao bug (texto e patches), incluindo estratégias e alterações de código de correções passadas: classificado como contexto e exemplos (recuperação que traz exemplos resolvidos). O estudo não detalha a forma exata como esse material entra no prompt (formatos no pacote de replicação, não consultado). Aplicada só aos bugs não resolvidos após a camada de repositório (79 para Llama 3.3 e 93 para GPT-4o-mini): contribuição cumulativa.

tecnicas.nome_original: progressive, hierarchical injection (escalonamento em camadas, contrastado com o baseline “all-at-once”)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 6 (Seção III-D, Baselines), p. 7 (Tabela II, duas últimas linhas), p. 9 (comparação com o baseline) do PDF
tecnicas.observacao: Ingrediente do pacote: injetar o contexto de forma progressiva, avançando à camada seguinte só para bugs cujo patch falha nos testes (outro). O baseline «All Knowledge Layers at Once» injeta simultaneamente as informações das três camadas em todos os bugs; segundo o estudo, serve para avaliar se a injeção progressiva e hierárquica é mais eficaz. Ressalva de comparabilidade: a condição hierárquica concede até três rodadas de 10 respostas aos bugs não resolvidos (resultado cumulativo), enquanto o baseline tem uma rodada; a diferença de orçamento de tentativas acompanha o ingrediente. Também tratado como componente, e não técnica focal distinta, porque é parte do sistema proposto.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 6 (Seção III-D), p. 7 (Tabela II), p. 9 do PDF
tecnicas.observacao: Comparador executado: mesmas informações das três camadas, injetadas de uma vez para os 314 bugs. Mecanismos acrescentados em relação ao prompt base (Bug Knowledge Layer), pelo mesmo critério aplicado às camadas. Os mecanismos do comparador não são isolados. Bugs mais complexos e estruturalmente isolados (sobretudo Program Anomaly, Network e GUI) continuam sem correção mesmo com todas as camadas: 85 bugs não resolvidos pelo GPT-4o-mini e 64 pelo Llama 3.3.

riscos.descricao: Os dados de treinamento dos LLMs proprietários não são divulgados, o que impede verificar se bugs ou conteúdo dos repositórios estavam no pré-treinamento. O estudo não afirma contaminação efetiva.
O não determinismo dos LLMs pode levar a resultados variáveis entre respostas.

A eficácia da camada de projeto depende da qualidade da documentação e do registro de issues de cada projeto; nos bugs não resolvidos, parte do contexto de repositório ou projeto não estava disponível (Tabela IV).

Validade externa: os achados podem não generalizar para outros LLMs; a distribuição dos tipos de bug é desbalanceada e categorias sub-representadas (por exemplo, Permission/Deprecation, 2 bugs) podem não gerar conclusões aplicáveis.

mitigacoes.descricao: Avaliação com pass@k e n = 10 respostas por prompt para lidar com o não determinismo.
Teste prévio em 10 bugs, 10 execuções por bug e por modelo (200 execuções), com saídas descritas como consistentes; critério de consistência nao_informado.
Revisão manual de todas as issues e pull requests vinculados para garantir que descrevam o bug sem revelar a correção.
Contra vazamento: desenho focado na eficácia relativa entre camadas, dois modelos distintos e citação de estudo que encontrou 11% de vazamento no BugsInPy com StarCoder (modelo não usado no estudo).
Anotação dos tipos de bug com duas rodadas de concordância (kappa 0,45 e depois 0,8) e resolução de divergências.
Patches plausíveis testados e verificados manualmente como correções corretas.

heterogeneidade.descricao: Inconsistência na camada de projeto do GPT-4o-mini: o texto diz «fixing 7 additional bugs» e a análise manual cita 7 bugs novos, mas Tabela II e linha Overall da Tabela III dão 229/314 após 221/314 (diferença de 8, cálculo próprio). A soma das linhas por tipo dessa coluna na Tabela III (129+38+21+26+13+1) dá 228 (cálculo próprio). Na RQ4, o total de 85 não resolvidos pelo GPT-4o-mini não bate com a soma das parcelas por tipo informadas no mesmo período (58+9+7+8+3+1 = 86, cálculo próprio); 85 é compatível com 229 e com a união de 99 (85+64−50). Não é possível decidir qual valor é o correto.

O «improvement of 23%» do resumo corresponde à diferença de 79% para 56%, isto é, 23 pontos percentuais (cálculo próprio), e não a variação relativa. citacoes.trecho: We propose a layered knowledge injection framework that incrementally augments LLMs with structured context.
By progressively injecting knowledge across layers, our approach achieves a fix rate of 79% (250/314) using Llama 3.3, a significant improvement of 23% over previous work.
We use Chain-of-Thought prompting, a proven strategy for guiding LLMs to process context step by step, as demonstrated in APR and other tasks [9], [20]–[22].
We enforce standardized outputs by requiring all code to be wrapped in triple backticks.
We also omit textual explanations to ensure the output contains only code.
Due to space constraints, we include the detailed prompt formats for each knowledge layer in our replication package.

The information types in this layer are adopted from Parasaram et al. [9], and serve as a baseline for evaluating the impact of injecting other contextual information in subsequent layers (RQ2 and RQ3).
We apply this knowledge injection to the bugs unresolved after the Bug Knowledge Layer, allowing us to assess the impact of repository-level context on repair outcomes.
Co-occurring files are not directly used in prompts.
We inject them to the unresolved bugs after the Repository Knowledge Layer.
These past issues often contain relevant knowledge about similar bugs and their resolutions [41], [42].
citacoes.localizador: p. 5 do PDF, Issue Resolution History

citacoes.trecho: We consider both the code (patches) and the natural language (titles, descriptions, discussions, and labels).
citacoes.localizador: p. 5 do PDF, Issue Resolution History

citacoes.trecho: We compare our approach against two baselines: (1) Parasaram et al. [9]’s approach, which leverages various bug-related contextual information to produce patches; and (2) an approach where information from all three layers (bug, repository, and project knowledge) is injected simultaneously for every bug.
The second baseline allows us to assess whether progressive, hierarchical injection is more effective than providing all context at once.
Since our focus is on generating patches for APR, for bug localization we use Function-granular Perfect Fault Localization, as recommended in prior work [9], [18].
It cannot determine which class attribute to modify and instead hallucinates the existence of a variable self._config.
These results suggest that providing all information upfront may prevent the model from distinguishing the most relevant context information for a bug, leading to degraded performance.

After applying all layers of contextual knowledge, GPT-4o-mini still fails to fix 85 bugs, consisting of 58 Program Anomaly, 9 Network, 7 GUI, 8 Configuration, 3 Performance, and 1 Permission/Deprecation bug.
GPT-4o-mini shows a 3% improvement, fixing 7 additional bugs and reaching a 73% fix rate.
The training data of proprietary LLMs is not fully disclosed.
This design isolates the impact of contextual knowledge and mitigates the influence of potential leakage.
The nondeterminism of LLMs can lead to varying outcomes across responses, which presents challenges when analyzing results.
We choose n = 10 and report Pass@k with k=1, 3, 5, following prior studies [9], [10].
All plausible fixes are tested and manually verified to be the correct fix.
We manually reviewed all linked issues and pull requests to ensure they only describe the bug and do not reveal the actual fix.
Moreover, the effectiveness of this knowledge depends heavily on how well a project maintains its documentation and issue reporting.
citacoes.localizador: p. 8 do PDF, Discussion da RQ3

citacoes.trecho: A threat to construct validity might arise from the manual bug type annotations.
Our findings may not generalize to all LLMs.
Over 66% of unresolved bugs lacked one or more pieces of injected repository or project-level context, limiting the model’s ability to see the full picture.
citacoes.localizador: p. 10 do PDF, Discussion da RQ4

citacoes.trecho: Injecting all contextual information at once underperformed our layered strategy for all bug types, reinforcing the importance of incremental, context-aware knowledge injection for maximizing repair performance.

tecnicas.nome_original: Chain of Thought (CoT) gerada por LLMs de raciocínio (CoT steps antes do código)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 1 (Resumo e Introdução); pp. 3-4 (Seção III.A); p. 8, Tabela I
tecnicas.observacao: Objeto de investigação do estudo: qualidade das CoTs produzidas por Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking, DeepSeek-R1 e o1 ao receberem diretamente os requisitos e contextos dos benchmarks (requisito/docstring → instrucao; contextos e trecho de código do repositório → contexto; passos de raciocínio → raciocinio). O estudo não reproduz o prompt de geração nem descreve se as CoTs são o raciocínio nativo do modelo ou passos solicitados no prompt (as figuras mostram 'CoT Steps' numerados). Não há condição sem CoT; a Tabela I é descritiva (Pass@1 e contagens de CoT correta/incorreta).

tecnicas.localizador: p. 2 (Introdução); p. 9, Seção IV.A e Tabela III
tecnicas.observacao: Três papéis (Verifier, Defender, Arbiter) instanciados com modelos diferentes, até três rodadas de debate com término antecipado; o estudo descreve o debate como 'feedback'. Comparado com detecção por um único LLM (pares indicados por cor na Tabela III). Pacote híbrido: além do prompting multiagente, combina três modelos distintos contra um único modelo (seleção de modelo), de modo que o ganho não é atribuível apenas ao debate. A tarefa avaliada é a detecção de CoTs de baixa qualidade (Recall, Precision, F1 da detecção), não geração, tradução, refatoração ou depuração de código; por isso não entra em extracoes. Prompts dos papéis não reproduzidos.

tecnicas.nome_original: Single LLM methods (detecção de CoT por um único LLM: DeepSeek-R1, Gemini-2.0, o1-2024-12-17)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 9, Seção IV.B e Tabela III
tecnicas.observacao: Linha de base da detecção de CoTs de baixa qualidade (tarefa fora do escopo). O template não é reproduzido; instrucao registrada só porque o método consiste em solicitar a detecção a um modelo; demais ingredientes nao_informado.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 9, Seção V.A; p. 10, quadro 'Simple Feedback' e Tabela IV
tecnicas.observacao: Primeiro dos três mecanismos de feedback de granularidade crescente; prompt: aviso de que os passos têm problemas e pedido de correção com base no requisito (feedback mínimo sobre a CoT, que é então usada para gerar código). Serve de base para as setas da Tabela IV e para o ganho de 2.7% descrito no texto. A única condição anterior é o pré-reparo com pass@1 de 0%, que vale por construção (só entram CoTs cujo código falhou), e não é condição comparável de prompting.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 9, Seção V.A; p. 10, quadro 'Error Type Feedback' e Tabela IV
tecnicas.observacao: Acrescenta ao Simple Feedback a lista de tipos de erro com definição breve e o requisito original explícito no template. A informação acrescentada pertence à categoria feedback, já presente no comparador (intensifica a informação de feedback). O contraste é entre templates: além da granularidade do erro, o template explicita o requisito, por isso o tipo é pacote e não ingrediente. Não se informa a origem dos tipos de erro fornecidos (anotação manual ou detecção automática).

tecnicas.localizador: p. 10, Seção V.A, quadro 'Detailed Error Feedback' e Tabela IV
tecnicas.observacao: Entrada: requisito original, CoT original e informação detalhada do erro. Acrescenta ao Simple Feedback a descrição específica do erro (categoria feedback, já presente no comparador) e explicita o requisito e a CoT original no template; pacote de template, não ingrediente isolado. A origem da 'detailed error information' não é descrita.

O MAD gera sobrecarga computacional significativa, e o estudo aponta o compromisso entre desempenho e custo; custo não quantificado. Refere-se à detecção de CoTs (tarefa fora do escopo).

citacoes.trecho: Furthermore, since the reasoning model can generate reasoning steps and final code based on user queries, we directly input the requirements and contexts from the original benchmark into three different LLMs to generate CoTs and final codes.
As the primary focus of this study is on code generation tasks, we selected a subset of 111 instances related to New Features from the Full version, termed SWE-bench-NF, for detailed analysis.
This study primarily focuses on the 230 Python tasks.
To ensure that the model achieves optimal inference performance, we strictly adhere to the preset parameter configurations.
Therefore, we introduce a Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) [24] framework, which leverages multi-party debate perspectives as feedback to identify low-quality CoTs.
We assign three specialized roles(Verifier, defender, and Arbiter) to automate detection.
The debate process consists of three rounds, with the provision to terminate early if a conclusion is reached before all rounds are completed.

Therefore, we focus on evaluating the self-repair capabilities of a single LLM under three granular feedback mechanisms— Simple Feedback, Error Type Feedback, and Detailed Error Feedback—to examine autonomous repair of CoT quality issues.
Error type feedback provides the LLM with information about the types of CoT quality issues, but does not offer detailed error specifics.
That is, during the repair process, we take the requirements, the original CoT, and the corresponding error information as input to let LLM repair the CoT.
The generated steps have quality issues. Please fix the steps based on the requirement description.
For each problem requiring repair, we generated one code solution.
Before the repair, the code generated due to CoT internal quality issues failed to pass the test cases, resulting in pass@1 values all being 0%.
Our findings reveal that even when the CoT is correct, 18.5% of the generated code still contains errors.
This issue arises mainly because LLMs sometimes fail to adhere to the steps in the CoT, resulting in discrepancies between the CoT and the code.
Furthermore, our analysis reveals that even when the generated code is correct, there is still an 11.9% chance of an incorrect CoT.
This ambiguity leads the LLMs to generate code using a placeholder variable like “c optimizations module name” instead of specifying the actual module name.

Furthermore, from the perspectives of security and robustness, when the target file exists and overwrite is False, the program should raise a FileExistsError exception to explicitly alert the user and prevent accidental overwriting of important files.

However, this performance advantage stems from the framework’s inherent design of multi-agent interaction, which also gives rise to significant computational overhead, making the trade-off between performance and cost a key challenge for its practical application.
The evaluation results may be sensitive to the prompt format.

To mitigate this issue, we conducted small-scale preliminary testing, experimenting with different prompts to select the prompts that yield the most consistent and optimal performance across various models.
Each sample was independently annotated by two participants to eliminate subjective bias, following the same procedure as the pilot analysis to refine and expand the taxonomy.
This paper empirically explores the external and internal factors of why LLMs generate unsatisfactory CoTs by analyzing 1,023 failed code samples on two widely used code generation benchmarks.
Finally, our analysis reveals that external factors constitute 53.6% of the total, while internal factors make up the remaining 40.1%.
We also investigate the distribution of these 649 factors across LLMs.
The results show that even when the CoT is correct, there is approximately an 18.5% probability of generating incorrect code.
Conversely, even when the CoT is incorrect, there is a 3.1% probability of generating correct code.
The MAD-series variants, MAD_DGO and MAD_OGD, demonstrate superior recall performance on CoderEval, achieving recall of 46.36% and 48.54%, respectively.
To address this issue, we created a preliminary categorization system for each category, and two of the authors were responsible for the verification process.
We provide the data and scripts online to facilitate replication or future work at: https://github.com/binquanzzz/CoT-Eval

Confidencialidade de dados: muitas empresas proíbem usar LLMs proprietários com dados sensíveis, como código da empresa; não se trata de vulnerabilidade do código gerado. O estudo usa o ponto para justificar o foco em modelos abertos.
Validade da métrica: a métrica binária de sucesso pode ser afetada desproporcionalmente por erros sintáticos sutis (por exemplo, imports ausentes) em vez de erros funcionais significativos.
Generalização limitada: dois conjuntos, três LLMs abertos, prompts testados possivelmente não ótimos e cinco linguagens; resultados podem não valer em outros conjuntos, modelos, prompts e linguagens.

citacoes.trecho: Using Open GPT4 8X7B and specialized StarCoder and CodeGen models on popular code translation benchmarks (CodeNet and AVATAR), we find that CoT with an intermediate NL summary performs best, with an increase of 13.8% and 6.7%, respectively, in successful translations for the best-performing model (Open GPT4 8X7B) compared to the zero-shot prompt.
Code translation is the task of converting code from one programming language (e.g., Java) to another (e.g., Python) [1].
However, manual code rewriting is a labor-intensive process that is inherently prone to human error, thereby impacting both efficiency and accuracy.

While early statistical efforts [3] have recently given way to methods based on large language models (LLMs), studies show that LLMs still produce buggy translations when using a zero-shot prompt [2].

We explore two approaches to incorporate IRs in code translation: (1) a two-step approach, where the LLM first translates the original code to IR and then translates this IR to the target language [8]; and (2) a CoT prompting approach, where the LLM is instructed to use IR to explain its reasoning during translation.
Our results show that CoT with NL summaries achieves the best performance, improving code translation accuracy by up to 13.8% compared to the zero-shot baseline.
They reported successful translation rates ranging from 2.1% to 47.3% across studied LLMs, with GPT-4 achieving the best performance.

Following work by Pan et al. [2], we use the percentage of successful translations as the performance metric, where a translation is “successful” if the code compiles, passes runtime checks, and passes existing tests (recall Section II-A).
All prompts were evaluated with a temperature of 0.2 to reduce randomness of the outputs.

Postprocessing was also conducted on the LLM outputs to remove the initial first line if it starts with “Here is” or “Here’s”, trim the first line of the file to remove any whitespace prefix, and delete any line that started with “End of Code”.
This sample contains 200 code snippets each of C++, C, Python, Java, and Go.
Zero-shot prompt (0SP), corresponding to previous work on code translation [2].
One-shot prompt (1SP), with one example of source-to-target language translation for each source-target pair, randomly selected from the CodeTransOcean dataset [35].

A zero-shot two-step approach of having the LLM translate the source language to either AST (2S-AST), NL (2S-NL), both AST and NL (2S-AST-NL), or both NL and AST (2S-NL-AST), followed by having the LLM translate the intermediate representation to the target language.
A one-shot CoT prompt in which the LLM is instructed to use either AST (CoT-AST), NL (CoT-NL), both AST and NL (CoT-AST-NL), or both NL and AST (CoT-NL-AST) to explain its reasoning.
The AST was obtained using the Python ‘ast’ method whereas the NL was obtained from the Rosetta Code website [36].
The same example used in the 1SP was also used here.
AVATAR contains 249 Java code snippets and 250 Python code snippets.

Table I shows that our results for Open GPT4 8X7B, averaged across all source-target language pairs, differ from those reported by [2], which reported an average of 82.0% for the CodeNet samples for the same zero-shot prompt with the proprietary GPT-4 model.
Similar to prior works on LLM few-shot learning [37], we also found that order matters: NL-AST achieved better results than the order AST-NL in the prompt.

Although the zero-shot performance with StarCoder on the AVATAR dataset was 7.3% higher than that reported by [2], the improvement exists for both Java and Python source languages and can be attributed to the inherent randomness in LLM outputs.
For the CodeGen model, Table II shows that the zero-shot prompt performs the best compared to CoT-NL and CoT-NL-AST.

However, we find our work to be more reflective of enterprise use cases for code translation as many companies have policies against using proprietary LLMs with sensitive data (such as company code) [42], [43], [44].

To mitigate this limitation, we also experimented with other formats and improvements such as using whitespace and custom examples for improving our prompts; however, we did not observe any performance improvements.

In this paper, we assess the quality of the code translation using a binary metric that measures whether the translation was successful, but future work should explore more robust evaluation metrics that penalize more for significant functional errors rather than subtle syntactic errors (e.g., missing imports) that disproportionately affect the binary metric.
Our work demonstrates that the general-purpose GPT-4 8x7B LLM outperformed larger, code-specialized LLMs; however, open-source models still lag behind the reported performance of proprietary models.

citacoes.trecho: Using SIMCODE, we evaluate three prominent LLMs, Gemini-2.0, GPT-4.1, and Qwen-3, across six prompt techniques.
In total, the dataset includes 400 simulation tasks.
Inspired by prior work on controlled generation [16, 17], we evaluate six template families that progressively enrich the input with structural cues, exemplars, or self-verification signals.
All prompts (i) cast the model as an ns-3 specialist, (ii) forbid commentary or markdown, and (iii) mandate C++17 compatibility for ns-3 ver. ≥ 3.41.
The templates differ, however, in the auxiliary scaffolding they provide.
It serves as a lower-bound baseline, absent any intermediate reasoning or examples.
Encourages the LLM to reason step-by-step about simulation components (nodes, network devices, protocols, parameters) before producing code, aiming for greater logical coherence and accuracy.
Provides a solved example that maps a simulation description to its code, helping the LLM generalize.
Employs a two-phase strategy: first reasoning about topology, configurations, and protocols, then “acting” by emitting the corresponding code.
Primes the model as a “renowned ns-3 developer,” explicitly requesting best practices (precise attribute configuration, helper usage).
citacoes.localizador: p. 4, Tabela II, linha Expert Prompt

citacoes.trecho: Embeds a draft–critique–rewrite loop (an enhanced CoT).
The model drafts, audits for common ns-3 pitfalls (missing headers, deprecated APIs, logical flaws), and outputs a corrected version.
For every LLM, CoT is better than the plain instruction prompt, giving about 2 to 3 percentage extra accuracy.
Self-consistency performs well for GPT-4.1, yet it hurts Gemini and Qwen-3.
Execution accuracy is paramount, as it is a binary metric that measures the proportion of generated code samples that successfully compile and execute.

However, upon analyzing the generated codes, we found that test cases often fail not because the solutions are incorrect, but because the implementation logic deviates from the reference, even when functionally correct.
Thus, similarity metrics give an illusion of uniform quality, while execution accuracy exposes the real functional gap.
It was observed that the most predominant fault derived from missing or outdated header/module references.
Tasks involving emerging technologies such as 5G, NR, or mmWave often led to hallucinated headers not part of standard ns-3 builds.
To mitigate these issues in future work, the recommended measures are also described in Table V.
Each data point was independently reviewed by at least two authors, who collectively bring academic experience from undergraduate and graduate-level networking and advanced networking courses.
For evaluation, we used only the instruction prompt to isolate the impact of fine-tuning from prompt engineering.
Results represent the average performance across 5 separate runs.
The codes and datasets were not shared during the review process to comply with the double-anonymized submission policy.

tecnicas.observacao: Para geração de código, o LLM recebe o prompt 'Generate a plan specifying the intermediate steps to <prob_st>' (instrucao + planejamento → decomposicao); o plano é refinado por pós-processamento com regex e, em prompt separado, combinado com o prompt original para produzir o código (etapas encadeadas → decomposicao). Os resultados da Tabela 2 foram obtidos com a variante Multi-Step (p. 6). O contrafactual é a avaliação zero-shot dos mesmos modelos e benchmarks na Tabela 1, comparada explicitamente pelo estudo ('compared to Table 1', p. 6). Pacote híbrido: inclui o refinamento por regex e a reamostragem do plano até três vezes quando não há passos no padrão esperado (componentes fora do escopo), e a fase de planejamento pode ter usado decodificação distinta (top-k 50, T = 0,89 'for specific LLMs', p. 9). O ganho é do pacote, não da decomposição isolada. O texto da descrição do problema usada na Tabela 2 (curta ou longa) não é informado.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 5, Seção 5.3.1; p. 6, Figura 2 (direita) e Seção 6.4
tecnicas.observacao: Variante de execução apresentada pelo estudo como formulação própria e avaliada em barras separadas (Figura 2, direita): plano e código são pedidos num único prompt (ex.: 'Generate a plan to design a 4-bit binary counter, then provide the final VHDL code'). O plano recebe a mesma categoria (decomposicao, planejamento) que na variante Multi-Step, pelo critério de consistência. Para geração de código, a única comparação é com a variante Multi-Step; não há condição zero-shot na Figura 2 nem valores impressos de Single-Step para geração, de modo que não há contrafactual com e sem o plano. A afirmação de pequena melhora sobre o zero-shot (p. 6) refere-se à sumarização (fora do escopo).

metricas: Pass@1 (TB): aprovação nos testbenches autoverificáveis (VUnit e GHDL), proporção (p. 3, Seção 4.2.1)
Pass@1 (SEC): correção funcional por verificação de equivalência sequencial com a solução canônica, proporção (p. 3, Seção 4.2.1)
SC1 (%): autoconsistência código→resumo→código com cadeia n = 1, verificada por SEC (p. 3, Seção 4.2.2)
PR (%): LLM Preference Rate com juiz Llama-3-70b-instruct (sumarização; VHDL-Eval e VHDL-Xform) (p. 3, Seção 4.2.4; p. 9, Figura 4)

riscos.descricao: Os testbenches podem não ser exaustivos, de modo que código aprovado no Pass@1 (TB) pode divergir da referência; o estudo atribui a diferença entre TB e SEC a isso.
Na geração zero-shot, o LLM produziu código para registrador de 4 bits quando o prompt pedia registrador de n bits (exemplo ilustrativo).

Risco de vazamento do benchmark (VHDL-Eval derivado do Verilog-Eval e de tutoriais públicos); o estudo reformula os enunciados para evitar reutilização direta. Não há discussão de vazamento para o VHDL-Xform.
O desempenho do CoDes depende fortemente da qualidade dos passos descritivos intermediários gerados pelo LLM (limitação declarada).
Validade externa: os conjuntos têm problemas autocontidos, sem a complexidade de projetos reais, o que pode dificultar o uso com problemas mais complexos.
Na sumarização (fora do escopo), a abordagem linha a linha torna-se cada vez mais demorada com o aumento do número de linhas (tempo de processamento); não quantificado.
O juiz Llama-3-70B usado no PR pode apresentar imprecisões; a variação com outros juízes não foi explorada (afeta métricas de sumarização).

mitigacoes.descricao: Reformulação dos enunciados do VHDL-Eval para evitar reutilização direta e vazamento do benchmark.
Uso de verificação de equivalência sequencial (SEC) além dos testbenches para avaliar a correção funcional.
Refinamento do plano e retorno de string vazia quando não há passos, para evitar instruções conflitantes ou ruidosas no prompt final.
Penalidade de repetição 1,2 para reduzir geração de texto redundante.

citacoes.trecho: To address this challenge, we propose Chain-of-Descriptions (CoDes), a novel approach to enhance the performance of LLMs for VHDL code generation and summarization tasks.
CoDes involves generating a series of intermediate descriptive steps based on: (i) the problem statement for code generation, and (ii) the VHDL code for summarization.
These steps are then integrated with the original input prompt (problem statement or code) and provided as input to the LLMs to generate the final output.
Our experiments demonstrate that the CoDes approach significantly surpasses the standard prompting strategy across various metrics on both datasets.
The LLM is then given a natural language prompt that follows a template: “Generate a plan specifying the intermediate steps to < prob_st >”.
The refinement includes: (a) Truncating boilerplate text with regex for conciseness, and (b) Ensuring consistency with a uniform style across steps.
In the Single-Step method, planning and execution occur in a single LLM prompt, instructing the model to outline steps and generate the final output in one interaction.
In the Multi-Step method, planning, refinement, and execution are divided into separate LLM prompts.
These results, obtained with the Multi-step plan execution strategy, demonstrate significant performance improvements.
Figure 2 (Left) shows that longer descriptions improve performance across all models, supporting our CoDes framework’s approach.
However, these test cases might not be completely exhaustive due to limitations in covering all possible scenarios, edge cases, and input combinations.
To ensure the model can make inferences and to prevent benchmark leakage, problem statements are reframed to avoid direct reuse.
If the generated plan does not contain any of these patterns, we sample the plan up to three times to extract intermediate steps.
In the zero-shot scenario, we primarily present scores derived from single sampling from the LLMs.
Additionally, we explored using a top-k value set to 50 and a temperature of T = 0.89 for specific LLMs during the plan formulation phase.
This method heavily relies on the quality of intermediate descriptive steps provided by the LLM being utilized.
Furthermore, the datasets used in our study feature self-contained problem sets and solutions, lacking the complexities found in real-life design scenarios.
Similarly, in the context of code summarization, employing a line-by-line approach becomes increasingly time-consuming as the number of lines of code increases.
This ensures clarity and avoids conflicting instructions when combining the plan with the input prompt.
To mitigate redundant text generation, a repetition penalty of 1.2 was applied.
