tecnicas.observacao: Pacote RAG de consulta única: instrução de tarefa ('You need to implement the function...', Box 1 → instrucao) mais quatro visões de contexto recuperadas do repositório por análise estática e similaridade (fragmentos similares, chamadores, cadeias de chamada previstas, funções similares → contexto) e serialização que preserva a hierarquia estrutural das entidades no prompt (formatação estrutural do contexto de entrada, sem categoria própria no dicionário → outro). Funções e fragmentos similares do repositório são código do repositório fornecido como insumo, não exemplos resolvidos da tarefa; por isso não se atribui exemplos. Em relação a Direct (sem recuperação, só contexto local), acrescenta o contexto recuperado e a serialização estrutural; Direct já contém contexto local, mas o contexto do repositório é ingrediente novo. Contra Direct é contrafactual de pacote; contra os demais baselines (DRACO, RLCoder etc.) as condições diferem em vários ingredientes. A alocação de tokens entre visões e a recuperação por embeddings (bge-small-en-v1.5) e K-means fazem parte do pacote; ver componentes_fora_escopo. O ganho é do pacote, não de um mecanismo isolado.

riscos.descricao: Contexto impreciso recuperado por similaridade pode levar o LLM a alucinar métodos inexistentes (get_parser_names, get_option_names) e produzir solução incorreta; ilustrado por um exemplo motivador.

Excesso de contexto irrelevante (por exemplo, oito métodos não usados trazidos por DRACO) pode obscurecer o código relevante e prejudicar o foco do LLM; omissão de contexto crítico pode gerar código em conflito com o conhecimento do repositório (constantes, APIs). Evidência de caso único.
riscos.localizador: p. 2, Introdução; p. 10, Seção 6.1 e Figura 4

riscos.descricao: Limitação do próprio método: a predição de cadeias de chamada pode degradar quando a função-alvo não tem funções similares (repositórios pequenos), quando funções similares não têm chamadas semelhantes ou quando as chamadas são esparsas; o estudo reconhece que a taxa de erro da predição ainda pode parecer alta em termos absolutos.

Abordagens com treinamento supervisionado extenso ou pipelines de agentes com várias consultas ao LLM têm custo computacional/temporal substancial; refere-se aos métodos comparados. O estudo relata apenas o tamanho médio do prompt em tokens; custo monetário e latência não quantificados.
pass@1 como única métrica de avaliação deixa de fora atributos como legibilidade e manutenibilidade (limitação de avaliação, não risco medido).

Ameaça interna: hiperparâmetros escolhidos por busca em grade em um pequeno subconjunto de dados, sem indicação de que o subconjunto seja disjunto dos conjuntos de avaliação; avaliação restrita a quatro LLMs por orçamento e a Python.

mitigacoes.descricao: Ajuste de parâmetros dos baselines para manter o tamanho médio do prompt aproximadamente no mesmo nível (exceto RepoCoder e CodeAgent, para os quais se alinhou o prompt da rodada final); procedimento de controle, sem comparação com e sem ele.
Temperatura 0 para saídas determinísticas; sem condição de comparação.
Mesmo modelo de embedding (bge-small-en-v1.5) para todos os métodos, exceto RLCoder.

citacoes.trecho: Evaluation on widely-used repository-level code generation benchmarks (CoderEval and DevEval) demonstrates that RepoScope outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to a 36.35% relative improvement in pass@1 scores.
RepoScope constructs a Repository Structural Semantic Graph (RSSG) and retrieves a comprehensive four-view context, integrating both structural and similarity-based contexts.
Additionally, we present a structure-preserving serialization algorithm for prompt construction, ensuring the coherence of the context for the LLM.
When supplied with this inaccurate context, LLMs may hallucinate non-existent methods (e.g., get_parser_names and get_option_names), leading to incorrect solution.

In terms of efficiency, approaches that depend on extensive supervised training [34, 41] or on agent-based pipelines with multiple LLM queries [30, 45] incur substantial computational/temporal cost, and often struggle to adapt across diverse repositories.
Together, these form a four-view context representation.
To achieve this, we propose a two-stage iterative prompt construction strategy.
You need to implement the function located at the end of the instruction based on relevant repository information.
Direct refers to generating code solely based on the local context without incorporating any retrieval.
SimpleRAG retrieves a fixed set of similar code snippets based on similarity and directly appends them to the prompt for one-shot generation.
Except for the temperature parameter, which is set to 0, all other decoding parameters are kept at their default values.

To minimize the impact of prompt token length—a extraneous variable—on the results and allow us to focus on the quality and accuracy of the prompt, we adjusted parameters in baselines during evaluation to make sure their average prompt token lengths were approximately at the same level.

We individually remove (1) the callers (w/o Ca), (2) the call chains (w/o CC), (3) the similar functions (w/o SF), and (4) the similar code fragments (w/o SCF), and then assess the impact on code generation performance.
However, it lacks a filtering mechanism for the retrieved code elements, leading to excessive irrelevant code being included in the context.
We performed a small-range grid search over RepoScope’s hyperparameters on a small subset of data, selecting the coefficients based on the best performance observed.
Besides, the current use of pass@1 as the sole evaluation metric limits a comprehensive assessment of code quality, overlooking important attributes such as readability and maintainability.

While this assumption holds in most cases, the prediction performance may degrade if the target function lacks similar counterparts (e.g., for small-scale repository), if similar functions do not exhibit similar calling behaviors, or if the calling behaviors are sparse.
Specifically, since both RLCoder and RepoCoder focus on similarity-based full-text retrieval, we replaced the similar code fragment context in RepoScope with the code retrieved by these two methods.

tecnicas.observacao: Pipeline de três etapas encadeadas (decomposicao): (i) geração de um redutor por prompt one-shot ao Qwen2.5-Plus, com a descrição da tarefa e um exemplo resolvido (ABC330D com seu reducer.py) (instrucao, exemplos, contexto); (ii) execução do redutor gerado (busca ddmin, fora do escopo) por até 60 s; (iii) prompt de reparo com descrição da tarefa, código com bug e par entrada-saída do contraexemplo reduzido (instrucao, contexto), com truncamento a um orçamento de L linhas. Comparada com 'Baseline (No Test)' e 'Origin Test' nos mesmos modelos e configurações (Tabelas 6, 7 e 13): contrafactual de pacote. Pacote híbrido: inclui a execução do algoritmo ddmin e o fallback para a entrada original quando a redução falha, que não são prompting; o ganho não se atribui a um mecanismo isolado. Mecanismos acrescentados tomados em relação ao Baseline (prompt base com enunciado e código) e ao Origin Test: o contraexemplo reduzido é contexto, categoria já presente na base. O redutor é sempre gerado pelo Qwen2.5-Plus, mesmo quando o modelo de reparo é outro. Na RQ-4, a mesma troca da entrada original pela reduzida é aplicada ao ChatRepair e ao CREF (pacote que então inclui também o feedback desses sistemas); na RQ-5 (OSS-Fuzz), o prompt de reparo inclui diagnósticos de crash, arquivos-fonte e formato SEARCH/REPLACE (contexto, restricoes), comuns às três condições. A geração de vários candidatos (N = 10) com validação pela suíte oculta é o procedimento de avaliação pass@k, igual em todas as condições, e não foi contada como amostragem.

citacoes.trecho: To address this, we propose ReduceFix, an LLM-based APR approach with a built-in component that automatically reduces test inputs while retaining their failure-inducing behavior.
ReduceFix prompts an LLM to generate a reducer that minimizes failure-inducing test inputs without human effort, and then feeds the reduced failure-inducing inputs to guide patch generation.

On this benchmark, ReduceFix shrinks inputs by 89.1% on average and improves overall pass@10 by up to 53.8% relative to a prompt that includes the original test, and by 17.6% compared with omitting the test entirely.

The overall process follows a three-stage pipeline: (i) reducer generation via a one-shot prompt with the problem description, (ii) time-bounded execution of the generated reducer to obtain the reduced input, and (iii) patch generation where the reduced input, buggy code, and problem description are jointly passed to the LLM.
Instead of directly reducing test inputs using LLMs, ReduceFix leverages one-shot learning to inject the knowledge of the ddmin algorithm [48] into the LLM.
The prompt, as shown in Listing 1, is sent to Qwen2.5-Plus [6] with a temperature of 0 (greedy decoding).
In our settings, the reducer runs reduction iteration for at most 60 seconds.
During candidate patch sampling, ReduceFix utilizes the LLM to generate at most N = 10 candidate patches.
Meanwhile, most of those benchmarks were released years ago and are drawn from popular open-source projects that large language models have almost certainly seen, which can overstate repair accuracy.
Therefore, we select all the satisfied tasks from ABC contests numbered 361 to 377, a span entirely after the knowledge cut-offs of the 4 LLMs we evaluate.

Although some OSS-Fuzz repositories may overlap with LLM pretraining corpora, we hold the LLM and evaluation instances fixed across strategies, so relative differences between prompt types remain valid despite potential data leakage.
The pure LLM baseline must embed the entire long test case in the prompt, which greatly inflates the token cost.

Because the defect depends on the absolute magnitude of vertex identifiers, this renumbering masked the failure, the interestingness predicate became false, and ddmin stopped without shrinking the input.
We can resolve the issue by adding one simple guard.
In contrast, prompting the unreduced test case often hampers performance.
Supplying the full failing test often hurts repair accuracy; in multiple LLMs and difficulty levels, it performs worse than the no-test Baseline.

To test whether the improvement is due to randomness, we leverage MWW tests [20, 35] to further confirm the improvement based on 4 LLMs, returning a two-sided p-value with < 0.05; therefore, the null hypothesis of equal success probabilities between ReduceFix and the “Origin Test” is rejected, establishing that the gain is statistically significant.
The Baseline prompt contains only the problem statement and the buggy code.
Diff Lines stays the same length but appends up to ten mismatched output lines, providing sparse evidence without increasing size.
Reduced + Origin concatenates the reduced and full tests, introducing redundant information as well as maximum length.
To isolate the effect of the initial prompt, we fix MAX_RETRY= 1 (one feedback round) and set the conversation window size to length=2 turns.

citacoes.trecho: Specifically, we propose a Python code generation framework utilizing state-of-the-art open-source LLMs to generate executable Pandas code via optimized prompting strategies.
Additionally, results show that Python code generation achieves superior performance in tabular question answering compared to alternative approaches.
However, LLM-based approaches introduce several challenges, including high computational costs and limited context length, making scalable and efficient tabular QA systems an open research problem.
A key feature of our system is its iterative error-handling mechanism.
If the initial code execution fails, the error message and faulty code are sent back to the LLM for correction, with a maximum of two iterations.
This mechanism significantly improves robustness, reducing failure rates in complex queries.
Additionally, handling multiple tables often leads to hallucinations, where models generate inaccurate or misleading responses.
Motivated by these challenges, we introduce a novel framework that integrates schema-guided prompting, controlled execution, and an error-handling mechanism.
Our extensive evaluations and prompt strategy experiments highlight the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing accuracy and robustness.
In contrast to these extensively annotated train and development splits, the test split only has question and dataset columns to ensure proper evaluation without data leak for the competition.
The schemas include each dataset’s name, each column, each column’s data type, 5 unique values from each column, and the total unique values that a column contains.
The example values are limited to a hundred characters total to avoid excessive verbosity and potential token overload.
We use the full dataset for schema creation for both full and sample datasets.
The code generation step is done with a prompt that includes the question, detailed instructions and the corresponding dataset schema.
The system captures the error message along with the faulty code and sends it to the LLM for automatic correction.
If the provided code is still faulty after the maximum number of attempts, execution is terminated for that query.
Additionally, we opted for a maximum of two iterations based on preliminary experiments, which showed that attempts beyond two iterations rarely produced further improvements.
To evaluate system performance, we used Accuracy, the official evaluation metric of SemEval 2025 Task 8.
However, we do not believe that every question-answer pair in these datasets can perfectly represent the real-world performance of the models.
We define Degenerate Loop errors as cases where an LLM repeatedly generates identical or nearly identical output sequences, continuing indefinitely until it reaches its maximum token limit.
As shown in Figures 2 and 3, although some Degenerate Loop errors are corrected, a notable portion still results in failures.
Results show that most initial failures are due to Runtime errors, while Syntax and Loop errors are less frequent but may persist across multiple correction attempts.

observacoes.descricao: Na RQ3, a informação de dependências permite construir um Data Flow Graph (DFG) que guia a geração de assinaturas de função e relações de chamada; o mecanismo exato e o prompt de geração não são descritos.
O diagrama de sequência aprimorado é construído manualmente por engenheiros (esforço manual descrito como parte do fluxo, sem ser tratado como custo).

O arcabouço foi encapsulado como ferramenta de apoio integrada ao sistema de projeto de diagramas, com inferência global ou local e avisos de compatibilidade de tipos; a demonstração (Figs. 5 e 6) é qualitativa, sem avaliação.

A Definição 5 categoriza dados produzidos e consumidos para que o LLM analise a dependência 'step by step'; o template da Fig. 2 não mostra instrução explícita de cadeia de raciocínio, por isso 'raciocinio' não foi registrado.
Número de execuções por condição não informado; a temperatura 0,1 não equivale a execução única.

citacoes.trecho: Second, recognizing the critical role of data flow, we introduce a dedicated data dependency inference (DDI) task.
To ensure reliability, we formalize DDI as a constrained mathematical reasoning task through novel prompting strategies, aligning with LLMs’ excellent mathematical strengths.
Furthermore, the integration of UML2Dep into the code generation pipeline also improves practical deployment, increasing compilation pass rate by 8.83% and unit test pass rate by 11.66%.
Particularly for large-scale sequence diagrams or exceptionally intricate logic, LLMs are highly susceptible to generating severe hallucinations when inferring data dependencies.
To overcome the ambiguity of natural language prompts in complex DDI tasks requiring precise reasoning, we propose a novel prompting approach using formal mathematical descriptions.

By parsing sequence diagrams into execution dependency graphs, we precisely identify reachable predecessor nodes for each target node in the execution flow, systematically removing logically unreachable context objects.
This refined context, combined with mathematical formalization prompting, enables the LLMs to infer the data dependency graph. This graph is subsequently used to generate the final code.
Cognitive Overload: Inclusion of irrelevant contextual information increases computational burden and may introduce spurious correlations that degrade inference accuracy.
Each dependency relation is reviewed and approved by three employees.

In our practical business scenario, it is crucial to ensure that all true dependency edges are identified (i.e., high Recall), as missing dependencies may lead to critical design or implementation errors.
For all experiments, we set the temperature parameter to 0.1 to ensure more deterministic and stable outputs.

To assess the effectiveness of each component in our framework, we compare three settings on the DDI task: (1) using mathematical formalization prompting with context pruning (our default method), (2) using natural language description, and (3) using mathematical formalization prompting without context pruning.
These cases involve enterprise-level, customized code frameworks, under which general-purpose large language models often struggle to generate syntactically correct and functionally complete code.
Our method introduces data dependency information into the generation process.

tecnicas.observacao: Descrição gerada pelo GPT-4.1-2025-04-14 a partir do prompt original e da solução de referência, com o pedido de descrever a função passo a passo e com todos os detalhes (Apêndice B), e refinada manualmente até pass@1 ≥ 0.8 com o Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (6 prompts do ParEval-Serial e 19 do ParEval-OMP editados ou regenerados). Mecanismos: instrucao (descrição em linguagem natural), contexto (preâmbulo e assinatura), restricoes (template de formato do HumanEval; além disso, a descrição traz especificações como alvos de complexidade e tratamento de casos-limite, temas 2.1 e 2.3 da taxonomia, Fig. 5), decomposicao (descrição em etapas numeradas, tema 3.4 «Implementation Sketch or Step Breakdown»). O p_top foi ajustado com o mesmo critério (pass@1 nos testes ocultos) e com um dos modelos avaliados (ver heterogeneidade).

citacoes.trecho: To answer this, we introduce PARTIALORDEREVAL, which augments any code generation benchmark with a partial order of prompts from minimal to maximally detailed.
Applying it to HumanEval and both serial and OpenMP subsets of ParEval, we measure how pass@1 scales with prompt specificity.

Our experiments with Llama-3.x and Qwen2.5-Coder demonstrate varying degrees of prompt sensitivity across different tasks, and a qualitative analysis highlights explicit I/O specifications, edge-case handling, and stepwise breakdowns as the key drivers of prompt detail improvement.
To give an example, we showed that LLM can indeed achieve higher pass@1 for two subsets of ParEval, even exceeding HumanEval figures—it suffices to add significantly more detail to the prompt.
Starting from an Original Prompt and its reference Solution, we use GPT-4.1 to draft a Maximally Detailed Prompt, manually refine it to ensure a pass@1 ≥ 0.8, and designate it as p_top.

citacoes.trecho: We illustrate our findings using Qwen results primarily but observed similar patterns in the Llama models.
For instance, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct climbs from 0.280 at p_bot to 0.799 at L = 50 and reaches 0.860 by L = 100 (matching p_top).
Its performance plateaus for L = 200 at 0.921, but declines back to 0.860 at p_top.
By contrast, PO-PAREVAL-SERIAL sees more gradual improvements—Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct reaches 0.867 at L = 75 and 0.900 at L = 150, yet remains below its p_top score of 0.983.
PO-PAREVAL-OMP is the most challenging: the same model rises slowly from 0.483 at p_bot to 0.800 at L = 200, but never attains its p_top accuracy of 0.967.

Additionally, the slight performance drop beyond L = 200 on PO-HUMANEVAL suggests that overly verbose prompts may introduce redundancy or cognitive overload, marginally impairing code-generation accuracy.

For instance, at r_p = 0.8 in paragraph sampling, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct achieves 0.747 on PO-HUMANEVAL—just 0.16 above the 1.5B model's 0.587—but the gap grows to 0.296 on PO-PAREVAL-SERIAL (0.933 vs. 0.637) and 0.338 on PO-PAREVAL-OMP (0.767 vs. 0.429).
For example, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B reaches 0.983 on PO-PAREVAL-SERIAL and 0.967 on PO-PAREVAL-OMP—versus only 0.800 and 0.667 on the unaugmented ParEval benchmarks.

tecnicas.observacao: Um dos quatro padrões de prompt comparados entre si (RQ2-1). Template de três partes (Instruction, Question, Reference Context, Fig. 1) acrescido de dois exemplos fixos de pedido e resposta (um específico e um geral), cuja ordem e número os participantes não podiam alterar. Mecanismos herdados da condição comum a todos os padrões: instrucao (parte Instruction e pedido em Question), contexto e restricoes (documento de projeto com especificação de classes, métodos, parâmetros, erros, e código esqueleto colados em Reference Context), feedback (iteração multi-turno em que os participantes colam mensagens de testes que falham; Fig. 10; p. 20). Não há condição sem padrão (por exemplo, zero-shot): os padrões diferem em mais de um ingrediente, por isso nao/nenhum. O documento de projeto também contém exemplos de entradas e saídas (p. 10), que os participantes podiam colar em qualquer condição; como a inclusão ficou a critério do participante e não é descrita por condição, exemplos não foi atribuído à base. Alocação aproximadamente balanceada, não aleatória (p. 13), e nível de GPT atribuído por preferência (p. 9).

O laço explícito de feedback do usuário é um acréscimo da instrução, mas a categoria feedback já está na condição comum (depuração guiada por testes), por isso não consta em mecanismos_acrescentados. As três perspectivas não são várias respostas com seleção, por isso não se atribuiu amostragem. Sem condição sem a técnica.

O texto do template não está reproduzido no artigo (remete ao repositório, não acessado). O estudo o apresenta entre seus achados principais (p. 3), por isso foi classificado como focal. A comparação com participantes que só colaram os materiais é post hoc, observacional, com 8 participantes por grupo, sem controle dos demais ingredientes (padrão de prompt, nível de GPT, experiência) e sem diferença estatisticamente significativa (p. 19); não é contrafactual em condições comparáveis, por isso nao/nenhum. Os ingredientes do padrão de prompt de cada participante variam e não são informados por grupo. Instrucao acrescentada: formulação manual de papéis e comportamentos esperados.

observacoes.descricao: Estudo com usuários: 36 participantes (12 no nível de função, 24 no de projeto), sessão de 15 min de introdução, 70 min de tarefa e 15 min de questionário; cada participante exposto a um padrão e a um nível de tarefa; pagamento de USD 50.

Atributos do usuário (idade, situação, gênero, experiência em programação, experiência industrial, uso de GPT, dependência do GPT, experiência com algoritmos) foram analisados como preditores; não são intervenções. A experiência com algoritmos teve associação negativa, que os autores relacionam a mais formulação manual de contexto.
Outros métodos de curadoria observados: geração automática de prompts pelo GPT (participante Rank 4) e uso de templates externos; não avaliados separadamente com resultado numérico.
Uso de código de casos de teste e mensagens de falha como contexto na depuração foi mais frequente entre os mais bem classificados; análise descritiva.

Gravações de tela ou registros de chat indisponíveis para alguns participantes; registros da OpenAI sem carimbo de tempo, com linha do tempo inferida.

citacoes.trecho: Lastly, we defined the well-known Few-Shot template by adding two pre-defined request-and-answer examples in the Example part below the three-part structure described in Fig. 1.

Fig. 1 illustrates the prompt template example for the reflection pattern used in our experiment, containing the pre-defined Instruction part to explain the Reflection pattern, and the Question and Reference Context parts where users can add any request and context information.
When I ask a question, explain the reasoning behind your answer by breaking down the steps you took to arrive at it.
Once I evaluate those perspectives and give feedback, update your response accordingly to provide a more refined and complete answer.
The Alternative Approach pattern aims to ensure that GPTs provide multiple methods for accomplishing a task.
We anticipate that this prompt pattern can offer various approaches for developing or fixing code, allowing users to select the best solution.
The Cognitive Verifier (a.k.a Chain-of-Thought) pattern enables GPTs to subdivide an original question into smaller questions that can ultimately yield a better answer to the original one.
Participants received a design document, skeleton code, executable tests, and a prompt-template format.

citacoes.trecho: Four prompt patterns were evaluated: Few-Shot, Reflection, Alternative, and Cognitive Verifier. Each pattern was assigned to 9 participants.

citacoes.trecho: RQ2-1. Which prompting patterns yield the highest productivity for both function-level and project-level software engineering tasks?
Based on the implications, we compared the TPR results from participants who only used CopyPaste with those who combined CopyPaste with the manual formulation.
GPT-generated codes, especially those involving multiple classes, often contain several faults, even after users spend significant time generating them.
Manual context formulation is not recommended without copying and pasting the original specification, as it increases the risk of hallucinations on missing details.
However, in all these cases, GPTs tend to recommend the second or third answer, which contains these hallucinated conditions, highlighting the persuasive strengths of its structure.
Our empirical inference suggests that the primary cause of these errors was related to the context window size.

During the debugging phase, GPT users should be aware of the risk of code overlap with the original code, particularly in multi-class fixing scenarios, where the side-effect errors need to be carefully reviewed.
Moreover, there may be data leakage concerns where GPTs directly respond to answer codes.
Candidate problems from LeetCode and HackerRank were screened by querying multiple GPT models with only the public task description.
To minimize the variance caused by the prompt pattern templates, we asked participants not to modify the order and number of examples in the Example part when using this pattern.

While this difference may seem trivial in function-level tasks, in project tasks that involve iterative and progressive development and debugging of code within a limited timeframe, the inefficiency of requesting more prompts results in a relative decrease in productivity.
Importantly, the project-level TPR was computed across all 228 test cases; therefore, participants who did not advance to Task 2 had zero solved tests for that second-stage task.
As a result, the final TPR reflects outcomes from a combination of GPT-generated code, iterative interactions between humans and GPT, and, in rare instances, participant corrections.

tecnicas.observacao: O prompt base (Zero Shot) já contém descrição da tarefa, instruções de formato e código inicial (starter code/input code), daí instrucao, restricoes e contexto na condição. A técnica acrescenta a seção de demonstração: no LeetCode, pares (questão semelhante, solução correta) recuperados, precedidos de uma dica em linguagem natural; no DevEval, trechos de código do mesmo repositório (funções, métodos, classes) precedidos de instrução para consultá-los. Recuperação que traz exemplos resolvidos → contexto e exemplos; a dica → instrucao. Contraste com Zero Shot na Tabela 1 (mesmo modelo, benchmark e métrica) isola o pacote (exemplos recuperados + dica), não cada ingrediente. Os retrievers são configurações da mesma técnica; Algorithm Tag só existe para LeetCode.

riscos.descricao: Conteúdo RAG com funções de nome idêntico ao alvo leva o LLM a copiá-las equivocadamente como solução; omissão de namespaces necessários.

Nomes ruidosos e enganosos nos exemplos causam degradação significativa; nomes verbosos podem distrair o modelo e levar a código incorreto (Fig. 8); modelos mais fracos são mais afetados por exemplos parcialmente relevantes.

citacoes.trecho: This paper systematically investigates the impact of different sources and internal features of code examples on ICL for code generation through controlled experiments on contest-style programming questions and repository-level tasks.

We construct retrieval-augmented ICL (RAG-ICL) systems for both scenarios, retrieve documents via multiple similarity metrics (sparse, dense, and tag-based retrievers), and embed the retrieved documents into prompts as ICL content.
### Hint: There are some other questions using similar algorithms. You can read their problem statements as well as their correct solutions.
### Format: You will use the following starter code to write the solution to the problem and enclose your code within delimiters.

Ground Truth (GT): Incorporates the ground truth for the target task directly, which is found meaningful to reveal the upper-bound performance of ICL when the database is ideally broad and adequate [77].
Zero Shot (ZS): Provides the target task and starter code shown in Figure 1 only, without any ICL demonstration examples, indicating LLMs’ native parametric capabilities.
Random: Following existing work [48], we include randomly retrieved documents as a baseline to isolate the effect of ICL content quality.

Specifically, we manually retrieve the ground truth solution, extract all the variables, functions, and class attributes that appear, then incorporate them into the prompt using JSON format with a brief instruction.
We also randomly retrieve one unittest function marked by DevEval and serve it as an ICL code example.
To assess the importance of repository structure, we incorporate explicit namespace metadata into RAG content for BM25, as well as the top-performing Embedding Model configuration (gist-large).
Specifically, we augment BM25-retrieved content with the required functions and variables extracted from ground-truth solutions.
We conduct a controlled ablation study to investigate the effect of each code feature on ICL separately.
We include the VOE mutation used in RQ2 that yields code incorporating the ordered variable names, and develop four additional operators to synthesize identifier names in different styles.
(2) The RAG content includes functions with identical names as the target, causing the LLM to mistakenly copy them as ground truth.

(2) The RAG content lacks helper functions or class attributes required by the target function, leaving the LLM unaware of their usage (as shown in Figure 5, where Qwen-32B hallucinates a non-existing class under Zero Shot, but effectively learns the required functions and class attributes from ICL examples).
Moreover, our experiments reveal that LLMs prefer semantically meaningful identifier names, while noisy and misleading names may cause significant performance degradation, especially in Python.
Comparative results across models further show that weaker LLMs (e.g., Qwen-7B) are more easily affected by partially relevant examples.
As demonstrated in Figure 8, verbose variable names may distract the model and prevent it from recognizing the usefulness of the code example.
Additionally, potential data contamination issues may arise from the exposure of benchmarks in the training process of LLMs.
This prevents inadvertent data leakage and ensures retrieved examples represent only external knowledge available to the model.
To avoid LLMs overfitting to visible test cases, we select 586 DevEval tasks with at least two unittests, ensuring the existence of hidden test cases and fair comparison.

To further substantiate that our findings are not driven by potential data contamination, we partitioned the LeetCode questions into two subsets for each model according to the knowledge cutoff date of each LLM: questions released before the cutoff (potentially seen during pre-training) and after the cutoff (guaranteed unseen).
For all LLMs, we adopt temperature=0 to minimize the randomness of LLMs and max_tokens=8000 to prevent the responses from being pruned due to the length limitation.

O ganho é do pacote, não de um mecanismo isolado. Possível pacote híbrido: o estudo descreve um pré-processamento manual (padronização de nomes de colunas, identificação de colunas tipo enum) e pós-processamento da saída sem dizer se se aplicam também à condição AG nem como se relacionam com o 'enhanced column selection'. citacoes.trecho: We developed a zero-shot pipeline that leverages an Large Language Model to generate functional code capable of extracting the relevant information from tabular data based on an input question.
In the event that the generated code fails, an iterative refinement process is triggered, incorporating the error feedback into a new generation prompt to enhance robustness.
Our results show that zero-shot code generation is a valid approach for Tabular QA, achieving rank 33 of 53 in the test phase despite the lack of task-specific fine-tuning.

Although our approach demonstrated strong performance in code generation and execution, subsequent analysis revealed that the model struggles with columns containing complex data types (lists, dictionaries, etc.) and ambiguous queries, particularly for list-based responses.
Moreover, we incorporate an error-fixing module that attempts to catch runtime errors and integrates them as part of a new prompt, guiding the LLM to refine its code generation.
Our template provides the list of column names and instructs the model to return only those that are essential for answering the query.
All our prompts are available in the code publicly available at GitHub.
As part of our prompt, we guided the LLM to generate Python programming code and postprocessed the output to ensure that only Python lines were passed throught the next module.
The final component of our pipeline captures execution errors that might occur due to incorrect syntax, schema mismatches, or runtime exceptions.
To achieve this, we used a structured prompt that includes the code that causes an error with the corresponding error description.

We standardized column names for simplified versions (removing emoji and all non-alphanumerical characters except punctuation symbols) to prevent possible errors in the Answer Generator caused by mismatches between the table structure and the generated code.
This way, no explicit training nor finetuning was conducted.
To do that, we analyzed the accuracy obtained with respect to the ground truth of the validation set, together with manual checks to assess the quality of the generated code.
Due to VRAM constraints, all models were executed with 4-bit quantization, using a greedy generation strategy with a temperature of 0.7.

Lastly, when integrating the Code Fixer (CF) with an enhanced column selection (ECS) to feed richer information about feature variations to the prompt, our final system setup (AG+ECS+CF) maintains almost the same performance over Subtask 2 but improves 7 points in Subtask 1, proving that integrating error feedback to the model assists the LLM for better querying larger databases.

Our results during the development phase (84 and 85 points for Subtasks 1 and 2, respectively) suffered a significant drop of 20 points (approx.) in accuracy with respect to the validation results, likely due to the greater complexity of datatypes presented in the test tables.
This might indicate that the LLM is not able to infer these complex schemes on the test set, producing errors that are propagated from the Column Selector module to the Answer Generator.

So, we ranked in the 32th (Subtask 1) and 31th (Subtask 2) positions out of 49 participants in the General category, and 23th (Subtask 1) and 21th (Subtask 2) positions out of 35 participants in the Open models category.
Columns µ and β indicate the average and baseline performance, respectively.

riscos.descricao: Alta frequência de violações de sintaxe, erros de referência inválida e conflitos de conhecimento de API no código gerado pelos três modelos online; com os prompts baseline e signal-augmented nenhum modelo chegou a solução correta.

riscos.descricao: Com o prompt baseline, os três modelos alucinaram sinais VSS inexistentes; com a lista de sinais, passaram a confundir sinais semelhantes (System.Mode em vez de Mode).
O reparo iterativo pode piorar o código: em algumas iterações a correção de um erro gerou vários novos erros e o score caiu (por exemplo, 0.0 na iteração 1 das Tabelas III, IV e V).

Segurança funcional (safety) em domínio automotivo crítico, não cibersegurança: o estudo destaca a necessidade de cautela e de mitigação para uso seguro e confiável de código gerado por LLM em sistemas de software automotivo; o risco não é medido.

citacoes.trecho: The task was to generate code, which turns off the windshield wipers, when the hood of the vehicle is open.

The task was evaluated across seven offline code generation LLMs including StarCoder (1B), TinyLLaMA, CodeLLaMA (7B, 7B-python, 7B-instruct), Phi-2 and Deepseek-Coder as well as three online LLMs being GPT-4o, GPT-4.1 and Codex.
To mitigate hallucinations, we applied the iterative repairing technique with feedback with static analysis and runtime errors proposed in Refining ChatGPT-generated code [21].
Baseline: a minimal one-liner prompt specifying the task.
Signal-augmented prompt: baseline prompt plus a list of 20 potentially relevant VSS signals
Template-augmented prompt: signal-augmented prompt plus a code skeleton with TODOs
To evaluate the correctness of the generated code, we define a heuristic scoring metric that starts at a maximum of 1.0 and penalizes occuring hallucinations in the following way:
Notably, all three models hallucinated VSS signals that do not exist indicating a reliability issue in generating code for unfamiliar domains.
In some iterations, the score got even worse as solving one error caused multiple new ones to arise.
The recorded types of hallucinations are syntax violations, invalid reference errors and API knowledge conflicts.
Moreover, hallucinations of non-existent VSS signals are no longer observed.
However, all models struggle to differentiate between similar signals, which means they use Vehicle.Body.Windshield.Front.Wiping.System.Model instead of the correct one.

This emphasizes the need for caution when relying on generated code in unfamiliar domains, because even with structured prompts and iterative feedback, correcting errors is not always straightforward and successful repair is not guaranteed.

The seven Offline code generation models were unable to generate any sensible code, highlighting their unsuitability for domain-specific tasks they sere not trained on even with context-enriched prompts.

These findings highlight the need for effective mitigation techniques to ensure the safe and reliable use of LLM generated code, especially in safety-critical domains such as automotive software systems.
Regarding the effectiveness of the mitigation strategy, the scores improved consistently across all prompting strategies demonstrating general effectiveness.
They comprise all signals related to the hood of the vehicle and the front windshield wipers.

tecnicas.observacao: Uma das três 'performance-aware prompts' investigadas na Seção 5.3. Herda do zero-shot o papel de especialista em tradução no system prompt (instrucao), o código-fonte inserido no prompt (contexto) e o formato de saída em bloco Markdown terminado por <|END|> (restricoes); acrescenta só a frase de sistema 'You are also a code optimization expert, ensuring the translated code is efficient and adheres to best practices' (instrucao). As Figuras 8 e 9 diferem apenas nessa frase, e ambas as condições são executadas com os mesmos três modelos na Tabela 5, o que configura contrafactual do ingrediente. A categoria acrescentada é a mesma já presente no prompt base.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 8, Seção 5.3 e Tabela 5; p. 23, Apêndice C.1; p. 25, Figura 10
tecnicas.observacao: Usa o mesmo system prompt do perf-zero-shot e acrescenta duas traduções eficientes de exemplo (fonte e tradução-alvo 'correct and efficient'), tiradas de outros problemas do TRACE na mesma direção de tradução (exemplos; o código das demonstrações também é contexto, já presente). Em relação ao comparador zero-shot, acrescenta instrução de eficiência e exemplos, por isso o contraste com zero-shot é de pacote. O par perf-few-shot × perf-zero-shot (Figuras 9 e 10; Tabela 5, p. 8) difere apenas nos exemplos e permitiria isolar esse ingrediente por contraste pareado; o estudo não analisa esse contraste. Critério de escolha dos dois exemplos além de 'other problems in TRACE following the same translation direction' não informado.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 8, Seção 5.3 e Tabela 5; p. 9; p. 23, Apêndice C.1; p. 26, Figura 11
tecnicas.observacao: Mesmo system prompt do perf-zero-shot; o prompt do usuário inclui a tradução produzida na rodada zero-shot anterior ('Reference Translation') e seu perfil de execução (resultado dos testes, feedback de execução, tempo e memória), pedindo melhoria se ela não for correta ou eficiente (feedback). Em relação ao zero-shot, acrescenta instrução de eficiência e feedback de execução: contraste de pacote. O par perf-self-refine × perf-zero-shot (Figuras 9 e 11; Tabela 5) difere no bloco de feedback, mas a tradução refinada parte da saída zero-shot, não da perf-zero-shot; o estudo não analisa esse contraste. Não se informa sobre quais testes (padrão ou de estresse) é gerado o perfil de execução nem se há mais de uma rodada de refinamento.

riscos.descricao: Ineficiência de execução em traduções funcionalmente corretas (não é cibersegurança): 23,5% das traduções corretas são mais de 2× mais lentas ou mais intensivas em memória que a melhor da tarefa; taxonomia em discrepância de implementação de algoritmo (11,93%), descompasso de construções da linguagem (66,36%) e ineficiência de gestão de recursos (21,71%). O estudo liga eficiência a 'operational cost', sem quantificar custo.

riscos.descricao: Traduções incorretas (falha de compilação, erro de execução ou excesso de recursos) são frequentes em alguns modelos (Pass de 62.5 a 95.5 na Tabela 2); na Seção 5.3, perf-self-refine reduz ligeiramente a correção do Claude-4 (93.4→91.9) ao melhorar o B_T.
riscos.localizador: p. 6, Seção 4 e Tabela 2; p. 9, Seção 5.3

riscos.descricao: Ameaça à validade de construto: o conjunto de referência de eficiência é derivado de LLMs; se for mais fraco que implementações otimizadas por humanos, o Beyond pode superestimar o desempenho dos modelos.

Limites de generalização declarados: só tempo de execução e pico de memória (sem latência de E/S, compilação ou energia); só C++, Java e Python; tarefas de nível de método, mais limpas que cenários de classe ou repositório.
Ruído de medição por carga do sistema na medição de ET e PM; o estudo relata coeficientes de variação tipicamente abaixo de 3,0% no ambiente controlado.

Possível vazamento de dados de avaliação no prompt few-shot: os dois exemplos do perf-few-shot vêm de outros problemas do TRACE na mesma direção. O estudo não discute contaminação por pré-treinamento dos problemas do TRANSCODER-TEST (coletados do GeeksforGeeks) nem apresenta esse procedimento como controle de contaminação.

mitigacoes.descricao: Estratégias de prompt orientadas a desempenho (perf-zero-shot, perf-few-shot, perf-self-refine) investigadas para reduzir ineficiências de tradução, comparadas com o zero-shot nos mesmos três modelos.

Ambiente controlado: cada comando fixado no núcleo de CPU menos utilizado (taskset -c) e cada perfil de execução calculado como média de cinco execuções para mitigar ruído; sem comparação com condição sem esse procedimento.
Limiar de diversidade ϵD = 0,05 escolhido acima da variância observada e do ruído relatado na literatura, para que as tarefas retidas reflitam diferenças reais de eficiência.

mitigacoes.descricao: Validação dos testes de estresse (Execution Integrity e Output Consistency nas implementações de referência em C++, Java e Python) para eliminar entradas sensíveis a comportamentos específicos de linguagem.

Verificação com linha de base humana em 50 tarefas sorteadas (Human 2.61 s × FastLLM 2.63 s) para examinar a validade do conjunto de referência; é checagem de sanidade, não comparação com e sem mitigação.
Classificação independente dos 327 casos ineficientes por dois autores, com resolução de divergências por discussão; concordância não quantificada.

citacoes.trecho: 3) Inference-time prompt strategies bring only modest improvements, indicating that simple prompting alone is insufficient to improve translation efficiency.
Execution efficiency determines how well a translated program performs, directly influencing responsiveness, scalability, and operational cost.
Notably, 23.5% of functionally correct translations are over 2× slower or more memory-intensive than the most efficient counterparts.
Few-shot prompting provides the most consistent yet modest efficiency gains, suggesting that improving translation efficiency likely requires more than prompt-level intervention.
This enriched prompt (E, Figure 12) incorporates: 1) two of the most effective synthesizers discovered so far; 2) the execution profiles of their outputs; and 3) chain-of-thought instructions.
For each task, the model generates a single translation using greedy decoding (temperature = 0.0) under a zero-shot prompt (Appendix C.1).
Translations that fail to compile, trigger runtime errors, or exceed resource limits (180s or 4096MB) are marked as incorrect and excluded from efficiency evaluation.
Correct translations are then executed on stress tests to measure ET and PM, with each metric reported as the arithmetic mean of five runs.
Two authors independently classified the cases and resolved disagreements through discussion.

Beyond the default zero-shot baseline, we experiment with three performance-aware prompts (Appendix C.1), inspired by recent code efficiency work (Shypula et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024a): 1) perf-zero-shot, which adds an explicit system instruction on efficiency; 2) perf-few-shot, which provides two efficient translation examples; and 3) perf-self-refine, which refines the initial translation based on execution feedback.
Overall, prompting yields modest and model-dependent gains.
Other strategies are mixed: perf-self-refine, for instance, improves Claude-4’s time efficiency (BT: 48.8→52.3) while slightly reducing correctness (93.4→91.9).

Taken together, the results suggest that prompt-based strategies can alleviate inefficiencies to a limited extent but fail to eliminate them, highlighting the need for more advanced methods to encode efficiency principles.
A potential threat to construct validity lies in using an LLM-derived translation set (efficiency reference set) as the evaluation anchor.
If the reference set were weaker than human-optimized implementations, the resulting scores could overestimate the model performance.
To examine this risk, we conducted a human-baseline sanity check on 50 randomly sampled tasks (18 C++, 21 Java, and 11 Python).
Meanwhile, we acknowledge that excluding other languages may pose risks to broader generalization.

We acknowledge that this setting is cleaner than real-world translation scenarios, which often involve class-level or repository-level contexts (Jimenez et al., 2023; Ibrahimzada et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025).
Each execution profile was averaged over five independent runs to mitigate noise from system load.
These models were utilized for both the curation of the benchmark and the evaluation of the work.

Four settings are considered: 1) zero-shot, which directly asks the LLM to translate code without additional guidance (Figure 8); 2) perf-zero-shot, which augments the zero-shot setting with explicit efficiency-oriented system instructions (Figure 9); 3) perf-few-shot, which provides the LLM with two efficient code translation examples, which are drawn from other problems in TRACE following the same translation direction (Figure 10); and 4) perf-self-refine, which includes the execution feedback of the translation produced in the previous zero-shot round and asks the LLM for further refinement or optimization (Figure 11).
You are also a code optimization expert, ensuring the translated code is efficient and adheres to best practices.

citacoes.trecho: We validate one of the proposed ideas regarding generating code out of UML model instances of software systems.
The RAG pipeline that we deploy incorporates sample Qiskit code from public GitHub repositories.
Experimental results show that well-engineered prompts can improve CodeBLEU scores by up to a factor of four, yielding more accurate and consistent quantum code.
RAG is a well-established, state-of-the-art concept to address the so-called LLM hallucination problem, which is abundant [7].
To overcome the LLM limitations that cause occasional hallucinations, a RAG approach is employed [26].
The input prompt given to the LLM entails the textual model instance that conforms to a meta-model.
We examine two types of prompts.
The first one is a more general prompt that simply instructs the LLM to generate quantum code based on the quantum circuit defined in the input model instance.
The second prompt variant is more specific, incorporating detailed implementation requirements, such as quantum gate mapping strategies and constraints on syntax and gate behavior.
Table II shows the results under the same generic prompt setting but with external context provided through a RAG pipeline that incorporates eight Qiskit GitHub repositories.
This external context does not significantly improve performance across most metrics, hence not validating RQ2 so far.

Comparing Table I with Table III, and Table II with Table IV further highlight that prompt-engineering has a far greater impact on the LLM’s code generation performance than the provided external context through the RAG pipeline in the current setup.

tecnicas.observacao: Uma das duas estratégias de mitigação que a RQ4 investiga («prompt-engineering techniques»); o estudo a descreve como prompt padrão de tradução acrescido de requisitos explícitos de segurança (genéricos), comparada com o Baseline na Tabela VII. O ingrediente acrescentado (requisitos de segurança, instruindo a preservar a correção funcional e evitar padrões comuns de vulnerabilidade) foi classificado como restricoes de segurança; também tem caráter de diretriz (instrucao), categoria já presente no prompt base. tecnicas.observacao: Proposta de mitigação do estudo. Recupera, por similaridade de cosseno entre embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), os três casos de código vulnerável mais semelhantes (limiar 0,5) de uma base de relatórios de análise de vulnerabilidade escritos manualmente e insere no prompt uma seção «Security Considerations» com tipos de vulnerabilidade, avaliação de severidade e relatórios, junto com o código-fonte e os requisitos de tradução. O contraste com o Baseline isola o pacote (recuperação + seção de segurança), não um ingrediente. O artigo não diz se o código dos casos recuperados entra no prompt (por isso exemplos não foi marcado) nem se os requisitos do Naive Prompt são mantidos. RAG e Naive diferem em mais de um ingrediente.

citacoes.trecho: To bridge this gap, we conduct a security-centric empirical study to investigate the risks of vulnerabilities being introduced or preserved during LLM-based translation.
Building upon our collected security-centric code corpus of 720 samples, we design 1,200 translation tasks for each subject LLM using a baseline prompt template without any enhancements.
Each prompt contains: (1) natural language instructions for the translation task; (2) source language; (3) target language and (4) the complete source code to be translated.
For file-level code translation in security contexts, we incorporate necessary constraints in the prompts to ensure basic translation quality while avoiding task-specific guidance.
All other hyperparameters are kept by default, and all evaluations are performed in a zero-shot setting.
RQ4 (Mitigation Effectiveness): To what extent do the prompt-engineering techniques reduce the risks?

To address security vulnerabilities in LLM-based code translation, we implement and evaluate two mitigation strategies: a naive security-aware approach and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) method [40].

The naive security-aware approach enhances standard translation prompts by integrating explicit security requirements, instructing models to preserve functional correctness while avoiding common vulnerability patterns.

This query embedding then undergoes a sophisticated similarity assessment against the entire stored vector database through cosine similarity calculations, efficiently identifying the three most semantically analogous code cases that exceed a predetermined similarity threshold of 0.5.

This meticulously crafted prompt synthesizes the source code, fundamental translation requirements, and a specialized Security Considerations section that enumerates specific vulnerability types, severity assessments, and detailed human-authored analysis reports corresponding to the retrieved cases.
The results reveal significant security degradation, with 28.6% to 45% of translations introducing new vulnerabilities.
The results reveal a trade-off: while mitigation strategies enhanced security, they incurred a cost to functional correctness.
Although some LLMs may have been trained on source code from our collected samples, they lack access to the corresponding correct translations, ruling out task-specific fine-tuning or reinforcement.

The data demonstrates that security vulnerabilities in translated code present significant detection challenges, with 90% of developers identifying them as the most difficult issues to verify – far surpassing syntactic errors (93.3% agreement on being easiest).
Temperature: Fixed at 0 to eliminate output randomness
The multi-level review mechanism operates as follows: each translated code sample is independently evaluated by two security researchers.
To assess functional correctness, we conducted an additional evaluation on a separate set of 67 samples, as the VIR test samples were inherently ill-suited for this metric.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote híbrido: detecção estatística de inliers (fora do escopo) seguida de geração de regras com Gemma-3-12B (prompt de três partes com papel/diretrizes → instrucao; exemplos genéricos, de domínio e de iterações anteriores → exemplos; esquema, perfis de colunas, base de conhecimento e amostras → contexto; formato JSON e comportamentos permitidos/proibidos → restricoes), enriquecimento com especificação e pseudocódigo e etapas encadeadas até a geração de código (decomposicao), filtros por LLM que descartam regras entre candidatas (conflitos e rubrica → amostragem) e reparo do código com a exceção da execução (feedback). Não há base de prompting identificável, por isso acrescentados vazio. O pacote é comparado apenas com detectores de erros que não usam LLM nem prompting (ED2, FAHES, KATARA, IQR, IF, SD, Max-Entropy, Min-K), que não constituem condição «sem o pacote» no mesmo pipeline; por isso tipo_contrafactual nenhum. Os papéis distintos (gerador, 'data-quality auditor', 'senior data-quality engineer') atuam em sequência, sem interação descrita; não classificados como multiagente.

citacoes.trecho: After filtering data samples through traditional clustering, we iteratively prompt LLMs to produce semantically valid quality rules and synthesize their executable validators through code-generating LLMs.
To generate reliable quality rules, we aid LLMs with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) by leveraging external knowledge sources and domain-specific few-shot examples.
Robust guardrails ensure the accuracy and consistency of both rules and code snippets.

Yet, existing LLM-based solutions—such as fine-tuned models, prompt-driven detectors (Heidari et al., 2019; Mehra et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), or in-context repair mechanisms (Chung et al., 2017; Biester et al., 2024; Ni et al., 2024a,b)—remain computationally expensive, either requiring per-row inference or dataset-specific training.
Each rule-generation prompt follows a structured, three-part format.
For wide tables, the schema is split into manageable batches to fit within Gemma’s context window while still preserving column-level details.
Cosine similarity selects the nearest domain; its representative rule cards for each rule type are then added to the prompt.
We employ an iterative prompting strategy inspired by the self-consistency technique in CoT (Wang et al., 2023) reasoning.
citacoes.localizador: p. 3, Few-shot examples from previous iterations

citacoes.trecho: In subsequent iterations, a randomly selected subset of these generated cards is included as additional exemplars in the prompt, progressively refining the model output.
citacoes.localizador: p. 3, Few-shot examples from previous iterations

citacoes.trecho: These contradictions stemmed primarily from two sources: (i) inconsistencies in the sample data frames used across iterations; (ii) LLMs hallucinations (see Appendix A.3 for examples).
An eight-point rubric (Hashemi et al., 2024) assesses each surviving rule card.
In the final stage, each rule card is translated into executable Python code using Qwen-2.5-Coder (32 B) (Bai et al., 2023), an LLM specialized for code generation.

We dynamically select these few-shot examples by embedding both the current table description and all stored code snippets using sentence embeddings, ranking them by cosine similarity, and inserting the most relevant samples into the prompt.
We run each snippet on a few rows; if it errors, the exception is fed back and the model repairs the code (see Figure 3).

As shown in Table 3, F1 scores declined significantly across all datasets (having 30% noise), emphasizing the filter’s critical role in providing clean context to the LLM to reduce false-positive rule generation.

We run the tests in two modes—one using domain-specific few-shot examples and one without—and report the resulting F1 scores side-by-side in Table 6, highlighting the merit of domain-specific examples.

Across ten data sets and three noise levels, our method records the top F1 in 26 of 30 settings, markedly surpassing the next best detector on challenging tables such as Bikes, Breast Cancer, and Soil-Moisture.
Evaluated on both REIN synthetic stress benchmarks and standard datasets from ED2 and RAHA, our approach consistently outperforms existing detectors in accuracy.
Table 21 shows the earlier F1 comparison with precision-recall breakdowns, offering a fuller view of detector performance across all datasets and noise levels.

Sem prompt base identificável: o comparador é a solução humana original, sem reescrita por SLM; por isso acrescentados fica vazio, com o mesmo critério para as quatro técnicas. O contrafactual é o pacote (SLM + prompt) contra o código humano não reescrito: a diferença mistura o efeito do modelo e o do prompt e não isola a persona. Contraste com Zero-Shot: as duas condições ficam nas mesmas categorias (a persona é instrucao), mas a redação das instruções também difere, logo não há contraste pareado de um ingrediente.

tecnicas.observacao: Duas etapas encadeadas: (1) a solução humana é enviada à API do GPT-5, que produz uma estratégia de otimização (raciocinio); (2) a estratégia e a solução humana são dadas ao SLM com a instrução de aplicá-la e devolver só o código (instrucao, contexto, restricoes; a cadeia estratégia → código conta como decomposicao). O raciocínio não é gerado pelo próprio SLM, mas por um modelo maior (GPT-5); pacote híbrido, porque inclui a escolha de outro modelo para a etapa de estratégia (ver componentes_fora_escopo). Template adotado de [14], [25]. Contrafactual de pacote (pipeline GPT-5 + SLM + prompt contra o código humano não reescrito); o ganho não pode ser atribuído ao raciocínio passo a passo do SLM nem a um mecanismo isolado. citacoes.trecho: In this study, we investigate whether prompt engineering can improve the energy efficiency of SLMs in code generation.
Each model is tested under four prompting strategies: role prompting, zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought (CoT).

Our findings show that CoT prompting provides consistent energy savings for Qwen2.5-Coder and StableCode-3B, while CodeLlama-7B and Phi-3-Mini-4K fail to outperform the baseline under any prompting strategy.
Importantly, we do not measure the energy consumed by running the language models themselves.
Results show that SLMs such as Qwen2.5-Coder and StableCode-3B achieve the best energy efficiency, with CoT prompting consistently outperforming the baseline across various difficulty levels.
We randomly chose 150 problems in total, with 50 from each category, ensuring that all had community-verified solutions.
These solutions served both as baseline references for comparison and as prompts to evaluate whether SLMs could generate more efficient and sustainable code.
For zero-shot and CoT prompting, we adopted the prompt templates introduced by [14], [25].
In each case, a human-written solution from LeetCode was provided to the SLM along with the corresponding prompt, instructing the model to optimize the code.
We instructed the SLMs to act as a senior software engineer with 10 years of experience in designing and optimizing software systems.
Each SLM was provided with a LeetCode human-written solution along with a direct instruction to optimize the code for efficiency.
For this setup, we constructed prompts containing a small set of code optimization examples, each showing an unoptimized piece of code followed by its optimized version.
In our setup, we first provided the human-written LeetCode solution to the GPT-5 API and asked it to outline a strategy for optimizing the code.
We then provided both the strategy and the original human-written solution to the SLMs, instructing them to optimize the code using the given reasoning steps.
In some instances, SLMs produced multiple solutions or echoed the provided human-written baseline solution and problem statement.
To address this, we performed a code-cleaning process using a combination of manual review and the ChatGPT API, retaining only the first valid solution.
Each code sample was executed ten times to account for variability and ensure reliable results.
A five-second cooling interval was applied between runs to maintain stable conditions.
To minimize external or nondeterministic influences, all executions were performed under identical virtualized settings.
In certain cases, prompting not only fails to improve performance but also increases energy consumption above the baseline.
This study focuses only on Python, a widely used programming language, so the results may not apply to other languages such as C++ or Java.
In addition, some benchmark problems may have been included in the training data of certain LLMs, which could lead to memorization and an overestimation of their performance.
Finally, although the experiments were conducted in a controlled Linux environment, minor system fluctuations and measurement overhead may have introduced small variations in the reported results.

citacoes.trecho: The retrieved relevant information is then incorporated into the LLM’s input prompt, guiding the model to generate more accurate and informed patches.
Initially, the BaseRepair stage attempts a straightforward repair using only the buggy function, error messages, failing test cases and perfect fault localization via LLM.

Our basic prompt—"You are an expert in program repair."—supplied to ChatGPT along with the buggy function, failing test, error messages and perfect fault localization, is sufficient for an initial patch attempt but inadequate for precisely retrieving relevant function signatures.
To overcome this, we leverage ChatGPT’s reasoning capabilities by prompting it (promptSIG) to generate two root causes and five candidate function names likely to repair the buggy line.
Since the effectiveness of this stage depends on the initial query rewriting stage, we repeat the Relevant Function Signature Retrieval process 20 times, each time producing a single candidate patch.
For each snippet, we generate 10 candidate patches and immediately validate them using the test suite; if all patches fail, we proceed to the next snippet.

We evaluate RELREPAIR against four state-of-the-art LLM-based APR techniques — ChatRepair [22], ThinkRepair [23], Mulpor [40] and RAP-Gen [41], as well as a baseline method, BaseChatGPT, which performs code repair by directly sampling from the ChatGPT model without access to any retrieved relevant code.
For baseline results, we reference reported outcomes from prior studies where available, ensuring a consistent and fair comparison across all approaches.
As a result, ChatGPT generates a plausible but incorrect function name, rehashIfNecessary(), based only on its general programming knowledge.
However, traditional RAG approaches face challenges, such as retrieving irrelevant, noisy, or incomplete information, which can negatively impact the accuracy and reliability of generated outputs.

(2) In contrast, the SnipRepair, although incurring significantly higher computational costs (up to $0.27 for 300 patches), exhibits consistent and substantial performance gains, increasing steadily from 21 correct fixes at 60 patches to 39 correct fixes at 300 patches.
Internal. The main internal threat arises from the manual validation performed to determine the correctness of plausible patches compared with reference developer fixes.
To mitigate this concern, following established practices in previous research [15, 20, 39, 47, 44, 43], we carefully examined each generated patch to ensure accurate validation.
External. The main external threat is the representativeness of the subjects used in our evaluation.

Specifically, when query rewriting is enabled (denoted as "w"), RELREPAIR successfully fixes a total of 54 bugs, whereas only 20 bugs are fixed without query rewriting ("w/o"), reflecting a considerable improvement.

citacoes.trecho: Each task input, consisting of complete context dependencies, a structured contract framework, and a concise task prompt, is independently annotated and cross-validated by experienced developers.

To guide the large language model in generating realistic and functional contract code, each code generation task takes the following three components as input, as illustrated in Figure 2: (1) context information, which includes relevant functions, variables, and contract definitions extracted from real-world repositories; (2) target contract framework, a structured scaffold that outlines contract-level elements; (3) task prompt, which specifies the task requirements, including the desired contract name and the compiler version for deployment.
// You task is to complete the smart contract {MerkleDistributor} strictly according to the provided context and description.
Note that the contract is deployed using compiler version {0.6.11}, and do not introduce any additional contracts, dependencies, or unrelated code.
To enforce this, we preserve the original function signatures and only leave the function bodies blank for the large language model to complete, while keeping all other structural elements intact.
For both metrics, greedy sampling is used when k = 1, while nucleus sampling is applied when k > 1.

Storage state inconsistencies expose the model’s shortcomings in variable management, which may cause subsequent transactions to operate on incorrect data or even lead to security vulnerabilities, such as reentrancy attacks or unauthorized access.
This oversight allows the function to be repeatedly called, leading to functional deviations.
In our evaluation of the Gemini-2.0-Flash-Exp model, we observe a recitation error in 12.54% of the tests.
In constructing the benchmark dataset, we recognize the potential risk of data leakage between the benchmark data and the model’s training data.

To mitigate potential data leakage, two developers with three years of smart contract experience independently rewrite the original comments into structured NatSpec documentation, ensuring semantic accuracy while significantly differing from the source.
Thus, our comparison should be interpreted as suggestive rather than as a rigorous quantitative evaluation of task difficulty.
Additionally, due to time and cost constraints, this study evaluates six LLMs, so findings may not fully represent all models.
We implement this on the Hardhat [36] local testing network, resetting blockchain state before execution to avoid cross-test interference.

citacoes.trecho: Within this framework, we assess large language models (LLMs) as repair agents under high- and low-context prompting conditions.

Extending this line of research, we explore how large language models perform syntax-only repair on uncompilable student code, examining how model type and prompting context influence repair outcomes.

Each submission was then processed under six experimental conditions, combining three language models (GPT-5, Claude 3.5 Haiku, and Gemini 2.5 Flash) with two prompting contexts (low and high), yielding a total of 600 repaired outputs for evaluation.

In the low-context condition, models received only the uncompilable student code and instructions to perform syntax-only repair with minimal edits that preserved control flow, identifiers, and formatting.
The high-context condition additionally provided the compiler message, problem statement, and few-shot examples of correct and incorrect repairs.
In the context of modeling students’ knowledge for feedback and analysis, semantic rewrites risk distorting the very evidence of learning we seek to model.

However, similar to the tendencies observed by Řechtáčková et al. [7], the models occasionally strayed from the intended pedagogical scope by making stylistic or structural edits that went beyond minimal correction.
Inter-rater agreement exceeding κ = 0.80 was achieved on the second round, after which the full set was coded and analysis conducted.
Compilation success rates were high and consistent across models, with GPT-5 achieving 98.5% (591/600), Claude 3.5 96% (576/600), and Gemini 2.5 95.5% (573/600) compilable repairs.
Edit distance, computed using normalized Levenshtein distance, measured how closely the repair aligned with the original code.

Prompting condition had no significant effect on edit distance (F(1, 594) = 0.004, p = 0.95), contrary to our hypothesis that providing additional context might encourage models to over-correct or attempt to solve the problem rather than perform syntax-only repairs.
Prompting condition had no significant effect on either measure (SP: χ2(1, N = 579) = 0.02, p = 0.88; LP: χ2(1, N = 549) = 0.00, p = 0.97).

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote de prompting do LLM Invoker: função C acompanhada só das expansões de macro, typedefs e definições de struct e função essenciais (contexto); pré-tradução das structs em invocações separadas, armazenadas em cache e fornecidas no prompt com a instrução de usar a definição pré-gerada (decomposicao, contexto, restricoes); usos de campos char* acrescentados ao pedido com instrução de considerá-los (contexto, instrucao); divisão de funções grandes em várias requisições (decomposicao); reenvio da mensagem de erro do compilador com a função C pedindo tradução corrigida e nova tradução quando há bloco unsafe ou chamadas a funções unsafe, até um número configurável de vezes (feedback, restricoes). O texto dos prompts não é apresentado. Não há condição sem o pacote no mesmo LLM nem ablação dos componentes: as comparações com CROWN (ferramenta sintática sem LLM, Tabela VI) e FLUORINE (outro sistema baseado em LLM, resultados do artefato, Tabela VII) contrastam sistemas distintos e não isolam o pacote. O verificador simbólico diferencial (Symbolic Analyzer) não realimenta o LLM na versão avaliada (a realimentação é apresentada como melhoria futura, Seção VII, p. 11); ver componentes_fora_escopo.

riscos.descricao: LLMs não garantem código correto e o código transpilado contém bugs sutis que podem escapar a testes unitários ou fuzzing (por exemplo, u8next_ com estado intermediário incorreto; 20 funções com bugs semânticos na Tabela IV).

riscos.descricao: Código Rust unsafe introduz potenciais vulnerabilidades de corrupção de memória; modelos diferentes do GPT-4o tendem a usar ponteiros brutos e blocos unsafe (Perc. unsafe de 3% a 79% na Tabela I).

riscos.descricao: Invocações diferentes do LLM geram definições Rust ligeiramente diferentes para as mesmas structs C (por exemplo, nomes de campos), causando erros de ligação.

Falsos positivos do verificador: funções C com bugs de corrupção de memória ausentes no Rust não são simbolicamente equivalentes; otimizações do KLEE ao modelar arrays também geram falsos positivos (FP de 0 a 3 por modelo na Tabela V).

citacoes.trecho: RustAssure presents a system that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically transpile existing C codebases to Rust.
RustAssure uses prompt engineering techniques to maximize the chances of the LLM generating idiomatic and safe Rust code.
RustAssure uses various prompt-engineering techniques to ensure that the code generated by the LLM compiles successfully, and also minimizes the use of unsafe Rust.
Therefore, RustAssure’s LLM Invoker includes only the essential macro expansions, typedef instructions, and struct and function definitions in the LLM request.

Then, for each function that uses these struct types, the pre-generated struct definition is provided along with the C function as the prompt, and the LLM is instructed to use the pre-generated definition.

To limit the amount of unsafe Rust code, the LLM Invoker extracts all uses of such char* fields and adds them to the LLM request, when pre-translating the struct types, and instructs the LLM to consider these field usages for the transpilation task.
To support these models, the LLM Invoker automatically chunks a function into multiple LLM requests if it does not fit within the LLM’s context window.

Like previous approaches [17], when the LLM produces a transpilation that does not compile, RustAssure re-attempts the transpilation, by sending the compiler error message along with the original C function to the LLM, requesting a corrected translation.

In addition to compilation errors, if the LLM-transpiled Rust code contains any unsafe block, or invokes unsafe functions such as the functions from the libc crate, the LLM Invoker requests a re-translation up to a configurable number of times.
However, LLMs are not guaranteed to always generate correct code [9].
Code generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) often contain subtle bugs.
Unsafe Rust code introduces potential memory corruption vulnerabilities in the program, therefore, the amount of unsafe Rust code generated by the LLM must be minimized.

We observed that due to the inherent non-determinism and randomness [15] of LLM models these different invocations can sometimes generate slightly different Rust struct definitions for the same C types.
When using these models, a single large function can exceed the context window length.

We note that C and Rust functions will not be symbolically equivalent if the C code has memory corruption bugs that are absent in Rust—a limitation that is present even when using concrete test cases.
The false positives arise due to optimizations KLEE performs when symbolically modeling arrays and aligning these differences is primarily an engineering effort.
RustAssure can be improved with a feedback loop from the Semantic Checker that returns divergences to the LLM for targeted re-transpilation.
GPT-4o outperformed all other LLM models across all codebases, successfully transpiling 89.8% of all C functions into compilable Rust functions.
The average percentage of unsafe code across all codebases is 13.05%, 20.88%, 31.03%, and 59.10%, for the GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5-turbo, and Claude-3.5-Sonnet models, respectively.
Figure 6 shows the simplified snippet of the scan_option function from the libcsv codebase.
The overall compilation success rate for RustAssure and CROWN is 89.8% and 97.3%, respectively.
We used a graph edit-distance-based comparison instead of SMT solving to simplify our implementation.

tecnicas.localizador: Seção III.B e Algoritmo 1, p. 3; Seção IV.A, p. 4; Figura 2 e Tabela I, p. 5
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote evolutivo: inicialização com M = 6 códigos CADQuery gerados a partir do prompt do usuário e de k = 5 exemplos sorteados de um conjunto de 40 amostras da documentação do CADQuery (instrucao; exemplos e contexto); uma tentativa de self-debugging com a mensagem de erro do compilador (feedback); a cada geração, renderização em imagem multivista, descrição textual pelo VLM com chain-of-thought (raciocinio), ranqueamento pelo RLM (o3-mini) repetido três vezes e promediado, seleção de pais por distribuição exponencial e elitismo (amostragem); crossover pelo LM com os dois códigos, suas descrições e o prompt, pedindo análise de semelhanças, pontos fortes e fracos (raciocinio, contexto, feedback visual); mutação com probabilidade de 50% pedindo refinamento do código (feedback); N = 4 gerações encadeadas (decomposicao); três modelos em papéis distintos (LM gerador, VLM descritor, RLM avaliador) cujas saídas alimentam uns aos outros (multiagente). mecanismos_acrescentados tomados em relação à população inicial (geração 0: instrucao, exemplos, contexto e feedback do self-debugging), que a Figura 2 reporta; feedback já está na base e por isso não é listado como acrescentado, embora a evolução acrescente feedback visual. Contrafactual: a Figura 2 mostra só a contribuição por geração dentro da mesma execução (cumulativo); a Tabela I compara com 3D-Premise e CADCodeVerify, sistemas diferentes com valores obtidos de [1], e não com uma condição sem a técnica em condições comparáveis. Pacote híbrido: inclui renderização, seleção probabilística com λ = 0,5, elitismo, temperatura e orçamento de população/gerações (ver componentes_fora_escopo). As variantes EvoCAD-4v e EvoCAD-4o diferem só no modelo (GPT-4V ou GPT-4o), não na técnica.
