citacoes.trecho: This paper presents a systematic comparative study built on the CodeEnhancer framework, evaluating five open-source LLMs—Qwen 2.5 Coder 7B, DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 2 9B, and Mistral 7B—across three prompt engineering strategies (Zero-shot, Few-shot, and Chain-of-Thought) using 81 Python prompts drawn from the LLMSecEval benchmark, yielding 1,215 experimental scenarios in total.
We evaluate three distinct prompt engineering strategies applied at the initial generation step.
The model receives the LLMSecEval natural language prompt with the docstring template but no explicit security guidance or examples.
citacoes.localizador: PDF p. 3, seção III-C, item a)

citacoes.trecho: Five secure code examples are prepended to the prompt, covering CWE-78, CWE-89, CWE-502, CWE-434, and CWE-22.
citacoes.localizador: PDF p. 3, seção III-C, item b)

citacoes.trecho: The model is instructed to execute a four-step security reasoning process before writing code: (1) identify external inputs, (2) enumerate associated CWE risks, (3) specify mitigations, and (4) generate code.
citacoes.localizador: PDF p. 3, seção III-C, item c)

citacoes.trecho: The original Stage 1 pipeline consists of: (1) structured code generation using a prompt template that enforces an embedded docstring with Input Prompt, Intention, and Functionality fields; (2) iterative validation using Bandit (security) and Pylint (syntax) to detect issues and generate structured feedback reports; and (3) LLM-driven code refinement based on the feedback, repeated up to a maximum of 5 iterations.
If the verdict is Incorrect, the reason is forwarded to the local generator model for a functional fix, and the file re-enters the SAST loop.

While this reflects realistic deployment profiles, it introduces a compound variable where improvements in Few-shot may stem from both the in-context demonstrations and the reinforced system directive.

Empirical studies confirm that LLM-produced code frequently replicates insecure patterns from training data, introducing vulnerabilities listed in the MITRE Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) Top 25 [5], [7]—such as command injection (CWE-78), SQL injection (CWE-89), and path traversal (CWE-22).
Mistral 7B triggered the most Incorrect verdicts across all strategies, indicating a tendency to generate functionally incomplete code even when SAST checks pass.
Empirically, we identified 9 scenarios in our CoT runs that ended in SyntaxError due to context or token limit truncation.
A key concern with few-shot prompting is data leakage: if the five examples cover the same CWEs as the test prompts, apparent improvements may reflect memorization rather than generalization.
Figure 3 disaggregates few-shot performance into seen CWEs (those covered by examples) and unseen CWEs (those not in the examples).
Although decoupling the evaluator via GPT-4o-mini successfully circumvents self-assessment divergence [19], relying on an LLM evaluator carries inherent stochasticity.
Bandit and Pylint detect static rule violations and syntax errors, but cannot verify deep semantic vulnerabilities or business logic flaws.

While SHA-256 resolves the immediate plaintext exposure, it represents an intermediate security level compared to salted hashing functions (e.g., bcrypt), highlighting both the repair capability and the nuanced boundary of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations.

Our mid-phase results validate this decision empirically: under the self-assessment framework (Self-Judge), Llama 3.1 8B achieved a low 15.6% resolution rate, and DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B scored only 20.0%.
All models used temperature = 0 (deterministic), max tokens = 2048, and context window (num_ctx) = 8192 to ensure identical context limits across all models and prompt strategies.

Os casos de teste foram categorizados como exemplos (entradas e saídas concretas; os autores aproximam TDP de few-shot) e como restricoes (especificações executáveis). A categoria restricoes já existe no prompt base (assinatura, formato de saída) e, em HumanEval, o enunciado do prompt base já traz exemplos de entrada e saída (Figura 2); em MBPP, segundo os autores, o prompt base só tem enunciado e assinatura. Contraste pareado com Normal Prompting nos mesmos problemas, modelos e hiperparâmetros, diferindo apenas nos casos de teste. Os autores reconhecem que o TDP tem cerca de 25% mais tokens, o que confunde estrutura de teste e volume de contexto (Seção IV-E1, p-17); o ganho é do acréscimo dos casos de teste, sem separar esses dois aspectos. Em RQ1 e RQ2 a comparação é feita na primeira tentativa e após o laço de remediação.

O desempenho de primeira tentativa é a fase inicial do mesmo orçamento de 5 tentativas («5-attempt budget's initial and post-correction performance»), por isso o contraste primeira tentativa vs pós-remediação é contribuição por rodada (cumulativo), não condição independente sem a técnica. Os mecanismos herdados variam conforme a estratégia sobre a qual o laço é aplicado (exemplos de teste só no TDP; exemplos de enunciado só em HumanEval).

riscos.descricao: Código gerado por LLM pode ser semanticamente incorreto, exigindo iterações de avaliação e refinamento.

Sobreajuste aos casos de teste públicos incluídos no prompt: o TDP regrediu em relação ao prompt normal em 26 instâncias únicas no HumanEval, 61 no MBPP e 10 no Code Contests; as soluções falham em casos-limite presentes só nos testes privados.
riscos.localizador: Seção IV-A (PDF p-15 e p-16; p. 22815-22816)

riscos.descricao: Dados de avaliação no prompt: 50% dos casos de teste de cada problema são incluídos no prompt TDP e também contam na avaliação, que usa 100% dos testes. O estudo controla parcialmente o risco exigindo aprovação também nos testes privados (ver mitigações). O estudo não discute contaminação dos benchmarks no pré-treinamento.
riscos.localizador: Seções II-C4 e II-D1 (PDF p-07 e p-08; p. 22807-22808)

riscos.descricao: Mesmo com temperatura 0,0 e semente 1000, a inferência é estocástica e os valores absolutos de acurácia podem variar entre execuções, versões de API e infraestrutura.

Em tentativa única, o TDP tem 25% mais tokens de entrada e 38% mais tempo de resposta, valores obtidos no estudo de caso da tarefa 51 do HumanEval (422 vs 315 tokens; 1,36 s vs 0,84 s). Os autores argumentam compensação em cenários de várias tentativas.
Citado na introdução, a partir da literatura: LLMs exibem alucinações; não avaliado no estudo.
Citado na introdução, a partir da literatura: LLMs memorizam segredos dos dados de treino e vazam informações; não avaliado no estudo.

Limitação de adoção apresentada pelos autores: o TDP exige que as organizações desenvolvam casos de teste antecipadamente, e a sobrecarga de desenvolvimento de testes pode superar os benefícios; não tratada como custo quantificado.

mitigacoes.descricao: Divisão 50% públicos / 50% privados, com avaliação em todos os testes, para reter testes não vistos que detectem sobreajuste; razão escolhida por análise de sensibilidade (0,25; 0,5; 0,75; 1,0) em HumanEval com quatro modelos, que mediu tamanhos de efeito do TDP, não o efeito da divisão sobre o sobreajuste.
mitigacoes.localizador: Seções II-C4 e II-D1 (PDF p-07 e p-08)

mitigacoes.descricao: Seleção sistemática dos primeiros 50% dos casos de teste como públicos, para evitar viés de escolha dos testes.
mitigacoes.localizador: Seção II-C4 (PDF p-07); Seção IV-E3 (PDF p-18)

mitigacoes.descricao: Temperatura 0,0 e semente 1000, e comparação pareada nas mesmas condições, para reduzir e equilibrar o efeito do não determinismo entre as estratégias.
mitigacoes.localizador: Seções II-D1 e IV-E1 (PDF p-08 e p-17)

mitigacoes.descricao: Laço de remediação aplicado igualmente às duas estratégias, para evitar a vantagem de aplicar TDP só após falha do prompt normal.
Teste de Wilcoxon como checagem de robustez ao pressuposto de normalidade do teste t pareado.

citacoes.trecho: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely adopted for Python code generation, the generated code can be semantically incorrect, requiring iterations of evaluation and refinement.
TDP, on the other hand, includes the same information as normal prompting but also supplies the first 50% of the test cases, obtained from the dataset, in the prompt for the programming problem.
The prompt includes (a) a description of the problem and (b) the signature of the function.
For each problem-prompt-model combination, models receive up to 5 attempts with error feedback after unsuccessful generations.

In our configuration, 50% of the test cases for each problem are designated as public tests (visible during prompting), while 100% of the test cases are used for evaluating the generated code (i.e., both public and private tests), to ensure that the generated code passes all test cases.
The 50% ratio balances specification clarity with validation rigor, retaining sufficient held-out tests to detect overfitting, unlike higher ratios that reduce or eliminate private evaluation.

According to qualitative analysis, these model-dependent regressions happen when models are excessively constrained by public test cases, producing solutions that do not work on edge cases, which are only included in private test cases.

First, even though deterministic generation settings were used (temperature = 0.0, seed = 1000), because LLM inference is intrinsically stochastic, absolute accuracy values can differ amongst evaluation runs, API versions, and infrastructure setups.
This indicates a 25% increase in TDP token costs.
Analyses at runtime show comparable overhead: Task 51 has a 38% increase in response time, taking 1.36 seconds under TDP as opposed to 0.84 seconds for normal prompts.
In addition, LLMs have been shown to exhibit hallucinations in which they assert that what is actually false is true [16], [17].
More relevant to the generation of code, LLMs have been proven to memorize secrets in training data, leaking valuable information about their models [14], [15].
On the other hand, TDP requires organizations to develop test cases upfront.
Another concern is that TDP prompts contain approximately 25% more tokens than normal prompts (Section III-A4), creating a potential confound between test-driven structure and additional context.

As a robustness check, we also performed the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which yielded consistent results (p < 0.001), confirming that our findings are not sensitive to the distributional assumption.
Our approach ensures both strategies receive equal remediation opportunities, enabling fair end-to-end effectiveness comparison.

tecnicas.nome_original: Multistage Bug Fixer (MBF), coluna «MBF» da Tabela 1 (sem informação de testes unitários no prompt)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 1 do PDF (impressa 34), resumo e seção 2; p. 2 do PDF (impressa 35), Algoritmo 1, Tabela 1 e seção 3 («Multistage Bug Fixer»)
tecnicas.observacao: Versão do Tree of Thoughts (BFS de profundidade 2, b = 1): fase 1 gera m = 5 hipóteses sobre localização e explicação do defeito (raciocinio) e o LLM vota (k = 5 votos, prompt de voto zero-shot) para escolher E*; fase 2 gera n = 5 propostas de correção a partir de E* e do código defeituoso e o LLM vota de novo (amostragem); as duas fases encadeadas → decomposicao; o código defeituoso fornecido como insumo → contexto; instruções zero-shot em cada etapa → instrucao. Os prompts exatos estão só no repositório (não acessado). O estudo não informa se, nesta coluna, o prompt traz a explicação do comportamento esperado presente no BBF (por isso restricoes não foi atribuída). Contrafactual de pacote: MBF contra BBF, mesmo GPT-4 e mesmos três casos em que o BBF falhou; ressalvas: casos escolhidos a posteriori pela falha do BBF em uma única tentativa, número de tentativas do MBF não informado e possível diferença de insumo (explicação do comportamento esperado). O ganho é do pacote, não de um mecanismo isolado.

tecnicas.nome_original: MBF w/UT (MBF com informação de testes unitários no prompt)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 1 do PDF (impressa 34), seção 2; p. 2 do PDF (impressa 35), Tabela 1 (coluna «MBF w/UT») e seção 3
tecnicas.observacao: Configuração de avaliação descrita na seção 2: nos passos 1a e 2a o prompt recebe, além do código defeituoso, detalhes da expectativa (testes unitários, entradas da rotina, saída esperada e saída obtida) → contexto e restricoes (mesma categorização dada ao ingrediente no BBF com testes). Mecanismos acrescentados em relação ao comparador de que deriva (BBF com informação de testes unitários). Contrafactual de pacote: o contraste com o BBF com testes unitários (mesmo ingrediente de teste, 2 sucessos em 15 tentativas) está só em prosa; na Tabela 1 o comparador listado é o BBF sem testes. Número de tentativas do MBF w/UT não informado.

tecnicas.nome_original: Unit test information in the prompt (inputs of the routine, expected output and actual output)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 1 do PDF (impressa 34), seção 2; p. 2 do PDF (impressa 35), legenda e colunas «MBF» e «MBF w/UT» da Tabela 1 e seção 3
tecnicas.observacao: Ingrediente de prompt: dados dos testes unitários (saída obtida → contexto de execução, fornecido uma única vez, sem ciclo de retorno, por isso não é feedback; saída esperada → restricoes como especificação). As categorias contexto e restricoes já podem estar presentes no prompt base (código defeituoso; explicação do comportamento esperado no BBF), mas o ingrediente é novo. Contraste com e sem o ingrediente dentro do MBF na Tabela 1 (mesmos três casos, mesmo modelo). Há também contraste em prosa no BBF (BBF com testes: 2 sucessos em 15 tentativas; BBF sem testes: uma tentativa por caso), com número de tentativas diferente.

tecnicas.localizador: p. 2 do PDF (impressa 35), seção 2 («Baseline Bug Fixer») e seção 3; Tabela 1 (coluna «BBF»)
tecnicas.observacao: Prompt zero-shot único com o código defeituoso (contexto) e uma explicação do comportamento esperado do programa (restricoes, como especificação), pedindo a correção (instrucao). Uma tentativa por caso; sem informação de testes unitários. Modelo de prompt só no repositório (não acessado). Comparador sem mecanismos isolados.

Comparador sem mecanismos isolados como técnica; o contraste com o BBF sem testes existe, mas com número de tentativas diferente (uma tentativa por caso contra 15 tentativas no total).

citacoes.trecho: Specifically, we ask a LLM to propose multiple hypotheses about the location of a bug, and based on the aggregated response we prompt for bug fixing suggestions.
A preliminary evaluation shows that our approach is able to fix multiple complex bugs previously unsolved by GPT-4 even with prompt engineering.
In phase 1, we ask LLM for multiple hypotheses E1,...,Em about fault location and explanation and then let LLM vote on its own solutions.
In phase 2, we ask LLM to generate multiple bug fix proposals F1,...,Fm given the highest voted explanation E∗ and the buggy code.

Note that in the evaluation we provide as input in Steps 1a and 2a not only buggy code but also details of the expectation, for example, the unit tests, or specifically the inputs of the routine, expected output and the actual output.
We used m = 5 and n = 5 as the number of explanations and the number of bug fixes, respectively.
A simple zero-shot vote prompt was used to sample k = 5 votes at both Steps 1b and 2b.
Here, the LLM is asked for a code fix via a single prompt containing buggy code and an explanation of the expected program behavior.

citacoes.trecho: We use GPT-4 (July/August 2023) with Azure OpenAI Services API via SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP).
As for arithm_expr_eval.py, BBF could correct the manually inserted bug but introduced another bug leading to a test failure.
Overall, BBF could fix 38 out of 41 cases with a simple zero-shot prompting, and failed for 3 cases.
Adding unit test information to BBF input did not help significantly for these 3 unsuccessful cases (only 2 successes in 15 trials).
Table 1 shows that MBF succeeded in all cases if the unit test information was added (last column).

As duas condições usam os prompts incluídos no HumanEval-XL, nos mesmos 80 problemas, mesmos casos de teste, mesmas 12 linguagens de programação, mesmos modelos e a mesma instrução de saída só com código executável; só a língua muda, daí `ingrediente`. O estudo não descreve o conteúdo dos prompts do benchmark (por exemplo, assinatura ou exemplos), por isso nenhum outro mecanismo foi atribuído.

citacoes.trecho: We examined how English and Spanish prompts influence the functional correctness of LLM-generated code.
RQ1 Does the prompt language (English vs Spanish) affect the functional correctness of code generated by LLMs?
For each problem in HumanEval-XL and each of the 12 programming languages, we used the benchmark’s included prompts, in English and Spanish.
Each prompt was submitted once to each model, so every combination of model (LLM), natural language prompt (problem), and programming language produced a single candidate solution.
In the prompt, in addition to the problem, we explicitly instructed the LLMs to output only executable code, avoiding explanations or chain-of-thought text.
This constraint was intended to prevent extra text from contaminating the output and causing failures during automatic execution.
Because executing arbitrary model-generated code is risky on a local machine, we ran all evaluations inside a sandboxed container.
We isolated executions using gVisor [7].
Finally, dataset contamination remains an important methodological concern.
When this happens, evaluation results can overestimate true generalization and understate remaining gaps, including potential language effects.
Due to the substantial time and financial resources required to evaluate the full HumanEval-XL benchmark, we restricted prompts to English and Spanish.
Totals were $0.52 for deepseek-V3.2, $24.45 for ChatGPT-5, and $64.59 for gemini-2.5-pro.
When the estimate is computed with n > k, pass@k benefits from lower variance and better reflects the effects of sampling diversity (for example, due to temperature) [14].
Future work could explore higher k values to obtain more precise performance estimates under multi-sample prompting strategies.
Accordingly, our results should be interpreted as evidence of correctness under benchmark conditions, not as a complete measure of software quality or production readiness.

For each API we used the provider’s default parameters to maintain comparable conditions across models, since at the time of writing, some model’s characteristics were unable to be modified using the API.
Across models and programming languages, English prompts generally yielded slightly higher correctness scores, although Spanish prompts matched or exceeded English in twelve programming languages.

We hypothesize that this reduced gap may be partly attributed to recent advances in LLM development, including wider use of chain-of-thought prompting, larger and more diverse multilingual training corpora, and improved fine-tuning and alignment procedures.

citacoes.trecho: Specifically, we present three creative strategies: XSP for improving problem comprehension, Syntax-Aware XSP (SA-XSP) for mitigating syntax errors, and Testcase-Driven Logic Error Debugging (TDLED) for resolving logic errors through test case feedback.

Our experiments on 30 LLMs, ranging from 0.5B, 70B, to 671B parameters and including 5 reasoning models, demonstrate that the proposed methods improve accuracy by up to 27.5%, especially in smaller models, with syntax error reductions of up to 60% and logic error corrections by up to 30%.
However, they often produce syntax and logic errors, which reduces their usability in production environments.
Moreover, this method often introduces new errors during the revision process, resulting in minimal overall gains and a cycle of diminishing returns.
We propose two new approaches, the Solution-Oriented Logic Error Debugging (SOLED) and the Testcase-Driven Logic Error Debugging (TDLED), to guide LLMs in correcting logic errors.

XSP mitigates these issues by clearly separating instructions, inputs/outputs, and examples into tagged sections, thereby reducing ambiguity and enhancing code-generation accuracy, particularly for smaller models with limited reasoning capacity.
While prior work has emphasized post hoc debugging, we propose a proactive approach: Syntax-Aware XML-Structured Prompts (SA-XSP), an extension of XSP.
We design three templates, each tailored to one of these common error types, to guide models toward generating syntactically correct code.
To evaluate this, we tested 30 LLMs on 3,000+ Codeforces problems, comparing unstructured prompts with the three SA-XSP variants.
For each problem, the model first generates an incorrect solution, which is then fed back to it with a prompt to revise and fix any errors.
This cycle repeats up to three times.
SOLED tests whether solution hints (English or pseudocode) help models overcome logic errors by asking them to re-generate solutions from scratch.
Fig. 12 illustrates how SOLED guides models using structured prompts that include a high-level algorithmic strategy and supporting pseudocode.
For each failed attempt, the model receives up to five structured test cases showing inputs, its incorrect outputs, and the expected outputs, encouraging it to reconcile discrepancies.
Across all sizes, TDLED plus reasoning consistently delivers the highest NI, offering a viable approach to reduce logic errors.

Our three methods - XML-Structured Prompt (XSP) for structural clarity, Syntax-Aware XSP (SA-XSP) for reducing syntax errors, and Testcase-Driven Logic Error Debugging (TDLED) for resolving logic errors via test-case feedback - are evaluated on 3,000+ Codeforces problems across 30 LLMs (0.5B–72B parameters).

tecnicas.nome_original: careful prompt engineering / (a suitable chain of) prompts for G-code manipulation
tecnicas.localizador: p. 1, Resumo e seção I (contribuição i); p. 2, seção II (Prompt Engineering) e Fig. 1; p. 3, seção III
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote de diálogo usado em todas as avaliações: prompt inicial com definições de comandos G-code (Fig. 1; `instrucao`, `exemplos`, `contexto`), envio do G-code inteiro ou em chunks (`contexto`; chunking como `outro`, ver técnica própria), prompts de tarefa (`instrucao`) e feedback do usuário a soluções incompletas ou dica adicional na depuração (`feedback`). O texto diz que os diálogos têm «atleast one of the following traits», de modo que a composição do pacote em cada diálogo, tarefa e modelo não é informada; os mecanismos listados são os do pacote descrito, não necessariamente os de cada diálogo. Não há condição sem o pacote nem prompt alternativo executado: as tabelas comparam modelos (seleção de modelo, fora do escopo), e o próprio estudo reconhece o uso ocasional de prompts diferentes entre modelos. Por isso `avaliada_isoladamente` = nao e `tipo_contrafactual` = nenhum. A afirmação de que os prompts são «effective» não é testada contra outra condição de prompting.

tecnicas.nome_original: Initial prompt to each LLM (Fig. 1): «Use these definitions for in-context learning» — chamado pelo estudo de «chain-of-thought» reasoning
tecnicas.localizador: p. 2, seção II (Prompt Engineering) e Fig. 1; p. 3, seção III, traço (i)
tecnicas.observacao: O prompt traz uma instrução («Use these definitions for in-context learning») e 13 comandos G-code de exemplo, cada um com sua descrição (por exemplo, «G28 homes all axes»), o que leva a `instrucao`, `exemplos` (exemplos ilustrativos de comandos) e `contexto` (documentação dos comandos). O estudo chama a técnica de «chain-of-thought» reasoning, «a form of in-context learning», mas o prompt impresso não pede raciocínio passo a passo nem explicação antes da resposta; por isso não se registrou `raciocinio`. Não há base identificável nem condição sem esse prompt.

tecnicas.nome_original: chunks of G-code (strategies for feeding large G-code files to context-length-limited LLMs)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 1, seção I (contribuição i); p. 3, seção III, traço (ii) e parágrafo sobre compreensão
tecnicas.observacao: `outro`: particionamento do G-code de entrada em chunks enviados ao longo do diálogo (500 linhas para GPT-3.5 e GPT-4), pedindo, na compreensão, que o modelo combine os chunks; não é decomposição da tarefa em subtarefas. Os demais mecanismos são herdados do pacote (prompt da Fig. 1, quando usado, e prompt de tarefa). Embora a contribuição (i) mencione «effective strategies» para alimentar arquivos grandes, o chunking é aplicado só aos modelos de contexto menor (GPT-3.5 e GPT-4), enquanto Claude-2, Llama-2-70b e Starcoder recebem o arquivo inteiro: a diferença coincide com a troca de modelo, e não há condição comparável com e sem chunking. Classificado como `componente` do pacote focal.

tecnicas.nome_original: user feedback to solutions that are incomplete or omit key parts of the g-code
tecnicas.localizador: p. 3, seção III, traço (iv)
tecnicas.observacao: Feedback humano no diálogo quando a solução é incompleta ou omite partes do G-code. Herda os mecanismos do pacote (Fig. 1, quando usada). O estudo não informa em quais diálogos, tarefas ou modelos o feedback foi dado nem quantas rodadas houve, e não relata resultado antes e depois do feedback.

tecnicas.nome_original: additional prompt saying that we are looking for an invalid command (additional hint)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 3, seção IV.A
tecnicas.observacao: Na depuração, o modelo recebe primeiro só o arquivo G-code com o pedido de procurar um erro; se entende a tarefa mas não acha a causa, recebe a dica de que se procura um comando inválido. É uma rodada adicional condicionada à falha, sem condição paralela sem a dica: só contribuição cumulativa (Claude-2 acerta após a dica). Se o prompt da Fig. 1 foi usado no diálogo de depuração não é informado (a Fig. 2 não o indica), por isso `exemplos` não foi listado. Não se informa se GPT-3.5 recebeu a dica.

tecnicas.nome_original: G-code for a single layer (G-code for the first layer on a conditional basis)
tecnicas.localizador: p. 3, seção III, traço (iii); p. 4, seção IV.B
tecnicas.observacao: Fornecimento apenas do G-code de uma camada em vez do arquivo inteiro, para avaliar o gargalo do tamanho de contexto. O texto relata, só em prosa e sem valores nem detalhe por modelo, que isso «led to more engaging and positive results» do que pedir a avaliação no G-code inteiro. As condições não são comparáveis: a camada única muda o próprio objeto da tarefa (transformar ou compreender uma camada em vez do objeto inteiro), e não se informa quais células das Tabelas I e II correspondem a cada condição. Por isso `avaliada_isoladamente` = nao e `tipo_contrafactual` = nenhum. Mecanismos acrescentados vazios porque o ingrediente muda o conteúdo do `contexto`, sem acrescentar categoria.

riscos.descricao: A maioria dos LLMs testados não consegue processar um arquivo G-code inteiro de uma vez, o que, segundo as observações empíricas dos autores, prejudica o raciocínio sobre a geometria; os modelos de código aberto têm desempenho fraco, e Starcoder e Llama-2-70b não reconhecem o arquivo como G-code na depuração. A atribuição ao limite de contexto é apresentada pelos autores como plausível, não demonstrada.
riscos.localizador: p. 3, seção IV.A; p. 4, seções IV.C e V

riscos.descricao: Segurança operacional, não cibersegurança: erros em G-code podem causar dano ao equipamento ou a pessoas. O estudo apresenta o risco como motivação para erros de G-code em geral; não o mede nem o atribui a saídas dos LLMs.

Diferenças de arquitetura, atenção, dados de treinamento e tamanho de contexto fazem os modelos responderem de modo diferente a prompts idênticos, exigindo ocasionalmente prompts diferentes para a mesma tarefa, o que limita a comparabilidade entre modelos.

Limite de janela de contexto: os modelos lidam melhor com camadas isoladas (2D) do que com o G-code inteiro (3D); o estudo aponta a deficiência na compreensão de geometrias complexas a partir do G-code.
riscos.localizador: p. 4, seções IV.B, IV.C e V

mitigacoes.descricao: Envio do G-code em chunks de 500 linhas para GPT-3.5 e GPT-4, por causa do tamanho de contexto; sem comparação com condição sem chunking no mesmo modelo.

Teste em G-code de uma única camada para avaliar o gargalo do contexto; o resultado é descrito só qualitativamente («more engaging and positive results») e a condição muda o objeto da tarefa, sem medida comparável contra o arquivo inteiro.
Uso, tanto quanto possível, dos mesmos prompts para todos os LLMs e uniformidade entre tarefas e modelos; procedimento de controle sem comparação.
maximum new tokens = 1024 no Starchat para permitir gerar G-code sem limite de tokens (parâmetro de decodificação, fora do escopo de prompting).

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we present the first extensive evaluation of numerous large language models (LLMs) for debugging G-code files for 3-axis 3D printing.

We design effective prompts to enable pre-trained LLMs to understand and manipulate G-code and test their performance on various aspects of G-code debugging and manipulation, including detection and correction of common errors and the ability to perform geometric transformations.

We present the first comprehensive evaluation of the state-of-the-art pre-trained LLMs for debugging and modifying G-code files for extrusion-based additive manufacturing (AM) without requiring fine-tuning or domain adaptation; our main technical challenge is demonstrating their generalization abilities by framing (a suitable chain of) prompts for G-code manipulation.
(i) We show how careful prompt engineering can enable pre-trained large language models (LLMs) to understand G-codes for AM.
We develop effective strategies for feeding large G-code files to context-length-limited LLMs.
In our evaluations below, we leverage the technique of “chain-of-thought” [27] reasoning, a form of in-context learning used to precondition an LLM for G-code-related tasks.
Use these definitions for in-context learning. For context, I have provided example commands for a 3D printer.
All our dialogues are performed with atleast one of the following traits: (i) We begin each conversation with the same prompt (Fig. 1).
(ii) We provide chunks of G-code, owing to the varying token lengths.
Empirically, we have found that a chunk length of 500 lines works for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
For Claude-2, Llama-2-70b, and Starcoder, we were able to provide the entire G-code as input.
(iii) Depending on the evaluation metric, we provide G-code for the first layer on a conditional basis.
(iv) We provide user feedback to solutions that are incomplete or omit key parts of the g-code.
Furthermore, we make a concerted effort to use the same prompts for evaluation across all LLMs.

However, owing to inherently different model architectures, attention mechanisms, different training datasets, and varying token lengths of the LLMs, such variance inherently affects the LLM’s response to identical prompts, necessitating the occasional use of different prompts to achieve the same task across different models.
We adhere to default settings for all LLMs except for Starcoder’s Starchat, where we set the maximum new tokens to 1024 to allow us to generate G-code sequences without token length limits.
We utilize three canonical shapes for experimentation: a cube, a cylinder, and an S-shape.
Translation transformation moves the object by a fixed distance (10mm in X and 20mm in Y) without changing its orientation or size.
For Scaling, we applied a uniform scaling factor of 2 and ask the LLM to scale the coordinates accordingly.
Shearing transformations were aimed at skewing the object by a factor of 0.5, and Rotation involved turning the objects 45 degrees (counter-clockwise) with respect to the Z axis.

We test various LLM chatbots on a simple 2D S-Shape (204 lines; suitable for all context lengths) for line-by-line debugging and replace the “G1” command in one line with “G13”, an invalid G-code command.
If the model understands the task but is unable to determine the cause of the error, we then provide an additional prompt saying that we are looking for an invalid command.
Claude-2 also performs well, getting the correct answer after receiving the additional hint.
Neither Starcoder nor Llama-2-70b are able to process the input and recognize that it is a G-Code file.
To assess the effect of this potential bottleneck we also test their performance on G-code for a single layer.
This led to more engaging and positive results than prompts asking for evaluation on the entire G-code.
A pervasive issue across most of the LLMs we tested is their inability to completely parse an entire G-code file in a single-shot manner.
Our empirical observations suggest that this shortcoming adversely affects the models’ capability to reason about the geometric intricacies represented in the G-code.

It would be premature to definitively claim that context length limitations impede an LLM’s spatial reasoning capability of the underlying geometry; it is plausible that this is a contributing factor and makes for an interesting direction for future research.
Debugging and modifying G-code for 3D printing involves complex syntactic, semantic, and geometric challenges, with errors potentially leading to equipment damage or human harm.
We also evaluated Bard [12], but the results are not included here since its incorporation into Gemini.
A full length version of our paper is on ArXiv and our results can be found on GitHub.

citacoes.trecho: To mitigate these challenges, we propose an API-aware stepwise prompting method for LLM-based workflow code generation.
This approach systematically decomposes the generation process into four steps: API selection, dataflow analysis, sequence diagram design, and workflow code generation.
These templates are designed to ensure consistency by incorporating requirements, API information, and intermediate outputs.
They also specify output formats (e.g., Mermaid or Python list) to facilitate structured extraction by the Autogen Manager.
You are a talented engineer. You want to develop an app that meets the requirements entered.
citacoes.localizador: p. 2 do PDF, Fig. 2(a) Prompt for API Selection

citacoes.trecho: All API specifications were included in the prompt context to isolate the effect of prompt decomposition rather than information availability.
1-step (exisiting): Code generation.
4-step (proposed): API selection, dataflow analysis, sequence diagram design, code generation.
The temperature and random seed were set to zero to ensure deterministic behavior.
The omission of the loop structure causes only the first element to be processed.
Despite the API expecting individual elements, the entire list is passed as a single parameter.
However, some outputs still contained issues, particularly in parameter assignment and loop handling, due to misalignment between data structures and control flow.

In addition, applying static analysis or simulation-based verification to the generated code—and feeding the results back to the model—can help it detect its own mistakes and improve the structural consistency of the output.
Future work will explore post-generation validation and feedback mechanisms to improve code reliability.

citacoes.trecho: This paper introduces Standard Conformant Prompting (SCP), a compliance-driven prompting architecture that embeds IEC 61131-3 rules, vendor syntax profiles, declaration discipline, and safety-oriented structural templates directly into the prompt to constrain first-pass synthesis toward TIA Portal-targeted PLC code.

Across validators, SCP achieves higher and more stable correctness ratings than CoVe while reducing safety-related failure modes and post-hoc correction needs; BLEU and expert Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) review are additionally reported as secondary comparisons.
As a result, LLM-generated PLC code often fails to compile or requires manual rework, limiting its practical adoption in industrial settings.
Consequently, even verified outputs may violate IEC 61131–3 rules, naming conventions, or vendor-specific syntax requirements, which are critical in safety-relevant industrial workflows.
A representative verification-centric approach is CoVe, which organizes generation as a post-hoc draft–verify–revise loop.
As illustrated in Fig. 2, SCP uses a fixed prompt skeleton that explicitly declares the target PLC platform, permitted language constructs, naming and datatype rules, and required output sections.
Avoid unsupported constructs (e.g., no POINTERS where disallowed).

Task specifications—including I/O definitions, timing and interlock constraints, safety requirements, and IEC 61131-3 reference implementations—are kept unchanged, and only the prompt template is varied.

To ensure reproducibility, PLC code is generated with a single model (DeepSeek), and all outputs are evaluated by independent validator LLMs using the same fixed evaluation prompt (Fig. 4) to score Correctness, Readability, Safety Compliance, and Modularity.
In contrast, CoVe shows lower and more variable scores, including a Fail due to a safety-relevant logic issue.
The interpretation is: larger α indicates tighter cross-validator agreement (higher robustness) for the semantic score signal produced at the Agreement Check stage of Fig. 5.

Important note for reviewers and reproducibility: Because Table II computes α from only two rated items (ST and IL) for a single benchmark instance (Robot Pick and Place), the estimate is statistically fragile.

Two certified PLC engineers independently scored the same Robot Pick and Place artifacts in both IEC 61131-3 representations (ST and IL) using a fixed rubric (Correctness, Readability, Safety, Modularity).
As summarized in Table II, SCP yields substantially lower observed disagreement than CoVe, indicating more consistent expert interpretation of semantic correctness and safety, particularly for IL.

Future work will strengthen industrial applicability by adding compiler- and simulation-in-the-loop validation, extending modular vendor constraint libraries, and integrating SCP into real engineering workflows (e.g., TIA Portal and TwinCAT) to quantify commissioning effort, maintainability, and certification readiness.

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we introduce COFT (Chain of Functional Triggers), a novel prompting strategy specifically designed for code generation tasks.
In challenging zero-shot scenarios and the Pass@1 metric, COFT can improve the performance of fundation LLMs by up to 35.3%.
As illustrated in Figure 1, in the field of code generation, the CoT generated using traditional methods is ambiguous and redundant, misleading to the wrong answer.

citacoes.trecho: First, a PLC-100 industrial dataset is constructed, which contains 10 types of 100 prompt words.
Second, a PLC code generation method based on GPT-4 with an adaptive evaluation system is proposed using the dataset.
Second, the PLC code generation capabilities of large models such as GPT-4o are evaluated through the Human-Based Evaluation Scores Algorithm.
We summarized and analyzed 100 answers from ChatGPT on Github.
The 100 data were divided into ten categories, with 10 data in each category.
In a follow-up prompt, we requested an MPC solution for this model, which ChatGPT provided as a basic implementation using the fmincon function.
The feedback from three MPC experts on the code was positive, but a more thorough evaluation was necessary.
Before using evaluation indicators to judge the quality of code generation, the code generated by the large model is first scored algorithmically.
Through the adaptive algorithm, different weights are given to different n and k values of BLEU and Pass@k, namely AdaptiveBLEU and AdaptivePass@k.
We propose an adaptive candidate generation strategy that dynamically adjusts the value of k to optimize generation efficiency and resource usage.
The version used by CODESYS is V3.5 SP13.3, which is compatible with the Windows operating system.
For the convenience of display, 10 types of PLC-ST data are displayed, and each type originally contains 10 data.

When the Human-Based Evaluation Scores Algorithm score is in the low segment, due to the limitations of the current general large model in the field of industrial control, the generated code may be significantly different from the traditional reference code.
After reproducing on codesys, the generation effect of the low segment is not feasible, ensuring the authenticity of the code generation.
From the experimental results, the compiled code cannot be directly used for copying and pasting for the time being.
It is still necessary to manually input information for the actual IO usage interface, and the generated code has certain warnings.
The generated code can be successfully run on codesys after manual input of the IO port, proving that the quality of the generated code meets the IEC-61131-3 standard.
The experimental results prove the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

citacoes.trecho: Due to token limitations encountered during fine-tuning, the process was shifted to Mistral-7B, where a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach was implemented using a knowledge base constructed from G-code manuals and reference guides.
Among the three approaches, the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B produced the most promising results, though both Mistral-based methods introduced a significant amount of noise and irrelevant outputs.
Significant improvements were observed with Mistral-7B, particularly after the transition from fine-tuning to instruction tuning and the use of example-rich, structured prompts.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was also explored as a means of enhancing performance by providing relevant code snippets at runtime; however, this approach often produced near matches rather than genuine generalization.
The dataset consisted of 15 curated examples of common 2D and 3D shapes, G-code for gears, and engraving patterns.
Combined the retrieved context with the user prompt.

citacoes.trecho: An evaluation of transformer-based models, namely StarCoder2-3B, Mistral-7B, and an instruction-tuned variant of Mistral-7B, indicated that instruction tuning combined with carefully structured few-shot prompting substantially enhanced the quality, organization, and geometric consistency of the generated G-code.

Additionally, the experiments with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) underscored its role in improving factual grounding, though its impact on generation quality is limited unless tightly integrated with the model’s core reasoning process.

citacoes.trecho: To overcome this, we propose a semantic-guided pruning method, which optimizes input length through coarse- and fine-grained pruning, retaining only the most semantically relevant tokens.
Our method improves LLM performance, increasing pass@1 accuracy by over 4% on the ClassEval benchmark.
Consequently, the model’s capacity to learn from and adapt to new examples is hampered, making it difficult to generate accurate and contextually relevant code.
Similar to our earlier study, we use the attention matrices from the SiT encoder and decoder to determine node importance.
While pruning the least important nodes one by one is intuitive, it is time-consuming as it requires recalculating node importance after each deletion.
To balance effectiveness and efficiency, we implement a two-phase pruning algorithm involving coarse-grained and fine-grained pruning.
The original prompt design for the class-level code generation task consists of three parts: the instruction, examples, and testing.
The instruction is the core of the prompt, containing the name and skeleton of the target code.

The examples section includes as many examples as possible to help LLMs better understand code generation, making it the longest part, and our pruning strategy focuses on this section to shorten the overall prompt length.
For each method, we use greedy sampling to generate code samples and evaluate performance with Pass@k for k = 1,3,5.
Success is measured by two criteria: all success, where both attempts pass all test cases, and partial success, where one attempt passes.
The first experiment compares performance between few-shot learning without pruning and our pruning strategy.
The second experiment, an ablation study, compares our semantic-guided pruning with random pruning to highlight the benefits of structured pruning over unstructured approaches.
For our experimental setup, we incorporated all 100 class-level code generation tasks from the ClassEval benchmark.
Notably, the desired code snippet for each task was randomly selected and did not appear in the example prompts provided.
To ensure the consistency and reliability of our results, we maintained uniform external conditions across all testing scenarios, including LLM hyperparameters and other relevant factors.
In the code generation phase, we utilized the GPT-3.5 model, specifically the GPT-3.5-turbo-0613 variant.
This model was configured with a temperature setting of 0, optimizing it for precision and stability in generating code snippets.
For example, in the Pass@1 all-success category, semantic-guided pruning achieves 9.5%, significantly higher than the 5.8% achieved by random pruning.

These results highlight a critical point: simply reducing token count randomly, as in random pruning, doesn’t effectively retain the essential structure or context needed for generating accurate class-level code.
We validated our method using the ClassEval benchmark, where it outperformed the unpruned and random pruning baselines, improving pass@1 accuracy by larger than 4%.

citacoes.trecho: We conducted an empirical study of real-world, single-turn interactions between developers and ChatGPT collected from GITHUB.

Regression analysis shows that readability metrics are strong predictors of usefulness and correctness, whereas structural features such as the number of sentences and task type significantly affect conceptual consistency.
We operationalized this dimension with a boolean value that indicates whether the prompt contains code examples or snippets.

citacoes.trecho: The metric was thus defined over the three remaining patterns, Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought, and coded as a binary variable, where 1 indicates that the prompt follows one of these patterns and 0 otherwise.

citacoes.trecho: In this stage, we decided to remove the Prompt Pattern metric, since the manual classification revealed that 90% of the prompts (164 out of 183) were Zero-shot.
After this adjustment, the dataset stabilized at a final set of 183 conversations (39 from commits, 138 from pull requests, and 6 from issues), extracted from 94 distinct GitHub repositories.

A possible explanation is that corrective tasks, such as bug fixing, are inherently more complex than perfective tasks, such as extending or generating code, which makes them harder for LLMs to handle.

Regarding task type, additive and corrective tasks showed positive coefficients compared to the perfective baseline, with corrective tasks approaching significance (p = 0.084), while preventive tasks were positively associated but non-significant.

citacoes.trecho: Both readability metrics—Flesch Reading Ease and Gunning Fog Index—were significantly and positively associated with correctness, indicating that prompts that are clearer and structurally more complex tended to yield more correct code.
Initial tests revealed violations of the proportional odds assumption for the number of difficult words and sentences.
Through the elicitation procedure, we selected seven independent variables covering both readability-related and structural properties of prompts.
Together, these eight variables capture complementary dimensions of prompt formulation.
After completing this step, we measured the three readability variables on the natural language text of each prompt.
With seven predictors and five ordered response categories (0–4), this implies a conservative requirement of N ≥ 70 conversations.
In cases where the two reviewers disagreed, an external reviewer was involved to provide clarification and resolve the conflict.
For example, each dataset entry was labeled by at least two authors independently, and disagreements were resolved by a third author.
Although the original formulation of ICE-Score employed GPT-4, in our study we opted for GPT-4.1-mini.

In line with the guidelines for SE studies using LLMs by Baltes et al. [97], we report that the LLM temperature was set to 0, and for prompting we used the original prompt setup reported by Zhuo et al. [34].
Another potential threat comes from the non-determinism of LLMs, as repeated executions of the same prompt may yield different outputs.
To mitigate this, we relied on a fixed dataset of already-executed conversations, ensuring that the analysis was performed on stable outcomes rather than re-generated outputs.
Our study identifies statistical associations between prompt characteristics and output quality, but it does not establish causality.

To mitigate the risk of overstating our findings, we carefully framed results in correlational terms, verified robustness across multiple model specifications, and excluded variables that violated model assumptions.
Moreover, the moderate explanatory power of our models (0.107 < pseudo-R2 <0.159) indicates that prompt-oriented metrics account for only part of the variability in output quality.
Finally, an initial exploratory analysis revealed that a single contributor accounted for more than 80% of the conversations.
Specifically, we computed the mean number of conversations per contributor and constrained over-represented contributors to this threshold (10 conversations).

Another potential limitation came from the evaluation of usefulness and correctness through ICE-Score with GPT-4.1-mini as the judging model, which may have introduced model-specific biases; we mitigated this by selecting a strong and widely adopted evaluator and by ensuring methodological transparency to enable replication with alternative judges.
We addressed this by inspecting the scripts used for data collection and processing and by manually validating a sample of the dataset.

Finally, we did not preprocess code (e.g., comment removal, normalization) before computing conceptual consistency between LLM-generated and developer-adapted code snippets, which may influence similarity scores.

In all such cases, an iterative strategy that progressively refines and validates outputs may be preferable to relying on a single response, whereas perfective tasks may already yield satisfactory results with simpler interactions.
The two prompts differ only in surface form, yet only the readable one yielded code that a developer could adopt without further intervention.

citacoes.trecho: This study evaluates the ability of modern LLMs to generate secure code using six established prompting strategies across 150 Python tasks (LLMSecEval).
Findings showed that Recursive Criticism and Improvement (RCI) prompting significantly improves security outcomes across all models.
Notably, LLaMA produced over 15,800 lines of vulnerability-free code under RCI.

These strategies are based on prior prompting taxonomies and experiments reported [6]: Baseline Prompting (Zero-Shot), Naive Secure Prompting (Zero-Shot), Comprehensive Prompting (Zero-Shot), Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (Zero-Shot CoT), RCI, Persona/Memetic Proxy Prompting.
These prompt types represent a spectrum from minimal guidance to rich, security-contextualized instructions.
Studies show LLMs often generate insecure code, with about %62 of programs containing vulnerabilities.
While widely adopted across domains, they often produce hallucinated or insecure code, especially when trained on unverified sources.

Overall, the findings suggest that security assessments vary depending on the static analysis tool used, underscoring the importance of employing multiple complementary tools for a comprehensive evaluation of LLM-generated code security.
The prompting techniques evaluated are highly text-dependent and assume structured input-output alignment, which may not reflect real-world developer behavior.
This study focuses solely on Python tasks, so results may not generalize to other programming languages with different syntax, libraries, or vulnerability patterns.
This review, performed by the authors, involves removing all comments and irrelevant information such as usage instructions and examples, descriptions of the code syntax, and guidelines.
The removal process could not be fully automated due to the complexity and variability of comment patterns in the generated code.
Besides, all models are configured to use same parameters: temperature, max completion tokens, and top p.
GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were also included as baselines, based on prior benchmarks in secure code generation [6].
Due to space limitations, the results related to GPT-family are not provided here, but can be found in [6].

DeepSeek, in contrast, had fewer Bandit-detected issues, but its CodeQL results were inconsistent, especially under the RCI prompt which unexpectedly yielded the highest CWE count (127) indicating sensitivity to CodeQL’s deeper static checks.
Comprehensive and RCI prompts reduce issues, while RCI and Persona improve security performance.

Gemini, while showing moderate vulnerability counts in Bandit, revealed significantly higher CWE detections in CodeQL, particularly with the Comprehensive and RCI prompts, suggesting broader weakness coverage by CodeQL.

Evaluating both proprietary (GPT family, Gemini) and open-source (LLaMA, DeepSeek) models with static analysis tools (Bandit and CodeQL), we found that strategies like Persona and RCI significantly reduce vulnerabilities across architectures.

Não é técnica para melhorar o código, e sim perturbação do prompt para avaliar robustez; classificada como 'outro' (paráfrase/perturbação lexical do enunciado). O prompt herda do prompt original do HumanEval a descrição do problema em linguagem natural ('instrucao'); o estudo não descreve o modelo de prompt enviado ao LLM (se inclui assinatura, docstring completa ou exemplos), por isso 'contexto' e 'exemplos' não foram atribuídos (nao_informado). O contrafactual é o pacote (prompts mutados por SPRoC contra o 'Original'/'Origin', HumanEval inalterado) no mesmo modelo e configuração. Pacote híbrido na construção: a mutação é gerada por modelo auxiliar (BERT) e tokenizador/etiquetador do NLTK, componentes fora do escopo; o efeito medido é o da perturbação do prompt, não de um mecanismo isolado.

citacoes.trecho: To address this, we propose SPRoC (Semantics-Preserving Robustness of Code generation), a method for evaluating LLM robustness through prompt mutation.
During the experimental process, SPRoC performs the replacement operation on the first identified replaceable word, limiting each sentence to the replacement of only one word.
Radamsa generates diverse new inputs by performing structural mutations on the original input samples.
Furthermore, the experiment retains the Original as a control baseline, where the unaltered HumanEval dataset is used to evaluate the LLM.
When faced with such semantically equivalent but syntactically diverse inputs, existing LLMs often produce code outputs with substantial structural or even functional differences.
This mismatch reduces the consistency and reliability of the evaluation.
In contrast, Radamsa’s random mutation strategy leads to more pronounced semantic drift and lower-quality mutated prompts.

Specifically, when the similarity between a candidate sentence and the original sentence is below a predefined threshold θ, the candidate sentence is directly discarded and not included in the Top-n ranking.
Additionally, to prevent the program from entering an infinite loop or executing for too long, a uniform timeout threshold of 3 seconds is set.
In addition, SPRoC achieves better performance in terms of similarity metrics like BLEU and BERTScore, improving by 12.96% and 1.83%, respectively.
Experimental results show that, compared to Radamsa, SPRoC improves the BERTScore by 1.8% and the BLEU score by 12.69%.
Additionally, SPRoC can detect robustness issues in code generation more effectively, leading to reductions in Pass@1, Pass@5, and Pass@10 by 0.3%, 2.7%, and 2.68%, respectively.
To evaluate the effectiveness of SPRoC, the following three research questions are set up in this paper.

In contrast, the Pass@5 and Pass@10 values of Radamsa are even slightly greater than those of the Original prompts, suggesting that although its random structural mutations introduce variation, they may fail to capture key semantic structures that influence code generation.
For each original prompt, ten mutated prompts are constructed using SPRoC, and the Pass@k values before and after mutation are recorded.
For each input sample, 10 candidate functions are generated, and the remaining parameters in the model are kept at their default values to ensure fairness and reproducibility of the experiment.

citacoes.trecho: Experimental results reveal that code description and BuggyLine are universal high-value information for all models, while PDG and TestOutput only benefit high-capability models, and TestFile acts as low-value noise with inhibitory effects in most cases.

High-capability commercial models exhibit significant synergistic effects with full-information combinations, achieving a maximum Repair Success Rate (RSR) of 97.5%, while low-capability models suffer from context overload due to redundant information.
BuggyCode: Directly extract the buggy code from the QuixBugs dataset with comment sections removed, as illustrated in Fig. 2.
Description: For each Python buggy code snippet in the QuixBugs dataset, a functional description of the code is provided immediately after the code block, as shown in Fig. 2.
BuggyLine: QuixBugs provides both buggy and correct versions of the code; the BuggyLine is identified by comparing these two versions.
PDG (Program Dependence Graph): Encompasses data dependencies and control dependencies associated with the buggy line within the target function.
TestFile: The test file corresponding to the buggy code in the QuixBugs dataset.

TestOutput: Execution results of buggy code from test file runs, autocapturing error-containing test logs with key info like test case pass/fail status, input parameters, expected/actual outputs and error code lines (e.g. for bucketsort in Quixbugs: “6 failed, 1 passed”, “input_data = [[8,5,3,1,9,6, …],10], expected = [0,1,2,3,4,5, …]”, “test_bucketsort.py:26: AssertionError”).
Evaluate the independent impact of each auxiliary information type on repair performance, identifying high-value and low-value information.
1 Test-related combination: BuggyCode + TestFile + TestOutput, integrate test-related information to explore the synergistic effect of test feedback (TestOutput) and test logic (TestFile) on repair.

1 Full-information combination: BuggyCode + Description + BuggyLine + PDG + TestFile + TestOutput, include all 6 information types to explore the upper limit of information integration and potential inhibitory effects between information.
To ensure that all LLMs follow the same repair constraints and output format, we design a unified Prompt template, which is divided into system prompts and task prompts:

You are a senior Python development expert, proficient in code debugging and bug fixing, especially in resolving Python semantic errors and runtime errors caused by logical flaws (e.g., incorrect loop conditions, wrong variable assignments).
1. Only return the fixed pure Python core code, without any additional content;
Single information enhancement scenario: Insert the corresponding auxiliary information into the prompt.

Combined information scenario: Arrange the information in the order of “ BuggyCode → TestFile → TestOutput” or “BuggyCode → Description → BuggyLine → PDG → TestFile → TestOutput” to ensure the logical coherence of the prompt and avoid information confusion.
Call each LLM with the Prompt, obtain the generated patch.
Execute the test case on the patch to verify whether it passes all tests; if passed, mark it as a successful repair.
Evaluation Metrics: Core metric: Repair Success Rate (RSR) = (Number of successfully repaired test cases / Total number of test cases) × 100%.

All base-lines are evaluated on the same QuixBugs Python subset (40 bugs) to ensure fair comparison, with the core metric being the Repair Success Rate (RSR) of our models versus the baselines under this consistent dataset.
Ambiguous native descriptions in QuixBugs may mislead high-capability models (e.g., DeepseekV3.2) to modify non-core code, causing temporary RSR drops.
Core reason: Test files contain a large proportion of redundant content, with valid test logic making up only a small fraction, which distracts models from defect localization.
Inhibitory mechanism: Low-capability models lack information weight assignment capabilities, leading to context overload and attention dispersion from redundant information.
Notably, CodeLlama:7B and CodeLlama:13B achieve nearly identical RSR (10% vs 12.5% in baseline), with no significant gain from parameter scaling.
Description and BuggyLine are universally high-value (improving RSR by 7.5–10pp for all models); PDG and TestOutput only benefit high-capability models.
TestFile is low-value noise (reducing RSR by 2.5–5pp).
Avoided information: Independent TestFile (low-value noise, only used in combination with TestOutput for commercial models after redundancy cleaning).
Dataset Limitations: The study only uses the QuixBugs Python subset (40 cases), which is small—results may not generalize to large-scale projects, syntax errors.

Model Coverage Limitations: Only 6 models are tested, lacking coverage of emerging code-specific LLMs (e.g., CodeLlama 70B, StarCoder) and multilingual models—future studies should include more diverse models to verify the generalizability of the “triple dividend” framework.

citacoes.trecho: In our study, we directly use a zero-shot fashion single conversation to perform FL.
To be more specific, we employ three types of information, namely source method code (i.e., src), bug-trigger assertion code (i.e., assert), and stack trace (i.e., stack).
FL Prompt 1: src + "There is a bug in the above code, please help me locate it."
FL Prompt 2: src + stack + "There is a bug in the above code, please help me locate it by considering the stack trace."
FL Prompt 3: src + stack + assert + "There is a bug in the above code, please help me locate it by considering the stack trace information and failure assertion code."
In the APR experiment, we also use a zero-shot fashion single conversation.
Additionally, to meet the generative task, we kept the code before the bug and the bug itself for LLM to fix.
In our pilot study, we found that LLMs rarely correctly fix the bugs without perfect localization, so we give either the line number of the bug or directly use the buggy statement.
APR Prompt 1: src + "There is a bug in line X of the code, please help me fix it."
APR Prompt 2: src + "There is a bug in S, please help me fix it."
APR Prompt 3: src + "There is a bug in the last statement, please help me fix it."
Note that if the length of the prompt exceeds the token limit of the LLM (e.g., ChatGPT 3.5 has a 4096 token limit), we truncate it.
Note that despite ChatGPT, few LLMs provide an API interface, which makes us engage in conversation with these models through their web pages.
All three LLMs only successfully fix less than 10% of the 120 bugs, and ChatGPT 3.5 achieves the best.
Then to reduce the threat of data leak, we will study their code capabilities on the datasets that are collected after the LLMs' training phase.

Contrary to our expectation that providing more information would enhance the performance of LLMs, surprisingly, the prompts that only code the source code of the buggy method achieve the best FL performance.

tecnicas.localizador: Resumo, p. 1 do PDF (impressa 2714); Seção III-F e Fig. 4, p. 5 (impressa 2718); Seção IV-F, p. 9-10 (impressas 2722-2723)
tecnicas.observacao: O prompt tem três partes: Description (tarefa: gerar dez programas Java que testem o tipo de refatoração → instrucao), Conditions (pré-condições comuns às engines e parâmetros da refatoração → restricoes) e Features (características finas recuperadas aleatoriamente, 1 ≤ n ≤ Max, de uma biblioteca construída manualmente a partir de relatórios de bugs e casos de teste → restricoes como especificação e contexto como conhecimento externo recuperado). Não há prompt base identificável executado no estudo, por isso mecanismos_acrescentados fica vazio. O único comparador executado (Gligoric's, Gligoric et al. [25]) é uma abordagem sem LLM que aplica refatorações aleatórias a aplicações de código aberto e não usa teste diferencial; não é a mesma condição sem o prompt nem sem as features, de modo que não isola a técnica de prompting. A abordagem é um pacote híbrido (biblioteca de features manual, teste diferencial entre engines, comparação por AST, confirmação manual). Não há condição sem Conditions ou sem Features com resultado relatado; a menção a «more than 80% in our initial study» de programas inúteis sem pré-condições não traz método nem valor da condição com pré-condições (p. 5).

tecnicas.localizador: Seção III-I e Fig. 5, p. 6 do PDF (impressa 2719); Seção IV-H e Fig. 6, p. 10-11 (impressas 2723-2724)
tecnicas.observacao: Classificada como focal porque o estudo a propõe (Seção III-I: «this section proposes a ChatGPT-based approach to automate the extraction») e a investiga na RQ4; é uma variante que substitui a extração manual de features (passo 2 do sistema). O prompt de extração (Fig. 5) tem persona e tarefa (instrucao), o programa de teste que dispara o bug e a mensagem de erro (contexto) e três exemplos construídos manualmente a partir dos três bugs mais antigos do tipo de refatoração (exemplos). As features extraídas alimentam o mesmo prompt de geração (instrucao, restricoes, contexto). O contrafactual é a mesma avaliação da Seção IV-E com as features extraídas manualmente; muda a origem das features. O estudo não informa se o orçamento, o número de programas gerados ou o número de execuções da nova rodada foram iguais aos da rodada com features manuais.

citacoes.trecho: To this end, in this paper, we propose a ChatGPT-based approach to testing refactoring engines.

The approach automatically generates prompts according to both predefined prompt templates and features randomly selected from the feature library, requesting ChatGPT to generate test programs with the requested features.
The prompt is composed of three parts: description, conditions, and features.
Please generate ten java test programs that test the move method refactoring and meet the following constraints
To this end, this section proposes a ChatGPT-based approach to automate the extraction.
To facilitate in-context learning, the prompt template also presents three examples of the same refactoring type.
As a result, most (more than 80% in our initial study) of the generated programs are useless for the testing of refactoring engines, wasting expensive testing resources.
To reduce the chance of generating such useless programs, we analyze the pre-conditions explicitly specified by the refactoring engines.
To this end, we compare the programs as AST and compare their AST-based similarity.
Only 216 out of the 3,053 suspicious cases were denied, resulting in a high precision of 92.9%.
First, it is not yet fully automated.
Notably, it is expensive to test refactoring engines because it involves expensive human intervention, and thus it is difficult to involve a large number of refactoring engines in the case study.
Because some of the involved refactoring engines, like Eclipse, only support Java, our initial implementation is confined to Java as well.
The experiment uses the default settings (including the temperature) of ChatGPT.
To make the comparison fair, we allocated the same time slots for Gligoric's and our approach, i.e., five days with three human participants.
It may lead to the well-known testing effect, i.e., the participants could become more effective after the first testing.
#Confirmed bugs is the total number of bugs we reported to the tool vendors.
Notably, 6 bugs were not reported to the tool vendors.
In total, the approach identified 28 inconsistencies among the three engines.
We also successfully identified 28 inconsistencies among the four refactoring engines that may cause confusion among programmers.

citacoes.trecho: Notably, Gligoric's does not employ differential testing, and thus it does not report any inconsistent cases.
The bug collection and feature extraction took the authors one man-months in total.
In our case study (with manual feature extraction), it took us 41 man-days to accomplish these tasks for 7 kinds of refactorings.
In total, invoking ChatGPT during the evaluation incurred a cost of $260.

O contrafactual é de pacote: contra Basic (Tabela I, mesmos 19 modelos e benchmarks); os contrastes contra ACT e contra Debugger retiram um estágio inteiro, cada um com vários ingredientes e orçamento de iterações diferente, e não isolam um único mecanismo. citacoes.trecho: To enhance the LLM’s code generation abilities, we investigate, in this paper, the combination of two complementary inference-time strategies: multi-agent collaboration and runtime execution-based debugging.
In particlular, on HumanEval benchmark, across 19 LLMs, our approach achieves 64.82% accuracy compared to 56.48% achieved by the basic one-shot prompting approach.
It also outperforms the individual multi-agent collaboration approach by more than 7.66%.
Within this stage, the Analyst Agent decomposes programming tasks into smaller, manageable components and formulates a comprehensive implementation strategy.

Following this strategic outline, the Coder Agent generates the solution, progressively improving the code through an iterative process informed by the Tester Agent’s evaluation, which includes code inspection, syntactic verification, and requirements validation.
To balance computational cost and effectiveness, this refinement cycle is limited to a maximum of three iterations (retriesCT=3).
A debugger agent receives this execution trace to analyze the errors and produce diagnostic explanations, which subsequently inform a coder agent that generates revised code.
We limit this iterative debugging process to 4 cycles (retriesD = 4), a reduction from LDB’s standard 10 iterations, to balance effectiveness with computational efficiency.

We begin by segmenting the HumanEval and HumanEval+ benchmark datasets into three components: task descriptions (function identifier and natural language requirement), visible test cases (for framework execution), and hidden test cases (for final evaluation).
All models were prompted with identical role-specific instructions to ensure experimental consistency.
For decoding, we set the temperature to 0, following common practice in code generation benchmarks, as this yields deterministic output and allows for fair comparison across models.

Baseline Approaches: To evaluate our ACT + Debugger combination, we compare against five approaches: (1) Basic: Direct LLM prompting without refinement, (2) AC: Analyst-Coder collaboration with single interaction, (3) ACT: Analyst-Coder-Tester three-agent collaboration with up to 3 iterations, (4) Debugger Only: Runtime debugging without prior ACT collaboration, and (5) AC + Debugger: Analyst-Coder two-agent collaboration followed by debugging.
AC and ACT showed substantial robustness drops (129.27 and 118.51), showing that agentic interaction introduces fragility.
ACT + Debugger, despite highest accuracy, showed largest robustness drop (137.74), suggesting compounded complexity reduces code resilience.

When implementing the complete ACT + Debug chain, the results demonstrate diminishing returns, as it demands the most extensive execution time (68.42 minutes) while achieving marginally reduced accuracy (61.195%).
When debugging significantly outperforms agentic approaches, combining them introduces unnecessary complexity.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote com três fases: Contextual Refactoring Extraction (RAG contextual que recupera exemplos de refatoração semelhantes como few-shot → contexto e exemplos; o código-fonte e informações de contexto são obtidos por ferramentas → contexto), Multi-Agent Workflow (agente desenvolvedor e agente revisor com papéis definidos → multiagente e instrucao; o revisor verifica refatoração, refatoração pura e estilo com RefactoringMiner, PurityChecker e StyleChecker e gera relatório de feedback → feedback) e Self-Refinement (substituição do código, compilação, teste e reparo com o log de compilação, até três tentativas → feedback; etapas encadeadas → decomposicao). Os agentes dispõem de conjuntos distintos de ferramentas (Fig. 1), mas o estudo não descreve restrições de ferramentas por etapa no prompt, por isso 'restricoes' não foi atribuído. Contrafactual de pacote: MUARF × RawGPT (Tabela I). Pacote híbrido: inclui ferramentas de análise (RefactoringMiner, PurityChecker), banco vetorial (chromdb) e BM25, além do prompting. O prompt de RawGPT não é descrito, por isso a lista de mecanismos acrescentados ficou vazia (base sem conteúdo identificável); o ganho não pode ser atribuído a um mecanismo do pacote.

citacoes.trecho: In this paper, we propose MUARF, an LLM-based solution designed to automate method-level code refactoring, aiming to generate correct, high-quality, and human-like refactored code.

MUARF leverages Contextual Retrieval-Augmented Generation to search for similar refactoring samples for few-shot learning, uses Multi-Agent Workflow to simulate the human refactoring process, and integrates advanced software engineering tools (e.g., RefactoringMiner, PurityChecker, StyleChecker) to assist refactoring.
Evaluation results show that MUARF achieves a compilation pass rate of 86.5% and a test success rate of 83.8% for the refactored code it generates.
The ablation results show that RefactoringMiner and Agentware made the greatest contribution to MUARF.
LLMs cannot obtain this feedback information from the initial prompt and are likely to generate code that changes the behavior of the program.
The implementation of a refactoring may cause design problems elsewhere.
We used Gson as the benchmark and the Oracle Refactoring Dataset as the source for few-shot examples.
Furthermore, we analyzed MUARF’s performance by comparing it with RawGPT, human-written code, and other LLM-based refactoring tools such as EM-Assistant and Move-Method Assistant.
Additionally, we examined their effectiveness across various refactoring types to better understand their impact.
To acquire suitable few-shot examples for LLMs, we constructed a pre-built database of refactored examples sourced from open-source projects.
Once a bad smell code is provided, a search algorithm retrieves relevant refactored code examples to serve as few-shot.

The developer agent is responsible for generating and optimizing the code, while the reviewer agent reviews the code and provides feedback or suggestions to the developer agent for further improvement.

This approach avoids the need for pre-set thresholds or fixed iteration counts, which are often required in traditional workflows, making MUARF more flexible and effective in handling diverse refactoring scenarios.
If the compilation fails, MUARF attempts automatic repair by providing the code and compilation log to ChatGPT, asking it to generate the corrected code.
If the compilation still fails, the process is retried up to three times before returning the final result.
The refactored code generated by MUARF was successfully compiled and tested in 32 out of the 37 refactorings.
In this ablation study, we analyzed the impact of removing specific components from MUARF.
The results reveal that feedback from RefactoringMiner and the Multi- Agent communications are the most critical contributors.
