citacoes.trecho: To address this limitation, we propose PseudoFix, a retrieval-based in-context learning framework using LLMs for refactoring structure distortions in pseudocode.

PseudoFix employs semantic retrieval to select the most relevant few-shot examples that provide structure distortion knowledge, and combines this with the well-structured coding patterns learned by LLMs from vast source code repositories, to efficiently refactor distorted pseudocode.
Following the standard in-context learning prompt paradigm, we distinguish between zero-shot learning (no examples) [45]–[47] and few-shot learning (multiple examples).
We select few-shot examples by retrieving the Top-K most relevant samples from the structure distortion dataset that match the given pseudocode pquery using information retrieval techniques [48].
We first employ a role-playing prompt method [52] in the task instruction TI to position the model as a “reverse engineering expert”.
The output format is constrained to {Yes,No}, and we prohibit model explanations to minimize unnecessary consumption.
Upon detecting a specific distortion, PseudoFix performs the corresponding refactoring.
This identify-then-refactor paradigm is intentionally designed to enhance the interpretability of our approach.
To eliminate the symbolic information in the source code s while preserving only structural features, we propose a novel source code stripping technique.
As shown in Table V, on average, retaining original identifiers yielded only 76.3% of the performance of the stripped method.

To handle the randomness of LLM outputs, we also design a twin-closure algorithm that performs semantic equivalence verification based on observed external program behaviors, ensuring each refactor is semantically consistent.
These two models are accessed via a unified API interface, with the temperature parameter set to 1.0.

To account for uncertainty of LLM output, we repeated each experiment three times, yielding a p-value of 0.8602 (> 0.05), which indicates no significant difference and confirms the stability of our results.
We manually annotate 200 samples for each type of distortion (totaling 1,200 samples) as ground truth.
To minimize the risk of data leakage, we further strip the symbol tables, rendering the data completely devoid of symbolic features and thus difficult to identify.
By concentrating on one distortion type at a time and constraining responses to {Yes,No} answers, we effectively reduce the risk of hallucination.
While our attempts prove it’s not feasible due to limitations in current model context length and hallucination, we believe this change remains promising as future model capabilities improve.
Symbolic execution-based approaches inevitably encounter the path explosion problem.
Furthermore, for excessively long execution paths, we implement both a maximum instruction execution length constraint and a timeout mechanism.
Notably, although PseudoFix performs relatively poorly in correctness in the D4 and D5 tasks, this does not prevent it from playing a substantial role in improving readability of pseudocode.
This demonstrates that our use of LLMs to optimize pseudocode, despite an average overhead of 7.1s, strongly achieves a groundbreaking breakthrough, pointing in a new direction.

In particular, under the 10-shot setting with GPT-4, we reduce Cyclomatic Complexity by 32% and Halstead Complexity Effort by 34% for the malware dataset, significantly easing comprehension challenges in malware analysis.
Following the original DeGPT paper, we focus solely on the Effort metric of Halstead Complexity, comparing the RVE module individually against PseudoFix’s refactoring of only D5-type distortions.
Notably, the manual annotation effort is negligible, and due to the powerful in-context learning capabilities of LLMs, in our work, only three golden examples per distortion category are required.

tecnicas.nome_original: SLM4PLC (correctness-by-construction framework: Agentic RAG + enhanced CoT prompting + syntax checking + CbC Debugging Agent)
tecnicas.localizador: Resumo, PDF p. 1; seção IV (Fig. 1, IV.C–IV.E), PDF p. 2–3; Tabelas I e III, PDF p. 4 (páginas sem número impresso)
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote híbrido: quatro agentes (Retrieval, Coding, Syntax-Checking, CbC Debugging) em pipeline fechado → multiagente e decomposicao; prompts estruturados com restrições de compilador, segurança e validação → instrucao e restricoes; CoT com análise de segurança e antecipação de erros → raciocinio; RAG com documentação PLC e exemplos/templates de ST validados → contexto e exemplos; laço com verificação sintática (RuSTy) e verificação formal (nuXmv) com depuração guiada por contraexemplo → feedback. Inclui também ajuste fino QLoRA do Phi-3 (fora do escopo) na linha Phi-3 3.8B (FT). Comparação com 'Naive LLM (Baseline)' nos mesmos modelos (Tabelas I e III) isola o pacote, não um mecanismo; para os modelos sem rótulo (FT) o estudo não declara explicitamente ausência de ajuste fino. O prompt do baseline ingênuo não é descrito, por isso não se identifica o que o pacote acrescenta (mecanismos_acrescentados vazio). A linha 'CbC Debugging Framework' da Tabela II é apresentada como 'The full CbC Debugging Framework', mas o modelo dessa tabela não é informado.

citacoes.trecho: The proposed framework integrates Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Agentic RAG) with structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to reduce reasoning errors, constrain safety-critical logic, and improve grounding in IEC 61131-3 programming patterns.
A lightweight SLM, fine-tuned using QLoRA, serves as the code generation engine.
Existing large-scale language models (LLMs) are too computationally demanding and lack the formal reliability for deployment on typical PLC hardware.
Cloud-based inference introduces additional concerns regarding latency, confidentiality, and predictable scan-cycle execution.
They help close the Computational Cost Gap that prevents larger LLMs like GPT-4 [15] from running on-site.
Reasoning quality is improved through Chain-of-Thought prompting [20] and RAG [24], both of which help reduce code hallucinations.
This combination prevents both syntactic errors and deeper logical flaws such as deadlocks, unsafe interlocks, or liveness violations, providing robust assurance for generated PLC control logic.

Studies also report persistent logical and semantic errors in LLM-generated PLC programs, motivating research into improved prompting, verification-aware workflows, and divide-and-conquer reasoning strategies.
SLM4PLC builds on this line of work by emphasizing lightweight model adaptation and formal assurance relative to a naive LLM baseline.

The system coordinates four agents—Retrieval, Coding, Syntax-Checking, and CbC Debugging—in a closed-loop pipeline that ensures the syntactic validity, logical correctness, and formal verifiability of PLC programs.
Fine-tuning was performed on the Phi-3-Mini-128K-Instruct (3.8B) model using QLoRA on a single NVIDIA GTX 950M GPU.
All samples were validated using the RuSTy ST compiler to ensure syntactic correctness, and organized into three task-oriented sets: Generation, Completion, and Fixing.
As shown in Fig. 2, the coder agent employs an enhanced Chain-of-Thought (CoT) strategy to guide the model through step-by-step reasoning.
This process includes a brief safety analysis to enforce safety constraints (e.g., interlocks and deadlock freedom) and an error anticipation step to identify common logic issues.
CoT is further supported by retriever-supplied code templates from the Agentic RAG module, enabling the model to generate more accurate and consistent Structured Text code.
Additional divide-and-conquer reasoning and hallucination-reduction techniques further enhance reliability.
It leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to ground code generation in curated PLC documentation and validated ST examples, reducing hallucinations.

Structured, domain-aware prompts encode compiler, safety, and validation constraints, and the agent operates in an iterative loop with syntax-checking and debugging components, enabling feedback-driven refinement and producing reliable, verifiable PLC code.
This trace is fed back to the Fixing Agent (the fine-tuned SLM), which is specifically prompted to perform a surgical code refinement [21], [22].

The evaluation validates the framework against key metrics, comparing six SLM configurations: Mistral 7B, CodeLlama 7B [12], Deepseek-Coder 6.7B [13], Qwen2.5-Coder 7B [14], Phi-3 3.8B, and Phi-3-Mini 3.8B (fine-tune).
To evaluate our framework, we constructed a benchmark dataset for generating IEC 61131-3 Structured Text from natural-language specifications and assessing correctness through formal verification.
The benchmark consists of 20 programming tasks with associated LTL specifications: 12 easy tasks with 52 properties and 7 medium tasks with 31 properties.
The Pass@k metric considers a task successful if at least one of the k generated candidates both compiles and satisfies the specified functional requirements.
As shown in Table I, all SLM4PLC variants achieve a perfect 100% first-pass compilation rate for both Easy and Medium tasks.
These results confirm that domain-aligned fine-tuning and structured prompting significantly improve syntactic robustness in IEC 61131-3 Structured Text generation.
On Easy tasks, verifiable rates increase from 50–58.3% under basic prompting to 66.6% when both components are applied.
The full CbC Debugging Framework achieves the highest performance, with a 75% verifiable rate and a 66.6% pass rate on Easy tasks, and a 57.1% verifiable rate with a 42.9% pass rate on Medium tasks.

citacoes.trecho: As shown in Table III, all SLM4PLC models achieve a perfect syntax compilation pass rate of 100%, successfully compiling all generated programs.
The framework attains a maximum verifiable rate of 66.7% and a pass rate of 58.3% with the fine-tuned Phi-3 3.8B model, demonstrating its superior capability in generating formally verifiable code.
No unexpected behavior or conflicting state updates were observed during execution.
SLM4PLC is designed as a fully offline deterministic workflow that aligns with industrial expectations for safety, confidentiality, and predictable behavior.

tecnicas.observacao: Prompt zero-shot em estilo de instrução ('Create a complete and ready-to-run RESTful API program based on this SQL DDL...') → instrucao; esquema SQL DDL do banco Chinook fornecido como insumo → contexto; framework ExpressJS, MySQL, entrega em ZIP e, no Experimento 3, 'Each resource is created in a separate file' → restricoes. O estudo compara diretamente duas representações alternativas do mesmo esquema (DDL e JSON) com o mesmo prompt; não há condição sem artefato de esquema nem prompt base do qual a representação derive, por isso não há condição com e sem a técnica e nenhum mecanismo é isolado. O contraste DDL × JSON difere só na representação do artefato e na menção a ela no prompt ('this SQL DDL' / 'this JSON file that contain structured SQL database information'); as duas condições recebem as mesmas categorias de mecanismo.

citacoes.trecho: This paper evaluates two database-related representations, JSON and Data Definition Language (DDL), on LLM for RESTful API code generation.

DDL achieves higher completeness (86.2–97.8%) and better handles more complex relational schemas, while JSON produces simpler, more readable code, but completeness degrades (to 46%) under complex scenarios.
This research aims to evaluate how different artefact representations affect LLM-generated outputs and to analyze the specific impacts of DDL and JSON inputs.
This DDL is the original representation of the Chinook database.
JSON representation was obtained by converting the original Chinook DDL representation [18].

Both representations contain the same database information to ensure that any observed differences in generated code can be attributed to the input artefact representation rather than to the schema difference.
Prompt type that uses zero-shot [21] with instruction-based style [22].
The same prompting strategy is applied consistently to both DDL and JSON input artefacts to maintain experimental fairness.
Each constructed prompt and its corresponding input artefact are submitted to ChatGPT 5.2 trough web interface with default configurations settings by its platform.
Create a complete and ready-to-run RESTful API program based on this SQL DDL.

citacoes.trecho: The results reveal that the PlaylistTrack resource exhibits the highest number of generation failures across all experiments (Table V).
This degradation occurs most often for the JSON input artefact representation, where only 5 resources are fully generated (46.2% complete) in experiment 3.
Minor variations are observed in the naming of generated resources across different experimental runs.
These variations do not affect functionality but indicate that, in the absence of explicit prompting, the LLM may apply different naming and endpoint prefixes during code generation.
As schema and prompt complexity increase, the LLM tends to simplify generated code by reducing internal logic and error handling.
DDL inputs consistently lead to more complex code structures, but JSON inputs result in simpler implementations with lower complexity.

Second, all experiments used zero-shot prompting with an instruction-based style.

tecnicas.nome_original: LLM-assisted workflow com multi-part prompt (structured prompting + automated compilation feedback)
tecnicas.localizador: Resumo, PDF p. 1 (impressa 0640); seções III e IV.D, PDF p. 2–4 (impressas 0641–0643); Fig. 2, PDF p. 3; Fig. 5, PDF p. 4
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote híbrido: prompt único com cinco componentes (system, structural, task, constraints, meta-control) e a especificação JSON embutida, extração por regex, compilação automática no Unity e ciclo de refinamento com resumo de erros. Mecanismos: papel e diretrizes do system prompt e descrição da tarefa → instrucao; formato de saída, scaffold de classe, restrições de API e especificação JSON → restricoes; ciclo de geração e correção com erros de compilação/validação → feedback; pipeline que encadeia geração, extração, compilação e execução da cena → decomposicao; identificador numérico anti-repetição → outro. Todas as condições executadas usam o mesmo prompt; a comparação executada é entre modelos (Qwen 3 Coder 30B, Code Llama Instruct 13B, DevStral Small 2507), não entre condições de prompting, por isso não há contrafactual. O próprio estudo diz que o objetivo do prompt não era otimizar desempenho, mas criar condições controladas.

tecnicas.localizador: Seção IV.B e Fig. 3, PDF p. 3 (impressa 0642); seção IV.D, PDF p. 4 (impressa 0643); 'Impact of Prompt Types', PDF p. 5 (impressa 0644)

Os efeitos atribuídos ('suppressed interleaved commentary') não vêm de condição sem o componente relatada no artigo; referem-se a observações qualitativas e ensaios preliminares não relatados.

citacoes.trecho: This paper investigates the feasibility of using large language models to assist in the early stages of digital twin development by generating Unity simulation components from structured descriptions.
A locally hosted pipeline was implemented to support this workflow, combining structured prompting, model-to-engine communication, code extraction, and automated compilation feedback.

Two models, Qwen 3 Coder 30B and Code Llama Instruct 13B, were evaluated using identical behavioral specifications to assess differences in generation time, compilation success, and functional correctness.
If validation fails, the workflow initiates a generation–correction cycle using the refinement prompt and error summary.
Inference parameters were fixed across all experiments, using a temperature of 0.25 and a top-p value of 0.9.
Three models were evaluated using this configuration:
Each model received the same multi-part prompt containing the behavioral description, JSON specification, class structure, and Unity-specific constraints.
The goal of the prompt design was not to optimize model performance, but to create controlled and reproducible conditions for comparison.
All five prompt components were delivered as a unified, single-turn payload to ensure context integrity and prevent the formatting drift observed in preliminary multi-turn trials.
The system prompt defined the model’s role and enforced a strict output format—valid Unity C# code enclosed in backticks, no commentary, and adherence to .NET Standard 2.1.
A structural scaffold specified the expected class layout, including required fields and the presence of Start() and Update().
The task prompt described the behavior to implement: create a primitive based on the JSON description, apply dimensions and color, and perform continuous rotation using the specified axis and speed.

A small number of Unity-specific constraints were added to avoid failure modes observed in preliminary trials, such as incorrect use of JsonUtility, improper collider selection, or coroutine-based rotation.
A lightweight numeric identifier was appended to each prompt to reduce repeated outputs during refinement cycles.
The JSON datasheet was embedded verbatim within the prompt, ensuring consistent structured parameters across all experiments.

The ordering of these components was also critical: placing the system and structural prompts first consistently reduced format drift and ensured that the model established a correct Unity-oriented coding context before receiving any behavior-specific instructions.

citacoes.trecho: Each model was tested multiple times with identical inputs to evaluate reproducibility.
Table I summarizes generation latency and output length across three attempts for each model.
Code Llama Instruct 13B required significantly longer decoding times (90–100 seconds) and generated longer outputs on average.

DevStral Small 2507 consistently failed to generate valid C# output and is therefore excluded from quantitative tables; its behavior serves only as a qualitative indicator of the workflow’s lower performance boundary.

These limits do not affect correctness but they do influence latency and token budgets, reflecting the conditions typical of security-sensitive or offline laboratory environments where cloud services are restricted.
Note: † Attempt recovered after prompt refinement.

citacoes.trecho: Qwen correctly implemented both rotation and color logic in two of three attempts, demonstrating strong semantic alignment with the JSON specification.
In the second attempt, a local-scope error caused the rotation behavior to be dropped; however, the scripting structure remained valid.
Code Llama produced correct behavior only after a refinement iteration (Attempt 3).
Earlier attempts failed due to JSON color parsing limitations and missing shape-scaling logic, both attributable to variable scope or object-access omissions (see Fig. 12).
Both models exhibited stability declines as prompts neared 1000 tokens, suggesting that current local workflows are sensitive to instruction density rather just model capacity.
Above this point, responses became slower and more variable.
This study validates that locally hosted LLMs can produce functional Unity C# scripts from structured specifications when supported by optimized prompt engineering.

tecnicas.observacao: Única condição de prompting aplicada aos dez LLMs avaliados: instruções específicas da tarefa em zero-shot → instrucao; a tarefa consiste em completar uma SCoT da qual foram removidos blocos semânticos, de modo que os blocos restantes da SCoT de referência são fornecidos como insumo → contexto (os autores atribuem o desempenho à dependência desse 'local context'). O texto do prompt não é publicado; não se informa se o programa Python ou o traço de prova Dafny entram no prompt nem se há formato de saída imposto. O objeto de investigação é a capacidade dos LLMs sob essa condição, não uma técnica de prompting; não há outra condição de prompting executada, por isso não há contrafactual. Papel focal por ser a condição avaliada no estudo.

tecnicas.observacao: Framework proposto pelo estudo: pipeline de LLMs que converte o traço de prova Dafny do PyPrep em passos de síntese em nível Spark (SCoT), usado para construir a referência do SCoT-Bench. Etapas: Synthesis Transformer (decomposicao), quatro agentes Synthesis Checker (lemma, invariante, pós-condição, comutatividade) em laço com o Transformer (multiagente, feedback), Synthesis Pruner e Synthesis Repair, que executa o código Spark em modo de verificação sintática do PySpark e devolve as mensagens de erro (feedback). Hierarquia de regras de prova que 'steers LLM attention' e filtro de abstração que instrui os checkers a ignorar passos triviais → instrucao; programa Python e prova Dafny como insumo e gramática do PySpark no prompt do agente de reparo → contexto; exemplos de reparo curados no prompt de sistema → exemplos (e contexto); mapeamento explícito obrigação→passo como saída estruturada dos checkers e regras de gramática → restricoes. Avaliado só por validação humana de uma amostra, sem condição sem o pacote; pacote híbrido (inclui a escolha de famílias de modelos por etapa, fora do escopo). Sem prompt base identificável, por isso mecanismos_acrescentados vazio.

Rubrica que aceita blocos semanticamente equivalentes (equivalência de lambdas, implicação mútua de invariantes, equivalência de asserções) em vez de correspondência token a token.
Comparação com o PyPrep restrita ao subconjunto expressível na IR e reavaliação com oracle abstain para dar aos LLMs opção de recusa comparável.

citacoes.trecho: Leveraging SCoT-Lift, we introduce SCoT-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark of 1,652 SCoT completion tasks for rigorously evaluating LLMs on the Python-to-Spark translation process.

Evaluation of ten state-of-the-art LLMs reveals severe fragility, indicating that current LLMs fall well short of the reasoning capabilities exhibited by automated theorem provers, and lag significantly behind the correctness guarantees of our formal Python preprocessor.
Judging a model solely by functional equivalence on a finite test suite cannot distinguish a model that constructs a sound deductive chain (as PyPrep does) from one that succeeds by chance.
In our prior work [1], we developed a Python preprocessor (PyPrep) that automates this translation using program synthesis and formal verification.
However, despite its formal correctness guarantees, the tool is limited to programs expressible in its IR and requires manual effort to extend to new patterns.
SCoT-Lift operates as a four-stage pipeline.
To address this, we introduce a Dafny proof rule hierarchy that explicitly steers LLM attention towards steps more likely to be semantically informative.
For each category, a dedicated checker agent verifies whether the Synthesis Transformer has produced a corresponding Spark-level step.

To reduce hallucinations, each checker must provide an explicit mapping from each high-level Dafny obligation to the corresponding Spark synthesis step, rather than issuing a binary completeness verdict.

The Synthesis Transformer is instantiated with Claude Sonnet 4.5; the four Synthesis Checker agents (lemma, invariant, postcondition, commutativity) are instantiated with GPT-5.2; the Synthesis Pruner uses Claude Sonnet 4.5; and the Synthesis Repair agent uses GPT-5.2 with the PySpark grammar and curated repair examples in its system prompt.
citacoes.localizador: Seção III, 'Models used inside SCoT-Lift', PDF p. 3

citacoes.trecho: Using two different model families across Transformer/Pruner versus Checkers/Repair reduces the chance that a single model’s blind spots silently propagate into the ground truth.
citacoes.localizador: Seção III, 'Models used inside SCoT-Lift', PDF p. 3

citacoes.trecho: When a checker signals incompleteness, the transformer reprocesses the entire proof, naturally recovering additional missing steps beyond the checker’s limited scope.
The Synthesis Repair stage ensures soundness by executing the transformed Spark program in PySpark’s syntax-checking mode and feeding error messages back to a repair agent.
Disagreements were reconciled by discussion to produce a single consensus label per step, used in the analysis below.
On the consensus labels, 96.4% of steps are judged sound, 91.6% of SCoTs are complete (no high-level Dafny obligation missing), and 88.3% of steps are concise.
At the SCoT (program) level, 43/50 (86%) pass all three goals jointly; the remaining 7 contain at least one violation but are not globally wrong.

We exclude the 7 failing SCoTs from SCoT-Bench-Org’s reference set; the remaining 113 programs (after the same review applied to the rest of the corpus, which yielded a comparable 86% joint pass rate) form the ground truth used in Section V.
The collection comprises 120 verified Python programs across domains including data filtering, aggregation, join processing, string matching, and numerical computation.
For each program containing N blocks, we generate N variants by removing between 1 and N blocks, yielding 967 SCoT completion tasks.

For each program, we generate up to three variants: Lambda-removal (all lambda blocks removed), Invariant-removal (all loop invariant blocks), and Assertion-removal (all assertion blocks), yielding 371 tasks.
We define three removal zones: Front (first 33% of the SCoT), Middle (33%–66%), and End (final 33%), yielding 314 tasks.
All models are prompted in a zero-shot setting with task-specific instructions.

We employ three metrics: Syntactic Accuracy (SynAcc), checked by executing the generated Spark code in syntax-only mode; Semantic Accuracy (SemAcc), evaluated by a specialized LLM-based judge guided by detailed rubrics and curated examples; and Overall Accuracy (Acc), a weighted combination.

The LLM judge is instantiated with Gemini 3 (a model family disjoint from the GPT-5.2 / Claude Sonnet 4.5 mix used inside SCoT-Lift, to limit shared-model bias between ground-truth construction and evaluation).
Against this gold standard, the judge attains a raw four-class agreement of 92.5% (185/200) with Cohen’s κ = 0.88 (almost perfect).

The largest residual confusion is between Level 1 and Level 2 (8/15 misclassifications), i.e., the judge occasionally disagrees with humans on whether a syntactically clean but semantically suspect program should be marked semantically correct; this affects Acc by at most ±1.4 percentage points under a worst-case re-assignment.
To avoid measuring chain-imitation rather than translation competence, the judge does not compare the model’s output to the lifted SCoT token by token.
citacoes.localizador: Seção V.A, 'Multiple valid reasoning chains', PDF p. 5

citacoes.trecho: Table I summarizes overall accuracy (%) at five representative removal levels and the per-model average; below the table we expand on five key findings.
With only 10% of blocks missing, the best model, Claude Sonnet 4.5, achieves 68.4% accuracy, while the weakest, CodeOSS-20B, reaches only 29.7%.
We therefore restrict this finding to the IR-expressible subset of SCoT-Bench-Org (94/113 programs, 78.6% coverage on which PyPrep produces a verified Spark translation).

On this subset, PyPrep is correct by construction (100%), while the best LLM, Claude Sonnet 4.5, attains 71.2% Acc at 10% removal and 16.1% at 100% removal—only marginally above its full-benchmark numbers.

Under this oracle-abstain protocol Claude Sonnet 4.5 reaches 81.4% precision at 62% coverage and GPT-5.2 reaches 76.8% at 58% coverage, both still well below PyPrep’s 100% at 78.6% coverage on the same subset.
Counterintuitively, Qwen 3’s thinking variant underperforms the non-thinking variant, and Gemini 3 Flash outperforms Gemini 3 overall.
In MapReduce translation, where PySpark requires precise API calls and commutativity checks, verbose “thinking” can introduce hallucinated operations or semantic drift.
At 100% removal, most models show a slight accuracy uptick.
This arises because single-block programs appear only at 100% removal, skewing the sample toward easier tasks.
Loop invariant completion achieves the highest accuracy but also the widest spread across models (65.2% to 9.4%, a 55.8% gap), making it the most discriminative construct type.

citacoes.trecho: To address these issues, this paper proposes SemCompress, a semantic-aware adaptive DocString compression method, which achieves a dynamic balance between compression efficiency and generation quality through three core modules: code-semantic-anchored structured parsing, dual-weighted token importance quantification, and dynamic-threshold-constrained iterative compression.

Experiments on three mainstream code generation benchmarks—HumanEval, CodeHarmony, and BigCodeBench—show that SemCompress achieves stable compression rates of 25% to 35%, outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by an average of 3.7 percentage points in Pass@1, reduces model inference floating-point operations (FLOPs) by an average of 18.7%, and shortens end-to-end inference latency by up to 21.4%.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have become core tools for industrial code generation, but DocStrings—the primary prompt carriers—often suffer from severe information redundancy, directly increasing model inference computational costs and third-party API expenses.

DocStrings-embedded at function heads—act as the critical bridge between user requirements and code, carrying function positioning, input/output constraints, exception rules, and examples that directly determine generation quality [3], [4].

General-purpose compression methods like LLMLingua2 [8] and Selective_Context [9] work well in NLP but fail in code generation: our pre-experiments show Pass@1 drops >15% above 10% compression, as they only evaluate token importance from text semantics, cannot identify code-critical units (e.g., parameter type constraints, exception rules), and eventually lead to functional errors.
However, it uses static compression settings, lacks robust core code semantic anchoring, and suffers significant performance degradation in high-difficulty industrial scenarios.

The overall framework of SemCompress (omitted Figure 1 due to space constraints) takes a code generation prompt containing a function signature and DocString as input, outputs the compressed DocString, and proceeds in three core stages.
To avoid semantic distortion, final filtering is only performed when post-filtering text semantic similarity ≥ 0.999 [13].

Construct a code generation keyword vocabulary based on million-level code corpus statistics, and assign an additional weight Impcode(di) (1.2–2.0) to code-critical tokens (type keywords, parameter names, exception identifiers, etc.) to strengthen core semantic protection.

Compression is only executed when both text semantic similarity ≥ 0.99 and code generation distribution similarity ≥ τdyn are satisfied, balancing text integrity and code generation task alignment [13].

This paper selects three mainstream Python code generation benchmarks (i.e. HumanEval, CodeHarmony, BigCodeBench) covering different difficulties to comprehensively verify the performance of SemCompress.
Random: Randomly prune tokens in DocStrings, set the same compression rate as SemCompress, and use it as the lower performance baseline.
ShortenDoc [10]: A code-scenario-specific DocString compression method, used as a direct comparison baseline for this paper’s method.

The core hyperparameters of SemCompress are set as follows: the base model is CodeLlama-7B-Instruct [14], the dynamic threshold range is 0.98–0.999, the text semantic threshold is 0.99, the maximum continuous compression sequence length is 3, and the compression upper limits of each semantic unit are consistent with the previous section.
Table I shows the average Pass@1 and compression rate comparison of different methods on three datasets, and all results are the average performance of six experimental models.

At an average compression rate of 30%, the average Pass@1 of SemCompress reaches 40.64, which is 2.14 percentage points higher than ShortenDoc, 7.66 percentage points higher than LLMLingua2, and 6.84 percentage points higher than Selective_Context, solving the core pain point of existing methods that generation quality drops sharply when compression rates increase.

On the HumanEval dataset, the compressed input increases the Pass@1 of CodeQwen1.5-7B from 77.44 (uncompressed) to 79.15, indicating that it filters redundant noise and helps the model focus more on core requirements.

After compression, the average inference FLOPs of the model are reduced by 18.75%, and the end-to-end latency is shortened by 21.38%, while the compression preprocessing latency is only 1.72s, and the additional video memory usage is less than 0.3GB, fully meeting the requirements of industrial real-time calls.

Taking the GPT-4o API pricing as an example, a 30% compression rate can reduce the total cost of a single call by 29.17%, which has extremely high economic value in enterprise-level large-scale call scenarios.
Experiments on three benchmarks show SemCompress achieves 25% to 35% compression, outperforms baselines by 3.7pp in Pass@1, and cuts inference costs and API expenses.

citacoes.trecho: In particular, our research answers the following questions:
RQ2: How do different prompts impact the vulnerability levels in the code generated by different open source LLMs?
For the purpose of our study we use three different prompts:
P1 (security-agnostic prompt): Write a code in the Python language to [Task].
P2 (task + role definition prompt): You are a computer security professional tasked with writing nonvulnerable code.
Make sure there are no potential vulnerabilities or security concerns with the code.

citacoes.trecho: The prompting strategies in this article were designed by following a controlled, incremental protocol so that we can isolate the effect of security awareness in prompts.
To ensure systematicity, all the given prompts share an identical structure and differ only in the presence and specificity of security-related instructions.
No task-specific or adaptive prompt tuning was performed.
In this study, we use multiple LLMs and feed each model with the three carefully designed prompts to evaluate their ability to generate secure and functionally correct Python code.

tecnicas.nome_original: Multi-objective optimization framework using the NSGA-II genetic algorithm (co-optimization of inference parameters and prompting strategies)
tecnicas.localizador: Resumo, PDF p. 1; seções III.B, III.D e III.E, PDF p. 4–5; Algoritmos 1 e 2, PDF p. 4–5; Tabela I, PDF p. 5; Tabela II e Fig. 1, PDF p. 6; Tabela III, PDF p. 7 (artigo sem paginação impressa)
tecnicas.observacao: Pacote híbrido: o NSGA-II busca simultaneamente parâmetros de decodificação (temperature, top-p, frequency penalty, presence penalty, max tokens; fora do escopo) e o tipo de prompt como variável categórica (zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, CoT), o que constitui seleção automática do prompt → otimizacao_prompt. Os mecanismos listados são os das estratégias disponíveis no espaço de busca; as soluções da frente de Pareto (Tabela II) usam apenas Zero-Shot, One-Shot e Few-Shot, e CoT não aparece em nenhuma solução relatada. O comparador executado é a busca sequencial em grade (seção III.F), não uma condição sem o pacote com o mesmo espaço de busca: a grade usa outros intervalos (penalidades de -2,0 a 2,0, temperatura de 0,0 a 2,0, top-p de 0,0 a 1,0), não inclui max tokens e a seção III.F não menciona tipo de prompt, embora a seção IV.A diga que a grade avaliou 'other prompt types'. Por isso o acréscimo de otimizacao_prompt em relação ao comparador é incerto. O 'sim' vale só para o pacote; o ganho não é atribuível à seleção de prompt nem a qualquer estratégia de prompting isolada.

tecnicas.localizador: Seção III.F, PDF p. 5; seção IV.A, PDF p. 6; Fig. 1, PDF p. 6; Tabela III, PDF p. 7

É essencialmente busca de parâmetros de decodificação. O prompt usado pela grade não é descrito na seção III.F (mecanismos não identificáveis, por isso lista vazia); a seção IV.A afirma que a grade avaliou 'other prompt types', sem detalhar. Sistema comparador cujos mecanismos de prompting não são isolados.

O Algoritmo 2 calcula accuracy = CorrectCount/|D| com D = conjunto HumanEval; o artigo não afirma explicitamente que os 164 problemas foram usados em cada avaliação de indivíduo nem quantas respostas foram geradas por problema.

riscos.descricao: Few-shot e CoT aumentam o consumo de tokens e, segundo o estudo, a latência e o custo computacional; o consumo de tokens é tratado pelo estudo como custo (objetivo de minimização). O custo em tokens é medido na Tabela II para as soluções da frente; o custo de CoT não é quantificado.
riscos.localizador: Seção III.B, PDF p. 4; seção I, PDF p. 1–2; Tabela II, PDF p. 6

riscos.descricao: Valores baixos de max tokens podem truncar a saída e produzir código incompleto (descrição geral na fundamentação, não medida).
Valores altos de max tokens podem aumentar custos e latência (descrição geral, não quantificada).
Temperaturas altas elevam o risco de erros factuais (descrição geral da fundamentação sobre texto, não medida para código).

A busca sequencial em grade é apresentada como significativamente mais custosa em tempo (aprox. 18 a 36 horas por modelo contra aprox. 3 horas do NSGA-II); trata-se do custo do procedimento de configuração, não da geração de código.

citacoes.trecho: The framework co-optimizes inference parameters and prompting strategies to simultaneously maximize code accuracy and minimize token consumption.

Validated on the HumanEval benchmark across three LLMs (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, and Mistral-7B), our approach identified Pareto-optimal fronts that surpassed the accuracy of a sequential search baseline while reducing optimization time by 6 to 12 times.
The approach aims to simultaneously maximize the quality of the generated code and minimize token consumption, a factor directly linked to computational cost.

The search space for the optimization was defined to include not only the standard inference parameters (such as temperature, top-p, Frequency penalty, and Presence penalty) but also the prompting strategy itself as a categorical decision variable.
The objective was to allow the algorithm to autonomously determine which prompt approach maximizes performance.
Zero-Shot Prompting: This approach consists of providing the direct instruction to the model, without including examples of how the response should be structured.
One-Shot Prompting: This technique provides the model with a single, complete example of the task (a prompt-completion pair) alongside the new instruction.
Few-Shot Prompting: Extending the one-shot approach, few-shot prompting includes several examples (typically 2-5) of the task within the prompt.
However, this comes at the cost of increased token consumption.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting: This technique encourages the LLM to externalize its reasoning process, breaking down the problem into logical steps before presenting the final solution [11].
CoT aims to increase robustness and accuracy on complex tasks but generally results in higher token consumption and, consequently, greater latency and computational cost.
This is a canonical dataset, developed by OpenAI, consisting of 164 unique, human-written programming problems in Python.
Finally, the two fitness values of the individual, accuracy and average token cost, are calculated and assigned.
To balance the exploration of the search space with the computational cost of the experiment, a population of 20 individuals was defined, with the evolutionary process occurring over 10 generations.

Notably, the Frequency penalty and Presence penalty parameters were restricted to non-negative values ([0,2.0]) to focus the optimization on configurations that penalize repetition, as negative values encourage token reiteration, a generally undesirable characteristic for the code generation task.
Max tokens [100,512]
citacoes.localizador: Tabela I, PDF p. 5, colunas Hyperparameter (Gene) | Search Range

citacoes.trecho: To provide a robust comparison for accuracy and execution time, a sequential grid search methodology was implemented as a baseline, inspired by the approach in [4].
The intervals and step sizes were defined as follows: frequency penalty and presence penalty both ranged from -2.0 to 2.0 (step 0.5).
To handle the codependency of the sampling parameters, temperature (varied 0.0–2.0, step 0.25) and top-p (varied 0.0–1.0, step 0.25) were optimized in separate passes.
This methodology resulted in a total of 1134 unique configurations being evaluated sequentially for each model.

citacoes.localizador: Tabela II, PDF p. 6, colunas Model | Ind. | Accuracy | Cost | temp. | top-p | max tokens | prompt type | frequency penalty | presence penalty

citacoes.trecho: The baseline spent significant computational time evaluating penalty values from -2.0 to 2.0 and other prompt types, regions that NSGA-II efficiently identified as suboptimal.

Furthermore, NSGA-II quickly identified that the optimal solutions for Qwen2.5 required frequency penalty values near 0.0 and very low presence penalty values (<0.4), while also converging on "Zero-Shot" as the dominant prompt strategy for that model.

Notably, for the Qwen and Llama models, the optimization not only matched but ultimately surpassed the performance of the sequential search in later generations, highlighting NSGA-II’s ability to find superior configurations in a complex search space.
Low values are ideal for ensuring concise answers, but they carry the risk of truncating the output, resulting in incomplete code or unfinished reasoning.

On the other hand, high values allow the model to generate detailed and comprehensive responses, essential for complex tasks, but can lead to increased costs, latency, and the risk of the model producing repetitive or unfocused content.
Higher values (e.g., τ > 1.0) increase diversity and creativity, making the text more surprising, but also elevate the risk of factual errors.
In stark contrast, the sequential search approach proved to be significantly more costly, with times ranging from 18 to 36 hours.

The results provide key insights into prompt strategy effectiveness and deliver a robust, automated approach that equips practitioners with a set of validated configurations for different operational needs.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote híbrido. Ingredientes de prompting: persona e conjunto de instruções com checklist (instrucao); trecho de código defeituoso, sinais estruturais da AST inseridos como anotações em linguagem natural e pedido de análise com projeto, arquivo, função e linhas defeituosas (contexto); exemplos de correções semelhantes recuperados por BM25 em formato lado a lado (contexto e exemplos); bloco <analysis> com causa raiz e plano antes do código (raciocinio); protocolo de saída estrito, cercas de código, mudança mínima, limite de 12 linhas (restricoes); até 10 candidatos com variação de ordem dos exemplos e da ênfase dos sinais estruturais, deduplicados e selecionados por testes (amostragem). O pacote também inclui componentes fora do escopo (decodificação variada, deduplicação por hash de AST, verificações de sintaxe, parada antecipada, limite de 2.048 tokens). Contrafactual: Qwen-ZeroShot recebe só o código defeituoso, com mesmo número de candidatos, semente, parâmetros de decodificação e validação; porém o artigo diz que o AgentRepair usa 'the Qwen [12] family' sem informar a versão, enquanto o comparador usa Qwen1.5-7B-Chat, de modo que a identidade do modelo não é declarada. O ganho é do pacote e não pode ser atribuído a um ingrediente. Não se classificou como multiagente: a 'arquitetura multiagente' é um pipeline de módulos (parser AST, BM25, execução de testes, orquestrador) em que só o Patch Generation Agent é descrito como chamando o LLM; não há interação descrita entre papéis de LLM. 'mecanismos_acrescentados' inclui contexto porque o pacote acrescenta novos ingredientes dessa categoria (sinais AST e casos recuperados) ao código defeituoso já presente no comparador.

tecnicas.localizador: Seções 2.3, 3.2 e 3.3, PDF p. 2, 4 e 5 (impressas 122, 124 e 125)

Só é avaliado dentro do pacote completo (por isso 'mecanismos' repete o pacote). Os autores reconhecem que as ablações não separam o efeito dos sinais AST; nenhuma ablação é relatada.

riscos.descricao: Fornecer só o código defeituoso leva a correções alucinadas; LLMs produzem patches incorretos ou alucinados, erros de sintaxe, ausência de cercas de código, refatoração desnecessária e código irrelevante.

riscos.descricao: Métricas baseadas em testes supõem suítes razoavelmente completas e podem gerar falsos positivos ou negativos (patch aprovado incorreto).

Ruído ocasional na recuperação BM25 e perda de contexto em defeitos longos ou multifunção por limites de tamanho do prompt; ganhos menores quando os exemplos recuperados são pouco relevantes ou o contexto não é localizado.
riscos.localizador: Seção 7, PDF p. 11 (impressa 131); seção 5.2, PDF p. 10 (impressa 130)

riscos.descricao: Desempenho pode variar com hiperparâmetros do BM25 e configurações de decodificação; a suíte de testes do BugsInPy pode ter comportamento instável (flaky) por dependências de ambiente e variação de tempo.

Resultados podem depender de possível sobreposição com código aberto no pré-treinamento; o estudo também trata do vazamento pelo índice de recuperação (controlado por leave-one-bug-out). Não se afirma contaminação efetiva.

citacoes.trecho: These clues and examples are combined into a detailed, evidence-filled prompt.
This prompt tells the LLM to create possible fixes, with strict rules to make only small, necessary changes.
In LLM-based automated program repair, providing only the buggy code as input often leads to hallucinated fixes, which are recognized as a major obstacle to practical applicability.
Any fixes for the same bug or clues directly derived from its associated tests were excluded from the retrieval index, thereby preventing data leakage.
Third, similar bug-fix exemplars retrieved by the Retrieval Agent pair real code with their corresponding patches, anchoring the model’s outputs in empirical evidence [10], [14].

The buggy snippet delineates the edit boundary; structural signals are inserted as natural-language annotations that emphasize specific failure modes, and retrieved bug-fix exemplars are supplied in a compact, side-by-side format so that the model can reference concrete precedents.
As shown in Figure 2, the instruction set forces the model to first articulate the bug cause and fix plan within the <analysis> block, then emit the corrected code as a complete function.
You are a senior Python bug-fix specialist.
In addition, prompt variation strategies such as reordering retrieved examples or altering the emphasis of structural signals are employed to provide multiple exploration paths.
The first candidate is always produced using greedy decoding to ensure reproducibility, while subsequent candidates are generated through probabilistic sampling to expand the search space.
Deduplication is performed using an AST-based hashing method [6], preventing identical patches from appearing across multiple candidates.

Following HAFix [8], we focus on the canonical single-line subset: from the 68 single-line, test-reproducible bugs reported by HAFix, we retain 51 cases that build and run end-to-end in our environment, exhibit the expected failing-to-passing transition between buggy and fixed revisions, and provide enough local context to fit within the model’s token budget without altering program semantics.
Patch generation uses the Qwen [12] family of code LLMs, producing up to 10 candidates per bug.
A patch was considered a bug-level success if all tests passed.
This model is built on Alibaba Cloud’s Qwen1.5-7B-Chat [12].
The input includes only the buggy code, excluding additional context such as repository history, retrieval evidence, or structural signals.
The number of candidate patches was limited to 10, and the random seed (42), decoding parameters, and validation procedures were configured identically to those used in our method.
We evaluated Google’s Gemma-7B-IT [20] under the same zero-shot conditions.
As shown in Table 2, AgentRepair successfully fixed 26 bugs, outperforming Qwen-ZeroShot ,Gemma-ZeroShot and DeepSeek-ZeroShot by +9 , +11, and +6 cases, respectively.
As shown in Figure 6, AgentRepair consumes on average about 2,400 tokens per candidate, which is roughly 2-3× higher than Qwen-ZeroShot (~800), Gemma-ZeroShot (~880), and DeepSeek-ZeroShot (~980).
AgentRepair averages 5.2 GB, comparable to Gemma-ZeroShot (5.3 GB) and Qwen-ZeroShot (5.5 GB), with DeepSeek-ZeroShot lower at 3.7 GB.

Internally, performance may vary with BM25 hyperparameters and LLM decoding settings, and the BugsInPy test suite [18] can exhibit flaky behavior due to environmental dependencies and timing variance.

We mitigated these issues by fixing random seeds, using a largely deterministic generation strategy, and logging all intermediate JSON outputs, retrieval evidence, and candidate patches, but individual repair outcomes may still depend on infrastructure conditions and potential pretraining overlap with open-source code.

Construct threats arise from our choice of pass@k and bug-level success [18] as primary metrics, which assume reasonably complete test suites and can yield false positives or negatives when that assumption is violated.

We did not perform statistical significance testing, which weakens the strength of our comparative claims, and our ablations do not fully disentangle the effects of AST signals [6], BM25 retrieval [10], and candidate diversification.

Limitations include occasional BM25 retrieval noise, context loss on long or multi-function defects due to prompt length constraints, potential AST parsing fragility on non-standard syntax, and a clear accuracy-cost trade-off as candidate counts grow.

citacoes.trecho: LLMs ChatGPT (GPT-4o) and DeepSeek (DeepSeek-V3) were used in this case.
Additional prompts were required to make sure that all the preconditions were correctly stated.
From the scenarios generated by ChatGPT (GPT-4o) 2 scenarios failed, and all scenarios generated by DeepSeek (DeepSeek-V3) passed the test.
But the two scenarios generated by GPT-4o failed because they lack a clearly defined precondition, and the LLM made an incorrect inference from the ST code (Listings 6 and Listings 7).
Based on these results lack of system context, inconsistency, and lack of traceability were observed on the generated scenario-based test suites, using LLMs based on the ST code.
Data is extracted from the Capella model in textual format (.txt), and given to LLMs; this time, only ChatGPT (GPT-4o) was used.
LLMs will generate the structured Text (ST) code, as well as functional requirements in JSON format.
When generating the functional requirements, the LLM (GPT-4o) was provided a format to follow to make the generated requirements formal, clear, structured, and traceable.
With a simple self-guiding prompt, the ST code and functional requirements were generated (Listings 8).

To generate the scenarios, LLM (GPT-4o) was provided with the Capella model data, ST code, and functional requirements (Listings 9) and a sample scenario JSON file from the previous work, which aided the process and eliminated additional prompts.
Even though the manually written code was not developed by an expert in this field the code generated by LLMs (GPT-4o) was found to be better.
Out of the ten scenario-based test suites generated, one failed S9.

The expected output is set as ” Counter += 1”, which is a value not readable by the current Python code, and also the simulation time needs to be adjusted if the aim is just to check the counters’ increment.

Whereas in” S6”, Python execution result on one of the expected outputs” Reset- fio-actuator” fails, or no result was found ”none”, but the rest of the expected outputs were found to be as intended, so the test passed.
This could be because” Reset-fio-actuator” is just a pulse within the PLC’s 20-ms scan cycle and disappears before Python, which implements a 3.7-sec. cumulative delay, has time to read and register.
Manual review and additional prompts were required to make sure preconditions and postconditions are stated correctly, and LLMs work better if provided with examples.

Additionally, the automatically generated ST code was found to be better in safety, readability, documentation, maintainability, and reusability, so besides saving time, this approach could aid in filling the gap in the absence of an expert.
The ST code generated by the LLMs was compared to the ST code written manually, and besides saving time, the quality of the code was found to be significantly better and more professional.
But manual checking is required because generated scenarios suffer from incorrect inference, and preconditions are not clearly defined.
The scenario-based test suites were generated in a single prompt because the LLMs have more data about the system, as well as example files from the previous work.

citacoes.trecho: This paper presents an empirical analysis of 12 ESLint information components’ impact on GPT-4 Turbo’s repair performance.
We measure the repair performance (CodeBLEU) of each of the 12 information components when used alone in the prompt across all 10,504 test cases.

citacoes.trecho: All experiments were conducted in a zero-shot setting without any additional fine-tuning.
It was followed by Rule Description (0.5013) and Fix Examples (0.4997), indicating that both general explanations and specific repair patterns contribute to performance.
The ’High-Synergy Pair’ combining Fix Examples with Code Block achieved 0.5279, reaching 99.5% of the full 12-component performance (0.5305) while using substantially fewer tokens.
While CodeBLEU provides comprehensive syntactic and structural assessment, we acknowledge it does not measure actual executability or test-passing rates.
Third, beyond syntactic similarity, future research should integrate test-based validation to ensure repairs actually fix the underlying issues.

This leads to three critical problems: inefficiency (full ESLint reports average 2,300 tokens, potentially incurring substantial API costs at scale), information overload (prior work shows excessive information can degrade LLM performance in certain scenarios [11]), and missed optimization opportunities through ’information toxicity,’ where useful components degrade performance when combined.
Each experiment was repeated 3 times with different random seeds to account for GPT-4’s stochastic generation.
The dataset is divided into training and test sets, with our experiments conducted on the complete test set of 10,504 cases to ensure comprehensive evaluation without sampling bias.
Our experiments were conducted on GPT-4 Turbo with JavaScript code from the TFix dataset, focusing on ESLint violations.
The generalizability to other contexts requires further validation.
This requires 12 additional API calls per test case (one for each ablation), totaling 126,048 calls for the complete test dataset.

The ’Naive Optimal’ strategy, combining the top two isolated components—Linter Message and Rule Description—achieved a CodeBLEU score of 0.5003, which is 0.005 lower than Linter Message alone (0.5053).
(3) Strategic component selection based on interaction analysis can achieve comparable performance to using all components while reducing token usage.

tecnicas.observacao: Pacote completo comparado com Direct (mesmo backend e, segundo o estudo, configurações de decodificação idênticas) na Tabela II; o ganho é do pacote e não autoriza atribuição a um mecanismo isolado. Pacote híbrido: inclui componentes de orquestração que não são prompting (deduplicação de falhas por similaridade com limiares, normalização de mensagens de erro, orçamento de iterações e de rodadas de debate, verificações programáticas de esquema JSON e alcançabilidade). Mecanismos: papéis e diretrizes dos agentes (instrucao); exemplares few-shot que ancoram o debate (exemplos); registro de problema com descrição do erro, evidências e plano de solução antes da edição (raciocinio); fluxo esqueleto, Policy Graph, meta-política e tradução para código em etapas (decomposicao); problema, Policy Graph, código candidato e traços de execução fornecidos aos agentes (contexto); refinamento com testes validados e traços de execução (feedback); agentes de estratégia, anjo, diabo, árbitro, auditor de risco, CaseCheckAgent, Merge Agent (multiagente); JSON com esquema e restrições estruturais C1–C7 (restricoes); duas propostas alternativas de reparo (anjo e diabo) seguidas de seleção pelo árbitro (amostragem). Mecanismos acrescentados calculados em relação a Direct, cujo prompt o estudo não descreve; Direct foi classificado como instrução direta (instrucao). O resumo descreve o debate como «between a strategy expert and a code expert», enquanto a Sec. III-D descreve anjo, diabo e árbitro (ver heterogeneidade).

tecnicas.observacao: Componente do sistema proposto, isolado por ablação (Full DDCoder contra w/o Policy Graph, Tabela III). Mecanismos da condição avaliada = pacote completo. Acrescenta grafo tipado serializado como JSON com esquema e restrições C1–C7 (restricoes) e modelagem em etapas (fluxo esqueleto → grafo → meta-política → código; decomposicao). citacoes.trecho: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly effective at generating code, but they still struggle on specification-intensive tasks where reliability is critical.
To address this gap, we introduce DeepDebateCoder, a closed-loop framework designed to improve robustness and structural consistency in LLM-generated code.
DeepDebateCoder first builds an explicit Policy Graph that captures module boundaries, branching logic, state transitions, and I/O constraints.
Finally, DeepDebateCoder uses execution feedback to drive an asymmetric debate between a strategy expert and a code expert.
Across HumanEval and APPS, DeepDebateCoder consistently improves pass@1 and robustness over competitive baselines.
In practice, we serialize G as schema-constrained JSON (metadata, nodes, edges), which makes validity checks straightforward and keeps the interface stable across agents.

While effective for reducing superficial mistakes, these methods often struggle on long-spec, corner-case-heavy problems: they may produce brittle defensive logic and exhibit weak handling of malformed inputs or boundary conditions [8].

To improve reliability, a common direction augments a single agent with lightweight planning or iterative refinement, including chain-of-thought prompting [9], Reflexion-style self-feedback [10], self-refinement/self-debugging [11], analogical prompting (APE) [12], and test-driven generation [4].
We evaluate DDCoder on three widely used benchmarks with increasing task complexity: HumanEval [3], HumanEval-ET [3], and APPS [26].
where n is the number of generated samples per task, ci is the number of correct samples for task i, and N is the total number of tasks.
citacoes.localizador: p. 5 do PDF, Sec. IV-A, após a Eq. 8

citacoes.trecho: All methods are evaluated under identical decoding settings on two commercial LLM backends (DeepSeek-Chat and Qwen-Plus).

On APPS—a benchmark with long specifications, multi-constraint reasoning, and hidden robustness checks—DDCoder improves pass@1 by 34 points on DeepSeek-Chat (32.00% to 66.00%) and by 17 points on Qwen-Plus (28.67% to 45.34%).
On HumanEval, where tasks are short and less constraint-heavy, DDCoder remains competitive but does not consistently surpass the strongest prompting baselines.
Removing the debate layer causes the largest performance drop (-12.67 pp), indicating that execution-grounded asymmetric debate is a major driver of gains on complex, long-specification tasks.
Overall, the improvements are driven by the synergy of Policy Graph modeling, test augmentation, and debate-based refinement rather than any single component.
DDCoder introduces additional inference-time computation due to its closed-loop design (Policy Graph construction, enhanced test generation/validation, and multi-agent debate refinement).

Experiments on the HumanEval-ET and APPS datasets with two LLM backends demonstrate consistent performance improvements for DeepDebateCoder, with the most significant gains achieved on harder, longer-specification tasks.

Specifically, ntest is set to 10, controlling the number of additional test cases generated for each problem; s is set to 1; Niter is set to 3, representing the maximum number of refinement iterations; and r is set to 2, specifying the number of debate rounds for each failed test case.
Our experiments use the OpenAI API [30] (via langchain-openai) for LLM calls, among other libraries.

tecnicas.observacao: O objeto do estudo é a variação das saídas de um único prompt fixo, submetido sem modificação por 16 participantes; não é uma técnica de prompting proposta nem comparada com outra condição. O prompt contém persona/papel ('You are an expert Laravel developer'), requisitos em linguagem natural (instrucao) e especificação da pilha tecnológica e de estilo ('PHP Laravel and MySQL', 'Use Tailwind CSS for the design') (restricoes). Não há prompt base identificável, por isso mecanismos_acrescentados está vazio. O prompt contém, por decisão dos autores, uma contradição interna ('3 roles' seguido de cinco papéis). A condição avaliada opera dentro do laço agêntico da Antigravity IDE (planejamento, execução de 'php artisan migrate' e autocorreção), que não é prompting do estudo e foi registrado em componentes_fora_escopo; por isso planejamento e autocorreção não foram contados como mecanismos da técnica.

O resultado 'first prompt' (FP) é definido como o estado final dessa trajetória.

citacoes.trecho: The prompt asked the model to take on the role of a Laravel developer and generate database migration files for a patient booking system called ClinicTrack.

You are an expert Laravel developer. I am building a patient booking website called ClinicTrack using PHP Laravel and MySQL. Requirements: Users can register and log in; 3 roles: Admin, Doctor, Patient, Receptionist, and Pharmacist; Use Tailwind CSS for the design. Please proceed to create the app database migrations files with seed data.
This was not corrected before the session; it was left in place so that we could observe how each session resolved it.

Gemini 3.1 in the Antigravity IDE operates as an agentic loop: after receiving the user message it may plan, write migration files, execute php artisan migrate, observe the output, and self-correct before returning control to the user.

Sixteen postgraduate researchers submitted an identical prompt to Gemini 3.1 during a hands-on web development workshop and received outputs that differed across five dimensions: how the model opened its response, which packages it chose, how many domain tables it generated (range: 4 to 18), whether the application ran on the first attempt (4 of 16 sessions), and how it resolved a role-count contradiction embedded in the prompt.
Taken together, 12 of 16 sessions (75%) required additional prompting beyond the first.

We argue that output variation carries heightened risk for non-technical users, who lack the background to detect differences in outputs and may proceed with incomplete or inconsistent code without realising it.
The model resolved the contradiction silently in every session.
This study documents output variation from a constant prompt; it does not isolate stochastic sampling from other sources.
Those who received a minimal or broken scaffold spent the workshop on errors that were not of their making.

First, non-technical users who rely on LLM-generated code scaffolds should submit the same prompt at least twice and compare outputs before proceeding, following the guidance of Cui and Alexander [9] to treat LLM outputs as distributions, not single answers.

Second, workshop instructors should not assume a shared prompt creates a shared starting point; a synchronisation step where participants verify their outputs cover the same major components before moving on would reduce the inequity we observed.

Third, tools aimed at non-technical LLM users could surface simple structural checks, such as table count or package list, that require no code-reading ability but would make inter-session variation visible.
All 16 sessions used Gemini 3.1 through the Antigravity IDE with fresh conversations, which controls the model version and interface.
The schema files (12 sessions) confirm this pattern.
Separately, 8 of 12 participants had laravel/breeze listed as a development dependency, indicating the model scaffolded authentication using the Breeze starter kit.
The post-workshop survey contained four question sections and three artifact upload sections.
Thirteen to fourteen completed the remaining sections.
No session implemented exactly the three roles specified; every session silently implemented four or five instead.

tecnicas.observacao: Prompt base de instrução direta: «Generate secure Python code for the following: <coding task>». O requisito «secure» foi classificado como restrição de segurança em linguagem natural. A tarefa (trecho de código incompleto com docstring) é o próprio enunciado e está em todas as condições; não foi classificada como contexto adicional. Condição de referência, sem contrafactual próprio.

tecnicas.observacao: Três passos (gerar, revisar procurando problemas de segurança, melhorar com base na crítica), com duas iterações do laço crítica-melhoria. O passo 1 é idêntico ao prompt baseline, de modo que a Tabela II contém a condição com e sem o laço de autocrítica (baseline vs. RCI) nos mesmos modelos e tarefas. É o comparador da RQ1 (técnica de referência da literatura, adotada de [7] e [2]); o isolamento é do pacote de autocrítica com duas iterações, não de um passo individual.

tecnicas.observacao: O prompt baseline recebe, anexadas, as 10 diretrizes de codificação segura mais similares (pares precondição-diretriz) recuperadas da base SecGuide (320 entradas derivadas de CWE/MITRE e recomendações do CodeQL) por similaridade de cosseno entre embeddings (text-embedding-3-small, ChromaDB). O acréscimo é um bloco único que combina conhecimento externo recuperado (contexto) e regras de segurança a seguir (restricoes; essa categoria já estava presente no baseline, em forma mais fraca, pelo termo «secure»). As diretrizes não são exemplos resolvidos. Baseline e RAG diferem apenas nesse bloco (Tabela I), mas o contrafactual é do pacote recuperação + diretrizes; não autoriza atribuir o ganho a um só mecanismo.

citacoes.trecho: In this work, we investigate the effect of incorporating secure coding guidelines, relevant to a given coding task, on the security of code generated by LLMs.
Here, the LLM was prompted to generate secure Python code for a given task without any additional security-related information.
Here, the model was first prompted to generate a secure Python implementation.
Lastly, based on this feedback, the model was prompted to refine its initial response to enhance the security of the code.
For our experiments, we performed two iterations of the feedback-improvement loop [2].
Once the relevant guidelines were retrieved, they were appended to the coding task and supplied to the LLM for code generation.
In our experiments, we retrieved the top 10 relevant guidelines per task (see Section III-C).
To address RQ2, we used the RCI+RAG as the fourth approach where we combined RCI and RAG by appending the relevant guidelines to the initial prompt used in the RCI process.
To ensure maximum reproducibility, we set the temperature to 0.0 [2] and the top_p to 0.1 [2] across all models.
However, RCI relies on the model’s ability to identify security flaws, which is constrained by its training data and susceptibility to hallucinations.
However, for CWE-78 (‘OS Command Injection’) and CWE-502 (‘Deserialization of Untrusted Data’), RAG resulted in a slight increase in detected weaknesses across all three models.

This problem may stem from RCI’s iterative three-step process (with two iterations in our setup), where the model refines its response at each step, potentially causing the code to drift from the initial task, compared to RAG’s direct single-step prompting.
Similar to RCI, RCI+RAG also resulted in fewer valid code snippets with respect to baseline and RAG.
However, the potential for direct contamination existed due to the publication of the SecurityEval dataset two years prior to this study.
We conducted a basic contamination test on the results of the main experiment using the Dolos toolkit [41] to quantify the impact of any potential leakage.
As this study exclusively utilized API access, indirect contamination was not a concern.
Additionally, RCI consumed, on average, twenty-two times more tokens per task due to its iterative and multi-step prompting process.
Integrating security guidelines at each step of RCI could address this issue, though at the risk of increased generation cost.
We also acknowledge that the responses generated by the LLMs were not evaluated for randomness.
The manual analysis of code validity and guideline relevancy was performed by a single author.
We used two tools for our analysis to increase the reliability of the findings gathered from the results.
Therefore, using CodeQL recommendations as a source for security guidelines does not provide any unintended advantage when the CodeQL tool is used to validate the generated code.

Additionally, as shown in Table IV, this approach took an average of 70.12 seconds for code generation per task, which is longer than RCI due to the overhead caused by the retrieval of guidelines with RAG.
For those 84 tasks, the retrieval process retrieved guidelines addressing the target CWE for 53 tasks (63.01%).
The analysis results from Bandit and CodeQL indicate that RCI+RAG produced the lowest average number of weaknesses in code generated by all three LLMs.
Even though RAG notably reduced security weaknesses compared to baseline, RCI delivered the best performance in contrast to the results obtained for tasks in the form of incomplete code snippets.

citacoes.trecho: We propose a novel system called DiCE, which takes serial code as input and automatically generates distributed version of the code and efficiently executes it on a distributed setup.

Since LLMs are quite sensitive to prompts, rather than us manually writing the prompt, we include a training phase in Synthia to automatically generate a system prompt, which will guide the LLM to generate syntactically correct and performant parallel code for the given input serial code (while ensuring that the output from the parallel code is the same as the output from the serial code).

We start with a basic seed prompt and iteratively revise the prompt automatically until we are able to generate syntactically correct and performant parallel code versions for each of the serial codes.
Revision occurs whenever the current system prompt is unable to generate syntactically correct and performant parallel/distributed code.
Input to this LLM includes the current system prompt, incorrect distributed code, and output from the serial and distributed code execution.
The serial code generated by the visual program synthesis tools is written in Python language, hence we guide the LLM to leverage libraries within Python language for parallel execution.
Synthia uses specific program semantics while generating the distributed code in order to make it easy to run on a distributed setup.
This LLM generates distributed code (based on the current system prompt) for the input serial code and user query.
Since we do not have any ground truth data and cannot run the serial code, we devise another LLM to perform some basic checks during inference.
If not (fail), then another version of distributed code is generated and compared.
We use the same system prompt for both these options.
We manually verify that the output from the distributed code matches the output from serial code for all the 100 example user queries.
Specifically, we pick the top 100 longest running serial codes generated by ViperGPT corresponding to user queries from “challenge_balanced_questions.json” file from the GQA dataset [3].
“mobius” and “rihanna-plus” are proprietary AI models being used behind “find” and “simple_query” APIs, respectively.

citacoes.trecho: This study aims to quantitatively compare the efficiency of the GPT-4.1 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet AI models using GitHub Copilot in Agent Mode, with a case study focused on developing a backend REST API application.
Independent Variable: The AI model used (GPT-4.1 or Claude 3.7 Sonnet).
Prompts were categorized into two types: a main prompt to initiate feature creation and follow-up prompts for corrections or refinements.
The main prompts were crafted with assistance from AI: the researcher provided the core problem context, and the AI helped structure a more comprehensive and effective prompt.
This main prompt, identical for both models in each task, typically included: project context, feature specifications, implementation steps, technical constraints, and logging requirements.
Follow-up prompts were necessarily adaptive, responding to the specific code generated by the model.
Initial Prompt: Give the main prompt to the selected AI model to generate the necessary code and corresponding unit tests.
If it does not meet requirements or if unit tests fail, use follow-up prompts to correct the code.
It is important to acknowledge that this measure is not purely AI processing time, as it includes user-incurred delays (e.g., time taken to confirm a command-line execution).
Context Isolation: To prevent context from a previous task from influencing the next one, a new chat session was initiated for each new feature being developed.
The final quantitative metrics for GPT 4.1 utilized data collected by both developers.
Overall, GPT-4.1 required fewer prompts (38) compared to Claude 3.7 (44).
GPT-4.1 had an average task completion time of approximately 1.5 minutes, whereas Claude 3.7 averaged over 3 minutes.
The total cumulative time starkly highlights this difference: GPT-4.1 completed all tasks in approximately 58 minutes, while Claude 3.7 required 137 minutes.
Weaknesses: Occasionally produced incomplete code, requiring follow-up prompts.
It also struggled with complex debugging tasks, sometimes getting stuck in ineffective, repetitive solution loops.
Over-engineering: Sometimes provided excessive code.

On occasion, after all functionality was verified, it would generate new, unnecessary test cases that introduced failures, requiring the researcher to forcibly stop the process to prevent project corruption.

citacoes.trecho: The experiment showed that GPT-4.1 required six fewer prompts than Claude 3.7 Sonnet and was significantly faster, with cumulative time savings of approximately 78 minutes.

Potential Researcher Bias: The evaluation process, particularly the formulation of follow-up prompts and the counting methodology, may contain subjective elements, although every effort was made to maintain objectivity.
Therefore, the success criterion for a task was primarily determined by the successful execution of AI-generated unit tests, which may not capture all aspects of the initial requirements perfectly.

citacoes.trecho: To address these challenges, this paper proposes a multi-agent collaborative 3D visualization code generation workflow based on Spatial-MLLM, which integrates the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) capability of ChatVis with the stepwise logic of multi-stage guided code generation (MSG).
The proposed workflow consists of five core modules: planning, design, generation, feedback, and evaluation.

We design the prompt template to include output examples, output requirements, and output formatting rules, explicitly instructing the LLM to convert the operations described in the natural language input into DAG nodes (tasks) and edges (data flows).

citacoes.trecho: If further errors are detected, the system continues the iterative loop until either a correct script is produced or the predefined maximum iteration limit is reached.
citacoes.localizador: p. 4 do PDF (p. impressa 515), seção III.C

citacoes.trecho: If the iteration limit is reached without success, the system outputs the error logs and source code to developers for manual debugging.
citacoes.localizador: p. 4 do PDF (p. impressa 515), seção III.C

citacoes.trecho: In our current implementation, the proposed framework adopts Qwen 3.0 as the underlying large language model (LLM).
citacoes.localizador: p. 4 do PDF (p. impressa 515), seção III.C

citacoes.trecho: For comparative experiments, we used ChatGPT-4 [19] as the language model, which operates on an engine with 1.7 trillion parameters.
citacoes.localizador: p. 4 do PDF (p. impressa 515), seção IV

citacoes.trecho: To ensure fair comparison, we evaluated the results generated by our method against those produced by GPT-4 without auxiliary prompts.
citacoes.localizador: p. 4 do PDF (p. impressa 515), seção IV

citacoes.trecho: Second, directly generated code often suffers from structural instability and low accuracy.

Furthermore, MSG’s use of SCoT for complex reasoning provides controllable intermediate representations, reducing hallucinations commonly observed in LLM-generated code and improving iterative correction efficiency.
In contrast, GPT-4 produced incorrect function calls, leading to execution errors and the failure to generate a valid visualization output.
citacoes.localizador: p. 5 do PDF (p. impressa 516), seção IV.B

citacoes.trecho: This experiment demonstrates that general-purpose LLMs, when used alone, often generate scripts containing syntax or API errors that prevent execution.
citacoes.localizador: p. 6 do PDF (p. impressa 517), seção IV.C

citacoes.trecho: From Table I, it can be observed that GPT-4 demonstrates relatively stable syntactic performance but lacks a complete understanding of ParaView’s parameter system, often leading to minor hallucinations or incorrect argument calls, which result in incomplete visual outputs.
citacoes.localizador: p. 6 do PDF (p. impressa 517), seção IV.D

citacoes.trecho: In addition, by applying RAG, our approach significantly reduces hallucination errors, thereby ensuring the correct generation of visualization scripts.

Compared to direct generation methods such as ChatGPT, our approach achieves notably higher task success rates and API invocation accuracy, providing domain experts with a low-barrier, high-reliability solution for automated visualization code generation.
Finally, the system performs a dual-level evaluation using SSIM/PSNR for image-level similarity and AST structural matching for code-level accuracy.

As regras são conhecimento externo selecionado por pré-filtragem top-k por sobreposição de palavras-chave e similaridade semântica (→ contexto) e funcionam como regras de codificação e de segurança obrigatórias (→ restricoes).
